indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B.6.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of variety of songs
indicator.objective: Relate the central messages in songs to personal experiences

skills.description: Identify the central message of a familiar song
Explain in own words what the song is teaching or telling listeners
Connect the song's message to a real personal experience
Point to a line or phrase in the song that supports the stated message

spec.difficultyPlan: 60% easy (identify or explain a clear message), 30% medium (link message to a specific personal experience), 10% harder (justify message with a line from the song). Songs used are familiar school, patriotic or value-based songs; short original song lines are provided in the stems so pupils work from the words in front of them.
misconceptions: Thinking the message is the tune or the mood rather than the lesson
Giving a one-word topic instead of a full message
Linking to an unrelated personal story
Confusing a song's story events with its central message

questions.stem: A class sings this song at assembly: 'Hold my hand, let us build, together we are strong.' What is the central message of the song?
options: Building is only for strong people.
We should sing loudly at assembly.
People achieve more when they work together.
Hands are the most important part of the body.
hints: Ask yourself what the song wants us to do, not how loud it is.
Look at the words 'together' and 'we are strong'.
questions.explanation: The song joins 'hold my hand', 'let us build' and 'together we are strong'. All three point to working as one group. So the central message is that people achieve more when they work together.
questions.misconception: Confusing the message with a detail about singing loudly or with the literal word 'hand'.

questions.stem: The national anthem is sung at the school assembly. Which of these is the central message it carries?
options: A story about a hunter and his dog.
Love for Ghana and a prayer for peace and freedom.
Instructions on how to plant maize.
A warning that rain is coming.
hints: Think about when and why the anthem is sung.
Patriotic songs speak to the whole nation, not to one farm.
questions.explanation: The national anthem is a patriotic song. It is sung to show love for Ghana and to ask for blessings of peace and freedom for the nation. It is not a story, an instruction song or a weather warning.
questions.misconception: Treating a patriotic song as if it were a story or an instruction song.

questions.stem: A class sings 'Ten Galloping Horses Came Through the Town'. What is this song mainly used for?
options: Teaching the letters of the alphabet.
hints: Count the horses as the song goes on.
Not every song carries a moral lesson.
questions.explanation: The song counts horses as they come through the town. Its main use is to practise counting while having fun, so its message is about numbers and enjoyment, not about traffic or the alphabet.
questions.misconception: Believing every song must teach a moral lesson.

questions.stem: Read these song lines: 'Little drops of water, little grains of sand, make the mighty ocean and the pleasant land.' Write the central message in one short phrase.
answer: little drops make a big thing
hints: Think about what many little drops can do together.
The message is about size, not about the sea.
questions.explanation: Many little drops of water make a mighty ocean. The song teaches that small things, added together, become great. So the message is that small things add up.
questions.misconception: Giving the topic (water and sand) instead of the message.

questions.stem: In a song, Kojo finds a purse on the road and returns it to its owner. What message does the song teach?
options: Money is more important than people.
Always tell the truth only when you are watched.
Lost things are never found again.
Honesty is the best way to live.
hints: What did Kojo do with the purse?
Returning what is not yours is a sign of a good character.
questions.explanation: Kojo found what did not belong to him and gave it back. That is honesty. The song teaches that honesty is the best way to live, not that money matters more than people.
questions.misconception: Choosing a message that contradicts the story or focuses on a small detail.

questions.stem: A song says: 'Wake up early, work with your hands, and your farm will feed you.' Explain the message in your own words.
answer: work hard and you will succeed
if you work hard you will get what you need
work hard and you will be rewarded
hints: What happens to a farmer who works early?
Say it in your own words, not the song's words.
questions.explanation: The song says that waking early and working with your hands will make the farm feed you. In other words, hard work brings success and enough food.
questions.misconception: Copying the song's words instead of explaining them.

questions.stem: Listen to the song your teacher sings about 'clean hands, healthy body'. In two sentences, explain the message in your own words.
hints: Think about what happens when we wash our hands.
Use your own words, not the words of the song.
questions.explanation: A good answer says that washing our hands keeps us healthy, and uses the pupil's own words in complete sentences.

criteria.description: States that washing hands keeps us healthy
Explains in own words rather than copying the song

questions.stem: A song line says: 'A friend in need is a friend indeed.' Which explanation best gives the message?
options: Friends are only useful when they need something.
A true friend helps you when you have trouble.
You should only make friends when you need them.
Friends should always share their food.
hints: 'In need' means a time of trouble.
The song is praising a certain kind of friend.
questions.explanation: A friend who stays with you when you are in trouble proves to be a true friend. So the message is that a true friend helps you when you have trouble.
questions.misconception: Explaining the message with a sentence that twists the meaning of the song.

questions.stem: Your school song says: 'Rise and shine, little stars, learn today to lead tomorrow.' Explain the message in your own words.
answer: learn now so you can lead later
education today prepares you for the future
study hard to become a leader
hints: What are you asked to do today?
What will you be able to do tomorrow?
questions.explanation: The song tells pupils to learn well now so that they can become leaders in the future. Learning today prepares you for tomorrow.
questions.misconception: Restating the topic of school instead of explaining the link between learning now and leading later.

questions.stem: In your own words, explain the message of the national anthem to a younger pupil in three sentences. Do not copy the words of the anthem.
hints: Think of two things the anthem asks for.
Use simple words a Basic 1 pupil will understand.
questions.explanation: A strong answer says the anthem shows love for Ghana and asks for peace and freedom, in simple words, across three sentences.

criteria.description: Identifies love for Ghana and prayer for peace and freedom
Explains in own words without copying the anthem
Uses simple language suitable for a younger pupil

questions.stem: After the class sings a song about sharing, tell the class about a time you shared something with someone. Say how you felt.
hints: Think of a time at home, at school or at the market.
Say what you shared and how you felt afterwards.
questions.explanation: The pupil should tell a clear, real experience of sharing and connect it to the song's message.

questions.stem: A song says: 'Help your neighbour, near or far.' Write two sentences about a time you helped someone at home or in school.
hints: Who did you help?
What did you do for them?
questions.explanation: A good answer describes a real or realistic act of help and links it to the song's message in two complete sentences.

criteria.description: Describes a clear experience of helping someone
Links the experience to the song's message

questions.stem: A song teaches: 'Be kind to the old.' Which personal experience best connects with this message?
options: I sang the song loudly at assembly.
I bought a new song book.
I helped an old woman carry her basket to the market.
I learned all the words of the song by heart.
hints: Which action actually shows kindness?
Singing about kindness is not the same as doing it.
questions.explanation: Carrying an old woman's basket is a real act of kindness to an older person, so it connects with the song's message. Singing or learning the words does not show the value in action.
questions.misconception: Confusing doing the value with singing about it.

questions.stem: After singing a song about honesty, tell the class about a moment when you told the truth even though it was hard. Explain how the song reminds you of that moment.
hints: What happened? What made telling the truth hard?
Which words of the song fit that moment?
questions.explanation: The pupil should describe the moment, show honesty, and connect the song's message to that experience.

criteria.description: Links the experience to the song's message
Maintains eye contact and speaks audibly

questions.stem: A song says: 'Work hard today, rest well tomorrow.' Write three sentences about how the message of this song is like something that has happened in your own life.
hints: Think of a time you worked hard and enjoyed the result.
Say clearly how the song and your experience are alike.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives one specific personal example and explains the link to the song's message across three sentences.

criteria.description: Explains how the example is like the song's message

questions.stem: A song teaches patience. Which line best supports this message?
options: Run, run, run, do not wait!
Wait for the seed to grow, wait for the rain to fall.
The sun is hot, the sun is bright.
Birds fly high, birds fly low.
hints: Which line tells us to wait?
A line that only mentions weather does not teach patience.
questions.explanation: Waiting for a seed to grow and for rain to fall shows patience. The other lines are about running, the sun and birds and do not support the message of patience.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that only mentions a related word without carrying the message.

questions.stem: Song: 'One good turn, one kind word, makes a happy home.' Which words in the song show that kindness matters at home?
hints: Look for the words about kind speech.
Copy the words exactly as they appear in the song.
questions.explanation: The words 'one kind word' show that speaking kindly at home brings happiness. They are the part of the song that supports the message of kindness.
questions.misconception: Copying the whole song instead of pointing to the words that carry the message.

questions.stem: A song teaches love for our country. Which line supports this message best?
options: My heart is glad when I see our flag flying high.
I like to eat rice and stew.
The market is full of people today.
My shoes are new and clean.
hints: Which line mentions a national symbol?
Love for country is not about food or shoes.
questions.explanation: The flag is a symbol of the nation, so feeling glad when the flag flies shows love for the country. The other lines are about food, the market and shoes.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line about personal likes rather than love for country.

questions.stem: Song: 'Stand up for what is right, even when you stand alone.' Write the message of the song, then copy the words that support your answer.
hints: What does the song want you to do when you are alone?
Copy the words exactly, then say why they show the message.
questions.explanation: The message is courage: we should do what is right even if no one else supports us. The words 'even when you stand alone' support that message.

criteria.description: States the message (courage or doing what is right)
Copies the correct supporting words from the song
Explains the link between the words and the message

questions.stem: A song says: 'Small hands can do great things.' Which line from the same song would best support the message that children can help their community?
options: We sing and dance till noon.
My kite flies in the wind.
Children sweep the market square and plant a tree.
hints: Which line shows children actually doing something useful?
Singing and dancing are fun, but do they help the community?
questions.explanation: Sweeping the market square and planting a tree are real actions that help the community, done by children. This line supports the message that small hands can do great things.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line about fun rather than the message of children helping.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B.6.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of variety of songs
indicator.objective: Compose songs around values discussed

skills.description: Identify the value(s) a given song teaches
Compose short meaningful song lines around a named value
Arrange composed lines into a singable order with a repeated chorus
Sing or perform the composed song with clear words and steady rhythm

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (name the value; produce one line), 35% medium (compose two or three connected lines), 15% harder (arrange lines into a short performable song). Values are limited to those treated in the curriculum: love, honesty, patriotism, patience, hard work, truthfulness, unity, kindness, generosity.
misconceptions: Composing lines that do not mention or reflect the chosen value
Writing sentences that cannot be sung
Copying an existing song word for word
Thinking any song automatically teaches a value

questions.stem: A class sings: 'Share your bread with a hungry friend, share your water too.' Which value does the song teach?
hints: What are the singers asked to do with what they have?
Think of a word that means 'giving freely'.
questions.explanation: The song asks us to give bread and water to a friend in need. Giving what we have to help others is generosity.
questions.misconception: Choosing a value that is named in the curriculum but is not shown in the song's words.

questions.stem: The song says: 'Sweep the yard, fetch the water, do your work well.' Which value is this song about?
hints: The song lists jobs to be done well.
Doing your work well is a sign of one particular value.
questions.explanation: Sweeping, fetching water and doing work well all show hard work. The song is not about music, punishment or travel.
questions.misconception: Thinking any song about school or home must be about obedience or punishment.

questions.stem: 'Love our land, keep it clean, green and peaceful.' Which value does this line teach?
hints: The line is about our land, not about one person.
There is a special word for love of one's country.
questions.explanation: The line asks us to love our land and keep it clean and peaceful. Love for one's country is called patriotism.
questions.misconception: Answering 'cleanliness' (a theme in the line) instead of the value being taught.

questions.stem: 'Speak the truth though it hurts, let your yes be yes.' Which value does this song teach?
hints: The song is about speaking the truth.
Which value is the opposite of telling lies?
questions.explanation: Speaking the truth even when it is hard is honesty. Courage may be needed, but the value being taught is honesty.
questions.misconception: Choosing a related value (courage) instead of the value the song directly names.

questions.stem: 'We stand together, one people, one nation, hand in hand.' Which value does this song teach?
hints: Look at 'together' and 'one people'.
Which value means oneness?
questions.explanation: Standing together as one people shows oneness. The value taught is unity.
questions.misconception: Confusing unity with patriotism, even when the song is about people being together rather than about the land.

questions.stem: Compose two short lines for a song about honesty. Your lines must be easy to sing and must mention telling the truth.
hints: Keep each line short, like something you can clap to.
Use the word 'truth' or 'true' in one line.
questions.explanation: Good lines are short, can be clapped or sung, and clearly show the value of honesty.

criteria.description: Lines clearly show honesty or telling the truth

questions.stem: Write one short line for a song about patience that a class can sing together.
hints: Patience means waiting without complaining.
One short line is enough, but it must be singable.
questions.explanation: A good line is short, mentions waiting or patience, and can be sung with rhythm.

questions.stem: Which line is the best first line of a song about hard work?
options: Sleep all day and let others work for you.
Rise early, work with your hands, and fill the barn.
The river is deep and the fish are many.
Sing a song and clap your hands.
hints: Which line shows someone actually working?
A line about fish or clapping does not show hard work.
questions.explanation: Rising early and working with your hands is exactly what hard work means. The other lines are about sleeping, fish and singing.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that is about another topic or even contradicts the value.

questions.stem: You are composing a song about kindness. Which line fits best?
options: Take what you want and run away.
The sun is hot at noon today.
Buy a new bag for school.
Lend a hand to the weak and the old.
hints: Kindness is about helping others.
Which line shows help to people who need it?
questions.explanation: Lending a hand to the weak and the old is an act of kindness. The other lines are about taking, the weather and shopping.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that sounds pleasant but does not show kindness.

questions.stem: Compose three short lines for a song about love for Ghana. The lines must be connected to one value and must be able to be sung by your class.
hints: Think of Ghana's land, people and peace.
Keep the lines linked to each other, not three separate ideas.
questions.explanation: Strong answers have three short connected lines, a clear value of patriotism, and a rhythm the class can sing.

criteria.description: Value of love for Ghana is clear
Lines are connected to one another

questions.stem: A group writes these song lines: 1. We will work together. 2. We will build our school. 3. We will work together. 4. We will keep the rule. Which line is being used as the chorus?
hints: The chorus is the line that comes back again and again.
Which words appear more than once?
questions.explanation: The words 'We will work together' appear in lines 1 and 3, so they form the repeated chorus. Line 3 is the chorus line shown.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that appears only once instead of the repeated one.

questions.stem: Song lines: 'Rise and shine, rise and shine, work till the sun goes down.' Which words are repeated to make the chorus?
hints: Look for the words that come twice.
Copy them exactly as they appear.
questions.explanation: The words 'rise and shine' are repeated at the start, so they form the chorus of the song.
questions.misconception: Copying the whole line instead of only the repeated chorus words.

questions.stem: Arrange these lines into a sensible song about unity: A. We are one people. B. Hand in hand we stand. C. We are one people. D. Together we are strong. Write the lines in the best order for singing.
hints: A and C are the same, so one of them is the chorus.
Put the chorus first and return to it at the end.
questions.explanation: A strong order uses 'We are one people' as the chorus, then the two supporting lines, then returns to the chorus: A, B, D, C (or C, B, D, A).

criteria.description: Uses the repeated line as a chorus
Places supporting lines in a sensible order
The order can be sung smoothly

questions.stem: Which of these makes a good chorus line for a song about cleanliness?
options: We keep our school clean, clean, clean.
My brother is ten years old.
hints: A chorus line must be easy to repeat.
It must also be about the value of cleanliness.
questions.explanation: The line about keeping the school clean is short, easy to repeat and clearly about cleanliness, so it works as a chorus.
questions.misconception: Thinking any short line can be a chorus, even when it is off the topic.

questions.stem: Write two chorus lines that can be repeated after every verse of a song about honesty.
hints: Short lines are easier to repeat.
Both lines should carry the value of honesty.
questions.explanation: Good chorus lines are short, repeatable, and clearly about honesty.

criteria.description: Lines can be repeated after each verse
Lines carry the value of honesty

questions.stem: In a group, sing the song you composed about honesty. Sing the words clearly and keep a steady beat.
hints: Say the words slowly enough for everyone to hear.
Clap softly to keep the beat together.
questions.explanation: The group should sing the composed words clearly, together, and with a steady beat.

criteria.description: The value of honesty can be heard

questions.stem: Sing one verse of your group's song about unity. Watch your group leader for the beat.
hints: Keep your eyes on the leader.
Do not rush ahead of the group.
questions.explanation: The pupil should follow the leader's beat, sing audibly, and use the correct words.

criteria.description: Uses the correct words of the song

questions.stem: Perform your composed song to another class. Use clapping to keep the rhythm and sing the chorus together.
hints: Practise the chorus so everyone starts together.
Stand where the audience can see and hear you.
questions.explanation: The group performs the whole song with a clear chorus, clapping rhythm and confidence before an audience.

questions.stem: After listening to another group's song, say two things they did well and one thing they can improve in their singing.
hints: Be specific: was it the words, the rhythm or the chorus?
Use polite words when you suggest an improvement.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives two clear positives and one helpful suggestion using polite language.

questions.stem: Perform your group's song. Make sure the value in the song can be heard clearly in the words.
hints: Say the value word or words distinctly.
Keep the beat steady from the first line to the last.
questions.explanation: The performance should make the value clear, with clear words and a steady rhythm.

criteria.description: The value can be heard clearly in the words

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the features of spoken language e.g. the use of modal expressions to convey tentativeness e.g. probably, not too sure etc.

skills.description: Identify features of spoken language: contractions and ellipsis
Identify modal expressions that show tentativeness
Use modal or tentative expressions appropriately in spoken sentences
Distinguish between definite and tentative expressions in speech

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify contractions and tentative words), 35% medium (use tentative expressions in speech), 15% harder (choose between definite and tentative expressions for a situation). Contexts: daily conversation, school and home.
misconceptions: Thinking 'probably' means 'certainly'
Confusing tentativeness with uncertainty about everything
Believing ellipsis is an error rather than a natural spoken feature
Using formal full forms in casual spoken exchanges where contractions are natural

questions.stem: Which of these is a contraction used in spoken English?
hints: A contraction joins two words with an apostrophe.
Which option is shorter and has an apostrophe?
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is the contraction of 'cannot'. The others are full forms.
questions.misconception: Thinking full forms are the only correct forms in speech.

questions.stem: In this short conversation, what is the ellipsis? A: 'Where are you going?' B: 'To the market.'
hints: Ellipsis means leaving out words that are understood.
What did B leave out in the answer?
questions.explanation: B answers 'To the market' instead of the full sentence 'I am going to the market.' The words left out make this an ellipsis.
questions.misconception: Thinking every short answer is a mistake.

questions.stem: Write the contraction for 'will not'.
hints: Replace 'will not' with a shorter form.
Use an apostrophe.
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'will not' is 'won't'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'willn't' or leaving out the apostrophe.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using contractions. Underline each contraction.
hints: Use words like can't, don't, won't, isn't.
Underline the contraction in each sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with contractions and underlines them.

questions.stem: In pairs, hold a one-minute conversation. Use at least two contractions and one ellipsis.
hints: Use contractions like 'don't' and 'can't'.
Use short answers like 'Yes, please' or 'Tomorrow.'
questions.explanation: The pair uses contractions and at least one ellipsis naturally in conversation.

questions.stem: Which word shows that you are NOT completely sure about something?
hints: Tentative words show doubt or uncertainty.
Which word means 'maybe'?
questions.explanation: 'Probably' shows that you think something is likely but not certain.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'probably' with 'certainly'.

questions.stem: Which phrase is the most tentative?
options: I am sure it will rain.
hints: Tentative means not certain.
Which phrase shows the most doubt?
questions.explanation: 'I think it might rain' is the most tentative because it uses both 'I think' and 'might' to show uncertainty.
questions.misconception: Thinking strong statements show tentativeness.

questions.stem: Write one tentative phrase you could use when you are not sure of an answer.
hints: Think of words that show doubt.
Phrases like 'I think' or 'maybe' work.
questions.explanation: Tentative phrases include 'I think', 'maybe', 'perhaps', 'probably' and 'I'm not too sure'.
questions.misconception: Using a phrase that shows complete certainty.

questions.stem: Write two sentences that use tentative expressions. Underline the tentative expression in each.
hints: Use words like probably, perhaps, maybe or might.
Underline the tentative expression.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses two tentative expressions correctly and underlines them.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks: 'Who wrote this poem?' You are not sure, but you have an idea. Which answer is best?
options: It was definitely Ama Ata Aidoo.
I think it might be Ama Ata Aidoo.
hints: You are not sure, so be tentative.
Use a phrase like 'I think it might be'.
questions.explanation: 'I think it might be' shows you have an idea but are not certain.
questions.misconception: Stating an unsure answer as if it were certain.

questions.stem: A visitor asks: 'Will the school team win the match tomorrow?' You are not certain. Which reply is best?
options: They probably will win, but I'm not too sure.
hints: You are uncertain, so use tentative language.
Which option shows uncertainty?
questions.explanation: 'They probably will win, but I'm not too sure' uses tentative words to show uncertainty.
questions.misconception: Giving a definite answer when you are not sure.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence to show tentativeness: 'It will rain this afternoon.'
answer: it probably will rain this afternoon
i think it will rain this afternoon
maybe it will rain this afternoon
i'm not too sure but it might rain this afternoon
hints: Replace 'will' with a word that shows doubt.
Words like 'might', 'may' or 'probably' help.
questions.explanation: Using 'might', 'may', 'probably' or 'I think' makes the sentence tentative.
questions.misconception: Keeping 'will' and adding no tentative word.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using tentative expressions in different situations (e.g. about the weather, about a test result, about where someone has gone).
hints: Use words like probably, maybe, might or I think.
Each sentence should show uncertainty.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences that each use a different tentative expression.

criteria.description: Each sentence uses a tentative expression

questions.stem: In pairs, ask each other two questions about tomorrow. Answer using a tentative expression such as 'probably', 'maybe' or 'I think'.
hints: Use tentative words in your answers.
Listen for the tentative words in your partner's answer.
questions.explanation: The pair asks and answers questions using tentative expressions.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows the most certainty?
options: I think it will rain tomorrow.
hints: Certainty means no doubt.
Which sentence uses 'will' without any tentative word?
questions.explanation: 'It will rain tomorrow' is the most certain because it uses 'will' without any tentative words.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'might' and 'will' show the same level of certainty.

questions.stem: Which situation calls for the most tentative language?
options: Predicting the score of a football match that has not been played.
Reading the time from a clock.
Reciting the days of the week.
hints: Tentative language is needed when the outcome is uncertain.
Which situation involves an unknown future result?
questions.explanation: Predicting a football score is uncertain, so it needs tentative language such as 'I think' or 'probably'.
questions.misconception: Thinking all situations need the same level of certainty.

questions.stem: Decide whether this sentence is certain or tentative: 'The sun will rise tomorrow.' Write 'certain' or 'tentative'.
hints: Is there any doubt that the sun will rise?
It is a fact of nature.
questions.explanation: The sentence states a fact of nature, so it is certain.
questions.misconception: Thinking every statement about the future is tentative.

questions.stem: Write two pairs of sentences. In each pair, one sentence should be certain and the other tentative. Use the same topic for each pair.
hints: Topic 1 could be the weather; Topic 2 could be a test result.
Use words like will (certain) and might/probably (tentative).
questions.explanation: A strong answer shows the difference between certain and tentative expressions on the same topic.

criteria.description: One sentence in each pair is certain
One sentence in each pair is tentative
The pairs are on the same topic

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of the differences between spoken and written forms of language (simplicity/complexity of sentence structures, formal/informal)

skills.description: State the main differences between spoken and written language
Turn a complex written sentence into a simpler spoken form
Identify formal and informal expressions in speech
Choose the appropriate register for a given situation

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (state differences; identify formal/informal), 35% medium (simplify or convert sentences), 15% harder (choose appropriate register for unfamiliar situations). Examples: 'I have not gone there' (written/formal) vs 'I haven't gone there' (spoken/informal).
misconceptions: Believing written language is always better than spoken language
Using contractions in a formal written letter
Thinking spoken language has no rules
Using slang in formal spoken contexts

questions.stem: Which statement about spoken and written language is true?
options: Spoken language is always more complex than written language.
Spoken language often uses simpler, shorter sentences than written language.
Written language never uses full stops.
Spoken language has no grammar rules.
hints: Spoken language is usually more relaxed.
Which statement matches how people actually speak?
questions.explanation: Spoken language often uses simpler, shorter sentences than written language, which tends to be more complex.
questions.misconception: Thinking spoken language has no rules at all.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more likely to appear in a formal written report?
options: I have not completed the work.
hints: Formal written language avoids contractions.
Which sentence uses full forms?
questions.explanation: 'I have not completed the work' uses full forms and is more formal, suitable for a written report.
questions.misconception: Thinking contractions are always appropriate in formal writing.

questions.stem: Write one way in which spoken language is different from written language.
answer: spoken language uses more informal words
hints: Think about how you speak compared to how you write a letter.
Contractions and simple sentences are good examples.
questions.explanation: Spoken language often uses contractions, shorter sentences and less formal words, while written language tends to be more formal and complex.
questions.misconception: Saying there is no difference between spoken and written language.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining the main differences between spoken and written language.
hints: Mention simplicity/complexity and formality.
Use complete sentences.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that spoken language is simpler and less formal, while written language is more complex and formal.

criteria.description: Explains the simplicity of spoken language
Explains the formality or complexity of written language

questions.stem: Which is the spoken form of this written sentence: 'I have not completed the assignment.'
options: I have not completed the assignment.
hints: Spoken language is simpler and uses contractions.
Which option sounds like natural speech?
questions.explanation: 'I haven't finished my homework' uses a contraction and simpler words, which is typical of spoken language.
questions.misconception: Thinking the spoken form should be longer and more complex.

questions.stem: Which is the spoken form of this written sentence: 'The pupils who had completed their homework were permitted to leave.'
options: The pupils were permitted to leave after completing their homework.
The pupils who had completed homework could go.
hints: Spoken form is shorter and simpler.
Which option sounds like something you would say?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils who had completed homework could go' is shorter and uses 'could go', which is more like natural speech.
questions.misconception: Choosing a long written sentence as the spoken form.

questions.stem: Rewrite this written sentence as a simpler spoken sentence: 'I have not gone to the market yet.'
answer: i haven't gone to the market yet
i haven't been to the market yet
hints: Use a contraction.
Make it shorter and simpler.
questions.explanation: The spoken form uses the contraction 'haven't' and may drop some words for simplicity.
questions.misconception: Keeping the full written form in the spoken version.

questions.stem: Rewrite these two written sentences as spoken sentences: (1) 'I have not eaten anything since morning.' (2) 'She cannot attend the meeting because she is unwell.'
hints: Use contractions.
Make the sentences shorter and simpler.
questions.explanation: A strong answer converts both sentences to natural spoken forms with contractions and simpler wording.

criteria.description: Converts the first sentence to spoken form
Converts the second sentence to spoken form

questions.stem: Which expression is informal?
options: May I please speak to the head teacher?
hints: Informal language is relaxed and casual.
Which option uses slang?
questions.explanation: 'Hey, what's up?' is informal and would not be used in a formal setting.
questions.misconception: Thinking all greetings are equally formal.

questions.stem: Which sentence is formal?
options: I would like to leave now, please.
hints: Formal language avoids slang and contractions that are too casual.
Which sentence sounds respectful and complete?
questions.explanation: 'I would like to leave now, please' is formal because it is polite and complete.
questions.misconception: Thinking slang is acceptable in all situations.

questions.stem: Write one formal and one informal way to greet a friend.
answer: formal good afternoon informal what's up
formal hello how are you informal hi
formal good morning how are you informal hey what's up
hints: Formal greetings are polite and complete.
Informal greetings are casual.
questions.explanation: Formal greetings use polite words like 'Good morning', while informal greetings use casual words like 'Hey' or 'Hi'.
questions.misconception: Using the same greeting for every situation.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one formal and one informal. Underline the formal sentence.
hints: Formal sentences avoid slang and use complete words.
Informal sentences can use contractions and casual words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one formal and one informal sentence and clearly underlines the formal one.

questions.stem: You are speaking to the head teacher at assembly. Which register is most appropriate?
options: A mix of slang and formal words.
hints: Speaking to a head teacher at assembly is a formal situation.
Formal register uses polite and complete language.
questions.explanation: A formal register with polite words is appropriate when speaking to the head teacher at assembly.
questions.misconception: Thinking informal language is fine in every situation.

questions.stem: You are chatting with your friends at break. Which register is most appropriate?
hints: Chatting with friends is a relaxed situation.
Informal register suits relaxed conversation.
questions.explanation: An informal register with casual words is appropriate when chatting with friends at break.
questions.misconception: Thinking formal register is always the best choice.

questions.stem: Name one situation where a formal register is appropriate.
hints: Think of places or people that require respect.
Examples include school assembly, church and interviews.
questions.explanation: Formal register is appropriate in situations such as speaking to the head teacher, at assembly, in interviews, or when writing formal letters.
questions.misconception: Thinking formal register is never needed.

questions.stem: Write two short situations: one where you would use formal language, and one where you would use informal language. Explain why for each.
hints: Formal situations involve unfamiliar adults or official events.
Informal situations involve friends or family.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names two situations and explains why each register is appropriate.

criteria.description: Names a formal situation and explains why
Names an informal situation and explains why

questions.stem: In pairs, practise greeting each other formally as if you were speaking to a visitor. Then greet each other informally as friends.
hints: Formal greetings are polite and complete.
Informal greetings are casual and relaxed.
questions.explanation: The pair uses formal and informal greetings appropriately in the two situations.

criteria.description: Uses a formal greeting for the visitor
Uses an informal greeting for a friend

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.1: Demonstrate knowledge of spoken grammar and register
indicator.objective: Demonstrate awareness of how meaning is conveyed through appropriate pace, stress, tone - through news reporting

skills.description: Identify good pace in news reporting
Identify how stress and tone change meaning in speech
Read or present news with appropriate pace, stress and tone
Explain how pace, stress or tone conveys meaning

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify good pace; identify stress/tone changes), 35% medium (read news with appropriate features), 20% harder (explain how meaning is affected). News items are kept short (30–60 seconds) and on familiar topics.
misconceptions: Thinking faster is always better
Reading every word with the same stress and tone
Believing tone does not affect meaning
Pausing in the middle of phrases rather than at natural breaks

questions.stem: What is a good pace for reading a news report?
options: Very fast so you finish quickly.
Moderate and steady so listeners can follow.
Very slow so everyone gets bored.
hints: Good pace means listeners can understand clearly.
Not too fast, not too slow.
questions.explanation: A moderate and steady pace allows listeners to follow and understand the news clearly.
questions.misconception: Thinking faster is always better.

questions.stem: A news reader is reading too fast. What problem does this cause for listeners?
hints: Fast reading is hard to follow.
What happens when you cannot follow?
questions.explanation: Reading too fast makes it hard for listeners to catch key details, so they may miss important information.
questions.misconception: Thinking speed is more important than clarity.

questions.stem: Write one rule for good pace when reading news aloud.
answer: pause at the end of sentences
hints: Think about the speed of speaking.
It should be comfortable for listeners.
questions.explanation: A good pace is moderate and steady, with pauses at natural breaks such as the end of sentences.
questions.misconception: Thinking you should read as fast as possible.

questions.stem: Read this news headline aloud at a good pace: 'Fire destroyed three stalls at Techiman market yesterday.'
hints: Do not rush.
Speak clearly and steadily.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the headline at a moderate, steady pace with clear words.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'I did not say that', which word you stress changes the meaning. If you stress 'I', what does the sentence suggest?
options: You did not say it at all.
hints: Stressing 'I' puts the focus on the person.
It suggests someone else is responsible.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'I' suggests that the speaker did not say it, but someone else did.
questions.misconception: Thinking stress does not change meaning.

questions.stem: Which tone is appropriate for reading a sad news story?
hints: The news is sad.
Which tone matches sadness?
questions.explanation: A serious, somber tone is appropriate for a sad news story because it matches the content.
questions.misconception: Thinking tone should always be cheerful.

questions.stem: Say one way the meaning of a sentence can change when you change the stress.
answer: stressing a different word changes the focus
stress on i shows someone else did it
hints: Think of the sentence 'I did not say that'.
Changing the stressed word changes who or what is important.
questions.explanation: Changing the stressed word shifts the focus of the sentence, which changes what the speaker means.
questions.misconception: Thinking stress has no effect on meaning.

questions.stem: Read this news item aloud with appropriate pace, stress and tone: 'The Ghana Education Service has announced that all schools will reopen on Monday.'
hints: Pause after 'Service'.
Stress 'all schools' and 'Monday'.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads with a steady pace, stress on key facts and a formal news tone.

criteria.description: Uses an appropriate formal news tone

questions.stem: In pairs, prepare and present a short news report (about 30 seconds) on a school event. Use good pace, stress and tone.
hints: Agree on the event and the main facts.
Practise pausing at natural breaks.
questions.explanation: The pair presents a short, clear news report with appropriate pace, stress and tone.

criteria.description: Report is about a school event

questions.stem: A news reader pauses at the wrong place: 'Fire destroyed three stalls at Techiman, market yesterday.' How does the misplaced pause change the meaning?
options: It sounds as if the market is in a different place.
It has no effect on meaning.
hints: The pause is between 'Techiman' and 'market'.
The audience may think the market is separate from Techiman.
questions.explanation: Pausing between 'Techiman' and 'market' makes them sound like two separate things, when they should be read as one place.
questions.misconception: Thinking pauses do not affect meaning.

questions.stem: Explain in one sentence why pace matters when reading news aloud.
answer: it helps listeners follow the news
a good pace helps people understand
if you read too fast people miss the information
hints: Think about the listener, not the reader.
Good pace helps the message get across.
questions.explanation: Pace matters because a steady, moderate pace helps listeners follow and understand the news.
questions.misconception: Thinking pace is only about speed and not about understanding.

questions.stem: Write three sentences explaining how pace, stress and tone help convey meaning in news reporting.
hints: Explain pace first.
Then explain stress and tone.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains each element and how it helps convey meaning.

questions.stem: Read the same sentence twice: once with a happy tone and once with a sad tone. Then explain how the meaning changed.
hints: Use the sentence 'The team won the match.'
The happy tone shows joy; the sad tone might suggest surprise or disbelief.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the sentence in two tones and explains how the tone shifts the meaning or feeling.

criteria.description: Reads the sentence in a happy tone
Reads the sentence in a sad tone
Explains how the meaning or feeling changed

questions.stem: In the sentence 'She said she would come', how does the meaning change if you stress 'she'?
options: It emphasises that SHE is the one who said it, not someone else.
It means she will not come.
hints: Stress puts emphasis on a specific word.
Stressing 'she' focuses on the person.
questions.explanation: Stressing 'she' emphasises that she — not another person — said she would come.
questions.misconception: Thinking stress can be moved with no effect.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.2: Demonstrate the ability to communicate with accurate pronunciation and appropriate intonation
indicator.objective: Speak at a good pace and with expression

skills.description: Speak at a good pace, not rushed and not dragging
Use expression, including voice variation and emphasis, while speaking
Deliver a short speech on a familiar topic
Use appropriate voice quality: volume, clarity and tone

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (speak at a steady pace on a familiar topic), 35% medium (use expression and appropriate volume), 20% harder (deliver a short speech with sustained good pace and expression). Topics: self, family, school and favourite things.
misconceptions: Speaking very fast to hide nervousness
Using a flat tone with no expression
Speaking too softly for the audience to hear
Using expression inappropriately, such as a dramatic tone for a simple fact

questions.stem: Which of these is a good pace when speaking to the class?
options: Speaking very slowly with long pauses.
Speaking at a steady, moderate speed.
hints: A good pace is neither too fast nor too slow.
Listeners should be able to follow easily.
questions.explanation: A steady, moderate speed allows the audience to follow what you are saying.
questions.misconception: Thinking speed shows confidence.

questions.stem: A pupil speaks very fast in a class presentation. What is the likely problem?
options: The class cannot follow the words easily.
The presentation becomes shorter and clearer.
hints: Fast speech makes it hard for listeners to keep up.
Which option describes the effect on the audience?
questions.explanation: Fast speech makes it hard for the class to follow the words, so they may miss important points.
questions.misconception: Thinking fast speech is always clearer.

questions.stem: Write one tip for keeping a good pace when speaking.
answer: pause at the end of sentences
listen to yourself as you speak
hints: Pauses help keep a good pace.
One clear tip is enough.
questions.explanation: Tips such as speaking slowly and clearly, pausing between points and not rushing help keep a good pace.
questions.misconception: Thinking you should speak without ever pausing.

questions.stem: Say this sentence at a good pace: 'Our school is the best place to learn and grow.'
hints: Do not rush.
Pause slightly after 'school'.
questions.explanation: The pupil says the sentence clearly at a steady, moderate speed.

criteria.description: Speaks at a steady, moderate pace

questions.stem: Which sentence should be said with excitement?
hints: Exciting news shows strong positive feeling.
Which sentence shows a happy event?
questions.explanation: 'We won the football match!' is exciting news and should be said with excitement.
questions.misconception: Thinking all sentences need the same expression.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be said with a serious tone?
options: The school has closed for the holidays.
We are all going to the beach.
There has been an accident on the road.
hints: Serious news involves something sad or important.
Which sentence reports an accident?
questions.explanation: News of an accident is serious, so it should be said with a serious tone.
questions.misconception: Thinking serious news should be said cheerfully.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence so it sounds more exciting when spoken: 'We went to the park.'
answer: we had an amazing time at the park
we went to the park and it was so much fun
what a wonderful time we had at the park
we went to the park and had great fun
we went to the park and it was fantastic
we went to the park and it was so exciting
hints: Add an expression of feeling.
Use words like 'wonderful' or 'amazing'.
questions.explanation: Adding expressive words like 'amazing' or 'so much fun' helps convey excitement.
questions.misconception: Keeping the sentence flat and unexpressive.

questions.stem: Say this sentence twice: first in a happy voice and then in a sad voice: 'The holidays are here.'
hints: In the happy voice, smile and speak with energy.
In the sad voice, slow down and lower your tone.
questions.explanation: The pupil shows expression by changing tone and energy for happy and sad voices.

criteria.description: Uses a happy voice for the happy version
Uses a sad voice for the sad version

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about one minute) about your favourite food. Speak at a good pace and with expression.
hints: Plan three main points.
Use expressive words to describe the food.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a short speech on a familiar topic with good pace and expression.

questions.stem: Deliver a short speech (about two minutes) about a person you admire. Use good pace and expression.
hints: Introduce the person first.
Explain why you admire them with one or two examples.
questions.explanation: The pupil delivers a two-minute speech on a familiar topic with good pace and expression.

criteria.description: Gives a clear introduction and conclusion

questions.stem: Which of these is the best voice quality for a class presentation?
options: Clear, loud enough for the class to hear, and steady.
hints: Good voice quality means everyone can hear clearly.
It should not be too loud or too soft.
questions.explanation: A clear, steady voice at an appropriate volume is best for a class presentation.
questions.misconception: Thinking louder is always better.

questions.stem: A pupil speaks too softly in a presentation. What should the pupil do?
hints: Speaking too softly means the class cannot hear.
What change would help the audience?
questions.explanation: Speaking louder and more clearly helps the class hear the presentation.
questions.misconception: Thinking volume does not matter.

questions.stem: Name one thing you should do with your voice when giving a short speech to the class.
answer: speak loudly enough for everyone to hear
hints: Think about volume and clarity.
The class should hear every word.
questions.explanation: Speaking loudly enough, clearly and with a steady voice ensures everyone hears.
questions.misconception: Answering with something unrelated to voice.

questions.stem: Say this sentence so that everyone in the class can hear you clearly: 'Good morning, my name is Kojo and I am in Basic 6.'
hints: Speak loudly enough to reach the back row.
Pronounce every word clearly.
questions.explanation: The pupil speaks loudly enough and clearly so the back row can hear every word.

criteria.description: Speaks loudly enough for the back row

questions.stem: In pairs, present a short introduction of each other to the class. Use a clear, steady voice and good pace.
hints: Introduce your partner in two to three sentences.
Speak clearly so the class can hear every word.
questions.explanation: The pair presents each other with clear voices and good pace.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.2: Demonstrate the ability to communicate with accurate pronunciation and appropriate intonation
indicator.objective: Read aloud clearly, at a good pace and with expression

skills.description: Read aloud clearly with correct pronunciation
Read at a good pace, neither too fast nor too slow
Read with expression: pause, stress and tone appropriate to meaning
Read different text types aloud, such as poems, stories and news, with appropriate style

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (read a short passage clearly), 35% medium (read with good pace and expression), 20% harder (read different text types with appropriate style). Texts are kept short and level-appropriate.
misconceptions: Reading word by word without phrasing
Reading too fast and stumbling over words
Using the same tone for a poem and a news item
Ignoring punctuation marks while reading aloud

questions.stem: What should you do to read aloud clearly?
hints: Clear reading means every word is heard.
Which option is about pronunciation?
questions.explanation: Pronouncing each word clearly helps listeners hear and understand what is being read.
questions.misconception: Thinking speed shows good reading.

questions.stem: A pupil reads aloud and says 'teef' instead of 'teeth'. What is the problem?
hints: The pupil said a word incorrectly.
Which skill is about saying words correctly?
questions.explanation: Saying 'teef' instead of 'teeth' is a pronunciation error, so the pupil needs to improve pronunciation.
questions.misconception: Confusing pronunciation errors with pace problems.

questions.stem: Write one thing you can do to read aloud more clearly.
answer: look at the words as you read
hints: Think about pronunciation.
Practising difficult words helps.
questions.explanation: Pronouncing each word clearly and practising difficult words help improve clarity.
questions.misconception: Thinking clarity is only about speaking louder.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud clearly: 'The pupils of Basic 6 planted trees along the school path.'
hints: Pronounce each word carefully.
Pause at the end.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the sentence with clear pronunciation of each word.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good pace for reading a short story aloud?
options: So fast that listeners miss words.
A steady speed that lets listeners follow.
So slow that listeners lose interest.
hints: Good pace helps listeners follow.
A steady pace is best.
questions.explanation: A steady speed lets listeners follow the story easily.
questions.misconception: Thinking reading fast is always best.

questions.stem: What should you do when you come to a full stop while reading aloud?
hints: A full stop marks the end of a sentence.
What does a full stop tell a reader to do?
questions.explanation: At a full stop, the reader should pause briefly before starting the next sentence.
questions.misconception: Thinking pauses should be ignored.

questions.stem: Read this passage aloud at a good pace: 'The sun was hot. The children ran to the shade of the mango tree. They sat and shared their water.'
hints: Pause at each full stop.
Do not rush the words.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads at a steady pace, pausing at each full stop.

questions.stem: Which sentence should you read with a surprised tone?
options: The pencil is on the desk.
hints: Surprise involves shock or amazement.
Which sentence shows strong surprise?
questions.explanation: 'I cannot believe we won!' expresses surprise, so it should be read with a surprised tone.
questions.misconception: Thinking all sentences should be read the same way.

questions.stem: When reading aloud, what should you do with a question mark?
options: Raise your voice slightly at the end of the question.
Read it as a full stop.
hints: A question mark signals a question.
The voice usually rises at the end of a question.
questions.explanation: A question mark tells the reader that the voice should rise at the end of a question.
questions.misconception: Thinking punctuation marks have no effect on reading.

questions.stem: Write one way to show expression when reading a sad story aloud.
answer: use a slow and soft voice
hints: Sad stories sound different from happy ones.
Slower and softer voices fit sadness.
questions.explanation: A sad story is read with a slow, soft voice and a sad tone.
questions.misconception: Reading a sad story with a cheerful tone.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud with expression: 'Oh no, I forgot my homework again!'
hints: Show worry or frustration in your voice.
Emphasise 'Oh no'.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads with expression, showing worry or frustration through tone.

criteria.description: Uses a worried or frustrated tone

questions.stem: How should you read a poem aloud differently from a news item?
options: A poem is read with rhythm and feeling; a news item is read clearly and neutrally.
A poem is read very fast; a news item is read slowly.
Both should be read the same way.
A poem is read in a whisper; a news item is shouted.
hints: Poems have rhythm and feeling.
News is reported clearly and neutrally.
questions.explanation: A poem is read with rhythm and feeling, while a news item is read clearly and neutrally.
questions.misconception: Thinking all text types are read the same way.

questions.stem: Which type of text is read with the most feeling and rhythm?
hints: Poetry has rhythm and emotional language.
Which text is meant to be performed?
questions.explanation: Poems are read with feeling and rhythm because they are meant to be performed and felt.
questions.misconception: Thinking any text can be read with rhythm.

questions.stem: Name one text type you would read aloud with rhythm and expression.
hints: Texts meant to be performed aloud.
Poems, stories and plays fit.
questions.explanation: Poems, stories, plays and songs are read with rhythm and expression.
questions.misconception: Answering with an instructional text.

questions.stem: Read this short poem aloud with rhythm and feeling: 'The moon is bright, the stars are high, / The night wind sings a lullaby.'
hints: Pause at the slash.
Let your voice rise and fall softly.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the poem with rhythm and feeling, pausing at the line break.

questions.stem: Read three short texts aloud: a poem, a story and a news item. Use a different style for each one.
hints: The poem should have rhythm and feeling.
The story should have pauses and expression.
The news item should be clear and neutral.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads each text with the appropriate style, showing awareness of text type.

criteria.description: Reads the poem with rhythm and feeling
Reads the story with pauses and expression
Reads the news clearly and neutrally
Adapts style to each text type

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Research and deliver speeches on given informational topics

skills.description: Select a topic of interest from informational texts
Research a topic using the library or print sources
Identify the purpose and audience of a speech
Deliver a researched speech to the class

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (select topic and identify purpose/audience), 35% medium (research facts and organise a short speech), 25% harder (deliver with clarity and confidence). Topics: health, environment, school, community and technology.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad to cover in a short speech
Copying from a source without understanding
Ignoring the audience by using vocabulary too advanced or too simple
Delivering a list of facts with no organisation

questions.stem: Which of these is the best topic for a short informational speech to your class?
options: The history of the whole world
How to keep our classroom clean
All the countries in the world
hints: A good topic is focused, not too broad.
Which topic can be covered in a short speech?
questions.explanation: 'How to keep our classroom clean' is focused and can be covered in a short speech. The others are too broad.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too wide to cover.

questions.stem: Write one suitable topic for a short informational speech about health.
answer: how to brush your teeth properly
the dangers of eating too much sugar
how to keep drinking water clean
hints: Think of one specific health habit.
The topic should be focused enough for a short speech.
questions.explanation: A good topic is focused, such as hand washing, malaria prevention, balanced diet or regular exercise.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too broad, such as 'all about health'.

questions.stem: You need facts for a speech on the environment. Which is the best place to find them?
options: The school library or the internet
hints: Research requires reliable sources.
Where do you find books and articles?
questions.explanation: The school library and reliable internet sources are good places to find facts for a speech.
questions.misconception: Thinking any object can be a research source.

questions.stem: Name one print source you could use to find facts for a speech about trees.
hints: Print sources are printed on paper.
Books, textbooks and newspapers are print sources.
questions.explanation: Print sources include textbooks, books, encyclopedias, newspapers and magazines.
questions.misconception: Naming a source that is not a print source.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech to your classmates about keeping the classroom clean. Who is your audience?
hints: Audience means the people listening.
Who is in your class?
questions.explanation: The audience for a speech to your classmates is your classmates.
questions.misconception: Confusing audience with a different group.

questions.stem: Write one purpose for a speech about exercise to your class.
answer: to inform them about the benefits of exercise
to show the importance of exercise
to get them to be more active
hints: Why would you give that speech?
The purpose could be to inform, persuade or entertain.
questions.explanation: The purpose of the speech could be to inform or persuade the class about the benefits of exercise.
questions.misconception: Giving a purpose unrelated to the topic.

questions.stem: Deliver a short speech (about one minute) about the importance of drinking clean water. Speak clearly and confidently.
hints: Start with an introduction.
Give two or three facts about clean water.
questions.explanation: The pupil delivers a short speech on clean water, clearly and confidently.

questions.stem: Research and deliver a speech (about two minutes) on a topic of your choice from the environment. Organise your points and speak clearly.
hints: Organise your points into introduction, body and conclusion.
Speak clearly and maintain confidence.
questions.explanation: The pupil delivers a researched and organised speech on an environment topic.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Draw on prior knowledge to identify subject matter and organisational structure of speech

skills.description: Identify the subject matter of a sample speech using prior knowledge
Identify the organisational structure of a speech: heading, vocative address, introduction, body and conclusion
Arrange the parts of a speech in the correct order
Link prior knowledge to a new speech topic

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify subject matter; order speech parts), 35% medium (identify structure with reasons), 15% harder (link prior knowledge to a new topic). Sample speeches are short and on familiar topics.
misconceptions: Confusing the heading with the introduction
Omitting the vocative address
Starting the speech with the body instead of the introduction
Believing every speech must follow the same strict format

questions.stem: A speech begins: 'Mr Chairman, our able Head Teacher, distinguished guests, teachers and fellow pupils... Today I want to talk about keeping our school clean.' What is the subject matter of this speech?
hints: The subject matter is what the speech is about.
Listen for the topic the speaker announces.
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'I want to talk about keeping our school clean', so that is the subject matter.
questions.misconception: Confusing the greeting of the audience with the topic.

questions.stem: A speech starts: 'Good morning, everyone. Today I want to discuss the importance of reading.' Write the subject matter of the speech.
hints: What topic does the speaker announce?
Look at the words after 'discuss'.
questions.explanation: The speaker announces the topic as 'the importance of reading'.
questions.misconception: Answering with the greeting instead of the topic.

questions.stem: Which part of a speech comes first?
hints: The vocative address greets the audience first.
It is the very start of the speech.
questions.explanation: The vocative address, such as 'Mr Chairman, distinguished guests', comes first in a formal speech.
questions.misconception: Thinking the body comes first.

questions.stem: Which of these is part of the body of a speech?
options: The main points and details of the topic
hints: The body develops the topic.
Which option gives the main points?
questions.explanation: The body of the speech is where the main points and details are presented.
questions.misconception: Confusing the vocative address or conclusion with the body.

questions.stem: Arrange these parts of a speech in the correct order: A. Conclusion. B. Vocative address. C. Body. D. Introduction.
hints: The vocative address comes first.
The conclusion comes last.
questions.explanation: The order is: vocative address (B), introduction (D), body (C), conclusion (A).
questions.misconception: Placing the conclusion before the body.

questions.stem: Write the three main parts of a speech in order, excluding the vocative address.
hints: The speech begins with an introduction.
It ends with a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The three main parts of a speech, excluding the vocative address, are introduction, body and conclusion.
questions.misconception: Listing the parts in the wrong order.

questions.stem: You are about to hear a speech about recycling. Which of your prior experiences would help you understand it?
options: You have seen people sorting plastics at home.
You have never heard of recycling.
You have only seen recycling on TV.
You have seen a speech on a different topic.
hints: Prior knowledge means what you already know.
Which experience relates directly to recycling?
questions.explanation: Seeing people sort plastics at home is a direct experience that helps you understand a speech about recycling.
questions.misconception: Choosing an experience unrelated to the topic.

questions.stem: A speech about good manners at school is about to begin. Write one thing you already know about good manners.
answer: we should say please and thank you
we should listen when others speak
we should not talk in class
hints: Think of polite behaviours at school.
Greeting, listening and saying 'please' are good examples.
questions.explanation: Good manners at school include greeting politely, saying 'please' and 'thank you', listening when others speak and respecting teachers.
questions.misconception: Giving a statement unrelated to manners.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Gather and select facts and ideas from one or multiple print and/or non-print sources, appropriate to the purpose, audience, context and culture

skills.description: Identify print and non-print sources
Select facts relevant to purpose, audience, context and culture
Organise gathered facts for a speech
Choose facts appropriate to the audience and cultural context

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify sources; select one relevant fact), 35% medium (gather and organise several facts), 20% harder (select facts appropriate to audience and culture). Topics from informational texts and community issues.
misconceptions: Using any fact found without checking relevance
Believing only the internet counts as a source
Including facts inappropriate for the audience
Gathering facts but not organising them logically

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-print source of information?
hints: Non-print means not on paper.
Which option is heard rather than read?
questions.explanation: A radio programme is a non-print source because it is heard, not printed on paper.
questions.misconception: Confusing non-print sources with printed texts.

questions.stem: Name one print source and one non-print source you could use for a speech about health.
hints: Print sources are on paper; non-print sources are electronic or spoken.
Give one of each.
questions.explanation: A print source could be a textbook or newspaper; a non-print source could be a radio or TV programme, or an interview.
questions.misconception: Naming two sources of the same type.

questions.stem: You are writing a speech on the importance of trees for your class. Which fact is most relevant?
options: Trees give shade and clean the air.
hints: Which fact shows why trees are important?
The purpose is to show importance.
questions.explanation: The fact that trees give shade and clean the air shows why trees are important, which is the purpose of the speech.
questions.misconception: Choosing an interesting fact that does not support the purpose.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech on keeping the school clean. Write one relevant fact you could use.
answer: keeping the school clean prevents sickness
we should put rubbish in bins
hints: The fact should relate to cleanliness and health.
Think about what happens when rubbish is not cleared.
questions.explanation: A relevant fact would be that rubbish attracts flies and rats, which can spread diseases.
questions.misconception: Giving a fact unrelated to cleanliness.

questions.stem: You have gathered five facts about the importance of exercise. How should you organise them in a speech?
options: In a clear order: introduction, main points and conclusion.
Only the most exciting fact, without order.
hints: Speech structure needs clear organisation.
Which option matches how a speech is usually organised?
questions.explanation: Facts should be organised into a clear structure: introduction, main points and conclusion.
questions.misconception: Thinking order does not matter in a speech.

questions.stem: You have these facts for a speech on water: (1) we need water to live; (2) we must not waste water; (3) clean water prevents disease. Organise them into an introduction, body and conclusion for a short speech.
hints: Start with the most important fact.
End with a call to action.
questions.explanation: A strong answer places the importance of water in the introduction, the consequences and prevention in the body, and the call not to waste water in the conclusion.

criteria.description: Places one fact in the introduction
Places other facts in the body
Places a call to action in the conclusion

questions.stem: You are speaking to pupils in Basic 1. Which fact is most appropriate?
options: Technical details about water purification chemicals.
Wash your hands before you eat.
hints: Younger pupils need simple, practical facts.
Which fact is easiest for young children to understand?
questions.explanation: 'Wash your hands before you eat' is simple and practical, which suits younger pupils.
questions.misconception: Thinking technical facts suit all audiences.

questions.stem: You are speaking to your class about malaria. Write one fact that is appropriate for your audience.
answer: sleep under a treated mosquito net
clear standing water near your house
keep the compound clean to stop mosquitoes
hints: Use facts that your classmates can understand and use.
Think of prevention or cause.
questions.explanation: A suitable fact for classmates would be that sleeping under a treated mosquito net prevents malaria, or that mosquitoes spread malaria.
questions.misconception: Giving a fact that is too technical for the audience.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Support ideas and points of view with concrete examples to convey meaning appropriate to purpose and context.

skills.description: Identify concrete examples in a sample speech
Support an idea or point of view with a concrete example
Choose examples relevant to purpose and context
Explain how the example clarifies the idea

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify examples), 35% medium (support an idea with an example), 20% harder (explain how the example clarifies the point). Examples are drawn from pupils' own environment: school, market, family and community.
misconceptions: Giving a general statement instead of a concrete example
Using an example unrelated to the point
Believing one example supports every point
Adding examples that confuse rather than clarify

questions.stem: In this speech, which part is a concrete example? 'We should keep our school clean. For example, the pupils of Basic 6 sweep their classroom every morning.'
options: We should keep our school clean.
For example, the pupils of Basic 6 sweep their classroom every morning.
hints: A concrete example gives a specific case.
Look for the part starting with 'For example'.
questions.explanation: The part starting with 'For example' gives a specific case of pupils sweeping their classroom, which is a concrete example.
questions.misconception: Confusing the general idea with the concrete example.

questions.stem: Speech: 'Exercise is important. For instance, Kojo runs to school every morning and he is very fit.' Write the concrete example in this speech.
answer: kojo runs to school every morning and he is very fit
kojo runs to school every morning
kojo running to school every morning
hints: Look for the specific person named.
It starts with 'For instance'.
questions.explanation: The concrete example is Kojo running to school every morning and being fit.
questions.misconception: Copying the general statement instead of the specific example.

questions.stem: Your point is: 'Reading helps pupils learn new words.' Which example supports this point?
options: Ama read a story book and learned ten new words.
Ama has a new school bag.
hints: The example must support the point about reading and new words.
Which option mentions reading?
questions.explanation: Ama reading a story and learning ten new words is a concrete example that supports the point.
questions.misconception: Choosing an example unrelated to reading.

questions.stem: Point: 'Eating fruits keeps us healthy.' Write one concrete example you could use to support this point.
answer: my sister eats oranges every day and she is rarely sick
i eat bananas and i feel strong
my friend eats mangoes and is healthy
eating an orange gives you vitamin c
eating fruit helps you grow strong
my mother eats fruit and is never sick
hints: Give a specific person or situation.
Mention the fruit and the result.
questions.explanation: A concrete example should name a specific person or situation and connect eating fruit with good health.
questions.misconception: Repeating the general point instead of giving an example.

questions.stem: Your speech is on 'Keeping our community clean'. Which example is most relevant?
options: Last Saturday the youth of Nima cleaned the market square.
The market square is very large.
Some people sell tomatoes in the market.
The market has a new roof.
hints: The example must be about cleaning.
Which option describes a cleaning action?
questions.explanation: The youth cleaning the market square is a relevant example of keeping the community clean.
questions.misconception: Choosing a fact about the market that is not about cleanliness.

questions.stem: Point: 'Pupils can be kind to one another.' Write one relevant example.
answer: a pupil shared her lunch with a hungry classmate
a pupil helped a classmate carry books
a pupil lent a pen to a friend
a pupil comforted a classmate who was crying
a pupil gave a pencil to a friend
a pupil invited a lonely child to play
hints: The example must show kindness.
Think of a specific action.
questions.explanation: A relevant example would be a pupil sharing lunch, lending a pen or helping a classmate — all concrete acts of kindness.
questions.misconception: Giving a general statement without a specific example.

questions.stem: Point: 'Water is important for good health.' Example: 'When Kojo stopped drinking water during football practice, he became dizzy and had to rest.' How does this example clarify the point?
options: It shows that football is dangerous.
It shows what happens when the body lacks water.
It shows that Kojo likes football.
It shows that resting is fun.
hints: The point is about water and health.
What happened to Kojo when he did not drink water?
questions.explanation: Kojo becoming dizzy without water shows the effect of lacking water on the body, which clarifies why water matters for health.
questions.misconception: Focusing on football rather than the water-health connection.

questions.stem: Point: 'Hard work brings success.' Example: 'Ama studied for two hours every evening and passed her exam with distinction.' Write two sentences explaining how the example clarifies the point.
hints: Connect Ama's study to the point.
Explain what happened because of her effort.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that Ama's consistent study is the hard work, and her distinction is the success, showing the connection clearly.

criteria.description: Connects Ama's study to hard work

questions.stem: Make a point about the value of sharing. Then give one concrete example and explain how it clarifies your point.
hints: State your point first.
Then give a specific example and explain the link.
questions.explanation: The pupil states a point, gives a concrete example and explains how the example supports the point.

criteria.description: Explains how the example clarifies the point

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a concrete example rather than a general statement?
options: Last Friday, the pupils of Basic 5 swept the school compound and picked up litter.
hints: A concrete example names specific people and actions.
Which option gives specific people and an action?
