questions.explanation: The sentence about Basic 5 pupils sweeping on Friday gives specific people, an action and a time, making it a concrete example.
questions.misconception: Thinking any statement about cleanliness is a concrete example.

questions.stem: Point: 'Reading for pleasure helps pupils do well in school.' Which example supports this point best?
options: Esi reads story books every evening and her vocabulary has improved greatly.
Esi has many story books on her shelf.
Esi likes the colour of her books.
Esi borrowed books from the library once.
hints: The example must show a link between reading and school success.
Which option shows an improvement from reading?
questions.explanation: The example of Esi reading every evening and her vocabulary improving shows a clear link between reading and doing well in school.
questions.misconception: Choosing an example about books without a result.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Identify and use the appropriate register for formal and informal contexts

skills.description: Identify formal register features
Identify informal register features
Choose the appropriate register for a given context
Use the appropriate register in spoken or written speech

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify formal/informal features), 35% medium (choose register for a situation), 15% harder (use register appropriately in a short speech). Contexts: assembly, classroom, market, church, mosque, home and peer conversation.
misconceptions: Using slang in a formal speech
Believing formal register means using big words unnecessarily
Using contractions in a formal written speech
Thinking informal register is rude

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of formal register?
options: Using full forms such as 'cannot' instead of 'can't'.
hints: Formal language is polite and complete.
Which option avoids casual words?
questions.explanation: Formal register uses complete words such as 'cannot' rather than the casual contraction 'can't'.
questions.misconception: Thinking slang belongs in formal speech.

questions.stem: Write one feature of formal register.
hints: Formal register sounds respectful.
Think about contractions and slang.
questions.explanation: Formal register uses full forms, polite words, complete sentences and avoids slang.
questions.misconception: Naming a feature of informal register.

questions.stem: Which expression is informal?
options: May I please have a seat?
hints: Informal language is casual.
Which option uses slang?
questions.explanation: 'Hey, what's up?' is an informal, casual greeting.
questions.misconception: Choosing a polite expression as informal.

questions.stem: Write one feature of informal register.
hints: Informal language is relaxed.
Think about contractions and slang.
questions.explanation: Informal register includes contractions, slang, casual words and shorter sentences.
questions.misconception: Naming a formal feature as informal.

questions.stem: You are giving a speech at a school assembly. Which register should you use?
hints: An assembly is a formal setting.
Formal register is more appropriate there.
questions.explanation: A school assembly is a formal setting, so formal register is appropriate.
questions.misconception: Thinking informal register is fine at assembly.

questions.stem: You are chatting with your friends at break. Which register should you use?
hints: Chatting with friends is casual.
Informal register suits relaxed talk.
questions.explanation: Chatting with friends calls for informal register because the situation is relaxed and casual.
questions.misconception: Thinking formal register is needed with friends.

questions.stem: Name one situation where you should use formal register.
hints: Formal situations involve respect or unfamiliar people.
Think of an official occasion.
questions.explanation: Formal register is used at assembly, with teachers or visitors, in interviews, in letters and in places of worship.
questions.misconception: Choosing an informal situation.

questions.stem: Which sentence is appropriate for a formal speech at a school assembly?
options: Good morning, Mr Chairman, teachers and fellow pupils.
hints: Formal greetings use titles and respect.
Which option is polite and complete?
questions.explanation: The formal greeting addresses the chairman, teachers and pupils politely and is appropriate for assembly.
questions.misconception: Using slang in a formal setting.

questions.stem: Write a short formal greeting (two sentences) that you could use at the start of a school assembly speech.
hints: Address the audience politely.
Use formal words like 'distinguished'.
questions.explanation: A strong greeting addresses the audience respectfully and sets a formal tone.

questions.stem: Greet a visitor to your school using formal register.
hints: Use polite words like 'Good morning' and 'sir' or 'madam'.
Speak respectfully.
questions.explanation: The pupil greets the visitor politely using formal register.

questions.stem: In pairs, role-play two situations: one where you greet a teacher formally, and one where you greet a friend informally. Use the correct register for each.
hints: The teacher greeting should be respectful and complete.
The friend greeting can be casual.
questions.explanation: The pair uses formal register with the teacher and informal register with the friend.

criteria.description: Uses formal register with the teacher
Uses informal register with the friend
Adapts tone and vocabulary to each situation

questions.stem: You are writing a letter to the head teacher about a school problem. Which register should you use?
hints: A letter to the head teacher is an official situation.
Formal register is appropriate here.
questions.explanation: A letter to the head teacher is a formal communication, so formal register is appropriate.
questions.misconception: Thinking informal register is acceptable in a letter to the head teacher.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Elaborate on points using experiences and feelings

skills.description: Elaborate a point with details such as facts, examples or explanations
Elaborate a point using a personal experience
Elaborate a point using feelings
Keep elaboration relevant to the point being made

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (add one detail to a point), 35% medium (elaborate with an experience or feeling), 20% harder (elaborate while staying relevant). Topics: school events, family, community and personal achievements.
misconceptions: Telling a long story that drifts from the point
Adding feelings without linking them to the point
Thinking elaboration means repeating the same idea
Sharing inappropriate personal details

questions.stem: Point: 'Our school has a beautiful garden.' Which sentence adds a good detail?
options: The garden has many kinds of flowers and tall green trees.
hints: A good detail tells more about the garden.
Which option describes what is in the garden?
questions.explanation: Mentioning flowers and tall green trees adds a useful detail that elaborates on the point about the garden.
questions.misconception: Repeating the point instead of adding detail.

questions.stem: Point: 'Reading is enjoyable.' Write one sentence that adds a detail to this point.
answer: reading stories takes me to faraway places
reading a good story makes me happy
i read every evening after school
reading is fun because it teaches new things
hints: Say what makes reading enjoyable for you.
Give one specific example.
questions.explanation: A good detail explains why reading is enjoyable, with a specific example.
questions.misconception: Repeating 'reading is enjoyable' without adding anything.

questions.stem: Point: 'Breakfast is important for pupils.' Write three sentences that elaborate on this point with details and examples.
hints: Give a reason first.
Add an example from your own or a classmate's experience.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives a clear reason, a specific example and a conclusion that stays on the point.

criteria.description: Gives a reason for the point

questions.stem: Point: 'Teamwork helps us achieve more.' Which sentence uses personal experience to elaborate?
options: In my group, each person did their part and we finished our project in one afternoon.
hints: A personal experience mentions something you have done.
Which option describes an actual group project?
questions.explanation: The sentence about the group project is a specific personal experience that shows how teamwork helped achieve more.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general statement instead of a personal experience.

questions.stem: Point: 'Helping at home is important.' Write one sentence from your own experience that elaborates this point.
answer: i help my mother carry water after school
i sweep the compound every morning
i help my father on the farm on saturdays
i look after my younger brother
i wash the dishes in the evening
i fetch water for my grandmother
hints: Think of something you really do at home.
One sentence with a specific action is enough.
questions.explanation: A personal example of a specific home task elaborates the point about helping at home.
questions.misconception: Restating the point without giving an experience.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about one minute) on the point 'Sport brings people together'. Use one personal experience to elaborate.
hints: State the point first.
Describe a real game or sports event you have been part of.
questions.explanation: The pupil makes the point and elaborates with a clear personal experience.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about the point 'Reading helps us learn about other places', using one personal experience.
hints: State the point.
Describe something you read about.
Say how it helped you.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the point, describes a personal reading experience and explains how it taught the pupil about another place.

criteria.description: Explains how it taught about other places

questions.stem: Point: 'Pupils feel proud when they win.' Which sentence elaborates with a feeling?
options: The pupils jumped and cheered with joy when the referee blew the final whistle.
The match was played on Saturday.
The referee was a tall man.
hints: A feeling shows emotion.
Which option describes how the pupils felt?
questions.explanation: Jumping and cheering with joy shows a clear feeling of pride and excitement.
questions.misconception: Choosing a fact rather than a feeling.

questions.stem: Point: 'Being late for school can make a pupil feel bad.' Write one sentence elaborating this with a feeling.
answer: i felt ashamed when i entered the class late
i was embarrassed when the teacher looked at me
i felt worried when i missed the assembly
i was upset when i could not answer the first question
i felt sad because everyone stared at me
hints: Name the feeling (ashamed, embarrassed, worried).
Describe what caused the feeling.
questions.explanation: A good sentence names a specific feeling and links it to the experience of being late.
questions.misconception: Describing the action without naming a feeling.

questions.stem: Point: 'Losing a friend's book can be upsetting.' Write three sentences elaborating this point using feelings and details.
hints: Describe what happened.
Say how you felt.
Say what you did about it.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the event, the feelings involved and how it was resolved, staying on the point.

questions.stem: Make a point about how helping someone makes you feel. Then elaborate with a feeling from your own experience.
hints: State the point first.
Name a specific feeling (happy, proud, glad).
questions.explanation: The pupil makes a point and elaborates with a clear personal feeling.

criteria.description: Links the feeling to a personal experience

questions.stem: Point: 'Cleanliness keeps us healthy.' Which elaboration is most relevant?
options: Washing our hands before eating prevents germs.
My friend has a new pencil case.
We play football at break time.
hints: The elaboration must connect to cleanliness and health.
Which option links a clean habit to health?
questions.explanation: Washing hands before eating is a clean habit that prevents germs, directly supporting the point about health.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated observation.

questions.stem: Point: 'Hard work pays.' Write one sentence of elaboration that is relevant to this point.
answer: my sister studied hard and passed her exam
a farmer who works hard gets a good harvest
kojo practised every day and won the race
if you work hard you will achieve your goals
ama worked hard and got a prize
hints: Give an example that shows hard work leading to a result.
Stay on the point.
questions.explanation: A relevant elaboration shows a clear connection between hard work and a positive result.
questions.misconception: Giving an example that drifts off the topic.

questions.stem: Point: 'Homework helps pupils understand lessons better.' A pupil elaborates: 'My brother plays football on weekends and he is a good goalkeeper.' How relevant is this elaboration?
options: It is relevant if the brother is younger.
It is not relevant to the point about homework.
It is relevant only at break time.
hints: Does the elaboration mention homework or lessons?
Which option matches how the elaboration connects to the point?
questions.explanation: The elaboration is about football and goalkeeping, not homework, so it is not relevant to the point.
questions.misconception: Believing any elaboration counts if it is interesting.

questions.stem: Point: 'Pupils should respect their teachers.' Write three sentences of elaboration that stay relevant to this point.
hints: Give reasons why respect matters.
Give a specific example.
Say what happens when respect is shown.
questions.explanation: A strong answer stays on the point by giving reasons and examples that show why and how pupils should respect teachers.

criteria.description: Gives a clear reason for respecting teachers

questions.stem: Make a point about the value of sharing. Elaborate with a relevant detail or example.
hints: State the point first.
Give a specific example that supports it.
questions.explanation: The pupil makes a clear point and elaborates with a relevant example.

questions.stem: Point: 'Our school has many clubs.' Write two sentences elaborating this point with details.
hints: Name at least one club.
Say what the club does.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names clubs and describes their activities, giving clear details.

questions.stem: Point: 'Working hard at school brings good results.' Which personal experience elaborates this point best?
options: I studied for one hour every day and my test score improved from 40% to 80%.
I like watching football on TV.
The school gate is painted green.
hints: The experience must connect study effort to good results.
Which option shows a clear improvement from effort?
questions.explanation: The pupil's study effort leading to an improved score is a clear personal experience that elaborates the point.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated personal fact.

questions.stem: Point: 'Coming late to school can make a pupil feel ashamed.' Which sentence elaborates this with a feeling?
options: I walked into class after assembly.
I felt small and my cheeks burned as the whole class turned to look at me.
hints: The sentence must name or show a feeling.
Which option describes how it felt?
questions.explanation: The description of feeling small and cheeks burning clearly shows the feeling of shame.
questions.misconception: Choosing a factual sentence instead of one that shows feeling.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.10.3: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Speak with confidence before different audiences using appropriate verbal and non-verbal cues to convey meaning

skills.description: Show confidence when speaking: steady voice, upright posture and eye contact
Use verbal cues: clear voice, appropriate volume and emphasis
Use non-verbal cues: gestures, facial expressions and posture
Adapt delivery to different audiences

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (speak to a small group with some confidence), 35% medium (use verbal and non-verbal cues), 25% harder (adapt delivery to different audiences). Topics: self, school, community and familiar stories.
misconceptions: Believing confidence means speaking loudly without preparation
Using gestures that distract from the message
Maintaining eye contact only with the teacher, not the audience
Using the same delivery style for peers and for adults

questions.stem: Which behaviour shows confidence when speaking to the class?
options: Looking at the floor while speaking.
Standing upright, looking at the audience and speaking clearly.
Whispering and hiding behind a desk.
Reading from a paper without looking up.
hints: Confident speakers face their audience.
They also stand tall and speak clearly.
questions.explanation: Standing upright, looking at the audience and speaking clearly are key signs of confidence.
questions.misconception: Thinking reading with no eye contact shows confidence.

questions.stem: Write one thing you can do to appear more confident when speaking.
answer: take a deep breath before speaking
hints: Think about your posture and eyes.
Practising helps confidence.
questions.explanation: Standing upright, making eye contact, practising and speaking clearly all help a speaker appear confident.
questions.misconception: Thinking confidence requires no preparation.

questions.stem: Introduce yourself to the class in three sentences. Stand upright, look at the class and speak clearly.
hints: Start with your name and class.
Look at different pupils as you speak.
questions.explanation: The pupil introduces themselves with upright posture, eye contact and a clear voice.

questions.stem: Give a short speech (about one minute) about your school to a group of younger pupils. Show confidence through your posture, eyes and voice.
hints: Practise your speech first.
Stand tall and look at your audience.
questions.explanation: The pupil delivers a short speech confidently with clear posture, eye contact and voice.

questions.stem: Which of these is a verbal cue used when speaking?
options: Emphasising important words with your voice.
hints: Verbal cues involve the voice.
Which option is about how you use your voice?
questions.explanation: Emphasising important words with the voice is a verbal cue. Smiling, standing upright and keeping hands still are non-verbal cues.
questions.misconception: Confusing non-verbal cues with verbal cues.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a good verbal cue for emphasis?
options: We must keep our school CLEAN!
We must keep our school clean.
We must... keep our school clean.
hints: Emphasis is placed on the key word.
Which option stresses 'CLEAN'?
questions.explanation: Stressing 'CLEAN' with emphasis is a strong verbal cue that draws the audience's attention to the key idea.
questions.misconception: Thinking flat delivery is as effective as emphasis.

questions.stem: Name one verbal cue you can use when speaking to make a point clear.
hints: Verbal cues use the voice.
Think about stress and pauses.
questions.explanation: Using stress, pauses, tone changes and emphasis are all verbal cues that make points clearer.
questions.misconception: Naming a body action instead of a voice cue.

questions.stem: Say this sentence aloud twice: once with emphasis on 'carefully' and once with emphasis on 'count'. 'Count the money carefully.' Explain how the meaning changed.
hints: Stressing a different word changes the focus.
The stressed word shows what the speaker cares about most.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses stress to change the focus of the sentence and explains how meaning shifts.

criteria.description: Uses emphasis on 'carefully' in the first reading
Uses emphasis on 'count' in the second reading

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-verbal cue?
options: Using hand gestures to show size.
hints: Non-verbal means without words or voice.
Which option uses the body?
questions.explanation: Using hand gestures is a non-verbal cue because it uses the body rather than words or voice.
questions.misconception: Confusing voice cues with body cues.

questions.stem: Which facial expression should you use when talking about something sad?
options: A serious face with a slight frown.
hints: Sad news calls for a sad expression.
A serious face fits sadness.
questions.explanation: A serious face with a slight frown matches the sad tone of the message.
questions.misconception: Thinking a smile is appropriate for all content.

questions.stem: Name two non-verbal cues you can use when giving a speech.
hints: Non-verbal cues use the body.
Gestures, facial expressions, posture and eye contact are examples.
questions.explanation: Gestures, facial expressions, posture and eye contact are all non-verbal cues.
questions.misconception: Naming voice cues as non-verbal cues.

questions.stem: Speak for 30 seconds about your favourite food. Use at least two gestures and one facial expression.
hints: Use a hand gesture to show size or shape.
Use a smile when describing what you like.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses appropriate gestures and facial expressions to support the message.

criteria.description: Uses at least one facial expression

questions.stem: How should you change your delivery when speaking to younger pupils instead of your classmates?
options: Speak faster and use big words.
Speak more slowly, use simpler words and smile often.
Read from a paper without looking up.
hints: Younger pupils need simple words and friendly delivery.
Which option suits young listeners?
questions.explanation: Slower speech, simpler words and friendly facial expressions are appropriate for younger pupils.
questions.misconception: Thinking the same delivery style suits all audiences.

questions.stem: Name one way you would change your speech when speaking to a group of adults instead of your classmates.
hints: Adults expect a more formal register.
Think about the words and tone you would use.
questions.explanation: Speaking more formally, using polite address and a serious tone are appropriate adjustments when addressing adults.
questions.misconception: Thinking the same style fits all audiences.

questions.stem: Speak for 30 seconds about the importance of reading. Then deliver the same speech to an imagined audience of adults, adapting your words and delivery.
hints: Keep the message the same.
Change the vocabulary and tone.
questions.explanation: The pupil adapts the same message to two audiences using different vocabulary and delivery.

criteria.description: Delivers the first version for peers
Delivers the second version for adults
Uses more formal language for adults

questions.stem: Present a short story to two different audiences: small group of classmates and imagined group of very young children. Adjust your tone, gestures and vocabulary for each.
hints: Use simpler words and more gestures for the children.
Use more detail and fewer gestures for the classmates.
questions.explanation: The pupil adapts the story presentation for both audiences, showing awareness of audience needs.

criteria.description: Delivers to the classmate audience appropriately
Delivers to the younger audience appropriately

questions.stem: Write three tips for speaking confidently before a new audience.
hints: Think about preparation, posture and eye contact.
Three short tips are enough.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three practical tips for confident speaking.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining how volume and emphasis help convey meaning in a speech.
hints: Volume shows importance or urgency.
Emphasis draws attention to key words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that volume and emphasis help the audience focus on key ideas and understand the speaker's intention.

questions.stem: Write three sentences explaining how gestures, facial expressions and posture help convey meaning when speaking.
hints: Gestures show size, shape or action.
Facial expressions show feelings.
Posture shows confidence or interest.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains each non-verbal cue and how it supports the spoken message.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Relate the central messages of poems to personal experiences

skills.description: Identify the central message of a short level-appropriate poem
Explain the poem's message in the pupil's own words
Link the poem's message to a real personal experience
Point to a line or word in the poem that supports the stated message

spec.difficultyPlan: 60% easy (identify or explain a clear message in a short poem), 30% medium (link to a specific personal experience), 10% harder (justify the message using a line from the poem). All poems used are short original four-to-six line poems printed inside the question stems.
misconceptions: Mistaking the topic of the poem for its message
Retelling the poem's events instead of stating its lesson
Offering a personal story unrelated to the message
Believing a poem's message must be stated directly in one line

questions.stem: Read the poem: 'The farmer waits for the maize to grow. He waters the soil and does not rush. When the rains come, the green shoots rise.' What is the central message of this poem?
options: Rain is more useful than sunshine.
Good things come to those who wait patiently.
Maize grows faster than other crops.
hints: Look at the words 'waits' and 'does not rush'.
Ask what the poem teaches about the farmer's behaviour.
questions.explanation: The farmer waits and does not rush, and only then do the green shoots rise. So the poem teaches that good things come to those who wait patiently.
questions.misconception: Choosing the topic (maize or rain) instead of the lesson about patience.

questions.stem: Read: 'One broom stick breaks alone. Many broom sticks hold as one. We are stronger together than we are alone.' What is the poem about?
options: Brooms should be kept in the kitchen.
hints: Compare one stick with many sticks.
What happens to people who stand together?
questions.explanation: Many sticks hold together while one stick breaks. The poem uses this to teach that unity makes people strong.
questions.misconception: Focusing on the broom as a household object rather than on the lesson it carries.

questions.stem: Read: 'Say what is true, even when your voice shakes. A lie is a heavy stone that you must carry alone.' What message does the poem carry?
options: Speak loudly when you are afraid.
Stones are too heavy to carry alone.
Always tell the truth, even when it is hard.
Keep quiet when your voice shakes.
hints: What does the poem ask you to say?
The poem calls a lie a heavy stone.
questions.explanation: The poem asks us to say what is true even when it is difficult. It calls a lie a heavy load, so the message is to always tell the truth.
questions.misconception: Confusing the image of shaking with the actual message about truth.

questions.stem: Read: 'Early in the morning, before the cockerel calls, Maame sweeps the compound and waters the plants.' Write the central message in a short phrase.
hints: What time does Maame start her work?
Which value does starting early and working show?
questions.explanation: Maame starts work before the cockerel calls, which shows that she is hardworking. The message is that hard work is good and should start early.
questions.misconception: Answering 'morning' or 'watering plants' instead of the value being taught.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market is loud, the market is wide, but my mother's smile is the best thing inside.' What is the poet saying?
options: A mother's love is worth more than anything money can buy.
The market is too wide to walk across.
Smiling people should sell in markets.
hints: What does the poet call the best thing in the whole market?
Think about the value of a mother's love.
questions.explanation: The poet says the best thing inside the wide, loud market is a mother's smile, not anything for sale. That means love is worth more than goods or money.
questions.misconception: Reading the poem literally as a complaint about a noisy market.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Hold the hand of the small one, share your water in the sun.' Which explanation gives the message best?
options: Keep your water because the sun is hot.
Small children should carry their own water.
Be kind and help those who are weaker than you.
Walk hand in hand only when the sun shines.
hints: What is the poem asking you to do with your water?
The poem is about the small and the weak.
questions.explanation: Holding a small child's hand and sharing water in the heat are acts of kindness to those who need help. So the message is to be kind and help the weaker ones.
questions.misconception: Explaining the message with a sentence that reverses the sense of the poem.

questions.stem: Poem: 'A man who greets his neighbour with a smile will never sleep hungry in the village.' Explain the message in your own words.
hints: What does the man do to his neighbour?
What happens to him when trouble comes?
questions.explanation: The man who smiles and greets his neighbour well is helped in return, so the poem teaches that kindness is rewarded and friendly people get help.
questions.misconception: Copying the poem's words instead of restating the meaning.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Stop for the old woman at the crossing. Her eyes are slow, her feet are tired.' In two sentences, explain the message in your own words.
hints: Who is the poem asking us to help?
Why does she need help?
questions.explanation: The poem asks us to help old people at crossings because they are slow and tired. The pupil should restate this in their own words.

criteria.description: States the message of helping elderly people
Explains in own words rather than copying

questions.stem: Poem: 'A tree that stands alone fears every wind. A forest laughs at the storm.' Which explanation of the message is correct?
options: Trees should be planted in one place only.
Standing alone is always the best choice.
People who work together can face difficulties better than people who work alone.
hints: What happens to a single tree in a storm?
What does a whole forest do in the same storm?
questions.explanation: The single tree fears the wind but the forest laughs at the storm. That shows that people who work together can face difficulties better than people alone.
questions.misconception: Taking the poem literally about trees rather than the lesson about people.

questions.stem: Poem: 'The learner asks, the learner grows, the learner who never asks, never knows.' Explain the message of this poem in three sentences.
hints: What does the poem say about asking questions?
What happens to someone who never asks?
questions.explanation: A good answer says that asking questions helps us learn, while refusing to ask leaves us without knowledge, and uses three sentences in the pupil's own words.

criteria.description: Explains that asking questions leads to learning
Explains that not asking leaves us ignorant
Uses own words, not the poem's words

questions.stem: The class read the poem about patience on the farm. Tell the class about a time you had to wait for something you really wanted.
hints: Think of a day you waited for a visitor, a meal or a gift.
Say how you felt while waiting.
questions.explanation: The pupil should describe a real waiting experience and connect it to the poem's message of patience.

criteria.description: Tells a clear personal experience of waiting
Connects the experience to the poem's message

questions.stem: The poem teaches that many hands are stronger than one. Write two sentences about a time you and others worked together at home or in school.
hints: What were you doing together?
Was the work easier or faster with others?
questions.explanation: A good answer describes a real group task and links it to the poem's message about unity.

criteria.description: Describes a clear experience of working together
Links the experience to the poem's message

questions.stem: The poem said: 'Say what is true, even when your voice shakes.' Which experience best connects with this message?
options: I helped my mother cook fufu on Saturday.
I told my teacher the truth about a broken chair, though I was afraid.
I read a poem aloud to the class at assembly.
I shared my bread with my friend at break.
hints: Which action actually shows telling the truth?
Speaking the truth is different from reading about it.
questions.explanation: Admitting the truth about the broken chair even though the pupil was afraid matches the poem's message about honesty and courage.
questions.misconception: Choosing an action that is good but does not show honesty.

questions.stem: The class read the poem about the man who greets his neighbour kindly. Tell the class about a time someone was kind to you or you were kind to someone, and explain why the poem reminds you of it.
hints: What exactly happened?
Which line of the poem fits that moment?
questions.explanation: The pupil should tell the incident clearly and connect it to the poem's message about kindness.

criteria.description: Links the incident to the poem's message
Maintains eye contact and speaks audibly

questions.stem: The poem says: 'A tree that stands alone fears every wind.' Write three sentences about a time you felt stronger because you were with others.
hints: Think of a group you belong to, at school or at home.
Say how the group made you feel stronger.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives one specific experience of being supported by others and explains the link to the poem.

criteria.description: Explains how the group made them stronger
Links the experience to the poem's message

questions.stem: Poem: 'The farmer waits for the maize to grow. He waters the soil and does not rush.' Someone says the message is about patience. Which words support this?
hints: Which words show waiting rather than doing?
Patience is about not rushing.
questions.explanation: The words 'The farmer waits' show patience directly, because waiting is the heart of the message.
questions.misconception: Choosing a phrase that names an object or action instead of the idea of waiting.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Say what is true, even when your voice shakes. A lie is a heavy stone that you must carry alone.' Which words show that a lie troubles the person who tells it?
answer: a lie is a heavy stone
hints: Which words compare a lie to something heavy?
Copy them exactly as they appear.
questions.explanation: Calling a lie 'a heavy stone' shows that telling lies weighs a person down and troubles them.
questions.misconception: Copying the whole poem instead of pointing to the supporting words.

questions.stem: Poem: 'One broom stick breaks alone. Many broom sticks hold as one.' The message is about unity. Which line supports the message best?
options: Many broom sticks hold as one
Brooms are kept in the kitchen
hints: Which line shows strength, not weakness?
Unity is about standing together.
questions.explanation: The line 'Many broom sticks hold as one' shows the strength that comes from being together, which is the message of unity.
questions.misconception: Choosing the opposite line, which shows what happens when you stand alone.

questions.stem: Poem: 'A tree that stands alone fears every wind. A forest laughs at the storm.' Which words in the poem show that being together brings courage?
answer: a forest laughs at the storm
hints: Look at what the forest does in the storm.
The tree fears; what does the forest do?
questions.explanation: The forest does not fear the storm, it laughs at it. Those words show the courage that comes from being together.
questions.misconception: Choosing the words about the lone tree instead of the words about the forest.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Early in the morning, before the cockerel calls, Maame sweeps the compound and waters the plants.' State the message of the poem, then copy the words that best support your answer and explain why.
hints: Which words tell you the time she starts?
Say why those words show your message.
questions.explanation: The message is that hard work should start early. The words 'before the cockerel calls' support this because they show Maame working before most people are awake.

criteria.description: States the message about hard work or early rising
Explains why those words support the message

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Discuss values in poems and talk about the importance of these values in society

skills.description: Identify the value expressed in a short poem
Explain why the identified value matters in society
Describe what happens in society when the value is present or absent
Discuss the value in a group and share views clearly

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (name the value and explain its importance simply), 35% medium (explain importance with reasons or describe consequences), 15% harder (describe consequences of presence and absence together and discuss in groups). Values are limited to those treated in the curriculum: honesty, love, patriotism, patience, hard work, truthfulness, unity, kindness, generosity, respect.
misconceptions: Confusing a value with an emotion or with the poem's subject
Giving importance that is too vague without a reason
Listing many values without linking any to the poem
Describing what happens when a value is absent but not when it is present

questions.stem: Poem: 'Sweep the yard before the sun is high, weed the garden, fetch the water.' Which value does the poem teach?
hints: The poem lists jobs to be done.
Doing work early and well shows one value.
questions.explanation: Sweeping, weeding and fetching water are jobs, and doing them before the sun is high shows hard work.
questions.misconception: Choosing a value that is not shown by the actions in the poem.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Our flag flies red, gold, green, with a black star in between. We love our land, Ghana.' Which value does this poem express?
hints: The poem is about our land and our flag.
There is a special word for love of one's country.
questions.explanation: The poem speaks of the flag and love for Ghana, which is patriotism.
questions.misconception: Confusing patriotism with general kindness or honesty.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Wait for the pot to boil, wait for the rice to swell. The hungry one who waits will eat well.' Which value does the poem teach?
hints: The poem says 'wait' more than once.
What do we call the ability to wait without complaining?
questions.explanation: The poem repeats the need to wait for the pot and the rice. That value is patience.
questions.misconception: Answering 'cooking' or 'hunger' instead of the value.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Hold the hand of the small one, share your water in the sun. A kind word costs nothing, but it warms a heart.' Which value is taught most clearly?
hints: Look at 'share', 'kind word' and 'warms a heart'.
Which value is about caring for others?
questions.explanation: Sharing water and speaking a kind word both show kindness, so that is the value taught most clearly.
questions.misconception: Choosing hard work because fetching water takes effort, when the poem's focus is caring for others.

questions.stem: Poem: 'One broom stick breaks, but many broom sticks hold. Let us stand together, let us be one.' Which value does the poem teach?
hints: Look at 'stand together' and 'be one'.
Which value means being joined as one people?
questions.explanation: The poem calls people to stand together and be one, which is the value of unity.
questions.misconception: Confusing unity with patriotism, even though the poem is about people joining together.

questions.stem: A poem teaches honesty. Why is honesty important in society?
options: It makes people speak more often.
It helps people trust one another.
It prevents people from asking questions.
hints: Think about what happens between people when everyone tells the truth.
Trust grows when people are honest.
questions.explanation: When people are honest, others can trust them. Trust is the reason honesty matters so much in a community.
questions.misconception: Choosing an answer that gives a benefit unrelated to honesty.

questions.stem: A poem teaches the value of hard work. Give one reason why hard work is important in society.
answer: it helps people achieve their goals
hints: What does hard work produce for a person or a country?
Think of farmers, teachers and traders.
questions.explanation: Hard work brings success, food, money and progress, which is why it matters to any society.
questions.misconception: Giving a reason that could apply to any value without linking it to work.

questions.stem: A class reads a poem about patience. Why is patience important at school?
options: It helps pupils wait for others and take turns fairly.
It means pupils never ask questions.
It allows pupils to do nothing all day.
It makes pupils finish work faster than anyone else.
hints: Patience is about waiting without quarrelling.
Think about the classroom line and sharing materials.
questions.explanation: Patience helps pupils take turns and wait fairly, which keeps the classroom peaceful and fair.
questions.misconception: Confusing patience with laziness or with speed.

questions.stem: A poem says the nation loves its land and keeps it clean. In three sentences, explain why love for one's country is important to society.
hints: What do people do when they love their country?
Think of keeping the environment clean and obeying laws.
questions.explanation: A strong answer says that love for country makes people care for the land, obey laws and work for peace, in three clear sentences.

criteria.description: Explains that patriotism makes people care for the country
Gives at least one specific example of caring

questions.stem: A poem teaches generosity. Write two reasons why generosity is important in a community.
hints: What happens to those who receive help?
What happens to the giver's character?
questions.explanation: Generosity helps those in need and builds good character and friendship in the community.

criteria.description: Gives one reason about helping those in need

questions.stem: Poem: 'Where there is unity, the harvest is big. Where there is quarrelling, the field is bare.' What happens when a community is united?
options: People work together and achieve more.
hints: What does the poem say unity leads to?
A big harvest means the community achieved something.
questions.explanation: When people are united they work together, so their harvest is big. Unity brings achievement.
questions.misconception: Choosing the consequence of quarrelling rather than the consequence of unity.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'One dishonest word can break a thousand promises.' What happens in a community where people are dishonest?
options: People trust each other even more.
People find it hard to trust one another.
People begin to speak more often.
hints: What does breaking promises do to trust?
Think about how you feel when someone lies to you.
questions.explanation: One dishonest word can destroy many promises, so people find it hard to trust one another.
questions.misconception: Choosing a neutral outcome instead of the loss of trust that dishonesty causes.

questions.stem: A poem says a patient farmer eats, but a rushing farmer throws away his seed. What happens in society when people lack patience?
hints: What did the rushing farmer do with his seed?
What does impatience usually produce?
questions.explanation: The rushing farmer wasted his seed. In the same way, people without patience make mistakes, spoil their work and lose what they have.
questions.misconception: Giving the consequence of patience instead of the consequence of lacking it.

questions.stem: Poem: 'Where the elders are respected, the village sits in peace. Where they are ignored, trouble sleeps at the gate.' Which statement best describes the consequence of respect?
options: The village experiences peace and order.
The elders become the village leaders.
The village makes more laws than before.
The elders stop speaking to the young.
hints: What does the poem say the village does when elders are respected?
Peace is the key word.
questions.explanation: The poem says the village sits in peace when elders are respected, so peace and order are the results.
questions.misconception: Choosing a consequence that sounds related but is not what the poem says.

questions.stem: A poem says: 'A land that keeps its rivers clean will feed its children for many years.' Describe what happens in a society where people do not care for their environment.
hints: What happens to rivers and land when people litter?
How does that affect food and health?
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the environment becomes polluted, water becomes unsafe and people fall sick or have less food.

criteria.description: Describes pollution or damage to the environment
Links the damage to a consequence for people

questions.stem: In your group, discuss the poem about honesty. Each member should say one reason why honesty is important at home. Share your group's views with the class.
hints: Wait for your turn before you speak.
Listen to what others say and add to it.
questions.explanation: The pupil discusses honestly, takes turns and shares the group's views clearly with the class.

criteria.description: Gives one clear reason about honesty
Shares the group's views with the class

questions.stem: With your partner, discuss the value of unity in the poem you read. Say how your class can show unity at school.
hints: Think of games, cleaning and group work.
Talk to your partner before you share with the class.
questions.explanation: The pupil should discuss unity with a partner and give practical examples of showing it at school.

criteria.description: Gives a practical example at school
Discusses with the partner before speaking

questions.stem: In groups of four, discuss the poem about kindness. Decide together which line shows kindness most strongly and explain your choice to the class.
hints: Each member should choose a line first.
Be ready to say why your group's line is the strongest.
questions.explanation: The group should agree on a line, justify the choice and report it clearly to the class.

criteria.description: Explains why the line shows kindness strongly

questions.stem: Write down two different views your group shared about why patriotism is important. Use sentences like 'One member said that...' and 'Another member said that...'.
hints: Write what your group members actually said.
Use the sentence starters in the question.
questions.explanation: A good answer records two different group views accurately and uses the reporting sentence starters.

criteria.description: Views are about patriotism and are clear

questions.stem: In your group, discuss why hard work is important for Ghana's development. Present two points to the class using polite and clear speech.
hints: Think of farmers, teachers, nurses and traders.
Ask for clarification politely if you do not understand a group member.
questions.explanation: The group should present two clear points about hard work and national development, speaking politely and clearly.

criteria.description: Points link hard work to national development

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.3.1: Appreciate poems and other pieces of literary materials
indicator.objective: Compose eight-line poems

skills.description: Write a single meaningful line on a given topic, matching the poem's theme
Build a poem with exactly eight lines
Arrange contributed lines into a meaningful order (beginning, middle, ending)
Make lines singable or readable with some rhythm or repeated pattern
Recite or perform the eight-line poem to the class

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (write one relevant line; count lines), 35% medium (order lines meaningfully; add rhythm/repetition), 25% harder (compose and perform an eight-line poem with rhythm). Topics drawn from pupils' environment: school, market, family, weather, animals, unity, work.
misconceptions: Writing prose sentences instead of lines that read like poetry
Producing fewer or more than eight lines
Making lines unrelated to each other or to the topic
Copying an existing poem rather than composing

questions.stem: Your class is composing an eight-line poem about the school garden. Which line fits the topic best?
options: The tall green maize sways in the breeze.
The tro-tro is full at the station.
I lost my pen on Monday.
hints: Which line describes the garden?
Look for words like maize, green and breeze.
questions.explanation: The line about tall green maize swaying in the breeze clearly belongs to a poem about the school garden. The others belong to different topics.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that is about a different place or situation.

questions.stem: Your poem is about a happy morning at school. Which line fits best?
options: The bell rings loud and the children laugh.
The night is dark and the owl cries.
The fish swim deep in the Volta.
My uncle sells tyres in Kumasi.
hints: The poem is about a happy morning at school.
Which line matches the place and the mood?
questions.explanation: The line about the bell and laughing children fits a happy morning at school. The other lines belong to a different time or place.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that is pleasant but does not match the set topic.

questions.stem: Write one short line for a poem about the rainy season. Your line must be easy to read aloud and must mention rain or rain clouds.
hints: Keep it short, like a song line.
Mention the rain or clouds in your line.
questions.explanation: A good line is short, mentions rain or clouds and can be read with rhythm.

criteria.description: Line is short and reads well aloud

questions.stem: Write two lines for a poem about your mother. Use words that show how you feel about her.
hints: Think of one thing she does for you.
Show feeling with words like warm, strong or kind.
questions.explanation: Good lines mention something the mother does and show the pupil's feeling about her in a short, readable form.

questions.stem: Your poem is about unity in the classroom. Which line fits best?
options: Each child works alone in the corner.
Together we sweep, together we learn, together we stand.
The rain beats hard on the tin roof.
I ate kenkey with my sister.
hints: The poem is about unity.
Look for the line that uses 'together' or 'we'.
questions.explanation: The line about sweeping, learning and standing together clearly carries the theme of unity. The other lines are about different things.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that is short but does not carry the theme.

questions.stem: A pupil writes this poem: Line 1: The sun is up, Line 2: The birds are singing, Line 3: The children run, Line 4: The bell is ringing, Line 5: The classroom door, Line 6: Is open wide, Line 7: We enter now, Line 8: With joy inside. How many lines does this poem have?
hints: Count every line the pupil wrote.
The last line is 'With joy inside.'
questions.explanation: Counting each line from 'The sun is up' to 'With joy inside' gives eight lines. So the poem has eight lines.
questions.misconception: Counting only the stanzas or counting words instead of lines.

questions.stem: A pupil has written five lines of an eight-line poem. How many more lines must the pupil write?
hints: The target is eight lines.
Take away the five lines already written.
questions.explanation: An eight-line poem needs eight lines. The pupil already has five, so 8 minus 5 = 3 more lines are needed.
questions.misconception: Answering '5' because that is the number already written.

questions.stem: A class is building an eight-line poem together. Four pupils have contributed one line each. How many more lines does the class still need?
hints: The poem must have eight lines in all.
The class already has four lines.
questions.explanation: Eight lines in all minus four lines already written gives four more lines needed.
questions.misconception: Giving the number already written instead of the number still needed.

questions.stem: A pupil writes nine lines for an eight-line poem. What should the pupil do?
hints: The task asks for exactly eight lines.
What happens if you have one line too many?
questions.explanation: The task is an eight-line poem. If the pupil has nine lines, one line must be removed so that the poem has exactly eight.
questions.misconception: Thinking extra lines do not matter so long as the poem is long enough.

questions.stem: Complete this eight-line poem by writing the missing lines. Lines 1–4 are: 'In our school yard, / The children play, / Running and jumping, / All through the day.' Write lines 5–8 to make the poem exactly eight lines.
hints: Keep the same topic (play in the school yard).
You need exactly four more lines.
questions.explanation: A good answer adds four lines on the same topic, producing exactly eight lines in all.

criteria.description: Lines stay on the topic of play in the school yard
Lines read like poetry, not prose

questions.stem: Four lines of a poem are jumbled: A. The rain falls soft on the dusty ground. B. The clouds turn grey and gather round. C. The children cheer and dance about. D. The dry earth drinks it in without a sound. Which order makes the best sense?
hints: The clouds come before the rain.
The dry earth drinks the rain after it falls.
questions.explanation: The clouds gather first, then the rain falls, then the earth drinks the rain and the children cheer. So B, A, D, C makes the best sense.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the natural sequence of events in the poem.

questions.stem: Arrange these three lines to make the best beginning of a poem about a market: A. Voices call out from every stall. B. The market wakes up early in the day. C. Traders spread their goods along the way. Write the letters in the correct order.
hints: The market wakes up first.
The voices call out after the goods are set.
questions.explanation: The market wakes up, traders spread their goods and then voices call out. So the order is B, C, A.
questions.misconception: Ordering lines by rhyme alone rather than by meaning.

questions.stem: Arrange these four lines into a good poem opening: A. In the beginning of the year we plant. B. With patient hands we water well. C. By harvest time the maize is tall. D. And all the village eats their fill. Which order fits best?
hints: Think of the farming year in order.
Planting, watering, growing, eating.
questions.explanation: The farming year goes: plant, water, the maize grows tall, then the village eats. So A, B, C, D is the natural order.
questions.misconception: Arranging the lines by length instead of by the order of events.

questions.stem: Your group wrote these lines for a poem about kindness: A. A kind word costs nothing at all. B. It warms the heart of a stranger too. C. A helper stands when another falls. D. Kindness will always come back to you. Write them in the best order, then say in one sentence why you chose that order.
hints: Start with the smallest act of kindness.
End with the reward or result.
questions.explanation: A strong order moves from the small act of kindness (A), through its effects on others (B, C), to its reward (D), with a clear reason given.

criteria.description: Arranges the four lines in a sensible order
Order moves from act to effect to result
Gives a clear reason for the order

questions.stem: A pupil is arranging an eight-line poem. The first line is 'The sun peeps over the eastern hill.' Which line should come last?
options: The cockerel sings his morning call.
The village wakes and starts to stir.
The night returns and rest is near.
The children run to fetch their water.
hints: The poem begins with morning.
What time of day usually ends a day poem?
questions.explanation: A poem that begins with the sun rising ends naturally with night returning, so the last line should be 'The night returns and rest is near.'
questions.misconception: Choosing a line that belongs to the middle of the day rather than the end.

questions.stem: Which pair of lines has a good, simple rhyme?
options: The moon is bright tonight / And I can see the light.
The moon is bright tonight / And I can eat kenkey.
The moon is bright tonight / And the goat is walking.
The moon is bright tonight / And there is a market.
hints: Listen to the ending sounds.
Which two ending words sound alike?
questions.explanation: The words 'tonight' and 'light' end with the same sound, so they rhyme. The other pairs do not rhyme.
questions.misconception: Choosing a pair that reads well but does not rhyme.

questions.stem: Which line has a steady rhythm for a poem about marching?
options: Left, right, left, right, we march along.
We march and sometimes we sing and walk.
Some days we walk and other days we do not walk.
Marching is something we do when it is not raining.
hints: Read each option aloud.
Which line sounds like a steady beat?
questions.explanation: The line 'Left, right, left, right, we march along' has a clear, steady beat that suits marching. The other lines are uneven or too long.
questions.misconception: Choosing a long line that describes marching without a steady beat.

questions.stem: Poem line: 'The wind whispers through the tall green trees.' Which word in this line sounds like the wind itself?
hints: Look for a word that sounds like soft blowing.
The word starts with 'wh'.
questions.explanation: The word 'whispers' sounds soft and breathy, like the wind. Poets choose such words to make the sound match the meaning.
questions.misconception: Choosing any word from the line instead of the word whose sound matches the wind.

questions.stem: Which of these four-line stanzas has the best rhythm and rhyme for an eight-line poem about the rainy season?
options: The rain comes down, the rain comes fast, / It beats upon the roof at last. / The children cheer, the children sing, / The rainy season now is king.
Rain is here / We like it / It is wet / We are happy.
The rain comes falling down upon the roof and all the children / cheer and sing because the rainy season now is king.
The rain comes down fast / The roof is beaten / The children sing / Rain is king.
hints: Look for lines of even length.
Listen for rhymes at the ends of lines.
questions.explanation: The first stanza has lines of even length, clear rhymes (fast/last, sing/king) and a steady beat. The others are too short, too long or without rhyme.
questions.misconception: Choosing a stanza that names the topic but lacks rhythm and rhyme.

questions.stem: Write the last two lines of an eight-line poem about a busy market. Make the lines rhyme and give them a steady rhythm.
hints: Choose a pair of words that rhyme (e.g. day/way, sound/ground).
Keep both lines about the same length.
questions.explanation: Good lines rhyme at the end, are similar in length and stay on the market topic.

criteria.description: Lines are about the busy market

questions.stem: Recite the eight-line poem your group composed about the school garden. Speak clearly and use some actions.
hints: Pause at the end of each line.
Use a hand action for the green maize.
questions.explanation: The pupil recites all eight lines clearly, with pauses and some actions.

criteria.description: Uses actions that match the words

questions.stem: Perform your eight-line poem about unity. Clap softly to keep the rhythm as you recite.
hints: Practise the rhythm by clapping first.
Keep the clap soft so the words can be heard.
questions.explanation: The pupil recites with a steady clap and clear words, and shows the value of unity through the poem.

criteria.description: The value of unity can be heard

questions.stem: In groups, perform your eight-line poem about hard work for another class. Use clear voice, actions and steady rhythm.
hints: Practise the poem together before the performance.
Make sure everyone starts and stops at the same time.
questions.explanation: The group performs the eight-line poem together with clear voice, actions and steady rhythm.

questions.stem: After listening to another group perform their eight-line poem, say two things they did well and one thing they can improve.
hints: Be specific: was it the rhythm, the actions or the voice?
Use polite words for the improvement.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives two specific positives and one helpful suggestion, using polite language.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Make connections between texts or stories and personal experiences.

skills.description: Retell a story heard or read sequentially using a story map or herringbone
Identify key story elements: characters, setting and events
Connect events or characters in a story to a similar personal experience
Explain how the personal experience is similar to or different from the story

spec.difficultyPlan: 55% easy (retell and identify elements), 30% medium (make a relevant personal connection), 15% harder (explain the similarity or difference clearly). Stories used are short original narratives printed in the question stems, with Ghanaian settings (school, market, village, home).
misconceptions: Retelling events out of order or leaving out the ending
Confusing the setting with the characters
Giving a personal story with no link to the text
Copying the story's words instead of linking it to own life

questions.stem: Read the story. 'Ama went to the market to buy tomatoes. On the way, she met her friend Esi. They walked together and talked about school. At the market, Ama bought her tomatoes and went home happy.' Which event happened first?
options: Ama bought tomatoes at the market.
Ama met her friend Esi on the way.
Ama and Esi talked about school.
hints: Follow the order of the sentences in the story.
The first thing that happened comes before the market.
questions.explanation: The story begins with Ama going to the market. On the way she met Esi. So meeting Esi is the first event listed among the options.
questions.misconception: Choosing an event that comes later in the story because it is more interesting.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi woke up late. He ran to school without eating. He missed the morning assembly. His teacher told him to sleep early.' What did Kofi do at the end of the story?
answer: his teacher told him to sleep early
the teacher told him to sleep early
teacher told him to sleep early
he was told to sleep early
he was asked to sleep early
hints: Read the last sentence of the story.
The ending tells what the teacher said.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says his teacher told him to sleep early. So the story ends with Kofi being told by his teacher to sleep early.
questions.misconception: Giving the beginning of the story instead of the ending.

questions.stem: Read the story. 'Adwoa found a small chick near the well. It was crying. She took it home and fed it. Soon the chick grew strong and followed her everywhere.' Retell the story in three sentences, using the correct order.
hints: What did Adwoa find first?
What did she do next? What was the result?
questions.explanation: A good retelling says that Adwoa found a crying chick, took it home and fed it, and the chick grew strong and followed her.

criteria.description: Mentions taking it home and feeding it
Events are in the correct order

questions.stem: Your teacher told the class the story of 'The Hawk and the Hen'. Retell the story in your own words, using a story map: beginning, middle and ending.
hints: Start with how the story began.
Say what happened in the middle and how it ended.
questions.explanation: The pupil should retell the story in the correct order, covering beginning, middle and ending in clear spoken sentences.

criteria.description: Events are in the correct order

questions.stem: Story: 'Kwame planted maize in April. He watered it every morning. In August the maize was tall and ready. Kwame and his family harvested it together.' Which part of the story is the middle?
options: Kwame and his family harvested the maize.
Kwame watered the maize every morning.
hints: The middle comes after the planting and before the harvest.
What did Kwame do between planting and harvesting?
questions.explanation: The story begins with planting in April, and ends with the harvest in August. The middle is the watering that Kwame did every morning between planting and harvest.
questions.misconception: Choosing the first or last event instead of the middle one.

questions.stem: Story: 'Akosua lived with her grandmother in a small village near Techiman. Every morning she carried water from the stream.' Who is the main character in this story?
hints: Who is the story mainly about?
The main character is the person who does the actions.
questions.explanation: The story follows Akosua and what she does every morning, so Akosua is the main character.
questions.misconception: Choosing a person or place that is mentioned but is not the main actor.

questions.stem: Story: 'Musah and his friends played football in the school park. They kicked the ball so hard that it flew over the wall.' What is the setting of this story?
hints: Setting is where the story takes place.
Where did Musah and his friends play?
questions.explanation: The story says Musah and his friends played football in the school park. The setting is the school park.
questions.misconception: Choosing an object mentioned in the story (like the wall) instead of the place where events happen.

questions.stem: Story: 'Maame Adjoa sells kenkey at the market. Her daughter Yaa helps her every Saturday. One day a heavy rain scattered the stalls, and Maame Adjoa and Yaa worked together to save the food.' Name the two main characters in this story.
hints: Who sells kenkey?
Who helps her every Saturday?
questions.explanation: The story names Maame Adjoa (who sells kenkey) and her daughter Yaa (who helps her). Those are the two main characters.
questions.misconception: Listing one character only, or naming a minor element like the rain.

questions.stem: Story: 'It was a hot afternoon in Tamale. Abena was walking home from school when she saw a small boy crying by the roadside. She stopped and helped him find his mother.' Which event is the most important one in the story?
options: Abena was walking home from school.
It was a hot afternoon in Tamale.
Abena stopped and helped the boy find his mother.
Abena was a girl who lived in Tamale.
hints: Which event makes the story worth telling?
What did Abena do that mattered most?
questions.explanation: The main event is the action Abena took: she stopped and helped the crying boy find his mother. The other options give background or setting.
questions.misconception: Choosing background information instead of the key action of the story.

questions.stem: Story: 'In the village of Berekuso, a young girl named Adjoa found a lost goat. She took it home, fed it and searched for the owner. After three days, an old farmer came to claim the goat and thanked her.' Identify the characters, the setting and the main events of this story.
hints: Look for names of people and the place name.
Write the main actions in the order they happened.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names Adjoa and the old farmer as characters, Berekuso as the setting, and lists the main events in order (finding the goat, taking it home, searching for the owner, and the farmer claiming it).

criteria.description: Names the characters (Adjoa and the old farmer)
Names the setting (Berekuso or the village)
Lists the main events in correct order

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi lost her pencil at school. She looked everywhere and was very sad. Her friend Abena gave her an extra pencil.' Which of your own experiences best connects with this story?
options: I once lost my pen and my brother gave me one of his.
I ate fufu with my family on Sunday.
I sang a song at assembly last week.
I bought a new school bag from the market.
hints: The story is about losing something and getting help.
Which experience is most like that?
questions.explanation: The story is about losing something and being helped by someone. Losing a pen and being given one by a brother is the closest personal experience.
questions.misconception: Choosing any personal experience instead of one that clearly matches the story's situation.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo was afraid of the dark. His father told him to be brave and gave him a small lamp. From that night, Kojo was no longer afraid.' Write two sentences about a time you were afraid of something and someone helped you.
hints: What were you afraid of?
Who helped you, and how?
questions.explanation: A good answer describes a real or realistic fear and how someone helped the pupil overcome it, in two complete sentences.

criteria.description: Describes something the pupil was afraid of

questions.stem: The class read the story of Adjoa, who found a lost goat. Tell the class about a time you found something that did not belong to you. What did you do?
hints: What did you find? Where?
What did you do with it?
questions.explanation: The pupil should describe a real experience of finding something and what they did, connecting it to the story of Adwoa.

criteria.description: Describes what was found and where
Explains what the pupil did with it
Connects the experience to the story

questions.stem: Story: 'Yaw's mother was sick. Every day after school he fetched water and cooked for the family. On Sunday, Yaw's mother thanked him in front of the whole family.' Which personal experience best connects with this story?
options: I went to the beach with my cousins.
I helped my aunt look after my baby cousin when she was sick.
I played football with my friends after school.
I bought a new pair of shoes at the market.
hints: The story is about helping a sick family member.
Which option involves caring for someone?
questions.explanation: The story is about a child helping a sick parent. Helping an aunt look after a sick baby cousin is the most similar experience.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated but pleasant personal experience.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama studied hard for her exams even though she had to help in her mother's shop every evening. When the results came, Ama had passed with distinction.' Write one way this story is like your own life or the life of someone you know.
answer: i help my mother and study
someone i know works hard and succeeds
i know someone who works and studies
my sister studies and helps at home
hints: Think of someone who had to work hard and study.
Say one clear way the two are alike.
questions.explanation: A good answer names one clear similarity, such as the pupil also helping at home and studying hard, or knowing someone who did.
questions.misconception: Giving a vague statement such as 'I am a good person' instead of naming the similarity.

questions.stem: Story: 'Musah saved his pocket money for weeks to buy a new football. He shared the ball with his friends every afternoon.' You once saved money to buy something. In three sentences, explain how your experience is similar to Musah's and how it is different.
hints: Say one way your experience is like Musah's.
Say one way it is different.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states a similarity (for example, both saved for weeks) and a difference (for example, the pupil kept the item rather than sharing it), in three clear sentences.

criteria.description: States one similarity to the story
States one difference from the story

questions.stem: After reading the story of Kofi, who woke up late and missed assembly, tell the class about a time you were late for something. Explain how your experience was different from Kofi's.
hints: What were you late for?
Say one way your experience was different.
questions.explanation: The pupil describes a real lateness experience and explains how it differed from Kofi's story, for example, they were late for a church service rather than school.

criteria.description: Describes a personal experience of lateness
States one difference from the story

questions.stem: Story: 'Abena was the only pupil who helped clean the classroom every Friday. The teacher gave her a prize at the end of the term.' A pupil says: 'Once I helped clean the school compound every Saturday and my teacher praised me.' How is the pupil's experience similar to the story?
options: Both the pupil and Abena helped clean and were praised.
Both the pupil and Abena won a prize at the end of the term.
Both the pupil and Abena were the only pupils who helped every day.
Both the pupil and Abena cleaned the compound for money.
hints: Look at what each of them did and what happened afterwards.
The praise is the shared outcome, not necessarily a prize.
questions.explanation: Both Abena and the pupil helped to clean and were praised by a teacher. That is the shared feature. The pupil did not win a prize, and neither cleaned for money.
questions.misconception: Choosing a similarity that is only partly true or that is not supported by the story.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi's family moved to a new town. She was lonely at first and cried for her old friends. After a few weeks, she joined the school choir and made many new friends.' Write three sentences explaining how Esi's experience is like a change you have gone through or a change someone you know has gone through.
hints: Think of a time of change: a new school, a new home or a new class.
Explain clearly how the changes are alike.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names a real change, explains how the person felt at first, and explains how they adjusted, linking each part to Esi's story.

criteria.description: Describes a real or realistic change
Explains how the change is like Esi's experience
Mentions the feelings at first and how things improved

questions.stem: The class read the story of Adjoa who found a lost goat. Tell the class about a time you found something or someone. Explain two ways your experience was like the story and one way it was different.
hints: Say clearly what you found.
Give two similarities and one difference.
questions.explanation: The pupil describes a real experience of finding something, names two similarities and one difference from the story, and speaks clearly.

criteria.description: Gives two similarities with the story
Gives one difference from the story
Speaks clearly and maintains eye contact

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Tell stories around given themes

skills.description: Identify the theme of a story heard or read
Match a given theme to an appropriate story idea or event
Tell a short story that clearly develops the given theme
Use appropriate vocabulary and expressions that depict the chosen theme
Tell the story with a clear beginning, middle and ending

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify the theme and match a theme to a story idea), 35% medium (tell a themed story with structure), 20% harder (use purposeful vocabulary to develop the theme). Themes are limited to those named in the curriculum: love, honesty, patriotism, hard work, truthfulness, unity, kindness, generosity, respect, perseverance.
misconceptions: Choosing a theme but telling an unrelated story
Stating the theme directly at the start and then not developing it
Ending the story abruptly without resolution
Using vocabulary that does not reflect the theme

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama saw a purse full of money on the road. She took it to the police station. The owner was very grateful and thanked her.' What is the theme of this story?
hints: What did Ama do with the purse?
Keeping what is not yours would be dishonest.
questions.explanation: Ama did the right thing by handing the purse to the police. The theme of the story is honesty.
questions.misconception: Choosing generosity because she gave something back, when the main theme is honesty.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo worked on his farm from morning till evening every day. At harvest time his barn was full, and his family ate well all year.' What is the theme?
hints: What did Kojo do every day?
What was the result of his effort?
questions.explanation: Kojo worked on his farm from morning till evening, and his hard work produced a full barn. The theme is hard work.
questions.misconception: Choosing patience because harvest requires waiting, when the story's focus is on effort.

questions.stem: Story: 'The pupils of Adenta Basic School cleaned their school compound every Friday. They planted trees, swept the yard and painted the walls. Their school became the neatest in the district.' Name the theme of this story.
hints: The pupils worked together on a shared task.
What one word describes their effort?
questions.explanation: The pupils worked together on a shared task and achieved a great result. The theme could be hard work, teamwork, unity or responsibility.
questions.misconception: Naming a theme that does not appear in the story, such as patriotism.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi and her little brother were walking home when it began to rain. Esi took off her own sandals and gave them to her brother. She walked home barefoot so he would not slip.' What is the theme?
hints: What did Esi give up for her brother?
Her action shows love in a strong way.
questions.explanation: Esi gave up her own comfort to help her little brother. The theme is love and self-sacrifice.
questions.misconception: Choosing honesty or patience because those words are positive, even though they do not describe the story.

questions.stem: You want to tell a story with the theme of unity. Which story idea fits best?
options: A boy who works alone all day and wins a prize.
A girl who lies to her teacher to avoid punishment.
A village that builds a new well together and shares the water.
A farmer who waits patiently for his crops to grow.
hints: Unity means working together.
Look for an idea that involves many people cooperating.
questions.explanation: A village building a well together and sharing it clearly shows unity. The other ideas fit other themes.
questions.misconception: Choosing an idea that involves hard work or honesty rather than working together.

questions.stem: You want to tell a story with the theme of perseverance. Which story idea fits best?
options: A girl who fails her exam once and studies every day until she passes.
A boy who finds a purse and returns it to its owner.
A family that shares their food with a hungry neighbour.
Two brothers who go to the farm together every morning.
hints: Perseverance means not giving up.
Which idea involves continuing after a failure?
questions.explanation: A girl who fails once and keeps studying until she passes shows perseverance. The other ideas fit honesty, generosity or unity.
questions.misconception: Confusing perseverance with hard work, even though the key is not giving up after a setback.
