questions.stem: Write two sentences describing a short story you could tell with the theme of kindness. Your idea must clearly show someone being kind to another person.
hints: Think of a simple act of help.
Make sure the act of kindness is clear.
questions.explanation: A good answer describes a simple act of kindness (such as giving food to a hungry person or helping an elderly person carry a load) that matches the theme.

criteria.description: Describes an act of kindness clearly
Idea fits the theme of kindness

questions.stem: Story: 'A young girl noticed that her neighbour had no food. Every evening she quietly left a small bowl of rice at his door. She never told anyone.' Which theme matches this story?
hints: What did the girl do, and did she want anyone to know?
The key is giving without seeking attention.
questions.explanation: The girl gave food quietly and never told anyone. This shows generosity without seeking praise.
questions.misconception: Choosing unity because she helped a neighbour, when the story's focus is on giving quietly.

questions.stem: Tell the class a short story (about one minute) that clearly shows the theme of honesty. Your story can be from your own experience or imagined.
hints: Think of a time someone told the truth.
Start with the situation, then say what happened.
questions.explanation: The pupil tells a short story in which honesty is clearly shown through the events and characters.

criteria.description: Story clearly develops the theme of honesty
Story has a beginning, middle and ending
The theme is shown through actions, not just named

questions.stem: Tell the class a short story (about one minute) with the theme of hard work. Use a character from your imagination.
hints: Give your character a name and a job.
Show the character working hard and enjoying the result.
questions.explanation: The pupil tells a short story with a named character who works hard and experiences a positive result.

criteria.description: Story clearly develops the theme of hard work
The story has a beginning, middle and ending

questions.stem: Write a short story (about six sentences) with the theme of unity. Your story must involve at least three people working together.
hints: What problem were the people facing?
How did they solve it together?
questions.explanation: A good story describes a problem, shows at least three people working together to solve it, and ends with a positive result.

criteria.description: Story involves at least three people
Story clearly develops the theme of unity
Story has a clear problem and resolution

questions.stem: In groups of four, prepare and perform a short play (about three minutes) with the theme of kindness. Each group member must have at least one line to say.
hints: Plan the story and who says what first.
Make sure the act of kindness is clear in the play.
questions.explanation: The group performs a short play that clearly shows kindness and gives every member a speaking role.

criteria.description: Theme of kindness is clear in the play
Every member has a speaking part
The play has a clear beginning, middle and ending

questions.stem: You are telling a story about hard work. Which word best fits your story?
hints: Which word means 'hardworking'?
The other words describe opposite qualities.
questions.explanation: Diligent means hardworking and careful, which is exactly what a story about hard work needs. The other words describe opposite qualities.
questions.misconception: Choosing an impressive-sounding word that does not match the theme of hard work.

questions.stem: You are telling a story about honesty. Write two words you would use to describe a person who is honest.
hints: Think of words that describe someone who tells the truth.
Words like 'truthful', 'trustworthy' and 'sincere' work well.
questions.explanation: Honest characters can be described with words like truthful, trustworthy, sincere, upright or honest.
questions.misconception: Giving unrelated words such as 'strong' or 'fast' that do not describe honesty.

questions.stem: You are writing a story about kindness. Write three sentences using words that clearly describe kind actions or a kind person.
hints: Use words like generous, caring, compassionate, thoughtful or gentle.
Make sure each sentence shows kindness.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses at least three vocabulary words that clearly describe kindness or kind actions, in three complete sentences.

criteria.description: Uses at least three vocabulary words that show kindness
Words fit the meaning in each sentence

questions.stem: You are telling a story with the theme of perseverance. Which sentence uses the best vocabulary to show the theme?
options: She tried once and gave up quickly.
She kept going, never giving up, until she finally succeeded.
She was unsure and decided to wait.
She thought about giving up but did nothing.
hints: Perseverance means continuing despite difficulty.
Which sentence shows someone refusing to give up?
questions.explanation: The words 'kept going', 'never giving up' and 'finally succeeded' show perseverance clearly. The other sentences show giving up, waiting or doing nothing.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence that mentions difficulty but does not show continuing through it.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama's mother sent her to the market. On the way she met a woman carrying a heavy load. Ama helped the woman carry it to her house. The woman thanked Ama, and Ama continued her journey.' What is the beginning of this story?
options: Ama helped the woman carry the load.
Ama's mother sent her to the market.
hints: The beginning introduces the situation.
Which sentence sets the story in motion?
questions.explanation: The beginning of a story introduces the situation. Here, it is Ama's mother sending her to the market, which starts the story.
questions.misconception: Choosing a middle or ending event as the beginning.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi's family had no water. Kofi decided to dig a well in the compound. After many days of digging, water came out. The whole family celebrated.' What is the ending of this story?
answer: water came out and the family celebrated
hints: The ending tells how the story is resolved.
What happened after the water came out?
questions.explanation: The ending tells how the story is resolved. Here, the family celebrated after water came out.
questions.misconception: Giving the middle event instead of the ending.

questions.stem: Write a short story (about six sentences) with the theme of honesty. Make sure it has a clear beginning, middle and ending.
hints: Begin with a situation that sets up a choice.
In the middle, show what the character decided.
End by showing the result of the choice.
questions.explanation: A strong story has a clear situation at the start, a decision in the middle and a result at the end, all tied to honesty.

criteria.description: Middle shows the key choice or action
Ending shows the result or resolution

questions.stem: Tell the class a story with the theme of love. Make sure you have a clear beginning (the situation), middle (what happens) and ending (how it works out).
hints: Who is in your story, and what is the situation?
How does the story end?
questions.explanation: The pupil tells a well-structured story that clearly shows love through the events and characters.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.5.1: Appreciate pieces of literary materials through dramatisation
indicator.objective: Dramatise/role-play whole/parts of stories/scenes, events

skills.description: Identify the plot of a chosen story: events at the beginning, middle and ending
Identify characters and assign roles for a dramatisation
Role-play a part or the whole of a story, scene or event showing the chosen theme
Use appropriate vocabulary and correct pronunciation while role-playing
Perform before an audience and respond to feedback

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify plot and characters), 35% medium (role-play a scene with appropriate words), 20% harder (sustain a whole scene/event and engage the audience). Scenes are drawn from familiar stories, folk tales and school/community events.
misconceptions: Retelling the story instead of acting it out
Forgetting the theme when performing
Speaking too softly or mumbling so the audience cannot hear
Adding content that changes the story's meaning

questions.stem: The story of 'Ananse and the Black Pot' has these three parts: Ananse finds the pot; Ananse uses the pot to trick the villagers; Ananse's trick is discovered and the pot is returned. Which part is the beginning?
options: Ananse uses the pot to trick the villagers.
hints: The beginning is where the story starts.
What happens before the trick?
questions.explanation: The story begins when Ananse finds the black pot. Only after that does he use it to trick the villagers, and finally the trick is discovered.
questions.misconception: Choosing a later event because it is more exciting.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama went to fetch water. At the stream, she slipped and her pot broke. She sat down and cried. A kind woman helped her mend the pot and they walked home together.' Which event is the middle of the story?
options: Ama slipped and her pot broke.
A kind woman helped her mend the pot.
hints: The middle is the problem the story builds around.
What makes Ama cry?
questions.explanation: The problem at the centre of the story is Ama slipping and her pot breaking. That is the middle event.
questions.misconception: Choosing the ending event instead of the problem in the middle.

questions.stem: Story: 'Two friends found a gold ring on their way to school. The first friend wanted to keep it. The second friend said they must find the owner. They took it to the chief, and the owner was found and rewarded them both.' What is the ending of this story?
answer: the owner was found and rewarded them
the owner was found and rewarded them both
hints: What happens after they take the ring to the chief?
The ending resolves the story.
questions.explanation: The ending resolves the story: the owner is found, and both friends are rewarded for their honesty.
questions.misconception: Giving the middle event (the argument) instead of the ending.

questions.stem: Story: 'Adjoa was chosen to lead the school choir at the festival. On the day of the festival, she lost her voice. She was afraid and wanted to run away. Her friends encouraged her, and she led the choir with a soft but sweet voice. The school won second prize.' Write the beginning, middle and ending of this story in three short lines.
hints: The beginning tells about the chance Adjoa got.
The middle is the problem she faced.
The ending tells how it turned out.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names the beginning (chosen to lead), middle (lost her voice and was afraid) and ending (led with a soft voice, the school won second prize).

questions.stem: Four pupils are planning a role-play of 'Ama and the Broken Pot'. Which event must come in the role-play after 'Ama slips at the stream'?
options: Ama sets out for the stream.
The kind woman helps mend the pot.
Ama's mother sends her to fetch water.
hints: Follow the order of events in the story.
What happens right after the pot breaks?
questions.explanation: After Ama slips and the pot breaks, the next event is the kind woman helping her mend it.
questions.misconception: Choosing the final event instead of the event that comes immediately after.

questions.stem: Your group is role-playing 'Ananse and the Black Pot'. How many main characters would you usually need to assign?
options: At least two characters: Ananse and someone he meets or tricks
Only a narrator and no characters
hints: A role-play needs at least a person doing and a person receiving the action.
How many people are needed for a scene with a trick?
questions.explanation: A role-play of Ananse tricking someone needs at least two characters: Ananse and the person he meets or tricks.
questions.misconception: Thinking one character alone can carry a whole scene.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi found a wallet and took it to the head teacher. The owner came to the school and thanked him. The head teacher praised Kofi at assembly.' Name three characters a group would need to assign for this role-play.
answer: kofi the head teacher and the owner
kofi, the owner, the head teacher
hints: Who found the wallet?
Who received the wallet? Who praised Kofi?
questions.explanation: The three characters are Kofi (who found the wallet), the head teacher (who received it) and the owner (who came to thank him).
questions.misconception: Listing only one or two characters and leaving out the owner or the head teacher.

questions.stem: You are role-playing a scene with four characters but only three pupils are present. Which is the best solution?
options: Drop one character from the scene.
Ask one pupil to play two characters in different parts of the scene.
Ask all four characters to speak at the same time.
Perform without any characters at all.
hints: How can one person take on more than one role?
The scene can still have all its characters.
questions.explanation: The best solution is for one pupil to play two characters in different parts of the scene. That way all characters are kept and the scene works.
questions.misconception: Choosing to cut a character and change the story.

questions.stem: In your group, choose a familiar story. Decide which characters are needed and assign a role to each member. Tell the class which role each member will play and why.
hints: Choose roles that fit each person's strengths.
Say why the role suits that member.
questions.explanation: The pupil should explain the assigned roles and give a reason for each assignment.

criteria.description: Gives a reason for each assignment

questions.stem: A group is acting out the scene where Ama slips at the stream. Which action best shows the scene without words?
options: The pupil stands still and smiles.
The pupil pretends to carry a pot, suddenly stumbles and reaches out to save it.
The pupil tells the audience what happened.
The pupil walks off the stage quickly.
hints: Acting means showing with the body, not telling.
What would Ama actually do when she slips?
questions.explanation: Pretending to carry a pot and stumbling shows the scene through action, which is what role-play requires.
questions.misconception: Choosing a pupil to narrate rather than act the scene.

questions.stem: Write a short role-play dialogue (about six lines) for the scene where Ama's pot breaks and the kind woman comes to help. Include at least two characters.
hints: Label each speaker's name before their line.
Show the kindness in the woman's words and Ama's reaction.
questions.explanation: A good dialogue names speakers, shows the problem clearly and shows the kind woman helping Ama.

criteria.description: Writes about six lines of dialogue

questions.stem: In pairs, role-play the scene where one pupil finds a lost wallet and the other is the owner who comes to claim it. Act out the moment of returning the wallet.
hints: Show the wallet clearly.
Show the owner's gratitude with words and action.
questions.explanation: The pair acts out the return of the wallet clearly, showing honesty and gratitude in speech and action.

criteria.description: Clearly shows the wallet being returned
Uses words that suit the scene

questions.stem: Role-play the whole of the scene where Kofi finds the wallet, gives it to the head teacher, and is praised at assembly. You may use two other pupils as other characters.
hints: Plan the beginning, middle and ending before you act.
Make the honesty of Kofi very clear.
questions.explanation: The group acts out all three parts of the scene, showing honesty and the resolution clearly.

criteria.description: Shows beginning, middle and ending of the scene

questions.stem: In groups of four, act out the scene where a village builds a well together. Show the problem, the working together and the celebration.
hints: Show each character doing their part of the work.
End with a clear celebration.
questions.explanation: The group shows the problem, the shared work and the celebration, making the theme of unity very clear.

criteria.description: Ends with a celebration that fits the story

questions.stem: You are role-playing a kind woman helping Ama. Which voice best fits the character?
options: A soft, warm voice with gentle words.
A whisper so no one can hear.
hints: A kind character should sound kind.
Choose a voice the audience can hear clearly.
questions.explanation: A soft, warm voice with gentle words fits the kind woman. A loud angry shout, a whisper or mumbling would not match the character.
questions.misconception: Thinking the loudest voice is the best voice for a role-play.

questions.stem: In a role-play, your character is very sad because she lost her mother's pot. Write one short sentence your character could say that fits the mood.
answer: oh no what will i tell my mother
i have lost my mother's pot
i am so sad i broke the pot
what am i going to do now
hints: The character is sad and worried.
The sentence should show how she feels about the pot.
questions.explanation: A good sentence shows the character's sadness or worry about the broken pot.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that is too cheerful for a sad moment.

questions.stem: Read this line aloud as your character in the role-play: 'Please, sir, I have found your wallet and I want to return it.' Say it clearly, with the correct pronunciation of 'wallet' and 'return'.
hints: Say 'wallet' clearly so it does not sound like 'water'.
Say 'return' with the stress on the second part.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the line clearly, pronounces 'wallet' and 'return' correctly and speaks audibly.

questions.stem: In pairs, role-play a scene where one character is angry and the other is calm. Use your voices to show the difference in mood.
hints: The angry character speaks faster and louder.
The calm character speaks slowly and softly.
questions.explanation: The pair shows the mood difference through voice: the angry character louder and faster, the calm character slower and softer.

criteria.description: Angry character uses a louder, faster voice
Calm character uses a softer, slower voice

questions.stem: Perform a short scene from 'Ama and the Broken Pot' for the class. Speak loudly enough for the back row to hear.
hints: Look at the audience while you act.
Project your voice so the back row can hear.
questions.explanation: The pupil performs the scene audibly, facing the audience and staying in character.

criteria.description: Speaks loudly enough for the back row

questions.stem: After watching another group's role-play, give them one compliment and one helpful suggestion about their performance.
hints: Be specific about what was good.
Be polite when suggesting an improvement.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives one specific compliment and one polite suggestion that could improve the performance.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.5.2: Appreciate key issues in stories/sketches
indicator.objective: Express personal opinion about moral lessons in sketches

skills.description: Identify the structure of a familiar story or sketch: beginning, middle, ending
Discuss the plot of a chosen story or sketch
Identify the moral values in a sketch or story
Express a personal opinion about the moral lessons and relate them to real life

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify structure, plot and moral), 35% medium (state opinion with a reason), 15% harder (relate moral to real-life situations). Short original sketches and stories are provided in the stems, with school, market, home and community settings.
misconceptions: Stating the plot instead of the moral
Giving an opinion without a reason
Treating every character as completely good or completely bad
Relating the moral to an unrelated real-life event

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Two boys are arguing over a football. Their teacher comes and asks them what happened. They explain and agree to share the ball every day.' What is the ending of this sketch?
options: The teacher comes and asks what happened.
They agree to share the ball every day.
hints: The ending resolves the problem.
How do the boys settle the argument?
questions.explanation: The problem is the argument, and the resolution is when they agree to share the ball. That resolution is the ending.
questions.misconception: Choosing the moment of tension instead of the resolution.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A girl named Aku is sent to buy kenkey. On the way, she loses the money. She meets an old man who lends her money to buy the kenkey. She returns home and her mother is happy.' Which part of the sketch is the middle?
answer: she loses the money and an old man lends her money
she loses the money and meets an old man
hints: The middle is the problem in the sketch.
What makes the story interesting or difficult for Aku?
questions.explanation: The middle is where Aku loses the money and meets the old man who helps her, creating the problem that is resolved at the end.
questions.misconception: Choosing the beginning (buying kenkey) or the ending (mother happy) instead of the problem.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil named Yaw borrows his sister's book without permission. He uses it and spills water on it. He is afraid to return it. His sister finds out and is upset. Their mother helps them talk it over, and Yaw promises to be more careful.' Write the beginning, middle and ending of this sketch in three short lines.
hints: The beginning sets up the situation.
The middle is the problem that arises.
The ending resolves it.
questions.explanation: The beginning is Yaw borrowing the book, the middle is the water spill and the fear, and the ending is the mother helping them talk it over.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Three pupils find a bag on the school field. One wants to keep it. One wants to take it to the head teacher. The third wants to leave it where it is. In the end, they take it to the head teacher and the owner is found.' Which part shows the conflict in this sketch?
options: The three pupils disagree about what to do with the bag.
They take it to the head teacher.
hints: Conflict is the disagreement among the characters.
Which part shows them disagreeing?
questions.explanation: The conflict is the disagreement among the three pupils about what to do with the bag. That disagreement is the heart of the sketch.
questions.misconception: Choosing the resolution (taking the bag to the head teacher) instead of the conflict.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Akua is rude to a new pupil in her class. The new pupil cries. Akua's friend tells her she is wrong. Akua apologises the next day and they become friends.' What is the main event of this sketch?
options: The new pupil joins the school.
Akua is rude to the new pupil, then apologises.
hints: What is the sketch mostly about?
Which action drives the whole sketch?
questions.explanation: The main event is Akua being rude to the new pupil and then apologising, because it sets up the whole sketch and its lesson.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail instead of the main event.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Musah and Adjoa want to watch TV. Their mother wants them to finish homework first. They argue, but the mother explains why homework matters. They finish their homework and watch TV afterwards.' Why did Musah and Adjoa argue with their mother?
answer: they wanted to watch tv instead of doing homework
because they wanted to watch tv
they wanted to watch tv first
hints: What did the children want to do?
What did their mother want them to do first?
questions.explanation: The children wanted to watch TV, but their mother wanted them to finish homework first. That disagreement is why they argued.
questions.misconception: Answering with what the mother wanted instead of what the children wanted.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Kofi borrows a bicycle from his neighbour without asking. He crashes it and bends the wheel. He hides the bicycle. The neighbour finds out and is upset. Kofi's father tells him to apologise and pay for the repair. Kofi apologises and pays.' Discuss the plot in three sentences: what happened, how it got worse, and how it was resolved.
hints: What did Kofi borrow without asking?
How did it become worse?
How was it sorted out in the end?
questions.explanation: A strong answer covers Kofi borrowing the bicycle without asking, the bicycle being damaged and hidden, and Kofi apologising and paying for the repair.

criteria.description: Describes how the problem was resolved

questions.stem: After watching a sketch in class, discuss its plot with a partner. Say what happened at the beginning, middle and ending in one minute.
hints: Talk with your partner before you speak.
Keep your answer to the point.
questions.explanation: The pupil discusses the plot with a partner and reports the beginning, middle and ending clearly in about one minute.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Adjoa found a purse with money. She took it to the head teacher, who found the owner. The owner thanked her.' What moral lesson does this sketch teach?
options: Be honest and return what is not yours.
hints: What did Adjoa do with the purse?
Was that a good or bad action?
questions.explanation: Adjoa returned the purse to its owner. The moral is that we should be honest and return what is not ours.
questions.misconception: Choosing a moral that contradicts the story's events.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Three pupils are told to clean the classroom. Two of them work hard, but the third sits and watches. When the teacher comes, the hardworking pupils are praised and the lazy one is asked to do his part alone.' What moral lesson does this sketch teach?
options: Sitting and watching is the best way to work.
Everyone should do their fair share of the work.
Only praise matters, not the work.
The teacher should clean the classroom.
hints: What was fair in the sketch?
Why was the lazy pupil asked to do his part alone?
questions.explanation: The moral is that everyone should do their fair share of the work, and people who do not will be asked to do their part.
questions.misconception: Choosing a moral that rewards the lazy pupil.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Akua laughs at a new pupil because of her old shoes. The new pupil cries. The other pupils comfort her and tell Akua her words are unkind. Akua feels ashamed and apologises.' What is the moral lesson of this sketch?
hints: How did the new pupil feel?
What should Akua have done instead?
questions.explanation: Akua laughed at the new pupil and made her cry. The moral is to be kind to others and not to laugh at or mock people.
questions.misconception: Answering 'apologise' (which is an action) instead of the moral lesson.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Kojo brags about how strong he is. He challenges Yaw to carry a heavy bag. Kojo lifts it but soon drops it. Yaw lifts it patiently and carries it safely. The onlookers clap for Yaw.' What moral lesson does this sketch teach?
options: Quiet effort and patience are better than boasting.
Never try to lift heavy things.
hints: Who worked quietly and succeeded?
Who boasted and failed?
questions.explanation: Kojo boasted and failed, while Yaw worked quietly and succeeded. The moral is that quiet effort is better than boasting.
questions.misconception: Choosing a moral that praises boasting.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Esi always comes late to school. One day she is late for an exam and misses it. She is very sad. From the next week, she wakes up early every day and never comes late again.' Write the moral lesson of this sketch in your own words.
hints: What was Esi's problem?
What did she learn from it?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says that lateness has consequences, and we should learn from our mistakes and change our behaviour.

criteria.description: Names the moral (lateness has consequences or learn from mistakes)
Links the moral to the sketch's events
Uses own words, not copying the sketch

questions.stem: After watching a sketch where a pupil gives up his seat on a tro-tro to an elderly woman, tell the class your opinion about that action. Say whether you think it was right and why.
hints: Say clearly whether you think it was right.
Give one reason for your opinion.
questions.explanation: The pupil states an opinion and gives a reason, showing awareness of the moral of the sketch.

criteria.description: Gives a reason for the opinion
Relates the opinion to the sketch

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A boy sees a classmate cheating in an exam. He does not report it, but tells his classmate quietly that cheating is wrong. The classmate stops cheating.' Which opinion about this sketch is best supported by the events?
options: The boy should have reported his classmate loudly in class.
The boy acted kindly by correcting his classmate quietly.
Cheating is not a problem if no one is hurt.
The boy was wrong to speak to his classmate.
hints: The boy corrected the classmate without humiliating him.
Which opinion fits the action he actually took?
questions.explanation: The boy stopped the cheating quietly, without humiliating his classmate. That supports the opinion that he acted kindly.
questions.misconception: Choosing an opinion that contradicts the events of the sketch.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A girl shares her lunch with a boy who forgot his food. Another girl laughs at the boy.' Which girl showed a better character, and why? Write two sentences giving your opinion.
hints: Which girl was kind? Which girl was unkind?
Say clearly why you think so.
questions.explanation: A good answer states that the girl who shared her lunch showed better character and gives a reason such as kindness or generosity.

criteria.description: States which girl showed better character
Gives a reason linked to the sketch

questions.stem: After watching a sketch where a group of pupils excludes a new pupil from their game, tell the class your opinion about their behaviour and what you would do in their place.
hints: Say clearly whether you agree with their behaviour.
Say what you would do differently.
questions.explanation: The pupil states an opinion, justifies it, and explains what they would do differently in the same situation.

criteria.description: States a clear opinion about the behaviour
Gives a reason for the opinion
Says what they would do in their place

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil named Kojo finds a wallet in the school compound. He puts it in his pocket and says nothing. Later, a girl is crying because she lost her bus fare. Kojo quietly returns the wallet.' Write three sentences giving your opinion about Kojo's actions and what the sketch teaches about honesty.
hints: Did Kojo do the right thing at first?
What changed by the end of the sketch?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says that keeping the wallet at first was wrong, returning it was right, and the sketch teaches that honesty should be shown from the start.

criteria.description: Gives an opinion about Kojo's first action
Gives an opinion about Kojo's later action
Names what the sketch teaches about honesty

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.5.2: Appreciate key issues in stories/sketches
indicator.objective: Write plays out of a story and perform them

skills.description: Turn a story into a play script with characters and dialogue
Use play-script features: character names, speaker labels, stage directions
Include the identified themes and values in the written play
Perform the written play for an audience
Respond to feedback on the performance

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (convert a short story into a short play; know play format), 35% medium (use play format correctly and show the theme), 25% harder (perform and improve from feedback). Stories used are short original narratives in the stems, with school, home, market and village settings.
misconceptions: Writing a narrative paragraph rather than a play script
Forgetting speaker labels and stage directions
Leaving out the theme or moral of the original story
Adding characters or events that change the story's meaning

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama found a purse. She took it to the head teacher. The owner was found.' Which is the best first line of a play made from this story?
options: Ama: (looking down at the ground) What is this purse doing here?
Once upon a time Ama found a purse and took it to the head teacher.
Ama walked to school one morning and saw a purse.
The purse was black and shiny.
hints: In a play, a character speaks the words.
Look for a line with the character's name and a stage direction.
questions.explanation: A play line shows the speaker's name and what the character says. Option A has the character name, a stage direction and the spoken words.
questions.misconception: Choosing a narrative sentence instead of a spoken play line.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo saw a boy fall from a tree. Kojo ran to help the boy. The boy's mother thanked Kojo.' Which is the best way to turn this into a play scene?
options: Write about Kojo and the boy in a paragraph.
Write Kojo and the boy as characters, with lines and actions for each.
Describe the tree and the boy's clothes only.
hints: A play needs characters who speak and act.
Which option makes the characters speak?
questions.explanation: To turn a story into a play, write the characters as speakers and add lines and actions for each.
questions.misconception: Believing a story becomes a play simply by being rewritten as a paragraph.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi found a lost goat. She took it home and fed it. The next day she searched for the owner and found an old farmer who thanked her.' Write a short play scene of about six lines showing Esi finding the goat and the farmer coming to claim it.
hints: Name the characters at the start of each line.
Add short stage directions in brackets.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes the scene in play form with speaker names, spoken lines and stage directions, and shows Esi finding the goat and the farmer thanking her.

criteria.description: Uses play-script form with speaker names
Shows the farmer claiming the goat and thanking Esi

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi borrowed a bicycle without asking. He crashed it. He apologised and paid for the repair.' Write a short play scene of about six lines showing Kofi's apology and payment.
hints: Who else should be in the scene besides Kofi?
Show the apology and the payment in the dialogue.
questions.explanation: A strong scene has Kofi and the bicycle owner, an apology in the dialogue and a clear action of payment.

criteria.description: Shows the payment or repair arrangement

questions.stem: Story: 'Two pupils are arguing about a football. Their teacher tells them to share.' Which of these is the best way to change the argument into play form?
options: Describe the argument in a paragraph.
Write the argument as a dialogue between the two pupils, then add the teacher's line.
Write the pupils' names on a page.
hints: Arguments in plays are shown through dialogue.
Who says what in the argument?
questions.explanation: The argument is best shown through dialogue between the two pupils, with the teacher's line to resolve it.
questions.misconception: Thinking a play can be written as a description of the argument.

questions.stem: Which of these is the correct way to write a play line?
options: Ama found a purse near the well.
Ama: (looking surprised) What is this purse doing here?
The purse was a small black purse.
Once upon a time Ama found a purse.
hints: Look for the speaker's name followed by a colon.
Stage directions usually appear in brackets.
questions.explanation: A play line begins with the speaker's name, a colon and the spoken words. Stage directions appear in brackets.
questions.misconception: Choosing a narrative sentence instead of a play line.

questions.stem: Look at this play line: 'Kojo: (running in) I have found the purse!' Which words in this line are the stage direction?
hints: Stage directions are usually in brackets.
They tell the actor what to do.
questions.explanation: The words in brackets — 'running in' — are the stage direction. They tell the actor what action to perform.
questions.misconception: Confusing the spoken words with the stage direction.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good stage direction for a scene where Ama has just found a purse?
options: Ama found a purse and it was black.
(bending down and picking up the purse, looking surprised)
The purse was on the ground.
hints: A stage direction tells the actor what to do.
Look for the option in brackets that shows an action.
questions.explanation: The stage direction in brackets tells Ama exactly what to do: bend down, pick up the purse and look surprised.
questions.misconception: Choosing a narrative sentence instead of an acting instruction.

questions.stem: Write a short play scene of about six lines showing Ama finding a purse and taking it to the head teacher. Include characters, speaker names and at least two stage directions.
hints: Use a colon after each speaker's name.
Put stage directions in brackets.
questions.explanation: A strong scene includes Ama and the head teacher as characters, speaker names with colons, spoken lines and at least two stage directions in brackets.

criteria.description: Names the characters at the top
Includes at least two stage directions in brackets
Shows Ama finding the purse and taking it to the head teacher

questions.stem: Turn this sentence into a play line with a speaker label and a stage direction: 'Kofi is afraid to tell his father the truth.' Write it as a proper play line.
hints: Start with the speaker's name and a colon.
Show Kofi's fear through the stage direction in brackets.
questions.explanation: A good answer starts with 'Kofi:' and uses a stage direction in brackets to show his fear, followed by words Kofi might say.

criteria.description: Includes a stage direction in brackets
The spoken words show Kofi's fear or hesitation

questions.stem: You are writing a play about a girl who returns a lost wallet. Which theme is the play developing?
hints: What value does returning a lost wallet show?
Keeping the wallet would be dishonest.
questions.explanation: Returning a lost wallet shows honesty, so the play develops the theme of honesty.
questions.misconception: Choosing a positive theme such as patience, even though the action shows honesty.

questions.stem: You are writing a play about a pupil who helps an old woman carry her basket. What theme does your play show?
hints: The action is helping someone who needs it.
Which value is about caring for others?
questions.explanation: Helping an old woman carry her basket shows kindness, generosity or respect. Any of these is a fitting theme.
questions.misconception: Answering with the action (carrying the basket) instead of the theme.

questions.stem: Story: 'A group of pupils clean the school compound every Friday. They plant trees and sweep the yard. The school becomes the neatest in the district.' Which two themes best fit a play made from this story?
hints: The pupils work together on a shared task.
They also put in a lot of effort.
questions.explanation: Working together shows unity, and their effort shows hard work. So the best pair of themes is unity and hard work.
questions.misconception: Choosing themes that are positive but not shown in the story.

questions.stem: Write a short play scene of about six lines that shows the theme of honesty. The scene should involve a pupil finding something that does not belong to them.
hints: Show the pupil deciding what to do.
Make honesty visible in the pupil's words and actions.
questions.explanation: A strong scene shows the pupil finding the item, deciding to do the right thing and acting honestly, with the theme clearly visible in the dialogue.

criteria.description: Honesty is clearly shown in words and actions

questions.stem: A play scene shows a girl giving up her seat on a tro-tro to an elderly woman. Which value is the scene teaching?
hints: The girl is showing care for someone older.
Which two values does this action show?
questions.explanation: Giving up a seat to an elderly woman shows both kindness and respect for older people.
questions.misconception: Choosing a value that sounds positive but is not shown by the action.

questions.stem: In groups of three, perform the short play you wrote about Ama finding the purse. Speak your lines clearly and use the stage directions.
hints: Say your lines loudly enough for the audience.
Follow the stage directions in brackets.
questions.explanation: The group performs the play clearly, using the speaker lines and following the stage directions.

questions.stem: Perform your scene where Kofi apologises for the broken bicycle. Use a serious voice and a sad expression for Kofi.
hints: Slow your voice down when you apologise.
Keep a serious face.
questions.explanation: The pupil performs the apology scene with a serious voice and expression that match the character's feelings.

criteria.description: Uses an expression that fits the apology

questions.stem: In groups, perform your play about a pupil finding a lost goat. Use simple props (a bag or a cloth for the goat) and speak clearly to the audience.
hints: Agree on who will bring the props before the performance.
Face the audience when you speak.
questions.explanation: The group performs the full play with simple props, clear voice and correct play-script structure.

questions.stem: After your group has performed, listen to a classmate's feedback. Reply politely and say what you will do better next time.
hints: Thank your classmate for the feedback.
Say one specific thing you will improve.
questions.explanation: The pupil listens politely, thanks the classmate and states one specific improvement for the next performance.

questions.stem: After your group's play, your teacher says: 'Your words were clear, but your stage directions were not followed.' Write two sentences saying what your group will do to improve.
hints: What did the teacher say went well?
What will your group do to follow stage directions better?
questions.explanation: A good answer keeps the clear speech and adds a specific plan for following stage directions better.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.5.2: Appreciate key issues in stories/sketches
indicator.objective: Justify the central messages in sketches performed

skills.description: Identify the central message(s) of a sketch performed
Point to actions, words or scenes in the sketch that support the message
Justify the central message with reasons drawn from the sketch
State the lessons in the sketch and relate them to life

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify message and lessons), 30% medium (give evidence from the sketch), 20% harder (justify message with reasons). Short original sketches are described in the stems, with school, home, market and community settings.
misconceptions: Giving a message not supported by the sketch
Retelling the sketch instead of justifying the message
Confusing the message with a character's name or the setting
Giving reasons unrelated to the actions in the sketch

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil finds a purse with money. Another pupil tells him to keep it. He refuses and takes it to the head teacher. The owner is found and thanks him.' What is the central message of this sketch?
options: Pupils should not tell each other what to do.
Money should never be picked up.
Head teachers should keep all lost items.
hints: What did the pupil do with the purse?
What value does refusing to keep it show?
questions.explanation: The pupil refused to keep the purse and took it to the head teacher. The central message is that honesty is the best policy.
questions.misconception: Choosing a message that fits a single event but not the whole sketch.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Three pupils are given a task. Two work hard, one sits doing nothing. At the end, the two finish the task and the third has nothing to show.' What is the central message?
options: Everyone should do their fair share of work.
The task should be given to one pupil only.
Only the fastest pupils should work.
hints: What happened to the pupil who did nothing?
What is the fair way to work in a group?
questions.explanation: The pupil who did nothing had nothing to show. The message is that everyone should do their fair share of the work.
questions.misconception: Choosing a message that rewards laziness or contradicts the sketch.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A new pupil joins a class. Some pupils laugh at her old sandals. Others welcome her and share their books with her. By the end of the week, the new pupil is happy and has many friends.' What is the central message?
hints: Which pupils helped the new girl?
What did their kindness achieve?
questions.explanation: The pupils who welcomed the new girl and shared with her helped her feel happy. The message is to be kind to others and not to laugh at them.
questions.misconception: Answering with a description of the events instead of the message.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A boy boasts that he can carry the heaviest load. He tries, but drops it. A quiet girl lifts the load patiently and carries it safely. The crowd claps for her.' What is the central message?
options: Quiet effort is better than boasting.
Heavy loads should not be carried by pupils.
hints: Who succeeded: the one who boasted or the one who worked quietly?
Which message does the crowd's clapping support?
questions.explanation: The boaster failed while the quiet girl succeeded, and the crowd clapped for her. The message is that quiet effort is better than boasting.
questions.misconception: Choosing a message that rewards boasting.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil finds a purse. He takes it to the head teacher. The owner is found and thanks him.' The message of the sketch is honesty. Which part of the sketch best supports this message?
options: The pupil took the purse to the head teacher.
The head teacher was in the office.
hints: Which action shows honesty?
Finding a purse is not honesty; returning it is.
questions.explanation: Taking the purse to the head teacher is the action that shows honesty. The other options are details that do not show the message by themselves.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that sets up the story rather than the action that shows honesty.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A boy laughs at a new pupil because of her old sandals. The other pupils welcome her and share their books. The new pupil becomes happy.' The message is to be kind to others. Which pupils' actions in the sketch show kindness?
answer: the other pupils welcome her and share their books
the other pupils shared their books
they welcomed her and shared books
hints: Who was kind in the sketch?
What did they do for the new pupil?
questions.explanation: The pupils who welcomed the new pupil and shared their books with her are the ones showing kindness.
questions.misconception: Naming the boy who laughed at the new pupil instead of the kind pupils.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Two pupils are told to sweep the classroom. Only one works. The teacher comes and asks the lazy pupil to finish alone. The hardworking pupil is praised.' The message is that everyone should do their fair share. Which part of the sketch best supports this message?
options: Both pupils are told to sweep.
The teacher asks the lazy pupil to finish alone and praises the hardworking one.
The teacher comes into the room.
hints: Which event shows what happens when someone does not do their share?
The praise and the extra work together make the point.
questions.explanation: The teacher's response — asking the lazy pupil to finish alone and praising the hardworking one — directly supports the message about doing your fair share.
questions.misconception: Choosing a scene-setting detail rather than the scene that shows the message.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Kofi borrows a bicycle without asking. He crashes it and bends the wheel. The neighbour finds out and is upset. Kofi's father tells him to apologise and pay for the repair. Kofi apologises and pays.' The message is that taking responsibility for your mistakes matters. Copy two actions from the sketch that support this message and explain why.
hints: Which two actions show Kofi taking responsibility?
Explain why each action shows responsibility.
questions.explanation: A strong answer copies two actions (apologising and paying for the repair) and explains that each shows Kofi accepting responsibility for the damage.

criteria.description: Copies two relevant actions from the sketch
Explains why each action shows responsibility

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Three pupils find a wallet. One wants to keep it. One wants to leave it. One wants to take it to the head teacher. In the end, they take it to the head teacher and the owner thanks them.' The message is that honesty is the best choice. Which reason best justifies this message?
options: The wallet might have been empty.
Taking the wallet to the head teacher led to the owner being found and thanking them.
The three pupils could not agree at first.
One pupil wanted to leave the wallet where it was.
hints: Which action had a good result in the end?
The best reason connects the honest action to the good result.
questions.explanation: Taking the wallet to the head teacher led to the owner being found and thanking the pupils. That good result justifies the message about honesty.
questions.misconception: Choosing a reason that describes the conflict rather than justifying the message.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil refuses to laugh at a new pupil, welcomes her and shares her books. The new pupil becomes happy.' The message is to be kind to others. Give one reason from the sketch that justifies this message.
answer: she made the new pupil happy
kindness made the new pupil happy
hints: What happened when the pupils were kind?
The reason must come from the sketch.
questions.explanation: Kindness made the new pupil happy and gave her a friend, which is a reason drawn from the sketch that supports the message.
questions.misconception: Giving a general statement about kindness that is not shown in the sketch.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil works hard all term. He helps his classmates, does his homework and never gives up when a problem is hard. At the end of the term, he wins the prize for the most hardworking pupil.' State the message and justify it with two reasons from the sketch.
hints: What actions show the pupil's hard work?
How does the ending prove the message?
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the message (hard work is rewarded) and gives two reasons from the sketch (helping classmates, doing homework, not giving up, or the prize).

criteria.description: States a clear message about hard work
Gives two reasons from the sketch

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A girl helps an old woman carry her basket. Later, the girl's own mother is helped by a neighbour when she is sick.' The message is that kindness comes back to you. Which reason best justifies this message?
options: The girl was younger than the old woman.
The girl's kindness was returned by someone helping her own mother.
The neighbour was strong enough to help.
hints: Look at what happened to the girl's own mother.
Which option shows kindness returning?
questions.explanation: The girl's kindness to the old woman was returned when a neighbour helped her own mother. That is the reason the sketch supports the message.
questions.misconception: Choosing a fact from the sketch rather than the connection that justifies the message.

questions.stem: After watching a sketch where a pupil returns a lost wallet, tell the class what the message of the sketch is and justify it with one reason from the sketch.
hints: State the message first.
Then give one clear reason from the sketch.
questions.explanation: The pupil states the message (honesty) and gives one clear reason from the sketch to justify it.

criteria.description: Gives one reason from the sketch
The reason clearly supports the message

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil is always late for school. One day he misses an exam. He is very sad. He starts waking up early every day.' What lesson does the sketch teach?
options: It is good to be late.
Lateness has consequences; we should learn from our mistakes.
Waking up early is bad for pupils.
hints: What happened when the pupil was late?
What did he do afterwards?
questions.explanation: The pupil missed an exam because of lateness, and then he changed his behaviour. The lesson is that lateness has consequences and we should learn from our mistakes.
questions.misconception: Choosing a lesson that contradicts the sketch's events.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A pupil lends his pen to a classmate who has none. The classmate passes the exam and thanks him. Later, when the pupil forgets his own pen, the classmate lends him one.' What lesson does this sketch teach?
options: Kindness is returned when you need help.
Exams are more important than friends.
You should always carry two pens.
hints: What did the classmate do in return?
What happens when you are kind to others?
questions.explanation: The classmate returned the kindness when the pupil needed a pen. The lesson is that kindness is returned when you need help.
questions.misconception: Choosing a lesson that focuses on a small detail rather than the main point.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Two pupils argue over a football. Their teacher reminds them that the ball belongs to the school and must be shared. The pupils agree and play together.' What lesson does this sketch teach?
hints: What did the teacher remind them about the ball?
How did the pupils settle their argument?
questions.explanation: The pupils agree to share the school ball and play together. The lesson is that we should share what belongs to everyone.
questions.misconception: Answering with the argument itself rather than the lesson.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'A boy finds a wallet on the school field. He hides it and says nothing. Later, he hears a girl crying because she has lost her bus fare. He quietly returns the wallet. The girl stops crying.' What lesson does this sketch teach?
options: It is fine to keep things you find.
Honesty should be shown from the start, not after someone suffers.
Crying gets you what you want.
Money should never be kept in a wallet.
hints: Was it right for the boy to hide the wallet at first?
When did he finally do the right thing?
questions.explanation: The boy hid the wallet at first and only returned it when the girl was crying. The lesson is that honesty should be shown from the start, not after someone suffers.
questions.misconception: Choosing a lesson that praises keeping the wallet, when the sketch shows the harm it causes.

questions.stem: Sketch: 'Two pupils make fun of a new pupil's English. The new pupil is silent for days. Their teacher explains that everyone is learning and asks them to apologise. They apologise and help the new pupil with her English. By the end of the term, she is one of the best speakers in the class.' Write the lesson of the sketch in two sentences and relate it to real life.
hints: What was the problem with how the pupils treated the new pupil?
How can you show the same lesson at school today?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says that making fun of others is wrong and help is better than mockery, and relates it to welcoming and helping new pupils at school.

criteria.description: States the lesson clearly (do not mock others; help instead)
Relates the lesson to real life at school or home

questions.stem: After watching a sketch where a pupil refuses to share his food with a hungry classmate, tell the class the lesson of the sketch and how you would apply it in real life.
hints: What was wrong with the pupil's behaviour?
What would you do if a classmate had no food?
questions.explanation: The pupil states the lesson (share with others) and describes how they would apply it in real life.

criteria.description: Explains how the lesson applies in real life

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.1: Explore certain culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Describe/talk about objects/personalities/ events in the country and the world

skills.description: Describe familiar objects using appropriate vocabulary
Talk about personalities — who they are and what they do
Talk about events — when, where, why and how
Talk about places and regions in Ghana and the world
Use appropriate vocabulary to describe objects, personalities and events
Ask and answer questions to clarify others' opinions

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (describe a familiar object, place or person simply), 35% medium (talk about a personality or event with details), 15% harder (clarify and respond to others' opinions politely). Contexts drawn from Ghana (regions, festivals, national figures) and a few global examples.
misconceptions: Giving only a name without describing the object, personality or event
Mixing up the roles of personalities
Describing an event without saying when, where or why
Using vague words instead of specific vocabulary

questions.stem: You are describing a school bag. Which description uses the best vocabulary?
options: It is a brown leather bag with a strong strap and two pockets.
hints: A good description uses words about colour, material and parts.
Avoid vague words like 'thing' or 'nice'.
questions.explanation: Option B gives colour (brown), material (leather), parts (strap, pockets) and a quality (strong). That is the most descriptive and useful vocabulary.
questions.misconception: Thinking a short vague answer is enough for a description.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes a clay pot well?
options: It is a round clay pot with a wide mouth and a smooth brown surface.
hints: Look for shape, material, mouth and surface.
The best description uses several words together.
questions.explanation: Option B describes the shape (round), material (clay), mouth (wide) and surface (smooth, brown). That is a full description.
questions.misconception: Thinking one detail alone (e.g. 'brown') is a full description.

questions.stem: Describe a local broom in one sentence. Use at least two describing words.
answer: it is made of grass and has a long handle
it is a long grass broom with a strong handle
it is a light broom made of grass
it is made of sticks and tied with rope
hints: Think about what it is made of.
Think about its shape and size.
questions.explanation: A good answer uses at least two describing words (colour, material, size or shape) to describe the broom clearly.
questions.misconception: Writing only 'it is a broom' without describing words.

questions.stem: Choose an object in your classroom and describe it to the class in three sentences. Do not name the object — let your classmates guess what it is.
hints: Start with what it is made of or what it looks like.
Give small clues that help your classmates guess.
questions.explanation: The pupil describes an object with three clear sentences using appropriate vocabulary and clues.

criteria.description: Describes the object in three sentences
The description is clear enough for the class to guess

questions.stem: Write four sentences describing a market stall you have seen. Include what the stall sells, how it looks and how it makes you feel.
hints: Say what the stall sells first.
Then describe the size, colour or arrangement.
End with how it makes you feel.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the stall's goods, appearance and the pupil's feelings in four sentences.

questions.stem: Who is the head of the Ministry of Education in Ghana?
hints: The Ministry of Education is a national ministry.
The leader of a ministry is called a Minister.
questions.explanation: The Ministry of Education is led by the Minister for Education. Regional Ministers lead regions, not ministries.
questions.misconception: Confusing the roles of regional and national leaders.

questions.stem: Name one role model in Ghana and say in one sentence what they are known for.
answer: the president of ghana leads the nation
a sports personality plays for ghana
a musician entertains people with music
a nurse cares for the sick
a footballer plays football for ghana
hints: A role model can be a sports person, a leader or a teacher.
Say what they do, not just their name.
questions.explanation: A good answer names a role model and gives one clear role or achievement.
questions.misconception: Naming a person without saying what they are known for.

questions.stem: You are asked to talk about a Regional Minister. Which sentence best describes their role?
options: They teach pupils in a school.
They lead all schools in the district.
They oversee the affairs of a region in Ghana.
They sell goods at the market.
hints: A Regional Minister is in charge of a region.
They do not teach directly in classrooms.
questions.explanation: A Regional Minister oversees the affairs of a region in Ghana. That is their main role.
questions.misconception: Confusing a Regional Minister's role with a teacher's or a head teacher's.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about a personality you admire (a sports person, a leader, a musician or a teacher). Say who they are, what they do and why you admire them.
hints: Start with the person's name and what they do.
Give one clear reason for your admiration.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names the personality, describes their role and explains why the pupil admires them.

criteria.description: Explains why the pupil admires them

questions.stem: Talk about a person in your community whom you respect. Say who they are, what they do and why you respect them.
hints: They might be a teacher, a nurse, a farmer or a chief.
Give one clear reason for your respect.
questions.explanation: The pupil talks about a community personality, describes their role and explains why they are respected.

criteria.description: Names the person and their role
Explains what they do in the community
Gives a clear reason for respect

questions.stem: Which sentence gives the most information about a festival?
options: The Homowo festival is celebrated by the Ga people in August to mark the harvest.
hints: Which sentence says who celebrates it, when and why?
A good description of an event gives several details.
questions.explanation: Option C names the festival (Homowo), the people (Ga), the month (August) and the reason (harvest). That is the most complete description.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'it was fun' counts as a full description of an event.

questions.stem: Name one festival celebrated in Ghana and say what it celebrates.
answer: homowo is celebrated by the ga people
abosom is celebrated by the ga people
damba celebrates the birth of the prophet
damba is celebrated by the dagomba people
odwira celebrates the harvest and purification
odwira is celebrated by the akuapem people
hints: Think of Homowo, Aboakyer, Damba or Odwira.
Say what the festival marks or celebrates.
questions.explanation: A good answer names a festival and gives a short explanation of what it celebrates.
questions.misconception: Naming the festival only without saying what it celebrates.

questions.stem: You are asked to talk about Independence Day in Ghana. Which detail should you include?
options: It is celebrated on 6th March to mark Ghana's independence from colonial rule.
It is only celebrated in Accra.
It is a day when schools are closed forever.
hints: Independence Day has a specific date and meaning.
The date is 6th March.
questions.explanation: Ghana's Independence Day is celebrated on 6th March to mark the nation's independence from colonial rule in 1957. That is the correct detail.
questions.misconception: Confusing Independence Day with other public holidays.

questions.stem: Write four sentences about a school event you attended (such as a sports day, a speech day or a cultural festival). Include the name, when it happened, what happened and how you felt.
hints: Start by naming the event.
Say when it happened and what happened.
End with how you felt.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names the event, gives the date or time, describes at least one thing that happened and describes feelings.

questions.stem: Talk to the class about a national event or holiday you have celebrated. Say what it is, when it is celebrated and why it is important.
hints: Choose a holiday you know well.
Say why the holiday matters to Ghanaians.
questions.explanation: The pupil names the event, gives the date or time and explains why it matters.

questions.stem: Which region is Kumasi the capital of?
hints: Kumasi is the seat of the Asantehene.
It is a large city in the middle of Ghana.
questions.explanation: Kumasi is the capital of the Ashanti Region.
questions.misconception: Confusing Kumasi with Accra or another regional capital.

questions.stem: Name the capital town of the Central Region of Ghana.
hints: It is a coastal town in Ghana.
It is known for its castle.
questions.explanation: The capital of the Central Region is Cape Coast.
questions.misconception: Confusing the Central Region capital with another regional capital such as Accra or Takoradi.

questions.stem: You are asked to talk about the Volta Region. Which description is the most suitable?
options: It is a region in the north.
It is a region in the east of Ghana with Ho as its capital and the Volta Lake nearby.
It is a region in the south with Accra as its capital.
It is a region where only fishermen live.
hints: The Volta Region has Ho as its capital.
It is in the eastern part of Ghana.
questions.explanation: The Volta Region is in the east of Ghana with Ho as its capital and the Volta Lake nearby. That is a clear description.
questions.misconception: Confusing the Volta Region with other regions.

questions.stem: Write four sentences about a place in Ghana you have visited or heard about. Include its name, where it is, one interesting fact and why you would like to visit or have visited.
hints: Choose a town, city or tourist site.
Say where it is in Ghana and one interesting fact.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names the place, locates it in Ghana, gives one interesting fact and explains the pupil's interest.

criteria.description: Explains the pupil's interest or reason

questions.stem: You are talking about a famous Ghanaian boxer. Which word best describes him?
hints: A boxer who wins titles is called by a special name.
The word 'champion' fits a winner.
questions.explanation: A famous boxer who wins titles is a champion. The other words describe different professions.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general profession instead of a word that fits a sports person.

questions.stem: Name two words you would use to describe a busy market.
hints: Think about the number of people and the sound.
Words like 'crowded' and 'noisy' describe a busy market well.
questions.explanation: A busy market can be described as crowded, noisy, lively, colourful or busy.
questions.misconception: Choosing words that do not match the idea of a busy market.

questions.stem: Your classmate says: 'The Homowo festival is the most important festival in Ghana.' Ask one question to find out more about their opinion.
hints: You want to know why they think that.
Use polite words like 'Could you' or 'May I ask'.
questions.explanation: The pupil asks a polite, clear question about the classmate's reason for their opinion.

criteria.description: Asks a clear question about the opinion

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'The Ashanti Region is bigger than the Northern Region.' Which question best clarifies their point?
hints: The best question asks about the reason for the statement.
'Why do you say that?' asks for the reason.
questions.explanation: 'Why do you say that?' invites the classmate to explain their reasoning, which is what clarifying means.
questions.misconception: Asking an unrelated personal question instead of asking about the opinion.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: View and listen attentively and for a sustained period, (e.g., look at the person speaking and maintain eye contact) and record the key issues in the discussion

skills.description: Identify attentive listening behaviours: eye contact, posture, not interrupting
Listen or view for a sustained period without losing focus
Record the key issues raised in a discussion, speech or video
Report recorded key issues accurately to the class

spec.difficultyPlan: 55% easy (identify attentive behaviours; record one or two key issues), 30% medium (sustain attention and record three or more key issues), 15% harder (report issues accurately and completely). Audio/video texts are described in the stems and kept short (about two minutes).
misconceptions: Thinking 'listening' means hearing without recording
Recording every word instead of key issues
Looking away or talking while someone is speaking
Reporting opinions as if they were the speaker's key issues

questions.stem: Which of these shows that a pupil is listening attentively to a speaker?
options: Looking at the speaker and keeping eye contact.
hints: Attentive listening involves your eyes as well as your ears.
Eye contact shows you are paying attention.
questions.explanation: Looking at the speaker and keeping eye contact shows that the pupil is paying attention. The other behaviours show distraction.
questions.misconception: Believing attention is only about hearing, not about looking.

questions.stem: Your teacher is giving instructions for homework. Which behaviour shows you are listening attentively?
options: Sitting still, facing the teacher and taking notes.
hints: Attentive listening means sitting still and facing the speaker.
Taking notes helps you record key issues.
questions.explanation: Sitting still, facing the teacher and taking notes shows attentive listening and helps you remember instructions.
questions.misconception: Thinking you can listen well while doing other noisy things.

questions.stem: Name two behaviours that show you are NOT listening attentively during a class discussion.
answer: playing with a pencil, looking away
hints: Think about what distracts you and the speaker.
Talking and looking away are two clear examples.
questions.explanation: Talking, looking away, interrupting and playing with objects all show that a pupil is not listening attentively.
questions.misconception: Listing behaviours that are actually attentive (e.g. sitting still, looking at the speaker).

questions.stem: Watch two pupils (one attentive, one inattentive) as your teacher demonstrates. Tell the class which one was attentive and why.
hints: Look at eye contact and posture.
Look at whether the pupil interrupted.
questions.explanation: The pupil identifies the attentive one and gives a clear reason based on eye contact, posture or turn-taking.

criteria.description: Explains the behaviour of the inattentive pupil too

questions.stem: Your teacher plays a two-minute audio about road safety. Which is the best way to listen for the whole duration?
options: Listen to the first 30 seconds and stop.
Look away and listen only with one ear.
Listen from the beginning to the end without interrupting.
Talk to your friend while it plays.
hints: Sustained listening means the whole duration.
Do not lose focus halfway.
questions.explanation: Listening from start to finish without interrupting is sustained listening, which is what the task requires.
questions.misconception: Thinking hearing the beginning is enough to answer questions.

questions.stem: Your teacher tells a three-minute story. What should you do to listen for the entire duration without losing focus?
answer: look at the speaker and take notes
sit still and look at the speaker
sit still and listen without interrupting
keep eye contact and take notes
listen quietly and look at the speaker
hints: Think about eye contact and sitting still.
Writing short notes helps you stay focused.
questions.explanation: Looking at the speaker, sitting still and taking short notes helps a pupil listen for the whole duration without losing focus.
questions.misconception: Thinking focus is automatic and does not need active effort.

questions.stem: Listen to your teacher read a short story for two minutes. Tell the class one thing you remember from the beginning, one from the middle and one from the end.
hints: Focus on the main events.
You need one detail from each part.
questions.explanation: The pupil listens for the full duration and recalls one clear detail from the beginning, middle and end of the story.

criteria.description: Recalls a detail from the beginning
Recalls a detail from the middle
Recalls a detail from the end

questions.stem: While listening to a short video about healthy eating, note down three key issues raised. Write them in short phrases.
hints: Write short phrases, not full sentences.
Focus on the main points, not every word.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three short key issues from the video on healthy eating.

criteria.description: Uses short phrases, not full sentences
The issues are accurate to the video

questions.stem: Your teacher gives a talk about keeping the school clean. Which of these is a key issue she raised?
options: The teacher wore a blue dress.
The school should be swept every morning.
The teacher walked into the classroom.
hints: A key issue is what the talk is about, not what the speaker wore.
Choose the statement that gives a main point.
questions.explanation: The talk is about keeping the school clean, so 'sweep every morning' is a key issue. The other options are unimportant details.
questions.misconception: Recording details about the speaker instead of the message.

questions.stem: During a class discussion, your teacher says: 'Pupils should come to school early. They should bring all their books. They should also do their homework every day.' Write two key issues raised.
answer: coming to school early and doing homework
coming to school early and bringing books
pupils should come early and do their homework
hints: Pick two of the three statements the teacher made.
Write them as short phrases.
questions.explanation: The key issues are coming to school early, bringing all books, and doing homework every day. Any two of these are correct.
questions.misconception: Copying the teacher's full sentence instead of picking out key issues.

questions.stem: A radio programme discusses three ways to save water at home. Which note is written as a good key issue?
options: The radio presenter had a nice voice.
The programme was on in the afternoon.
The radio was small and black.
hints: A key issue is something you can act on.
Closing taps tightly is a practical way to save water.
questions.explanation: Closing taps tightly is one of the ways to save water, so it is a key issue. The other options are details about the radio programme.
questions.misconception: Recording information about the radio programme rather than its message.

questions.stem: Listen as your teacher reads a short speech on the importance of reading. Write three key issues from the speech in short phrases.
hints: Focus on why reading is important.
Write each key issue in a few words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists three key issues about the importance of reading (e.g. reading improves vocabulary, reading builds knowledge, reading is fun).

criteria.description: Issues are about the importance of reading

questions.stem: After listening to a short audio about road safety, tell the class two key issues you recorded.
hints: Say the key issues in short phrases.
Make sure they are about road safety.
questions.explanation: The pupil reports two clear key issues about road safety from the audio.

questions.stem: You recorded three key issues from a talk: (1) wash hands before eating, (2) cover food, (3) drink clean water. Which sentence reports them accurately?
options: The speaker said we should eat more food.
The speaker said we should wash hands, cover food and drink clean water.
The speaker wore a white shirt.
The speaker talked for a long time.
hints: Choose the report that matches what you recorded.
Do not add or change the key issues.
questions.explanation: Option B matches all three key issues you recorded. The other options are inaccurate or about the speaker.
questions.misconception: Adding new information or replacing key issues with details about the speaker.

questions.stem: You recorded these key issues from a discussion: (1) keep the classroom clean, (2) do not litter, (3) plant trees. Write one sentence reporting them.
answer: the class should keep the classroom clean not litter and plant trees
keep the classroom clean do not litter and plant trees
we should keep the classroom clean avoid littering and plant trees
keep the class clean and do not litter and plant trees
clean the classroom do not litter and plant trees
hints: Use all three key issues in one sentence.
Start with 'The class should...'.
questions.explanation: A good report mentions all three key issues in one clear sentence.
questions.misconception: Reporting only one or two of the key issues.

questions.stem: After listening to a short video about the environment, write three sentences reporting the key issues you recorded. Use 'The video said that...' to begin each sentence.
hints: Use the sentence starter given.
Make sure each sentence reports a different key issue.
questions.explanation: A strong answer reports three different key issues accurately using the sentence starter 'The video said that...'.

questions.stem: After listening to a classmate's short presentation about healthy eating, report two key issues they raised to the class.
hints: Listen carefully during the presentation.
Report only what the speaker actually said.
questions.explanation: The pupil reports two accurate key issues from the classmate's presentation, without adding or changing the speaker's points.

criteria.description: Does not add or change the speaker's points

questions.stem: In a group, each pupil reports the key issues they recorded from the same audio. Compare your reports and agree on the three most important issues.
hints: Listen to each member's report.
Decide together which issues matter most.
questions.explanation: The group reports, compares and agrees on three key issues from the audio.

criteria.description: Each member reports their key issues
The group agrees on three most important issues

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.2: Demonstrate positive listening and viewing attitudes and behaviour by showing attentiveness and understanding
indicator.objective: Listen and view for the entire duration of text/speech/presentation/video etc.

skills.description: Stay focused for the entire duration of a text, speech, presentation or video
Identify character traits in a text or speech heard and discuss them
Role-play characters from a text or speech heard
Answer questions about a text or speech heard, including inferential questions

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (stay focused; identify a character), 35% medium (identify traits with evidence), 20% harder (role-play a character and answer inferential questions). Texts and speeches are kept short (3–5 minutes) and their content is provided in the stems.
