misconceptions: Losing concentration before the end and guessing
Describing a character's appearance instead of their traits
Role-playing in a way that contradicts the character's words
Answering from memory of a similar story rather than the one heard

questions.stem: Your teacher plays a three-minute video about the water cycle. Which behaviour shows you listened and viewed for the entire duration?
options: You can describe the beginning, middle and ending of the video.
You watched the first minute only.
You talked to your friend while it played.
You looked at your phone during the video.
hints: Listening for the whole duration means you know the whole message.
Which option shows you followed the whole video?
questions.explanation: Being able to describe the beginning, middle and ending of the video shows that you paid attention for the entire duration.
questions.misconception: Believing that watching part of the video is enough for understanding.

questions.stem: During a five-minute speech by the head teacher, Kofi stops listening after two minutes because he thinks he already knows the topic. What is the likely result?
options: He will understand the speech completely.
He will miss important new points made later.
He will remember the speech better than others.
He will be given a prize.
hints: Even familiar topics can have new information.
If you stop listening halfway, what do you miss?
questions.explanation: If Kofi stops listening after two minutes, he will miss the points made in the last three minutes, so he will not have full understanding.
questions.misconception: Thinking prior knowledge of a topic means you can stop listening.

questions.stem: Give two behaviours that help you stay focused for the whole duration of a speech.
answer: take notes and keep eye contact
keep eye contact and sit still
sit still look at the speaker
take short notes and listen carefully
hints: Think about your eyes, your posture and your hands.
Two behaviours that prevent distraction.
questions.explanation: Sitting still, keeping eye contact, taking short notes and staying quiet all help a pupil stay focused for the whole speech.
questions.misconception: Thinking focus happens automatically without any active effort.

questions.stem: After listening to a two-minute audio about keeping the environment clean, tell the class two key points from the end of the audio.
hints: Listen right to the end.
The end of an audio often contains the most important points.
questions.explanation: The pupil reports two key points specifically from the end of the audio, showing attention to the whole duration.

criteria.description: Points are from the end of the audio

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Ama always gives her food to her hungry classmates. She never complains and always helps when her mother is tired.' Which trait describes Ama best?
hints: What does she do with her food?
Which trait means giving freely to others?
questions.explanation: Ama gives her food to hungry classmates and helps her mother, so the best trait is generous.
questions.misconception: Choosing a negative trait when the character's actions are good.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Kojo never tells lies. Even when he broke his neighbour's window, he went and told the neighbour himself.' What trait does Kojo show?
hints: What does he never do?
What did he do when he broke the window?
questions.explanation: Kojo never tells lies and admits his mistakes. That shows honesty.
questions.misconception: Confusing honesty with stubbornness or cowardice.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Esi finds an old woman struggling with her load. Esi helps her carry it all the way to the market, refusing any reward.' Name one trait that describes Esi.
hints: What did Esi do for the old woman?
She refused a reward too.
questions.explanation: Esi helps without expecting a reward, so she shows kindness, generosity or selflessness.
questions.misconception: Answering with an action (helping) rather than the trait.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Adjoa always boasts about her marks. She laughs at those who score lower. When she fails a test, she blames the teacher.' Which trait describes Adjoa?
options: Proud and unwilling to accept her mistakes
hints: She boasts and laughs at others.
She blames the teacher when she fails.
questions.explanation: Boasting, laughing at others and blaming the teacher show pride and unwillingness to accept her own mistakes.
questions.misconception: Assuming a pupil who gets good marks must be hardworking and humble.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Yaw works hard on his farm every day. When his neighbour is sick, he waters the neighbour's crops too. He refuses payment and says he is happy to help.' Write three sentences describing Yaw's character traits, giving evidence from the story for each.
hints: Think of hard work and generosity.
Use words from the story as evidence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names traits like hardworking, generous and kind and supports each with evidence from the story.

criteria.description: Gives evidence from the story for each trait

questions.stem: After listening to a short story in class, tell the class one trait of the main character and give a reason from the story.
hints: Start by naming the trait.
Give one clear action from the story that shows it.
questions.explanation: The pupil names a trait and gives one clear piece of evidence from the story.

questions.stem: You are role-playing Kojo, who is honest but shy. Which behaviour fits your role best?
options: Speak loudly and boast about your honesty.
Look down at your feet and quietly admit what you did.
Shout at everyone in the room.
Laugh and tell jokes about the story.
hints: Shyness means speaking quietly and looking down.
Honesty means admitting your actions.
questions.explanation: Looking down and quietly admitting what you did matches a shy, honest character. The other behaviours do not fit.
questions.misconception: Choosing behaviours that contradict the character's personality.

questions.stem: You are role-playing Ama, a generous classmate. Write one sentence Ama would say to a hungry friend.
answer: here is some food i have plenty to share
please take some of my food i have enough
take this food i can share with you
do not worry i will share my food with you
hints: Ama is generous.
Her words should show sharing.
questions.explanation: A generous character would offer to share food with a hungry friend. The sentence should show willingness to give.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that shows selfishness or refusal to share.

questions.stem: Role-play a character from a story you heard who is very kind. Use a soft voice and kind words to speak to another pupil in the role of someone in need.
hints: Use a gentle tone.
Say kind words that help the other person.
questions.explanation: The pupil stays in character, using a soft voice and kind words suited to a kind character.

questions.stem: In pairs, role-play a scene from a story you heard: one character is boastful and the other is humble. Use voices, actions and facial expressions to show the difference.
hints: The boastful character speaks loudly and uses big gestures.
The humble character speaks softly and listens more than talks.
questions.explanation: The pair clearly shows the difference between boastful and humble characters through voice, actions and expressions.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Kwesi helped his mother carry water. Then he did his homework. Then he fed the chickens.' Which did Kwesi do first?
options: He helped his mother carry water.
hints: The word 'then' shows the order.
What did he do first in the story?
questions.explanation: The story says Kwesi first helped his mother carry water, then did his homework and then fed the chickens.
questions.misconception: Choosing a later action instead of the first one.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Ama looked at her mother's tired face and quietly picked up the broom. She swept the whole compound before her mother came back.' Why did Ama sweep the compound?
options: She saw her mother was tired and wanted to help.
She was told to sweep by a teacher.
hints: The story says she looked at her mother's tired face.
Why did she pick up the broom after that?
questions.explanation: Ama noticed her mother was tired and chose to help by sweeping. The inference is that she acted out of love and care.
questions.misconception: Choosing an answer that is not supported by the story.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Kojo lost his money on the way to school. He did not tell anyone. During break, he sat alone and did not eat. His friend Esi noticed and shared her food with him.' Why did Kojo sit alone during break?
answer: he had no money to buy food
hints: What had Kojo lost?
Why does not eating make him sit alone?
questions.explanation: Kojo had lost his money, so he could not buy food and sat alone during break. Esi noticed and shared her food.
questions.misconception: Answering with a feeling (sad) instead of the reason.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Adjoa wanted to enter the school singing competition, but she was afraid of singing in front of people. Her music teacher encouraged her every day. On the day of the competition, Adjoa stood up, closed her eyes and sang with all her heart. She won first prize.' Why do you think Adjoa closed her eyes when she sang?
hints: Adjoa was afraid of the crowd.
What does closing your eyes help you do when you are nervous?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says that Adjoa closed her eyes because she was nervous and wanted to block out the crowd so she could focus on singing.

criteria.description: Connects closing eyes to her fear or nervousness
Suggests she wanted to focus or block out the crowd

questions.stem: After listening to a short speech about the importance of reading, answer one question the teacher asks about it (such as 'What does the speaker say reading does for us?').
hints: Listen carefully to the question.
Answer using what the speaker said, not your own opinion.
questions.explanation: The pupil answers the teacher's question accurately, using what the speaker said.

criteria.description: Answer is based on what the speaker said

questions.stem: After listening to a short story, answer this question: 'Why do you think the main character made the choice she did?' Give a reason from the story.
hints: Think about the character's feelings and situation.
Support your answer with something from the story.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a thoughtful answer about the character's motivation, supported by evidence from the story.

criteria.description: Gives a clear answer about the character's motivation
Supports the answer with evidence from the story

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Engage in collaborative conversation with unfamiliar audience

skills.description: Initiate or enter a conversation on a given topic with an unfamiliar audience
Take turns in conversation without dominating or interrupting
Use appropriate facial expressions and maintain eye contact
Contribute relevant ideas to the conversation
Use polite and appropriate language with unfamiliar people

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (greet and enter; take one turn), 40% medium (contribute relevant ideas; use facial expressions and eye contact), 20% harder (sustain a collaborative conversation with unfamiliar adults or visitors). Topics drawn from the curriculum list: social issues, social values and manners.
misconceptions: Talking over others or staying silent throughout
Giving irrelevant contributions to the topic
Using informal or slang language with unfamiliar adults
Avoiding eye contact or looking at the floor

questions.stem: A visitor comes to your class to talk about keeping the environment clean. Which is the best way to enter the conversation politely?
options: Say 'Hello, please may I ask a question about your talk?'
Shout your question from the back of the class.
Interrupt the visitor while they are speaking.
hints: Polite greetings come before questions.
Wait until the speaker has paused.
questions.explanation: Greeting politely and asking permission to speak is the right way to enter a conversation with an unfamiliar person.
questions.misconception: Thinking you can interrupt or shout in a conversation with an unfamiliar adult.

questions.stem: Write one polite opening sentence you could use to start a conversation with a visitor about the value of honesty.
answer: good morning please may i ask you about honesty
excuse me sir please may i ask a question about honesty
good afternoon could i ask what you think about honesty
please may i ask your opinion on honesty
excuse me please could you tell me about honesty
hello please may i ask you about honesty
hints: Start with a polite greeting.
Ask for permission before asking your question.
questions.explanation: A good opening sentence uses a polite greeting and asks permission to raise the topic of honesty.
questions.misconception: Starting rudely with 'Hey!' or 'Tell me about honesty.'

questions.stem: You want to start a conversation with a teacher you have not met before on the topic of good manners. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Excuse me, please. May I ask you about good manners?
You, come here and talk about manners.
hints: Use polite language with unfamiliar adults.
Ask permission before raising the topic.
questions.explanation: Option B uses polite language and asks permission, which is appropriate for unfamiliar adults.
questions.misconception: Thinking a direct, rude command is fine with unfamiliar adults.

questions.stem: With a partner playing the role of an unfamiliar visitor, start a conversation about children and mobile phones. Use a polite greeting and an opening question.
hints: Greet first.
Then ask one clear question about the topic.
questions.explanation: The pupil greets the visitor politely, then introduces the topic of children and mobile phones with a clear opening question.

criteria.description: Uses polite tone and eye contact

questions.stem: You are in a conversation with a visitor and two classmates. Which behaviour shows good turn-taking?
options: Waiting for the speaker to finish before you speak.
Staying completely silent the whole time.
hints: Turn-taking means everyone gets a chance to speak.
Do not interrupt the speaker.
questions.explanation: Waiting for the speaker to finish before you speak is polite turn-taking. Talking over others and staying silent all the time are not good conversation behaviours.
questions.misconception: Confusing turn-taking with staying silent and never contributing.

questions.stem: Name two polite phrases you can use to take your turn in a conversation without interrupting.
answer: excuse me and may i add something
excuse me, please may i speak
may i add something and sorry to interrupt
excuse me and please may i add
sorry to interrupt and may i say something
please may i add and excuse me
hints: One phrase apologises for a pause in your turn.
One phrase asks permission to contribute.
questions.explanation: Polite phrases such as 'excuse me', 'may I add something', 'sorry to interrupt' and 'please may I speak' help pupils take turns without interrupting.
questions.misconception: Thinking you can just start speaking whenever you like.

questions.stem: During a discussion, one classmate has spoken for five minutes without letting anyone else speak. What should the group do?
options: Shout at the classmate to stop.
Politely ask to take a turn after they finish their point.
Repeat their points until they stop.
hints: The classmate should be treated politely.
Wait for a natural pause and ask for a turn.
questions.explanation: Politely asking for a turn after the classmate finishes is the right way to ensure everyone contributes without being rude.
questions.misconception: Thinking shouting or leaving is the solution to dominating speakers.

questions.stem: In a group of four, hold a two-minute conversation on the topic 'Should pupils use phones in school?'. Make sure each pupil speaks at least once.
hints: Use polite phrases to take your turn.
Wait for pauses.
questions.explanation: The group converses on the topic with each member contributing at least once, using polite turn-taking.

criteria.description: Each member contributes at least once

questions.stem: With a partner playing an unfamiliar visitor, hold a short conversation about the value of honesty. Take turns speaking and respond politely to what the visitor says.
hints: Listen to the visitor's point before you respond.
Use 'I agree because...' or 'May I add...' to respond.
questions.explanation: The pair sustains a short, polite conversation on honesty with clear turn-taking and respectful responses.

criteria.description: Responds politely to the other's point
Stays on the topic of honesty
Uses facial expressions and eye contact

questions.stem: Which facial expression best shows that you are listening to someone politely?
options: A frown with your eyes looking down.
A calm, interested face with eyes on the speaker.
A wide yawn with your head turned away.
A smile while looking at the ceiling.
hints: Faces show attention.
Look at the speaker with an interested expression.
questions.explanation: A calm, interested face with eyes on the speaker shows polite listening. The other expressions show boredom, distraction or rudeness.
questions.misconception: Thinking any expression is fine as long as you can hear.

questions.stem: Give one reason why keeping eye contact with a speaker is important in a conversation.
answer: it shows you are paying attention
it helps the speaker know you are following
hints: Eye contact shows something to the speaker.
It is a sign of respect or attention.
questions.explanation: Eye contact shows the speaker that you are paying attention and respecting what they are saying.
questions.misconception: Thinking eye contact is unimportant in conversation.

questions.stem: With a partner, hold a one-minute conversation on a topic of your choice. Make sure you maintain eye contact and use expressions that match the topic.
hints: Look at your partner as you speak.
Match your expression to your words.
questions.explanation: The pair holds a clear conversation with steady eye contact and matching facial expressions.

criteria.description: Uses facial expressions that match the topic

questions.stem: The class is discussing 'How can we keep our school compound clean?'. Which contribution is most relevant to the topic?
options: I like to eat rice at home.
We should place bins at the corners of the compound.
hints: The topic is about keeping the compound clean.
Which idea would actually help?
questions.explanation: Placing bins around the compound is a direct way to keep the school clean. The other ideas are not about the topic.
questions.misconception: Confusing a related but irrelevant comment with a relevant contribution.

questions.stem: The class is discussing 'How can pupils show respect to elders?'. Write one relevant idea you could contribute.
answer: stand up for them on the bus
listen to them when they speak
hints: Think of everyday actions that show respect.
Greeting, helping or listening are good examples.
questions.explanation: A relevant contribution names a specific action that shows respect to elders, such as greeting them politely or helping them.
questions.misconception: Giving a contribution that is not linked to respect.

questions.stem: In a conversation with a visitor about 'Good manners at home', a pupil says: 'My cousin plays football well.' How is that contribution relevant to the topic?
options: It is not relevant because it does not relate to good manners at home.
It is relevant only if the cousin plays at home.
It is relevant only at break time.
hints: Does playing football relate to good manners at home?
Which option matches what the contribution says?
questions.explanation: The contribution about football does not relate to good manners at home, so it is not relevant to the discussion.
questions.misconception: Believing any statement in a conversation is automatically relevant to the topic.

questions.stem: In a group conversation about 'Good manners at the market', contribute one clear idea that fits the topic.
hints: Think of things you should or should not do at the market.
Say 'please' and 'thank you' to sellers.
questions.explanation: The pupil contributes one clear idea on good manners at the market, such as greeting sellers politely or waiting for their turn.

criteria.description: Idea relates to the topic of good manners at the market

questions.stem: You want to ask an unfamiliar adult a question. Which is the most polite way to ask?
options: Excuse me, please, could I ask you something?
I want to ask you now.
Tell me what I want to know.
hints: Polite language uses words like 'please' and 'could I'.
Avoid commands when asking an adult.
questions.explanation: Option B uses polite words ('excuse me', 'please', 'could I'), which is the right way to address an unfamiliar adult.
questions.misconception: Thinking a direct command is acceptable with unfamiliar adults.

questions.stem: Write one polite sentence you could use to disagree with a visitor in a conversation, without being rude.
answer: i understand your point but i think differently
with respect i see it another way
i see your point but i have a different view
excuse me i would like to disagree politely
i appreciate your view but i think otherwise
thank you but i have another opinion
hints: Start by acknowledging the other person's point.
Then state your difference politely.
questions.explanation: A good answer acknowledges the visitor's point first, then politely expresses a different view.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing with a rude phrase such as 'That is wrong!'

questions.stem: With a partner playing an unfamiliar visitor, hold a short conversation about social values. Use polite language throughout, including greeting and respectful disagreement.
hints: Greet politely at the start.
Use 'I understand, but...' when you disagree.
questions.explanation: The pair holds a polite, respectful conversation on social values, including greeting and polite disagreement.

criteria.description: Stays on the topic of social values

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate turn taking in conversation on different topics and follow agreed-upon rules for conversation and express thoughts coherently

skills.description: State or identify the rules of conversation: listen, one at a time, do not interrupt
Practise turn-taking in pairs or groups on different topics
Express thoughts coherently in complete, connected ideas
Use appropriate vocabulary, with hints or word cards where needed
Use repair phrases such as 'Sorry?', 'Excuse me', 'Can you repeat that?'

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (state rules; use repair phrases), 35% medium (take turns and express a coherent thought), 20% harder (sustain turn-taking on an unfamiliar topic and express connected thoughts). Topics drawn from current and recent events and school life.
misconceptions: Believing turn-taking means waiting silently without contributing
Giving fragmented ideas that do not connect
Interrupting to correct others rather than waiting
Using repair phrases inappropriately, such as 'What?' instead of 'Sorry, could you repeat that?'

questions.stem: Which of these is a rule of good conversation?
options: Speak one at a time and listen to others.
Speak as loudly as you can.
Interrupt whenever you have something to say.
Only one person should speak the whole time.
hints: Good conversation is shared.
Everyone should get a chance to speak.
questions.explanation: The main rule of conversation is to speak one at a time and listen to others so that everyone gets a turn.
questions.misconception: Thinking conversation means speaking as much as you can.

questions.stem: During a class discussion, which rule should everyone follow?
options: Pupils should interrupt each other to be heard.
Pupils should raise their hands and wait to be called.
Pupils should speak all at once.
hints: Raising hands keeps order.
Waiting to be called shows respect for others.
questions.explanation: Raising hands and waiting to be called is the rule that keeps a class discussion orderly so everyone gets a turn.
questions.misconception: Thinking the loudest or quickest speaker should always go first.

questions.stem: Write one rule of conversation that helps everyone get a turn to speak.
answer: one person speaks at a time
wait for the speaker to finish
hints: Think about what happens when one person interrupts.
One clear rule is enough.
questions.explanation: Rules such as 'do not interrupt', 'one person speaks at a time', 'wait for your turn' and 'listen when others speak' all help everyone get a turn.
questions.misconception: Writing a rule that encourages interrupting or shouting.

questions.stem: Write three rules for a good class conversation.
hints: Think about listening, waiting and not interrupting.
One rule per sentence is enough.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three clear rules such as listening, waiting for a turn and not interrupting.

questions.stem: Tell the class two rules your group agreed on for a good conversation and explain why each rule matters.
hints: Choose rules that help everyone speak.
Explain why each rule matters.
questions.explanation: The pupil states two clear rules and gives a reason why each matters.

questions.stem: Two pupils are talking about the recent school sports day. Which shows good turn-taking?
options: Ama speaks while Kwame is speaking.
Ama finishes her point, then Kwame responds to it.
Ama repeats her point three times.
Kwame interrupts Ama to correct her grammar.
hints: Turn-taking means each person finishes before the other begins.
Responding to what the other said is part of good conversation.
questions.explanation: Ama finishing her point and Kwame responding to it shows good turn-taking. Interrupting or repeating does not.
questions.misconception: Believing speed of speech shows good conversation.

questions.stem: You are in a pair conversation about the school sports day. Write one polite phrase you could use to take your turn.
answer: excuse me may i add something
sorry may i add a point
hints: Start politely.
Ask permission to contribute.
questions.explanation: A polite phrase such as 'Excuse me, may I add something?' or 'Please, may I say something?' shows good turn-taking.
questions.misconception: Thinking you can just start speaking without checking whether the other has finished.

questions.stem: In pairs, hold a two-minute conversation about 'My favourite school subject'. Take turns and each of you should speak at least twice.
hints: Wait for your partner to finish before you speak.
Respond to what your partner says.
questions.explanation: The pair holds a short conversation on the topic with clear turn-taking and at least two turns each.

criteria.description: Each partner speaks at least twice

questions.stem: In groups of four, hold a short conversation about 'A recent event in Ghana'. Each pupil should take at least one turn to speak and respond to at least one other pupil.
hints: Agree the rules of the conversation before you begin.
Listen to each speaker and respond to their point.
questions.explanation: The group holds an ordered conversation in which each member speaks, and each responds to at least one other member's point.

criteria.description: Each pupil takes at least one turn
Each pupil responds to at least one other point

questions.stem: In groups, hold a conversation on the topic 'Should pupils wear uniform every day?'. Follow the agreed rules: one person at a time, listen before responding, no interrupting.
hints: Use polite phrases to take your turn.
Wait for the speaker to finish.
questions.explanation: The group holds a polite conversation on the topic, following the agreed rules and clearly taking turns.

questions.stem: Which of these expresses a thought most coherently?
options: Sports day, yes, running, my friend, happy.
On sports day I ran a race with my friend, and we were both very happy.
I ran friend race happy sports day.
hints: Coherent thoughts use complete, connected sentences.
Look for a sentence with all the ideas joined clearly.
questions.explanation: Option B is a complete, connected sentence that expresses a clear thought. The others are fragments that do not connect ideas.
questions.misconception: Thinking a string of words is the same as a coherent sentence.

questions.stem: Rewrite this disconnected idea as one coherent sentence: 'Homework. My sister. Hard. Me. Tired.'
answer: my sister and i were tired after doing our homework
my sister and i felt tired after homework
homework was hard and my sister and i were tired
my sister and i found the homework hard and we were tired
we were both tired after the hard homework
i was tired and my sister was tired after homework
hints: Join the ideas into one complete sentence.
Use 'and' or 'because' to connect the ideas.
questions.explanation: A coherent sentence joins the ideas into one clear thought, such as 'My sister and I were tired after doing our homework'.
questions.misconception: Believing a list of words can be a coherent sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses a clear, coherent thought about the market?
options: Yesterday I went to the market and bought fresh tomatoes for my mother.
I to market went buy tomatoes.
Market many people too much noise.
hints: Look for a complete sentence with a clear meaning.
Which sentence uses correct grammar and clear ideas?
questions.explanation: Option B is a clear, complete sentence that expresses a coherent thought about the market.
questions.misconception: Choosing a broken sentence that only lists words.

questions.stem: Write three connected sentences on the topic 'A day I enjoyed at school'.
hints: Each sentence should connect to the one before it.
Use words like 'first', 'then' and 'finally'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences that clearly tell about one day, using connecting words so the ideas flow.

questions.stem: Tell the class about a recent event at school in three connected sentences. Make sure each sentence connects to the one before it.
hints: Start with what happened first.
Use 'then' and 'after that' to connect the ideas.
questions.explanation: The pupil tells about an event in three connected sentences with clear flow.

questions.stem: You are talking about the value of honesty. Which word is most appropriate to add to your conversation?
hints: Choose a word that fits the topic of honesty.
Which word is related to telling the truth?
questions.explanation: 'Truthful' is directly related to honesty. The other words describe food, size and shape.
questions.misconception: Choosing any impressive-sounding word regardless of the topic.

questions.stem: Your class is discussing 'Good manners in the community'. Write one word or phrase you would use to add to the conversation.
hints: Think of a word that means good behaviour towards others.
Words like 'respect', 'politeness' or 'kindness' fit.
questions.explanation: Words such as respect, politeness, kindness, courtesy and consideration all relate to good manners.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word unrelated to manners.

questions.stem: In a group conversation about 'Keeping the environment clean', use one new word from the word cards your teacher has displayed. Explain its meaning as you speak.
hints: Choose a word you understand.
Say what the word means before you use it in your point.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses a new word from the word cards in a relevant way and explains its meaning clearly.

criteria.description: Uses a word from the word cards
Uses the word correctly in a sentence

questions.stem: You did not hear what your partner said in a conversation. Which phrase should you use to ask them to repeat it politely?
options: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?
hints: Polite repair phrases start with 'Sorry' or 'Excuse me'.
Ask politely for a repeat.
questions.explanation: 'Sorry, could you repeat that, please?' is polite and clear. The other options are rude or unclear.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'What?' is a polite way to ask someone to repeat.

questions.stem: Write one polite phrase you can use when you need someone to repeat what they said.
answer: excuse me could you say that again
i am sorry i did not hear you could you repeat
pardon me could you repeat that
sorry i missed that could you say it again
hints: Start politely.
Ask for a repeat clearly.
questions.explanation: Polite repair phrases such as 'Sorry, could you repeat that?', 'Excuse me, could you say that again?' or 'Pardon me, could you repeat that?' help keep the conversation going respectfully.
questions.misconception: Using 'What?' or 'Eh?' without any polite words.

questions.stem: Your partner in a conversation speaks too softly. Which is the most polite way to respond?
options: Shout at your partner to speak louder.
Excuse me, I did not hear you clearly. Could you speak a little louder, please?
Ignore what your partner said and talk to someone else.
Tell the class your partner cannot speak well.
hints: Be polite when asking for a louder voice.
Do not embarrass your partner.
questions.explanation: Option B politely explains the problem and asks for a louder voice, without embarrassing the partner.
questions.misconception: Thinking shouting or embarrassing your partner is acceptable.

questions.stem: With a partner, practise this conversation: your partner speaks softly, and you politely ask them to repeat. After the repeat, continue the conversation.
hints: Use a polite repair phrase.
Continue the conversation after the repeat.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses a polite repair phrase, listens to the repeat and continues the conversation.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.6.3: Use knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Ask and answer questions about key details on topics under discussion.

skills.description: Ask relevant questions about key details on a topic
Answer questions about key details accurately
Ask questions for clarification
Use appropriate topic vocabulary when asking or answering

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (ask or answer one detail question), 35% medium (ask or answer several connected detail questions), 15% harder (clarify and extend answers). Topics drawn from the curriculum list: holidays, future career, school, family and current events.
misconceptions: Asking yes or no questions only when details are needed
Answering with a single word when a detail is expected
Asking questions unrelated to the topic
Using vague vocabulary such as 'that thing' or 'somewhere'

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I spent my holidays in Kumasi.' Which question asks for a key detail about the holiday?
options: How did you travel to Kumasi and what did you do there?
hints: A detail question asks about the specific facts of the story.
Which question asks about travel and activities?
questions.explanation: Option B asks for two key details (how he travelled and what he did), which are specific to the holiday story.
questions.misconception: Thinking any question asked after a statement counts as a detail question.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'My future career is to be a nurse.' Write one question that asks for a key detail about this career choice.
answer: why do you want to be a nurse
which school will you attend to become a nurse
how long will it take to become a nurse
where do you want to work as a nurse
who inspired you to become a nurse
hints: A detail question asks about a specific part of the career.
Think about why, how, where or when.
questions.explanation: A key-detail question asks about the reasons, training, location or timing of the career choice.
questions.misconception: Asking a yes or no question such as 'Do you like nursing?' when details are needed.

questions.stem: Your class is discussing a recent event in the community. Which question asks for the most useful key detail?
options: What happened, and who was involved?
hints: A useful detail question asks for facts.
Open questions such as 'what' and 'who' give more information.
questions.explanation: Option A asks for facts (what happened and who was involved) that give useful information for the discussion.
questions.misconception: Thinking yes or no questions give as much information as open questions.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I went to the beach during the holidays.' Write three questions you could ask to find out key details about the trip.
hints: Ask about who, what, when and how.
Three different questions are enough.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three different questions about the beach trip (who went with them, what they did, when they went, how they travelled).

criteria.description: Questions ask for key details about the trip
Questions are clear and different from one another

questions.stem: With a partner, ask two questions about the details of their future career. Make sure your questions ask for specific information.
hints: Ask open questions, not yes or no questions.
Listen carefully to the answer before asking the next question.
questions.explanation: The pupil asks two clear, open questions that invite specific details about the career.

criteria.description: Questions are on the topic of future career

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Where did you spend your holidays?' Which answer gives the best key detail?
options: I spent my holidays in Cape Coast with my aunt.
hints: A good answer gives specific details.
Which answer tells where and with whom?
questions.explanation: Option B gives the place (Cape Coast) and the person (my aunt), which are specific key details.
questions.misconception: Thinking a one-word or vague answer is enough for a detail question.

questions.stem: Your classmate asks: 'What do you want to be in future and why?' Write a two-part answer.
answer: i want to be a nurse because i want to help sick people
i want to be a teacher because i love teaching children
i want to be a doctor because i want to save lives
i want to be a farmer because i love growing crops
i want to be an engineer because i like building things
i want to be a pilot because i love travelling
hints: State the career first.
Then give one reason.
questions.explanation: A good answer names the career and gives a clear reason for choosing it.
questions.misconception: Answering only one part of the question.

questions.stem: A classmate asks: 'Tell me about a festival you celebrate at home.' Which answer gives the best key details?
options: We celebrate Homowo in August with drumming and a family meal.
hints: Which answer names the festival and says when and how?
Look for specific details.
questions.explanation: Option B names the festival (Homowo), the month (August) and the activities (drumming and family meal), which are useful key details.
questions.misconception: Choosing a vague answer that gives no useful details.

questions.stem: Answer these three questions about your school in complete sentences: (1) What is the name of your school? (2) What is your favourite subject and why? (3) What is one thing you would like to improve in your school?
hints: Answer each question separately.
Use complete sentences, not single words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three complete, specific answers that address each question.

questions.stem: A classmate asks: 'What did you do during the last holidays?' Answer with at least two key details in a clear sentence.
hints: Give at least two specific things you did.
Use complete sentences.
questions.explanation: The pupil answers clearly, giving at least two specific details about the holiday activities.

criteria.description: Gives at least two key details

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I want to be a doctor, but not the kind you think.' Which question best clarifies what they mean?
options: What do you mean by 'not the kind you think'?
hints: A clarifying question asks about something unclear.
Which part of your friend's statement is unclear?
questions.explanation: Option A asks about the unclear part of the statement, which is exactly what clarification means.
questions.misconception: Asking a personal question unrelated to the unclear statement.

questions.stem: Your classmate says: 'I want to visit the most beautiful place in Ghana.' Write one question to clarify which place they mean.
answer: which place are you referring to
what is the name of the place
where exactly do you want to go
which beautiful place do you mean
can you tell me the name of the place
hints: The unclear part is the name of the place.
Ask for the name or location.
questions.explanation: A clarifying question asks for the name or location of the place so the statement becomes clear.
questions.misconception: Asking a question about something else in the statement.

questions.stem: Your friend says: 'I went to the big market.' Which question best clarifies which market they mean?
options: Which big market do you mean?
hints: The unclear part is the name of the market.
Which question asks about the market itself?
questions.explanation: 'Which big market do you mean?' asks directly for the specific market, which is the unclear detail.
questions.misconception: Asking a question about the trip rather than about the unclear detail.

questions.stem: A classmate says: 'We should all help to keep our school clean, especially during exam week.' Write two clarifying questions you could ask to understand their point better.
hints: Ask about what 'help' means in this context.
Ask why exam week matters especially.
questions.explanation: A strong answer asks two clear questions about the specific actions and the reason for the focus on exam week.

criteria.description: Questions are clear and on the topic

questions.stem: In pairs, discuss 'What makes a good friend?'. When your partner says something unclear, ask a clarifying question before you respond.
hints: Ask for clarification politely.
Do not respond until you understand.
questions.explanation: The pupil asks a clear, polite clarifying question when something is unclear, then responds to the clarified point.

criteria.description: Asks a clarifying question when needed

questions.stem: You are asking questions about a career in nursing. Which word best fits this topic?
hints: Choose a word related to a hospital or nursing.
Which word do nurses use every day?
questions.explanation: 'Patient' is directly linked to nursing. Football, kente and fufu belong to other topics.
questions.misconception: Choosing any familiar word regardless of the topic.

questions.stem: You are asking and answering questions about 'My future career'. Write two words or phrases you would use in that conversation.
hints: Think about what is needed for a career.
Words like 'training', 'salary' and 'qualification' fit.
questions.explanation: Words such as training, salary, qualification, skills, career and profession all fit a conversation about a future career.
questions.misconception: Choosing words that do not fit the career topic.

questions.stem: Write five sentences asking and answering questions about a topic of your choice (for example 'My future career' or 'My school holidays'). Use at least three words from the topic vocabulary in your sentences.
hints: Choose a topic you know well.
Use at least three topic words, such as 'training', 'salary' and 'skills'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes five clear question-and-answer sentences on one topic, using at least three topic-specific words.

criteria.description: Writes five sentences in question-and-answer form
All sentences relate to one topic
Uses at least three topic-specific words

questions.stem: In pairs, hold a one-minute conversation about 'My school holidays'. Use at least two topic words (such as 'travel', 'visit', 'journey' or 'relatives').
hints: Choose topic words you understand well.
Use them naturally in the conversation.
questions.explanation: The pair holds a clear conversation on the topic and uses at least two topic words naturally.

criteria.description: Holds a conversation on the topic
Uses at least two topic words

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Employ Think Aloud and visualisation strategies to make meaning from level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Use the Think-Aloud strategy to say aloud what one is thinking while listening
Create a mental picture of what is heard and describe it
Construct meaning from a text heard using the two strategies
Explain how Think-Aloud or visualisation helped make meaning

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (describe a mental picture; state a thought while listening), 35% medium (construct meaning from a short text), 15% harder (explain how the strategy helped). Short texts are provided in the stems.
misconceptions: Thinking Think-Aloud means reading the text aloud rather than sharing thoughts
Visualising details not in the text (adding invented content)
Believing visualisation is only for pictures, not for words heard
Reporting the strategy name without showing its use

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The market was noisy and full of people.' Which Think-Aloud thought shows you are making meaning?
options: I can see a busy market with many people talking and selling.
hints: Think-Aloud means saying what you picture or understand.
Which thought shows you have understood the scene?
questions.explanation: The first option shows the pupil making a mental picture of the market, which is a Think-Aloud thought about meaning.
questions.misconception: Confusing counting words or describing the teacher's voice with making meaning.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The sun rose over the hills.' Write one Think-Aloud thought you could say about this sentence.
answer: i can see the sun coming up over the hills
i can see orange light on the hills
i think it is morning now
i can imagine the sun rising slowly
i see the sun over the hills
hints: Say what you picture in your mind.
Say what the sentence tells you about the time.
questions.explanation: A good Think-Aloud thought describes what the pupil pictures or understands from the sentence.
questions.misconception: Repeating the sentence word for word without adding a thought.

questions.stem: You hear: 'The pupils were excited about the football match.' Which Think-Aloud thought shows you are making meaning?
options: I wonder why they were excited and what the match is about.
hints: Think-Aloud includes wondering and predicting.
Which thought shows you are trying to make sense of the sentence?
questions.explanation: Wondering why the pupils are excited shows that the pupil is actively making meaning, which is what Think-Aloud aims for.
questions.misconception: Thinking letter or word counts count as making meaning.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a short paragraph. While listening, say aloud one thought that comes to you about what is happening.
hints: Say what you picture or wonder.
Do not repeat the paragraph word for word.
questions.explanation: The pupil shares a thought aloud while listening that shows active meaning-making.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'Ama looked at the dark clouds and hurried home.' Write two Think-Aloud thoughts that show how you are making meaning.
hints: Think about why Ama hurried home.
Predict what might happen next.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives two thoughts such as 'I think it is going to rain' and 'Ama wants to reach home before the rain'.

criteria.description: Thoughts relate to the sentence read

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'A yellow taxi stopped in front of the school gate.' Which picture matches the sentence?
options: A yellow car at a school gate.
A green tro-tro on a highway.
A blue boat at the beach.
A red bicycle at the market.
hints: Look for the colour and place named.
The vehicle is yellow and it is at a school.
questions.explanation: The sentence mentions a yellow taxi at the school gate, so the correct picture matches those details.
questions.misconception: Choosing a picture that matches only one word from the sentence.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The rain fell hard on the rusty roof of the old house.' Describe the picture you see in your mind in one or two sentences.
answer: i see an old house with rain falling on a rusty roof
i picture rain beating down on a rusty roof
i see an old broken house in heavy rain
i imagine a small house with a rusty roof and heavy rain
i see water splashing on a rusty old roof
hints: Mention what you see, hear and feel.
Use the words from the sentence as clues.
questions.explanation: A good visualisation uses the words from the sentence to create a clear, detailed mental picture.
questions.misconception: Describing a house that is not part of the sentence or leaving out the rain.

questions.stem: You hear: 'The old fisherman pulled a big silver fish from his net.' Which picture is best?
options: An old man with a silver fish in a net.
A boy catching a small fish with a hook.
A young woman swimming in the sea.
A dog running on the beach.
hints: Look for the age and the object mentioned.
The fisherman is old and the fish is silver.
questions.explanation: The correct picture shows an old man, a silver fish and a net, which are all mentioned in the sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing a picture that matches only one detail.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a short paragraph about a busy market. Describe to the class the picture you see in your mind.
hints: Think about colours, sounds and people.
Use words from the paragraph.
questions.explanation: The pupil describes a clear mental picture that matches the paragraph.

questions.stem: Your teacher reads: 'The children ran laughing down the green hill while the wind blew through their hair.' Write three sentences describing the picture you see in your mind.
hints: Mention the hill, the children's laughter and the wind.
Use the words from the sentence as clues.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes three clear details that fit the sentence (green hill, running children, wind).

questions.stem: You hear: 'Adjoa's mother was sick, so Adjoa cooked dinner and swept the house.' What does this tell you about Adjoa?
options: She is lazy and does not help.
She is angry with her mother.
She is too young to help.
hints: What did Adjoa do when her mother was sick?
Think about what her actions tell you about her character.
questions.explanation: Adjoa helped when her mother was sick, showing she is helpful and responsible.
questions.misconception: Choosing a character trait that contradicts Adjoa's actions.

questions.stem: You hear: 'Kwame looked at his torn school bag and sighed.' What do you think Kwame is feeling?
answer: he is sad about his bag
hints: A sigh often shows a feeling.
Why would a torn bag make someone sigh?
questions.explanation: Looking at a torn bag and sighing shows that Kwame is sad or worried about the bag.
questions.misconception: Answering with a physical action instead of a feeling.

questions.stem: You hear: 'The pupils whispered and pointed at the new teacher.' What does this suggest?
options: The pupils were curious about the new teacher.
The pupils were angry with the new teacher.
The pupils did not see the new teacher.
hints: Whispering and pointing show something about attention.
Why do people whisper and point?
questions.explanation: Whispering and pointing show the pupils were curious about the new teacher.
questions.misconception: Choosing a feeling that is not shown by the action.

questions.stem: You hear: 'Kofi counted his coins again and again, but they were still not enough for the football.' What does the sentence tell you about Kofi and his situation? Write two sentences.
hints: Why is Kofi counting his coins again and again?
What does 'still not enough' tell you about his feelings?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says Kofi really wants the football and is disappointed that he cannot afford it.

criteria.description: Explains Kofi's wish for the football

questions.stem: Your teacher reads a short passage about a hungry family. Tell the class what you think the passage is mainly about.
hints: What is the main problem?
Say it in one or two sentences.
questions.explanation: The pupil states the main idea of the passage, showing constructed meaning.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I pictured the yellow taxi at the gate, and that helped me understand where the story was taking place.' Which strategy is the pupil describing?
hints: The pupil pictured something in their mind.
The strategy is named after creating a mental picture.
questions.explanation: Picturing something in the mind is visualisation. That is the strategy the pupil is describing.
questions.misconception: Confusing visualisation with spelling or reading aloud.

questions.stem: Explain in one sentence how visualisation helps you understand a story you hear.
answer: it helps me picture the story in my mind
it helps me see what is happening
it makes the story feel real
it helps me understand what the words mean
it helps me imagine the characters and places
it helps me follow the story
hints: What do you do in your mind when you visualise?
How does that help your understanding?
questions.explanation: Visualisation helps the listener picture the story, which makes the words easier to understand and remember.
questions.misconception: Answering with 'it helps me read' rather than with how it helps understanding.

questions.stem: During a story, a pupil says: 'I wonder why the girl is crying. Maybe she lost something.' Which strategy is the pupil using?
hints: The pupil is saying their thoughts aloud.
Which strategy is about sharing thoughts while listening?
questions.explanation: Sharing thoughts aloud while listening is the Think-Aloud strategy. The pupil is also making a prediction.
questions.misconception: Confusing Think-Aloud with visualisation.

questions.stem: Write three sentences explaining how you use the Think-Aloud and visualisation strategies when listening to a story.
hints: Explain what Think-Aloud means in your own words.
Explain what visualisation means.
Say how each strategy helps you.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains each strategy and how it helps understanding in three clear sentences.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Relate the sequence of events (E.g. beginning, middle and end)stories/drama/texts

skills.description: Identify events at the beginning, middle and end of a story, drama or text heard
Arrange events in the correct order
Relate the sequence of events to the whole story, drama or text
Identify the plot structure of a story heard

spec.difficultyPlan: 55% easy (identify beginning, middle or end), 30% medium (order events), 15% harder (relate sequence to the whole). Stories are short and printed in the stems.
misconceptions: Confusing the middle with the end
Ordering events by when they were heard rather than when they happened
Thinking every story has only three events
Giving a summary instead of a sequence

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Ama woke up early. She swept the compound. She fetched water from the well. Then she went to school.' What did Ama do first?
options: She fetched water from the well.
hints: Which event begins the story?
The word 'first' refers to the very start.
questions.explanation: The story begins with Ama waking up early. That is the first event.
questions.misconception: Choosing the most interesting event instead of the first one.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Kojo planted maize. He watered the plants every day. The maize grew tall. He harvested it with his family.' What is the ending of the story?
options: He harvested it with his family.
hints: The ending comes after all the other events.
What happens after the maize is fully grown?
questions.explanation: The harvest is the last event, so 'He harvested it with his family' is the ending.
questions.misconception: Choosing the middle event (the maize growing tall) as the ending.

questions.stem: Story heard: 'Adjoa lost her pencil. She searched her bag. She found it in her pocket.' What is the middle event of this story?
answer: she looked in her bag for the pencil
hints: The middle event comes after the pencil is lost.
It comes before the pencil is found.
questions.explanation: After losing the pencil, Adjoa searches her bag before finding it in her pocket. That search is the middle event.
questions.misconception: Choosing the beginning (losing the pencil) or the ending (finding it) as the middle.

questions.stem: After listening to a short story, tell the class what happened at the beginning, in the middle and at the end.
hints: Say one clear event for each part.
Keep your answer in the order of the story.
questions.explanation: The pupil states one event from each part of the story in the correct order.

criteria.description: Gives one event from the beginning
Gives one event from the middle
Gives one event from the ending

questions.stem: Four events from a story are jumbled: A. Adjoa found the purse. B. She went to the head teacher. C. The owner was found. D. The owner thanked Adjoa. Which order is correct?
hints: Start with what Adjoa found.
The thanks come last.
questions.explanation: The natural order is: Adjoa finds the purse, takes it to the head teacher, the owner is found, and the owner thanks Adjoa.
questions.misconception: Ordering by what feels important rather than by time.

questions.stem: Arrange these events in the correct order: A. The rain stopped. B. Dark clouds gathered. C. The children played outside. Write the letters in order.
hints: Clouds come first.
Children play after the rain stops.
questions.explanation: Clouds gather first, then the rain stops, then the children play. So the order is B, A, C.
questions.misconception: Ordering by length of the sentences rather than by events.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kwame walked to the market. He bought tomatoes. On his way home, it began to rain. He ran all the way home.' Which sentence should come first in a retelling?
options: He ran all the way home.
hints: The story starts with Kwame's journey.
What did he do before he bought the tomatoes?
questions.explanation: The story starts with Kwame walking to the market, so that is the first event in the retelling.
questions.misconception: Choosing the event that comes second or later.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi made a greeting card for her mother. She drew flowers on it. She hid it under her mother's pillow. Her mother found it and smiled.' Write the events in the correct order using sentences.
hints: Start with Esi making the card.
End with the mother finding it.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes the four events in order: making the card, drawing flowers, hiding it, mother finding it.

criteria.description: Events are in the correct order

questions.stem: After listening to a short story, arrange the main events in the correct order and tell them to the class.
hints: First list the events in your head.
Then say them one by one in the correct order.
questions.explanation: The pupil arranges the main events in the correct order and tells them clearly.

criteria.description: Puts them in the correct order

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama lost her book. She searched everywhere. A kind classmate lent her a book. Ama was happy again.' Why is the classmate's action important in the story?
options: It solves the problem that Ama faced in the story.
It happens before the story begins.
It is not important at all.
hints: What was Ama's problem?
Who solved the problem?
questions.explanation: Ama's problem is that she lost her book. The classmate's kindness solves that problem, so it is an important part of the story.
questions.misconception: Choosing an event because of its position rather than its role in the story.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo's mother sent him to the market. He lost the money. He cried. A trader helped him find it. He bought the food and went home.' Why does Kojo's crying matter to the story?
answer: it shows how sad he was
it leads to the trader helping him
it shows he had lost the money
hints: Think about what Kojo's crying tells the listener.
How does his crying lead to what happens next?
questions.explanation: Kojo's crying shows the problem and makes the trader's help meaningful. It is an important part of the sequence.
questions.misconception: Answering that the crying is just an action with no role in the story.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi worked hard in the garden. She watered the plants. At harvest, the vegetables were big and healthy. Her family ate well for weeks.' How do the events show the message of the story?
options: The story shows that the family was greedy.
The story shows that hard work brings reward.
The story shows that gardens are small.
The story shows that the family was angry.
hints: Think about what Esi's work led to.
What did the family enjoy at the end?
questions.explanation: Esi's hard work leads to big vegetables and food for her family, showing that hard work brings reward.
questions.misconception: Choosing an interpretation that does not fit the sequence of events.

questions.stem: Story: 'Adjoa wanted a new bag. She saved every coin for months. She finally bought the bag. She was very happy.' Explain how the events in this story are connected in three sentences.
hints: How does saving connect to buying the bag?
What does buying the bag lead to?
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains the chain: Adjoa wanted the bag, so she saved, which allowed her to buy the bag, which made her happy.

criteria.description: Explains how the events are connected
Identifies cause and effect between events

questions.stem: Story: 'Kwame wanted a football. He had no money. He worked for a neighbour to earn money. He bought the football.' What is the problem in this story?
options: Kwame had no football and no money.
hints: The problem is what the character must solve.
What did Kwame want and what was he missing?
questions.explanation: Kwame wants a football but has no money. That is the problem that drives the story.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail rather than the central problem.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama saw a dog. The dog had hurt its leg. Ama took the dog home and bandaged it. The dog was safe.' What is the ending of the story?
hints: The ending tells how the story turns out.
What happened after Ama helped the dog?
questions.explanation: The story ends with the dog being safe, which is the resolution of the story.
questions.misconception: Choosing the problem (the hurt leg) rather than the ending.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi lost his way in the market. He sat down and cried. A woman asked him where he lived and took him home.' What is the middle of this story?
answer: he lost his way and cried
he could not find his way home
hints: The middle is the problem.
What made Kofi cry?
questions.explanation: The middle of the story is when Kofi loses his way and cries, which is the problem the woman helps to solve.
questions.misconception: Choosing the ending (woman takes him home) as the middle.

questions.stem: Story: 'Esi was afraid to sing in public. Her teacher encouraged her. Esi practised every day. On the day of the concert, she sang beautifully. Everyone clapped.' Write the beginning, middle and ending of this story in three short lines.
hints: What was Esi's problem at the start?
What did she do in the middle?
How did it end?
questions.explanation: The beginning is Esi's fear, the middle is her practice and encouragement, and the ending is her successful performance and applause.

criteria.description: Writes a beginning that sets up the problem
Writes a middle that develops the story
Writes an ending that resolves the story

questions.stem: After listening to a short story, tell the class the problem the character faced and how it was solved.
hints: State the problem first.
Then say how it was solved.
questions.explanation: The pupil states the problem clearly and explains how it was resolved.

criteria.description: Explains how the problem was solved

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Ask relevant questions to improve on understanding of moral lesson in text.

skills.description: Identify the moral lesson in a story, drama or text heard
Identify characters and their roles in the text
Identify the setting of the story or text
Ask relevant questions to improve understanding of the moral lesson

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify moral, characters or setting), 35% medium (ask relevant questions), 15% harder (ask questions that deepen understanding of the moral). Texts kept short and value-based.
misconceptions: Stating the plot as the moral lesson
Asking questions already answered in the text
Confusing the setting with the characters
Asking only yes or no questions

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo found a wallet with money. He took it to the head teacher. The owner was found and thanked him.' What is the moral lesson of this story?
options: Money should never be picked up.
Head teachers keep all lost items.
hints: What did Kojo do with the wallet?
What did that action show?
questions.explanation: Kojo was honest by returning the wallet, so the moral lesson is that honesty is the best policy.
questions.misconception: Choosing a message that contradicts the story's action.

questions.stem: Story: 'A girl laughed at a new pupil's old shoes. The new pupil cried. The teacher told the girl that kind words are better than unkind ones.' What is the moral lesson?
options: New pupils should stay away from others.
Be kind to others and do not mock them.
hints: What did the girl do that was wrong?
What did the teacher say was better?
questions.explanation: The teacher corrected the girl for laughing at the new pupil. The moral is to be kind to others and not mock them.
questions.misconception: Choosing a lesson about shoes rather than about kindness.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi worked hard on his farm every day. When harvest came, he had more than enough food, and he shared with his neighbours.' What is the moral lesson of this story?
answer: work hard and share with others
hard work and generosity are rewarded
share what you have with others
hints: What did Kofi do every day?
What did his hard work lead to?
questions.explanation: Kofi worked hard and shared the results. The moral lesson is that hard work pays and generosity matters.
questions.misconception: Answering 'farming' or 'food' instead of the lesson.

questions.stem: Story: 'A boy was always late for school. One day he missed an important test. From the next week, he woke up early every day and was never late again.' What is the moral lesson?
options: Lateness has consequences, so learn from your mistakes.
Waking up early is bad for pupils.
It is fine to be late sometimes.
hints: What happened when the boy was late?
What did he do afterwards?
questions.explanation: The boy suffered a consequence and changed his behaviour. The moral lesson is that lateness has consequences and we should learn from our mistakes.
questions.misconception: Choosing a lesson that ignores the consequence in the story.

questions.stem: Story: 'A girl saw an old woman struggling with a heavy basket. She helped her carry it all the way home. The old woman thanked her, and the girl felt happy.' Write the moral lesson of this story in two sentences.
hints: What did the girl do for the old woman?
What did she feel afterwards?
questions.explanation: A strong answer says the moral lesson is that helping others is good and brings happiness.

criteria.description: Moral lesson relates to helping others

questions.stem: Story: 'Akua found a lost book. She took it to the library. The librarian thanked her and returned it to the owner.' Who are the characters in this story?
hints: Characters are the people in the story.
Which two people act in the story?
questions.explanation: The characters are Akua, who found the book, and the librarian, who helped return it. A library and a book are not characters.
questions.misconception: Confusing objects or places with characters.

questions.stem: Story: 'Kofi lost his bag. A kind girl found it and gave it back. Kofi thanked her.' What is the role of the girl in the story?
options: She found the bag and returned it.
She kept the bag for herself.
She took the bag to the market.
hints: What did she do with the bag?
Her action is helpful.
questions.explanation: The girl found the bag and returned it to Kofi, which is her role in the story.
questions.misconception: Confusing the girl's action with Kofi's or with another character's.

questions.stem: Story: 'Musah and his friends were playing football. The ball went over the wall. Musah's mother told him to ask the neighbour for the ball.' What role does Musah's mother play in the story?
answer: she tells musah what to do
she tells him to ask the neighbour
hints: What does she say to Musah?
How does her advice help the story?
questions.explanation: Musah's mother gives advice that helps him solve the problem, so her role is to guide him.
questions.misconception: Answering with what Musah did instead of what his mother did.

questions.stem: Story: 'Adjoa found a wallet. She took it to the police station. The police officer contacted the owner. The owner thanked Adjoa.' Describe the role of each of the three characters in the story in three sentences.
hints: Say what Adjoa did.
Say what the police officer did.
Say what the owner did.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes each character's role: Adjoa found and reported the wallet, the officer contacted the owner, and the owner thanked Adjoa.

questions.stem: After listening to a short story, tell the class who the main character is and what they do in the story.
hints: The main character is the one the story follows.
Say what they do and how their actions affect the story.
questions.explanation: The pupil names the main character and describes their actions clearly.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama was walking to school when she found the purse. She took it to the head teacher's office.' Where does the story take place?
hints: Where was Ama walking?
Where did she take the purse?
questions.explanation: Ama was walking to school and took the purse to the head teacher's office, so the setting is at school.
questions.misconception: Choosing any place mentioned in a typical story rather than the one in this story.

questions.stem: Story: 'The fishermen pulled their nets onto the sandy shore as the sun set over the sea.' What is the setting of the story?
hints: Fishermen, nets and the sea give a clear clue.
Where would you find these things?
questions.explanation: Fishermen, nets, a sandy shore and the sea all point to a beach near the sea.
questions.misconception: Confusing the sea with other water bodies or settings.

questions.stem: Story: 'The noisy market was full of traders calling out their prices. The smell of fresh fish filled the air.' What is the setting of this story?
hints: Where would you find traders calling out prices?
What place smells of fresh fish?
questions.explanation: Traders, prices and fresh fish point to a market setting.
questions.misconception: Answering with an object like 'fish' instead of the place.

questions.stem: Story: 'The children gathered under the big mango tree. They sang songs and played games until the sun went down.' Describe the setting of the story in two sentences. Explain how you know.
hints: Where do the children gather?
What time of day is it?
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the mango tree setting and says the clues are the tree, songs, games and sunset.

criteria.description: Explains how the clues show the setting

questions.stem: Story: 'Kojo found a purse. He took it to the head teacher. The owner was found.' Which question helps you understand the moral lesson better?
options: Why did Kojo decide to take the purse to the head teacher?
How many pupils were in the school?
What is the head teacher's name?
hints: A question about the moral lesson should ask about reasons or values.
Which question asks about Kojo's choice?
questions.explanation: Asking why Kojo took the purse to the head teacher helps us understand the moral lesson about honesty.
questions.misconception: Asking about irrelevant details rather than the reason behind the action.

questions.stem: Story: 'Ama helped an old woman carry her basket. The old woman thanked her.' Write one question that would help you understand the moral lesson better.
answer: why did ama help the old woman
what does this teach us about kindness
what is the lesson of the story
how did ama feel after helping
what can we learn from ama
what made ama help the old woman
hints: Ask about the reason or the lesson.
Questions starting with 'why' or 'what can we learn' help.
questions.explanation: Questions about the reason for helping or the lesson of the story help deepen understanding of the moral.
questions.misconception: Asking about irrelevant details (e.g. the old woman's age).

questions.stem: Story: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom together. They finished quickly and played after.' Which question deepens your understanding of the moral lesson?
options: Why was the cleaning finished quickly?
How many pupils were in the class?
hints: The moral is about working together.
Which question links the quick finish to the lesson?
questions.explanation: Asking why the cleaning was finished quickly links the action to the moral lesson about teamwork.
questions.misconception: Choosing a question about a detail that does not affect the moral.

questions.stem: Story: 'Adjoa was always polite. She greeted everyone she met. People loved her and helped her whenever she needed it.' Write three questions that would help you understand the moral lesson of this story more deeply.
hints: Ask why the story ends the way it does.
Ask what the story teaches about politeness.
Ask what we can learn from Adjoa.
questions.explanation: A strong answer asks three questions about reasons and lessons, such as why people helped Adjoa, what politeness brings, and what we can learn from her.

criteria.description: Questions focus on the moral lesson
Questions ask about reasons or lessons, not irrelevant details

questions.stem: After listening to a story about a boy who told the truth even when it was hard, ask the class one question that would deepen everyone's understanding of the moral lesson.
hints: Ask about the boy's choice.
Ask what the story teaches us.
questions.explanation: The pupil asks a clear question about the reasons or lesson of the story to deepen understanding.

criteria.description: Asks a question about the moral lesson

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Use background knowledge to understand and build new knowledge while listening to informational text

skills.description: Activate background knowledge before listening (K and W of KWL)
Link background knowledge to new information in the text
Identify the main ideas of an informational text heard
Share what was newly learnt from the text (L of KWL)

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (state what is already known; identify one main idea), 35% medium (link known to new), 15% harder (share new knowledge clearly). Informational texts are short and printed in the stems, on familiar topics such as health, environment, school and community.
misconceptions: Treating background knowledge as the whole answer and ignoring the text
Confusing 'what I know' with 'what I learnt'
Listing details instead of main ideas
Rejecting new information that differs from prior belief

questions.stem: Before listening to a talk about keeping the school clean, which question best activates your background knowledge?
options: What do I already know about keeping a place clean?
How many pupils are in my class?
hints: Activating background knowledge means thinking about what you already know.
Which question connects to the topic of cleanliness?
questions.explanation: Asking what you already know about cleanliness activates background knowledge and prepares you to link it to the new talk.
questions.misconception: Thinking background knowledge activation is about unrelated personal details.

questions.stem: Your teacher is about to read an informational text about malaria. Write one thing you already know about malaria.
answer: malaria is caused by mosquito bites
malaria makes people sick with fever
we should sleep under mosquito nets
it is spread by female anopheles mosquitoes
hints: Think about how malaria is spread.
Think about how we prevent it.
questions.explanation: Any correct statement about malaria (its cause, symptoms, prevention) shows activated background knowledge.
questions.misconception: Giving a statement unrelated to malaria.

questions.stem: Before listening to a text about the water cycle, which question from the 'W' of KWL would best guide your listening?
options: What did I eat for lunch?
What do I want to learn about how water moves?
How many words are in the text?
hints: The 'W' in KWL stands for 'Want to know'.
Which question asks about the content of the text?
questions.explanation: The 'W' question asks what the pupil wants to learn about the water cycle, which guides listening.
questions.misconception: Confusing the W question with unrelated personal or technical questions.

questions.stem: Your teacher is about to read a text about road safety. Write two things you already know about road safety (K) and two things you want to know (W).
hints: The K column lists what you already know.
The W column lists what you want to learn.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists two known facts and two questions about what they want to learn.

criteria.description: Writes two questions to find out

questions.stem: You already know that washing your hands keeps you healthy. Your teacher reads: 'Washing your hands before eating prevents germs from entering your body.' How does this link to what you already know?
options: It adds a reason to what I already know.
It has nothing to do with what I know.
It tells me to stop washing my hands.
hints: The new information gives a reason for the old information.
Do the two ideas agree or disagree?
questions.explanation: The new information adds a reason (preventing germs) to what the pupil already knew about hand washing.
questions.misconception: Thinking new information must contradict prior knowledge.

questions.stem: You know that trees give shade. Your teacher reads: 'Trees also help prevent soil erosion.' How does this new information connect to what you already know about trees?
answer: it adds a new benefit of trees
it shows trees are more useful than i thought
it adds another reason trees are important
it connects because both are about trees being useful
