it adds to my knowledge about trees
hints: The new information is another benefit of trees.
Does it contradict or add to what you know?
questions.explanation: The new information adds to what the pupil already knows by showing another benefit of trees.
questions.misconception: Thinking new information must replace old information.

questions.stem: You know that exercise keeps the body fit. Your teacher reads: 'Regular exercise also helps the mind to stay sharp and happy.' Write three sentences explaining how this new information connects to what you already know.
hints: State what you already knew.
State the new information.
Explain how the two are linked.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states prior knowledge, the new information and how they connect (both about the benefits of exercise).

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Malaria is spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It causes fever and headaches. People can prevent malaria by sleeping under treated mosquito nets.' What is the main idea?
options: Malaria is caused by mosquitoes and can be prevented.
hints: The main idea covers all the sentences.
Which idea connects the cause and the prevention?
questions.explanation: The text explains that malaria is spread by mosquitoes and can be prevented, which is the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Keeping the environment clean helps us stay healthy. Rubbish attracts flies and rats. These animals can bring diseases. We should throw rubbish in bins and keep our surroundings tidy.' What is the main idea?
options: Flies and rats live in rubbish.
Keeping the environment clean helps us stay healthy.
hints: The first sentence often states the main idea.
What does the whole text teach us to do?
questions.explanation: The whole text is about keeping the environment clean for good health, which is the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail (flies and rats) instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Eating a balanced diet gives the body all the nutrients it needs. It includes fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins. A balanced diet helps children grow strong and healthy.' What is the main idea of this text?
answer: a balanced diet is good for health
eating a balanced diet keeps children healthy
a balanced diet helps children grow strong
balanced diet is important for health
eating healthy food helps us grow
hints: What does the whole text talk about?
What does a balanced diet do for children?
questions.explanation: The main idea is that eating a balanced diet is good for the body and helps children grow strong and healthy.
questions.misconception: Listing the types of food mentioned instead of stating the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Reading is important for many reasons. It improves our vocabulary and helps us learn new things. It also allows us to travel to different places without leaving our seats. Reading for fun can be a great hobby.' Write the main idea of this text in one sentence, then two supporting details.
hints: The main idea covers the whole text.
Supporting details give specific reasons.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the main idea (reading is important) and gives two supporting details from the text.

questions.stem: You knew that trees give shade. After listening to a text about trees, you learn that trees also help hold the soil in place. Which statement correctly shares your new knowledge?
options: Trees give shade and also help hold the soil in place.
Trees have nothing to do with soil.
Trees are only important for birds.
hints: New knowledge adds to what you already knew.
Which statement shows the new information you learnt?
questions.explanation: The new knowledge adds that trees hold the soil in place, so the correct statement combines the old and new knowledge.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the new information or replacing what was already known.

questions.stem: After listening to a text on hand washing, write one new fact you learnt.
answer: we should wash hands before eating
we should wash hands after using the toilet
germs are too small to see
hints: Think about one specific new fact from the text.
It should be a fact you did not know before.
questions.explanation: Any specific new fact learnt from the text on hand washing is correct.
questions.misconception: Restating something that was already known instead of new knowledge.

questions.stem: You did not know that mosquitoes breed in standing water. After a text on malaria prevention, you learn this fact. Which question could you now answer that you could not answer before?
options: How many legs does a mosquito have?
How fast can a mosquito fly?
hints: The new fact is about where mosquitoes breed.
Which question does the new fact answer?
questions.explanation: The new fact about standing water answers the question 'Where do mosquitoes breed?', which the pupil did not know before.
questions.misconception: Choosing a question that is not answered by the new fact.

questions.stem: After listening to a text about road safety, write three sentences sharing what you already knew, what you learnt, and why the new knowledge matters.
hints: Start with what you already knew.
State one new fact.
Explain why that fact matters.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states prior knowledge, one new fact from the text and the importance of that new knowledge.

criteria.description: Explains why the new knowledge matters

questions.stem: After listening to a short text about keeping the environment clean, share with the class one new fact you learnt and one fact you already knew.
hints: Say the new fact first, then the fact you already knew.
Use complete sentences.
questions.explanation: The pupil shares one new fact and one prior fact about the environment clearly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Express own opinions about the details of texts

skills.description: Identify details in a story, drama or text heard
Form a personal opinion about the details of a text
Express the opinion clearly and respectfully
Give a reason for the opinion based on the text

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify details), 35% medium (state an opinion), 20% harder (support opinion with a reason). Texts are short and value-based.
misconceptions: Stating a fact as an opinion
Giving an opinion with no reason
Using disrespectful language when disagreeing
Confusing the author's opinion with one's own

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Adjoa found a wallet on her way to school. She took it to the head teacher. The owner was found and thanked her.' What detail is given about Adjoa?
options: She found a wallet on her way to school.
She found a bag in the market.
hints: Where was Adjoa going?
What did she find?
questions.explanation: The text states that Adjoa found a wallet on her way to school.
questions.misconception: Confusing the details with a similar but different event.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Kojo's mother was sick. He cooked and fetched water. He also swept the compound. In the evening, he read his notes.' Write two things Kojo did for his mother.
answer: he cooked and he fetched water
hints: Focus on the actions done for his mother.
Any two of his tasks are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Kojo cooked, fetched water and swept the compound. Any two of these tasks are correct.
questions.misconception: Including reading his notes (done for himself, not for his mother).

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils of Adenta Basic School cleaned the compound every Friday. They planted trees and swept the yard. At the end of the term, they won the cleanest school award.' Why did the pupils win the award?
options: They cleaned the compound and planted trees.
hints: The award is for cleanliness.
What actions made the school clean?
questions.explanation: The pupils cleaned the compound and planted trees, which earned them the cleanest school award.
questions.misconception: Choosing an action that has nothing to do with cleanliness.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Esi and her brother walked to the market. Esi bought tomatoes and onions. Her brother bought pepper. They carried their goods home in a basket.' Write three details from this text.
hints: Focus on what they bought and how they carried their goods.
Write three clear details from the text.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three specific details (e.g. they walked to the market, Esi bought tomatoes and onions, they carried goods in a basket).

criteria.description: Details are accurate to the text

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Kofi refused to share his food with a hungry friend.' Which statement is an opinion about this detail?
options: Kofi refused to share his food.
Kofi was unkind to refuse to share.
hints: An opinion tells what someone thinks or feels.
A fact can be checked; an opinion is a personal view.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi was unkind' is a personal judgment, while the other statements are facts that can be checked in the text.
questions.misconception: Confusing a fact from the text with an opinion about the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Ama helped an old woman carry her basket to the market.' Write one opinion you have about Ama's action.
hints: An opinion tells what you think about her action.
Use words like 'good', 'kind' or 'right'.
questions.explanation: Any opinion that expresses a judgment about Ama's helpful action is correct.
questions.misconception: Restating the fact (Ama helped) without giving an opinion about it.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils had to clean the classroom during break instead of playing.' Which of these is a personal opinion?
options: The pupils should be allowed to play sometimes too.
hints: An opinion says what should or could be different.
Which option is a personal view about fairness?
questions.explanation: Saying pupils 'should be allowed to play sometimes too' is a personal opinion. The other options are facts from the text.
questions.misconception: Choosing a factual statement as an opinion.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Akua laughed at a new pupil because of her old sandals.' Write two opinions you have about Akua's behaviour and one fact from the text.
hints: One sentence should state a fact.
Two sentences should give your opinion.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the fact (Akua laughed at the new pupil) and two opinions (e.g. that it was unkind and that she should apologise).

criteria.description: States one fact from the text
Gives two opinions about the behaviour
Opinions are clearly different from the fact

questions.stem: Text heard: 'A classmate always finishes his homework but refuses to help others.' Which statement expresses your opinion respectfully?
options: He is the worst pupil in the class.
I think he should help others sometimes.
hints: Respectful opinions avoid rude or insulting words.
Which statement uses 'I think' and suggests a solution?
questions.explanation: 'I think he should help others sometimes' expresses an opinion respectfully without insulting anyone.
questions.misconception: Thinking strong insults count as clear opinions.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Ama gave her only pencil to a classmate who had none.' Express your opinion about her action in one polite sentence.
answer: i think ama did a very kind thing
in my opinion ama was generous
i believe ama did the right thing
i think it was very kind of ama
i think ama is a good friend
hints: Use 'I think' or 'In my opinion'.
Keep the language polite.
questions.explanation: A polite opinion about Ama's generosity uses phrases like 'I think' or 'In my opinion'.
questions.misconception: Expressing an opinion without polite or respectful language.

questions.stem: After listening to a story where a pupil refused to share, tell the class your opinion respectfully.
hints: Say 'I think' or 'In my opinion'.
Avoid insulting the character.
questions.explanation: The pupil expresses a clear, respectful opinion about the character's action.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils cleaned the market square on Saturday instead of going to the beach.' Write three sentences expressing your opinion about this. Use respectful language.
hints: Start with 'I think' or 'In my opinion'.
Give your view clearly and respectfully.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives a clear opinion, uses respectful language and keeps to the topic in three sentences.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Adjoa returned a wallet she found.' You say: 'I think Adjoa did the right thing.' Which reason best supports this opinion?
options: Returning what is not yours is honest.
hints: The reason must support the opinion.
Why is returning a wallet the right thing to do?
questions.explanation: The reason 'returning what is not yours is honest' directly supports the opinion that Adjoa did the right thing.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated detail from the text as a reason.

questions.stem: You think Kojo should have told the truth earlier. Write one reason from the text that supports your opinion. Text: 'Kojo hid the broken vase for three days. His sister was blamed unfairly.'
answer: his sister was punished for something she did not do
his sister suffered for his mistake
she was blamed for what kojo did
hints: Look at who was affected by Kojo's silence.
The reason should come from the text.
questions.explanation: Kojo's sister being blamed unfairly is the reason from the text that supports the opinion that Kojo should have told the truth earlier.
questions.misconception: Giving a reason that is not found in the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Esi shared her lunch with a hungry boy.' You say: 'Esi is a generous person.' Which detail from the text supports this opinion?
options: Esi shared her lunch with the hungry boy.
hints: Choose the detail that shows generosity.
Sharing food is the action that shows the trait.
questions.explanation: The action of sharing her lunch with a hungry boy is the detail that supports the opinion that Esi is generous.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that does not show generosity.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'A classmate made fun of a new pupil's English. The new pupil became quiet and stopped speaking in class.' Write three sentences giving your opinion about this and two reasons from the text that support your opinion.
hints: State your opinion clearly.
Give two reasons from the text that support it.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives a clear opinion and supports it with two reasons from the text, such as the new pupil becoming quiet and stopping speaking.

criteria.description: Gives two reasons from the text

questions.stem: After listening to a story, state your opinion about a character's action and give one reason from the story to support it.
hints: State your opinion first.
Give one clear reason from the story.
questions.explanation: The pupil states an opinion and supports it with a reason from the story.

criteria.description: Gives a reason from the story

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Identify the problems and solutions in texts

skills.description: Identify the problem(s) in a text heard
Identify the solution(s) in the text
Analyse causes and effects of the problem
Relate the problem and solution to the events and values in the text

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify problem or solution), 35% medium (analyse cause and effect), 15% harder (relate problem-solution to events and values). Texts are short and on familiar issues such as conflict, waste, lateness and bullying.
misconceptions: Confusing the problem with a character's feeling
Naming a solution not found in the text
Confusing cause with effect
Thinking every text must have only one problem

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils of Adenta Basic School had no clean water. They walked two kilometres to a stream every morning. The water made some of them sick.' What is the problem in this text?
options: The school had no clean water.
hints: The problem is the main difficulty.
Why did the pupils walk to the stream?
questions.explanation: The main problem is that the school had no clean water. The long walk and sickness are effects of that problem.
questions.misconception: Choosing an effect (walking far, sickness) instead of the root problem.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Some pupils in Basic 6 always come late to school. They miss the morning assembly and the first lesson.' What is the problem?
options: The morning assembly is too long.
The pupils are always late to school.
hints: What is the main difficulty in the text?
What happens because of the pupils' behaviour?
questions.explanation: The problem is that the pupils always come late, which causes them to miss assembly and the first lesson.
questions.misconception: Choosing an effect (missing assembly) instead of the root problem.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Two pupils always quarrel during group work. Other pupils refuse to work with them. The group work is never finished on time.' What is the problem in this text?
answer: the pupils fight during group work
the pupils always quarrel during group work
hints: What behaviour is causing the problem?
The problem is what starts the chain of events.
questions.explanation: The problem is that two pupils always quarrel, which makes others refuse to work with them and causes work to be unfinished.
questions.misconception: Answering with the effect (unfinished work) instead of the root problem.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Rubbish is thrown all around Adabraka market. Flies gather on the rubbish. Some traders and buyers get sick. The market is no longer clean.' Write the main problem and two effects of the problem.
hints: The main problem is about rubbish.
Effects follow from the rubbish.
questions.explanation: The main problem is rubbish being thrown all around the market. The effects include flies gathering, people getting sick and the market becoming dirty.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils had no clean water. The head teacher asked the PTA for help. The PTA built a borehole. The pupils now have clean water.' What is the solution in the text?
options: The head teacher asked the PTA for help.
The pupils walked to the stream.
hints: The solution is what actually fixes the problem.
What gives the pupils clean water?
questions.explanation: The solution is the borehole built by the PTA, which gives the pupils clean water.
questions.misconception: Choosing the step taken to find the solution (asking for help) instead of the solution itself.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The classroom was always dusty. The pupils' books got dirty. Their teacher asked them to water the compound before sweeping. The classroom stayed clean afterwards.' What is the solution?
options: The pupils watered the compound before sweeping.
hints: Which action fixed the problem?
The solution comes after the problem.
questions.explanation: Watering the compound before sweeping is the action that fixed the dusty classroom problem.
questions.misconception: Choosing the problem statement instead of the solution.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Some pupils always come late. Their teacher told them to sleep early and set an alarm. The pupils came on time every day after that.' What was the solution to the lateness problem?
answer: sleep early and set an alarm
the pupils slept early and set an alarm
the teacher told them to sleep early
set an alarm and slept early
hints: What did the teacher tell them to do?
What did the pupils do that solved the problem?
questions.explanation: The solution was sleeping early and setting an alarm, which helped the pupils come to school on time.
questions.misconception: Answering with the problem (lateness) instead of the solution.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The school compound was littered with plastic bags. The pupils started a clean-up club. They collected the plastics every Friday and sold them to a recycling company. Within three months, the compound was clean.' Write the solution and two results of the solution.
hints: What did the pupils start?
What were the results of their action?
questions.explanation: The solution is starting a clean-up club and collecting plastics for recycling. The results are a clean compound and earning money.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Rubbish was thrown into the drain. The drain got blocked. Water could not flow, so the compound flooded.' What caused the flooding?
options: The drain was blocked by rubbish.
The pupils played in the water.
hints: Trace the chain of events.
What happened before the flooding?
questions.explanation: Rubbish blocked the drain, which stopped water from flowing, causing the compound to flood.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unstated cause (heavy rain) rather than the cause given in the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils skipped breakfast. They became tired in class. They could not concentrate on the lesson.' What was the effect of skipping breakfast?
options: They became tired and could not concentrate.
hints: What happened after they skipped breakfast?
The effect comes after the cause.
questions.explanation: The effect of skipping breakfast was that the pupils became tired and could not concentrate on the lesson.
questions.misconception: Choosing an event that is not linked to the cause.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Kojo forgot his homework. His teacher was unhappy. He promised to write it that evening.' What caused the teacher to be unhappy?
answer: kojo did not do his homework
he did not bring his homework
kojo forgot to do his homework
he had not done his homework
hints: What did Kojo forget?
The cause comes before the effect.
questions.explanation: The cause of the teacher's unhappiness was Kojo forgetting his homework.
questions.misconception: Answering with the effect (the teacher was unhappy) instead of the cause.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils used to buy sugary drinks every day. Many of them had tooth problems. Their teacher showed them how to make fruit juice. The pupils started drinking fruit juice instead. Their teeth became healthier.' Identify the cause of the tooth problems, the effect, and the cause of the healthier teeth.
hints: What were the pupils drinking before?
What did they change to?
questions.explanation: The cause of tooth problems was drinking sugary drinks daily. The effect was tooth problems. The cause of healthier teeth was switching to fruit juice.

criteria.description: Identifies the cause of the tooth problems
Identifies the cause of healthier teeth

questions.stem: After listening to a short text, tell the class the cause of the main problem and one effect.
hints: Say what started the problem.
Then say one thing that happened because of it.
questions.explanation: The pupil correctly identifies a cause and an effect from the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Adjoa was often late. Her teacher helped her plan her morning routine. Now she wakes up early, eats breakfast and arrives at school on time. She has become a school prefect.' How do the problem and solution relate to the values in the text?
options: Adjoa's lateness and her improvement show the value of hard work and responsibility.
Adjoa's story shows the value of laziness.
Adjoa's story shows that teachers are strict.
Adjoa's story shows that lateness cannot be fixed.
hints: What values does Adjoa's change show?
Which option connects the problem and solution to a value?
questions.explanation: Adjoa's improvement shows responsibility and hard work, connecting the problem and solution to the values in the text.
questions.misconception: Choosing an answer that does not relate the solution to a positive value.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The class was divided and pupils would not help each other. A new pupil suggested they form study groups. Soon, everyone was helping one another and the class did better in exams.' What value does the solution of the story show?
hints: The solution brings pupils together.
Which value is about working as one group?
questions.explanation: The solution of study groups shows unity, teamwork or cooperation.
questions.misconception: Choosing a value that does not match the solution (e.g. honesty).

questions.stem: Text heard: 'A pupil found a wallet and kept it. He was uncomfortable all week. His friend told him to return it. He took the wallet to the head teacher and felt relieved when the owner thanked him.' How do the problem and solution relate to the events and values?
options: Keeping the wallet caused him to be comfortable, and returning it was a mistake.
Keeping the wallet caused him discomfort, and returning it brought relief and showed honesty.
Returning the wallet was too late to make a difference.
The story shows that keeping found things is the right choice.
hints: What happened when he kept the wallet?
What happened when he returned it?
questions.explanation: Keeping the wallet caused discomfort, and returning it brought relief and showed honesty, which connects the problem and solution to the events and values of the text.
questions.misconception: Choosing an answer that contradicts the cause and effect in the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The village had a problem with dirty water. Many people became sick. A nurse taught the villagers to boil water and use clean containers. The sickness reduced. The villagers were grateful.' Write three sentences explaining how the problem and solution are connected to the values in the text.
hints: State the problem.
State the solution and the value it shows.
State the result.
questions.explanation: A strong answer connects the problem to the solution and identifies the value shown (e.g. care, community action, responsibility) and the result.

criteria.description: Identifies a value shown by the solution
Explains how the events connect to the value

questions.stem: After listening to a short text, tell the class the problem, the solution and one value shown by the solution.
hints: State the problem first.
Then state the solution and a value it shows.
questions.explanation: The pupil clearly states the problem, solution and a value linked to the solution.

criteria.description: Identifies a value connected to the solution

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Make simple generalisations based on the main ideas and key details of a text

skills.description: Identify the main ideas of a text heard
Identify key details supporting the main ideas
Make a simple generalisation from the main ideas and key details
Support the generalisation with evidence from the text

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify main ideas and key details), 35% medium (make a simple generalisation), 20% harder (support the generalisation with evidence). Texts are short and informational or value-based.
misconceptions: Making a generalisation from one detail only
Overgeneralising from a single story
Confusing a summary with a generalisation
Giving a generalisation not supported by the text

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Exercise makes the body strong. It helps the heart beat properly. It also keeps the mind fresh. Children who exercise regularly stay healthy.' What is the main idea of this text?
options: The heart beats faster during exercise.
Exercise is good for the body and mind.
The mind is part of the body.
hints: What does the whole text talk about?
Which idea covers all the sentences?
questions.explanation: The main idea is that exercise is good for the body and mind. All the sentences support this idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing one supporting detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. It causes fever and body pain. Children and pregnant women are at risk. Sleeping under treated nets can prevent it.' What is the main idea?
options: Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes that can be prevented.
hints: Which idea links all the details?
The main idea covers spread, symptoms and prevention.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes that can be prevented.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated statement instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Trees give shade. They hold the soil in place. They give us fruits and wood. They also make the air fresh.' Write the main idea of this text.
answer: trees are very important to us
trees help us in many ways
hints: What do all the sentences have in common?
They all describe what trees do for us.
questions.explanation: All the sentences describe what trees give us, so the main idea is that trees are important or useful.
questions.misconception: Listing what trees give (shade, wood) instead of stating the main idea.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Reading is important. It improves our vocabulary. It helps us learn new things. It lets us travel to other places without leaving our seats.' Which of these is a key detail supporting the main idea?
hints: The main idea is 'reading is important'.
Which option gives a reason that supports the main idea?
questions.explanation: 'Reading improves our vocabulary' is a key detail that supports the main idea that reading is important.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general statement rather than a specific supporting detail.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Keeping the environment clean is good for our health. Rubbish attracts flies. Flies spread diseases. We should use bins and keep our surroundings tidy.' Write two key details that support the main idea.
answer: rubbish attracts flies and flies spread diseases
rubbish attracts flies and we should use bins
flies spread diseases and we should use bins
hints: Which details show why cleanliness matters?
Which details tell us what to do?
questions.explanation: Key details that support the main idea include: rubbish attracts flies, flies spread diseases, and we should use bins to keep the environment clean.
questions.misconception: Giving only one detail or giving details not in the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Eating a balanced diet gives the body all the nutrients it needs. It includes fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins. It helps children grow strong and healthy.' Which detail does NOT support the main idea?
options: Fruits and vegetables are part of a balanced diet.
A balanced diet helps children grow strong.
The market sells fresh fish every Tuesday.
hints: Which detail is unrelated to a balanced diet?
The main idea is about balanced diet and health.
questions.explanation: The statement about the market selling fish every Tuesday does not support the main idea about balanced diets.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that is loosely related instead of the unrelated one.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Adjoa studies every day. Kojo studies every day. Esi studies every day. All three pupils pass their tests.' What generalisation can you make from this text?
options: Pupils who study every day are likely to pass their tests.
All pupils in the school pass tests.
Studying does not help pupils pass tests.
hints: Look at what all three pupils have in common.
What result follows from their common behaviour?
questions.explanation: All three pupils study every day and all three pass, so the generalisation is that pupils who study every day are likely to pass.
questions.misconception: Overgeneralising to all pupils in the school.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom. The pupils of Basic 5 cleaned the library. The pupils of Basic 4 cleaned the dining hall. The whole school was clean on Friday.' What generalisation can you make?
options: Only one class can clean the school.
When pupils work together, the whole school can be clean.
The school is always clean every day.
The dining hall is the largest place.
hints: What happened when every class did its part?
Which generalisation follows from the results?
questions.explanation: When each class cleaned a part, the whole school became clean. The generalisation is that when pupils work together, the whole school can be clean.
questions.misconception: Overgeneralising (e.g. saying the school is always clean) without support from the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Rubbish was thrown in the yard. Rubbish was thrown in the drain. Rubbish was thrown near the well. The whole school became dirty and unsafe.' Write one generalisation based on this text.
answer: throwing rubbish everywhere makes a place dirty
throwing rubbish everywhere makes a place unsafe
we should not throw rubbish everywhere
throwing rubbish around makes a place unsafe and dirty
littering makes places dirty and unsafe
keeping the school clean is important
hints: What was the common behaviour in the text?
What was the common result?
questions.explanation: The text shows that littering in different places makes the school dirty and unsafe. So a valid generalisation is that throwing rubbish everywhere makes a place dirty and unsafe.
questions.misconception: Giving a generalisation not connected to the text.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Esi helped an old woman carry her basket. Kojo helped his blind neighbour cross the road. Adjoa helped her sick mother cook.' Write a generalisation based on the text and explain how it fits.
hints: What did all three pupils do?
What generalisation follows from their actions?
questions.explanation: A strong answer generalises that helping others is good, and explains that all three pupils performed acts of kindness.

criteria.description: Explains how the generalisation fits the text

questions.stem: After listening to a text in which several pupils help others, make one generalisation to the class and say why you made it.
hints: State the generalisation clearly.
Explain how it fits the events you heard.
questions.explanation: The pupil states a clear generalisation and explains the basis for it from the text.

criteria.description: Explains why the generalisation is based on the text

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Ama sweeps the school yard. Kojo picks up litter. Esi waters the flowers.' A pupil makes the generalisation: 'Pupils can help keep the school clean.' Which details best support this generalisation?
options: The pupils sweep, pick up litter and water flowers.
hints: Which details show pupils keeping the school clean?
Look for actions related to cleanliness.
questions.explanation: Sweeping, picking up litter and watering flowers are all actions that keep the school clean and support the generalisation.
questions.misconception: Choosing details that do not show cleanliness.

questions.stem: Generalisation: 'Breakfast is important for pupils.' Write one detail from the text that supports this. Text: 'Pupils who ate breakfast were alert in class. Pupils who skipped breakfast were tired and sleepy.'
answer: pupils who ate breakfast were alert
pupils who skipped breakfast were tired
eating breakfast made pupils alert in class
pupils who ate breakfast were more alert
students who skipped breakfast were sleepy
hints: Look for what happened to pupils who ate breakfast.
Look for what happened to pupils who did not.
questions.explanation: The text says pupils who ate breakfast were alert in class, while those who skipped breakfast were tired. Either detail supports the generalisation.
questions.misconception: Giving a detail that does not directly support the generalisation.

questions.stem: Generalisation: 'Regular exercise keeps pupils healthy.' Which detail best supports this?
options: Pupils who exercise every day have fewer sicknesses.
The school has a big field.
hints: Which detail links exercise to health?
Look for a statement about health outcomes.
questions.explanation: The statement that pupils who exercise daily have fewer sicknesses directly supports the generalisation about health.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail about playing sports without a health link.

questions.stem: Text heard: 'Kojo returns lost items. Ama tells the truth even when it is hard. Esi admits her mistakes.' Generalisation: 'Honesty is a quality of good pupils.' Write two details from the text that support this generalisation.
hints: Which actions show honesty?
Copy or paraphrase two details from the text.
questions.explanation: Two details such as 'Kojo returns lost items' and 'Ama tells the truth even when it is hard' support the generalisation about honesty.

questions.stem: After listening to a text, make a generalisation and support it with one detail from the text.
hints: State the generalisation first.
Then give a detail from the text.
questions.explanation: The pupil makes a clear generalisation and supports it with a detail from the text.

criteria.description: Supports it with a detail from the text

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions correctly
indicator.objective: Answer "Yes" or "No" questions correctly using the expressions that show the future

skills.description: Identify future time expressions (tomorrow, next week, next month, later, soon)
Answer yes or no questions about future actions correctly
Use future expressions in answers: Yes, I will / No, I won't
Choose the correct future form (will/won't) to match the question subject

spec.difficultyPlan: 55% easy (identify future expressions; give a yes/no answer), 30% medium (use the correct future expression in the answer), 15% harder (match will/won't correctly with the question subject). Contexts: school, home, market, community, travel.
misconceptions: Answering 'Yes, I do' instead of 'Yes, I will' for future questions
Confusing 'won't' with 'don't'
Using 'will' for past time expressions
Giving only 'Yes' or 'No' without the future expression when the full answer is expected

questions.stem: Which word shows that something will happen in the future?
hints: Future means time that has not come yet.
Which word points to the day after today?
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' refers to a day that has not yet come, so it is a future time expression. 'Yesterday', 'last week' and 'before' refer to the past.
questions.misconception: Confusing past time words with future time words.

questions.stem: Which sentence talks about the future?
options: I will visit my grandmother next week.
I am reading a book now.
I went to the market last Monday.
hints: Look for a future time expression.
Which sentence has 'will' and 'next week'?
questions.explanation: 'I will visit my grandmother next week' uses 'will' and 'next week', which show the future.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence about the past because it sounds familiar.

questions.stem: Write one future time expression you could use in a sentence about school.
hints: Think of a time that has not come yet.
One expression is enough.
questions.explanation: Words such as tomorrow, next week, next month, later and soon all show future time.
questions.misconception: Writing a past time expression such as 'yesterday'.

questions.stem: Write two sentences about what you will do at school tomorrow. Underline the future time expression in each sentence.
hints: Use 'tomorrow' or 'next week' in each sentence.
Underline the future time expression.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with future time expressions clearly underlined.

criteria.description: Uses future time expressions in each sentence

questions.stem: Tell the class one thing you will do next weekend. Use a future time expression in your answer.
hints: Start with 'Next weekend I will...'
Make sure your sentence shows the future.
questions.explanation: The pupil states one future activity using a clear future time expression.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Will you come to school tomorrow?' Which answer is correct?
hints: The question uses 'will'.
The answer should use the same future form.
questions.explanation: The question uses 'will', so the correct answer is 'Yes, I will.'
questions.misconception: Answering with 'do' or 'am' instead of 'will'.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks: 'Will you finish your homework tonight?' Which answer is correct?
hints: The question uses 'will'.
The negative future form is 'won't'.
questions.explanation: The question uses 'will', so the correct negative answer is 'No, I won't.'
questions.misconception: Using 'don't' for a future question.

questions.stem: Question: 'Will you go to the market on Saturday?' Write a complete answer.
answer: yes i will go to the market
no i won't go to the market
hints: Start with 'Yes' or 'No'.
Use 'will' or 'won't'.
questions.explanation: A complete answer uses 'Yes, I will' or 'No, I won't' (or the full sentence).
questions.misconception: Answering only 'Yes' or 'No' without the future expression.

questions.stem: Write two questions about the future and answer each one with 'Yes, I will' or 'No, I won't'.
hints: Start each question with 'Will you...?'
Answer each question clearly.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two future questions and gives correct future answers.

questions.stem: In pairs, ask your partner two 'Will you...?' questions about next week. Your partner answers with 'Yes, I will' or 'No, I won't'.
hints: Ask about school, home or a trip.
Listen for the future form in the answer.
questions.explanation: The pair asks and answers two future questions with correct 'will' or 'won't' answers.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Will you come to my birthday party?' You plan to go. What is the best answer?
hints: The question uses 'will'.
Use the same future form in your answer.
questions.explanation: The best answer is 'Yes, I will.' It matches the future question.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'Yes, I do' because it is a common answer.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: 'Will you help me with my homework?' You do not plan to help. What is the best answer?
hints: The question uses 'will'.
The negative future form is 'won't'.
questions.explanation: The best answer is 'No, I won't.' It is the correct negative future form.
questions.misconception: Using 'don't' or 'didn't' for a future question.

questions.stem: Answer the question with a future expression: 'Will you travel to Kumasi next month?'
answer: yes i will travel to kumasi next month
no i won't travel to kumasi next month
hints: Use 'will' or 'won't'.
Mention the future action if possible.
questions.explanation: The answer should use 'will' or 'won't' to match the future question.
questions.misconception: Answering with 'do' or 'am' instead of 'will'.

questions.stem: Write three answers to future questions: (1) Will you attend the school assembly tomorrow? (2) Will you play football next week? (3) Will you visit your grandparents next holiday? Use 'Yes, I will' or 'No, I won't'.
hints: Answer each question separately.
Use 'will' or 'won't'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three answers that clearly use 'will' or 'won't'.

questions.stem: Question: 'Will they arrive on time?' Which answer is correct for a group?
hints: The question uses 'will' with 'they'.
The answer must match the subject and the future form.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Yes, they will.' It matches the subject 'they' and the future form 'will'.
questions.misconception: Using 'do', 'are' or 'did' for a future question.

questions.stem: Question: 'Will she come to the party?' Which answer is correct?
hints: The question uses 'will' with 'she'.
The negative future form for 'she' is 'won't'.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'No, she won't.' It matches the subject 'she' and the future form.
questions.misconception: Using 'don't' or 'isn't' for a future question.

questions.stem: Question: 'Will the bus leave at six o'clock?' Write a complete answer using 'will' or 'won't'.
answer: yes the bus will leave at six o'clock
no the bus won't leave at six o'clock
yes it will leave at six
no it won't leave at six
hints: The subject is 'the bus' (it).
Use 'will' or 'won't'.
questions.explanation: The answer should use 'will' or 'won't' with the subject 'it'.
questions.misconception: Using 'does' instead of 'will'.

questions.stem: Write four short answers to future questions: (1) Will you come? (2) Will they help? (3) Will she sing? (4) Will we win? Use 'Yes, I will' / 'No, I won't' and match the subject.
hints: Match the subject: I → will, they → will, she → will, we → will.
Use 'won't' for negative answers.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives four answers with correct subjects and future forms.

questions.stem: In pairs, ask each other three future questions with different subjects (you, they, she). Answer with 'will' or 'won't'.
hints: Use 'Will you...?', 'Will they...?', 'Will she...?'
Match the answer to the subject.
questions.explanation: The pair asks and answers three future questions with correct subject-verb matching.

criteria.description: Asks three future questions with different subjects

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.8.2: Identify and use question tags correctly in speech
indicator.objective: Use positive tags, negative tags and auxiliaries in speech

skills.description: Identify positive and negative tags in spoken sentences
Form the correct question tag (positive after negative, negative after positive)
Match the auxiliary in the tag to the auxiliary in the statement
Use tags in speech with appropriate intonation

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify positive/negative tags), 35% medium (form correct tags and match auxiliaries), 15% harder (use tags with correct intonation in speech). Contexts: school, home, market, community.
misconceptions: Using the same polarity in statement and tag
Using the wrong auxiliary
Forgetting to contract the tag
Using rising intonation for a tag where falling is expected

questions.stem: Which of these sentences has a question tag?
options: You are coming to school, aren't you?
You come to school every day.
hints: A question tag is a short question at the end of a statement.
Look for a short phrase like 'aren't you?' at the end.
questions.explanation: The first sentence has the tag 'aren't you?' at the end, which is a question tag.
questions.misconception: Confusing a full question with a question tag.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence is the tag? 'You like fufu, don't you?'
hints: The tag comes after the comma.
It is a short question at the end.
questions.explanation: The tag is 'don't you?' — the short question at the end of the statement.
questions.misconception: Choosing the whole statement as the tag.

questions.stem: Underline the tag in this sentence: 'She can sing well, can't she?'
hints: The tag is at the end.
It is a short question.
questions.explanation: The tag is 'can't she?' — the short question at the end of the statement.
questions.misconception: Underlining part of the main statement instead of the tag.

questions.stem: Write two sentences with question tags and underline the tag in each.
hints: End each sentence with a short question.
Underline the tag.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two statements with tags and clearly underlines each tag.

criteria.description: Underlines the tag in each sentence

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'You are coming to the party, _____?'
hints: The statement is positive ('are coming').
The tag should be negative.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag must be negative: 'aren't you?'
questions.misconception: Using a positive tag after a positive statement.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'She doesn't like fish, _____?'
hints: The statement is negative ('doesn't like').
The tag should be positive.
questions.explanation: The statement is negative, so the tag must be positive: 'does she?'
questions.misconception: Using a negative tag after a negative statement.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'They will come, _____?'
hints: The statement is positive ('will come').
The negative form of 'will' is 'won't'.
questions.explanation: The statement is positive, so the tag is 'won't they?'
questions.misconception: Using 'will they' instead of 'won't they'.

questions.stem: Write four sentences with question tags: (1) You like kenkey, _____? (2) He isn't tall, _____? (3) We can go, _____? (4) They won't be late, _____?
hints: Match positive with negative and negative with positive.
Use the correct auxiliary in each tag.
questions.explanation: A strong answer provides correct tags: don't you, is he, can't we, will they.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'You have a pen, _____?'
hints: The statement uses 'have'.
The tag should use the same auxiliary.
questions.explanation: The statement uses 'have', so the tag uses 'haven't you?'
questions.misconception: Using 'don't you' when the statement uses 'have'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'He is a teacher, _____?'
hints: The statement uses 'is'.
The tag should use the same auxiliary.
questions.explanation: The statement uses 'is', so the tag uses 'isn't he?'
questions.misconception: Using 'doesn't he' when the statement uses 'is'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct tag: 'They are playing football, _____?'
hints: The statement uses 'are'.
The negative form is 'aren't'.
questions.explanation: The statement uses 'are', so the tag is 'aren't they?'
questions.misconception: Using 'don't they' instead of 'aren't they'.

questions.stem: Write four sentences with question tags using the correct auxiliary: (1) She can swim, _____? (2) You will come, _____? (3) He doesn't know, _____? (4) We are late, _____?
hints: Match the auxiliary in the statement.
Use the correct negative or positive form.
questions.explanation: A strong answer provides correct tags: can't she, won't you, does he, aren't we.

criteria.description: Matches the auxiliary in each statement

questions.stem: Say this sentence aloud with the correct intonation: 'You are coming to school, aren't you?'
hints: The tag often has a rising intonation for a real question.
Make your voice rise at the end.
questions.explanation: The pupil says the sentence with a rising intonation on the tag, which is appropriate for a real question.

criteria.description: Uses rising intonation on the tag

questions.stem: Say this sentence aloud with the correct intonation: 'You don't like fish, do you?'
hints: The tag is a real question.
Let your voice rise at the end.
questions.explanation: The pupil says the sentence with rising intonation on the tag.

criteria.description: Uses rising intonation on the tag

questions.stem: Work in pairs. One pupil makes a statement, and the other adds the correct tag and says it with appropriate intonation. Take three turns each.
hints: Listen to the statement before adding the tag.
Match the auxiliary and polarity.
questions.explanation: The pair takes turns making statements and adding correct tags with appropriate intonation.

questions.stem: Say these two sentences aloud with the correct intonation and explain the difference: (1) 'You are coming, aren't you?' (2) 'You are coming, aren't you.' (with falling intonation)
hints: Rising intonation makes it a real question.
Falling intonation suggests you expect agreement.
questions.explanation: The pupil says both sentences with the correct intonation and explains that rising intonation asks a real question, while falling intonation expects agreement.

criteria.description: Uses rising intonation for the question
Uses falling intonation for the expected agreement

questions.stem: In a group, take turns making statements and adding tags. The group listens and says whether the intonation was appropriate.
hints: Listen carefully to the rise or fall of the voice.
Give polite feedback.
questions.explanation: The group takes turns making statements with tags and gives feedback on intonation.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.9.1: Explore the use of verbs in commands, instructions, requests and directions appropriately in speech.
indicator.objective: Create and present simple instructions or a manual on how to play a game

skills.description: Identify the rules or steps of a familiar game
Arrange instructions in the correct order (first, next, then, finally)
Use imperative verbs correctly to give instructions
Write clear and complete instructions
Present instructions orally to the class with confidence

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify game rules and steps), 35% medium (order steps and use imperatives), 20% harder (present clear instructions to an audience). Games chosen are familiar Ghanaian and international games that pupils actually play (ampe, oware, ludo, football, hopscotch).
misconceptions: Giving instructions in random order rather than logical sequence
Using descriptive statements instead of imperatives
Leaving out steps that seem obvious but are necessary for a newcomer
Presenting instructions in a disorganised or unclear manner

questions.stem: In the game of ampe, what do players mainly do?
options: Kick a ball into a goal.
Clap hands and jump on one leg to match the leader's moves.
hints: Ampe is a jumping and clapping game.
Players follow the leader's actions.
questions.explanation: In ampe, players clap their hands and jump on one leg while trying to match the leader's moves. The other options describe football, oware and athletics.
questions.misconception: Confusing ampe with another game.

questions.stem: In the game of oware, what do players do?
options: Move seeds from one hole to another on a wooden board.
Throw a ball into a basket.
hints: Oware is played on a wooden board.
The pieces are usually seeds or stones.
questions.explanation: In oware, players move seeds around holes on a wooden board, trying to capture the opponent's seeds.
questions.misconception: Confusing oware with a ball game.

questions.stem: Write one rule of the game of ludo.
answer: you need a six to move out of home
move your counters around the board
roll the dice and move your counter
you must roll a six to begin
be the first to get all counters home
move your pieces from start to finish
hints: What do you need to roll to start?
What do you move around the board?
questions.explanation: A key rule of ludo is that you need to roll a six to start, then move your counters around the board and try to get them home.
questions.misconception: Giving a rule that belongs to a different game.

questions.stem: Write three rules of a game you know well (for example football, ampe, ludo or hopscotch).
hints: Think of how the game starts.
Think about what players must do and must not do.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three clear rules that belong to the chosen game.

criteria.description: Rules belong to the chosen game

questions.stem: Tell the class two rules of a game you enjoy playing.
hints: Choose a game you know well.
Say what players must do.
questions.explanation: The pupil states two clear rules of a familiar game.

criteria.description: Rules belong to the chosen game

questions.stem: Four steps for starting a game of ludo are jumbled: A. Roll the dice. B. Place your counters in the home circle. C. Move a counter out when you roll a six. D. Wait for your turn. Which order is correct?
hints: Where do the counters go before the game starts?
You must roll a six before you can move out.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: place counters in home (B), wait for your turn (D), roll the dice (A), and move a counter out when you roll a six (C).
questions.misconception: Ordering steps by what feels exciting rather than by game sequence.

questions.stem: Arrange these instructions for playing hopscotch in the correct order: A. Throw a stone into square 1. B. Draw the hopscotch squares on the ground. C. Hop through the squares to pick up the stone. D. Skip the square with the stone. Write the letters in order.
hints: You must draw the squares before you can play.
You throw the stone before you hop.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: draw the squares (B), throw the stone into square 1 (A), then hop through, skipping the square with the stone (D), and pick up the stone (C).
questions.misconception: Placing the drawing step last instead of first.

questions.stem: Instructions for making a paper boat: A. Fold the paper in half. B. Open the paper and fold the corners to the centre. C. Fold the bottom edges up. D. Pull the sides apart to make a boat. Which instruction should come first?
hints: What is the very first thing you do with the paper?
You must fold the paper before you can fold the corners.
questions.explanation: The first step is to fold the paper in half, because all other steps build on that fold.
questions.misconception: Starting with a later step that sounds more interesting.

questions.stem: Write four instructions for playing a simple game of your choice in the correct order. Use the words 'first', 'next', 'then' and 'finally'.
hints: Start with 'First...'
End with 'Finally...'
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes four instructions in the correct order using the connecting words.

criteria.description: Instructions are in the correct order

questions.stem: In a group, prepare a set of four instructions for playing a game. Present them to the class in the correct order.
hints: Agree on the steps first.
Use 'first', 'next', 'then' and 'finally' as you speak.
questions.explanation: The group presents four clear instructions in the correct order.

criteria.description: Instructions are in the correct order

questions.stem: Which sentence is written as a command (imperative)?
options: The ball is passed to Kojo.
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
It usually starts with a verb.
questions.explanation: 'Pass the ball to Kojo' is an imperative because it tells someone to do something and starts with the verb 'pass'.
questions.misconception: Confusing a descriptive statement with an imperative command.

questions.stem: Which of these is a correct imperative for a game instruction?
options: Throw the stone into the first square.
hints: Imperatives start with a verb.
Which option tells the player exactly what to do?
questions.explanation: 'Throw the stone into the first square' is a clear imperative instruction.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence that describes rather than commands.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence as an imperative command: 'You should roll the dice.'
hints: Remove 'you should'.
Start with the verb.
questions.explanation: The imperative form removes 'you should' and starts with the verb: 'Roll the dice.'
questions.misconception: Keeping 'you should' in the command.

questions.stem: Write four imperative instructions for playing a game. Each instruction must start with a verb.
hints: Use verbs like 'roll', 'move', 'throw', 'jump'.
Do not use 'you should' or 'the player'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives four instructions that each start with a verb.

criteria.description: Each instruction starts with a verb

questions.stem: Give three imperative instructions to a partner on how to play a simple game.
hints: Start each instruction with a verb.
Speak clearly so your partner can follow.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives three clear imperative instructions.

questions.stem: Which instruction for playing ampe is clearest for a new player?
options: Do the thing with your hands.
Clap your hands once, then jump on your right leg.
hints: A clear instruction tells exactly what to do.
Avoid vague words like 'thing'.
questions.explanation: The clear instruction tells exactly what action to take: clap once and jump on the right leg.
questions.misconception: Thinking a general statement counts as a clear instruction.

questions.stem: Improve this unclear instruction: 'Do something with the dice.' Write a clearer instruction.
answer: roll the dice on the table
pick up the dice and roll it
hints: Say exactly what to do with the dice.
Use a clear verb.
questions.explanation: A clear instruction says exactly what to do with the dice, such as 'Roll the dice once.'
questions.misconception: Leaving the instruction vague with words like 'something'.

questions.stem: Which set of instructions is the clearest for a new player?
options: First, stand at the start line. Then, throw the stone into square 1. Next, hop through the squares. Finally, pick up the stone and hop back.
Hopscotch is easy once you try.
hints: Look for step-by-step detail.
Which option explains every action?
questions.explanation: Option C gives step-by-step instructions in order with clear actions, which is easiest for a new player to follow.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general statement instead of step-by-step detail.

questions.stem: Write four clear instructions for how to play a simple game of your choice. Each instruction must be specific and complete.
hints: Tell exactly what to do at each step.
Include order words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes four specific instructions that a new player could follow.

questions.stem: Write a short manual (about six instructions) on how to play a familiar game. Make each instruction clear enough for someone who has never played the game before.
hints: Start with 'First...' and end with 'Finally...'
Include all the steps a beginner would need.
questions.explanation: A strong manual gives six clear, complete, ordered instructions that a beginner could follow.

criteria.description: Instructions are in the correct order

questions.stem: Present your manual on how to play a game to the class. Speak clearly and explain each step.
hints: Stand where the class can see you.
Speak clearly and slowly.
questions.explanation: The pupil presents the manual clearly, explaining each step in order.

questions.stem: In groups, prepare a set of instructions for a game and present them to another group. The other group must be able to play the game after hearing your instructions.
hints: Practise the presentation first.
Make sure the instructions are complete.
questions.explanation: The group presents clear, complete instructions that allow another group to play the game.

criteria.description: Instructions are clear and easy to follow
The other group can play the game

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.1.9.1: Explore the use of verbs in commands, instructions, requests and directions appropriately in speech.
indicator.objective: Make and respond to polite requests for help from unfamiliar people

skills.description: Identify polite request forms
Make a polite request to an unfamiliar person
Respond politely to a request (grant or decline)
Use appropriate tone and facial expression when making or responding to requests
Role-play making and responding to requests in given situations

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify polite forms), 35% medium (make and respond to requests), 20% harder (role-play appropriate tone and expression in unfamiliar situations). Situations: asking a stranger for directions, asking a shopkeeper for help, asking a teacher for permission, asking a visitor for information.
misconceptions: Using 'Give me' or 'I want' without 'please' as a polite request
Confusing a command with a request
Responding with 'No' without a polite reason when declining
Using an aggressive or impatient tone with unfamiliar people

questions.stem: Which of these is the most polite way to ask a stranger for help?
options: Excuse me, please could you help me?
hints: Polite requests use words like 'excuse me' and 'please'.
Avoid commands with unfamiliar people.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, please could you help me?' uses polite words and asks rather than commands.
questions.misconception: Thinking a direct command is a polite request.

questions.stem: Which phrase is a polite request for permission?
hints: Polite permission requests start with 'May I' or 'Could I'.
Which option asks rather than demands?
questions.explanation: 'May I please go out?' is a polite request for permission.
questions.misconception: Confusing a demand with a polite request.

questions.stem: Write one polite phrase you could use to ask a stranger for directions.
answer: excuse me please could you tell me the way
excuse me could you help me find
please could you show me the way
excuse me please may i ask for directions
sorry to trouble you could you tell me how to get to
please can you direct me to
hints: Start with 'Excuse me' or 'Please'.
Ask, don't command.
questions.explanation: A polite request for directions uses 'excuse me', 'please' and 'could you'.
questions.misconception: Writing a direct command such as 'Tell me the way.'

questions.stem: Write two polite requests: one to ask a teacher for help and one to ask a shopkeeper for a bag.
hints: Use 'please', 'could you' or 'may I'.
Keep the tone respectful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two polite requests that use appropriate polite words for each person.

questions.stem: Which of these is a polite way to decline a request?
hints: Polite declines include an apology or explanation.
Look for 'sorry' or 'I'm afraid'.
questions.explanation: 'I can't, sorry' is polite because it includes an apology and softens the decline.
questions.misconception: Thinking a blunt 'No!' is a polite response.

questions.stem: You are lost and need to ask a stranger for directions to the market. Which request is best?
options: Excuse me, please could you tell me the way to the market?
hints: Start politely with 'Excuse me'.
Ask clearly for directions.
questions.explanation: Option B is polite, clear and respectful — it uses 'excuse me', 'please' and 'could you'.
questions.misconception: Thinking a command or a single word is a polite request.

questions.stem: You want to ask a stranger to help you carry a heavy bag. Write one polite request.
answer: excuse me please could you help me carry this bag
please would you help me carry my bag
excuse me could you kindly help me with my bag
please could you help me with this heavy bag
excuse me please may i ask you to help me carry my bag
sorry to trouble you please could you help me carry this bag
hints: Start with 'Excuse me' or 'Please'.
Ask, don't command.
questions.explanation: A polite request uses 'excuse me' or 'please' and asks the stranger for help clearly.
questions.misconception: Making a command like 'Carry my bag.'

questions.stem: With a partner playing a stranger, ask politely for directions to the nearest bank.
hints: Start with 'Excuse me'.
Use 'please' and 'could you'.
questions.explanation: The pupil makes a polite request for directions using appropriate words.

questions.stem: Write three polite requests for help from unfamiliar people in these situations: (1) asking a stranger for directions; (2) asking a shopkeeper for change; (3) asking a visitor for information.
hints: Use 'please', 'excuse me' and 'could you'.
Keep the tone respectful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives three polite requests, each suited to the situation.

questions.stem: A stranger politely asks you for directions to the post office. Which response is most polite?
options: Yes, of course. Go straight, then turn left at the market.
hints: A polite response helps if you can.
Which option gives clear, kind directions?
questions.explanation: Option B is polite, helpful and gives clear directions.
questions.misconception: Thinking a blunt 'I don't know' is always acceptable.

questions.stem: Someone asks you to lend them your phone, but you do not want to. Which response is most polite?
options: I'm sorry, but I can't lend my phone.
hints: A polite decline includes an apology or a soft word.
Which option uses 'sorry' and is polite?
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, but I can't lend my phone' is polite because it includes an apology.
questions.misconception: Thinking any 'No' is automatically rude, or that rudeness is acceptable.

questions.stem: A stranger asks you for directions to the hospital. You know the way. Write a polite response.
answer: yes of course go straight and turn left at the market
certainly it is just down this road
yes it is not far go straight and take the second turning
of course i can help go down this street and turn right
yes please go straight ahead and turn left
hints: Start with 'Yes, of course' or 'Certainly'.
Give clear directions.
questions.explanation: A polite response agrees to help and gives clear directions.
questions.misconception: Answering with a blunt 'Go straight' without any polite words.

questions.stem: Write two polite responses: (1) a polite refusal to a stranger asking for your pen; (2) a polite agreement to help someone who asks you for directions.
hints: For refusal, use 'I'm sorry, but...'.
For agreement, use 'Yes, of course' or 'Certainly'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives one polite refusal and one polite agreement.

questions.stem: Which tone is best when making a polite request to a stranger?
hints: Polite requests need a pleasant tone.
Which tone sounds friendly and respectful?
questions.explanation: A calm and friendly tone is best for polite requests to strangers.
questions.misconception: Thinking a loud or bossy tone makes a request clearer.

questions.stem: Name one facial expression that shows politeness when making a request.
hints: Think about what a kind face looks like.
It can be a small smile.
questions.explanation: A smile or friendly expression shows politeness when making a request.
questions.misconception: Answering with an angry or blank expression.

questions.stem: With a partner, practise making a polite request with a calm tone and a friendly expression.
hints: Speak softly and clearly.
Smile as you ask.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses a calm tone and friendly expression when making a request.

questions.stem: In pairs, role-play this scene: a stranger asks you for directions to the police station. Respond politely.
hints: The stranger should greet and use polite words.
The response should be polite and helpful.
questions.explanation: The pair role-plays a polite request for directions and a polite response.

questions.stem: In groups of three, role-play: one is a visitor, one is a pupil who helps, and one is a pupil who politely declines. Practise making and responding to requests for help.
hints: The visitor asks for help politely.
One pupil agrees politely, the other declines politely.
questions.explanation: The group role-plays a polite request with both a polite grant and a polite decline.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.10.1: Read and summarize passages read
indicator.objective: Summarise level-appropriate passages/text orally

skills.description: Identify the most important idea(s) in a sentence or short paragraph
Restate the main idea in own words
Summarise a single sentence in fewer words
Summarise a short paragraph orally
Present the summary orally in a clear, concise way

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify main idea and summarise a sentence), 30% medium (restate in own words), 20% harder (summarise a whole paragraph orally). Passages kept short (1–3 sentences or a short paragraph).
misconceptions: Copying the original sentence instead of restating
Including minor details in the summary
Omitting the main idea while keeping details
Making the summary longer than the original
Confusing a summary with a personal opinion

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom, swept the floor and arranged the desks.' What is the main idea?
hints: What is the whole sentence about?
All three actions are part of cleaning.
questions.explanation: The sentence is about the pupils cleaning the classroom. Sweeping and arranging are details.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up early, swept the compound, fetched water and cooked breakfast.' What is the main idea?
hints: What do all the actions have in common?
They are all morning tasks.
questions.explanation: All the actions are morning chores, so the main idea is that Ama did her morning chores.
questions.misconception: Choosing one action as the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo found a wallet, took it to the police station and the owner thanked him.' Write the main idea in one sentence.
answer: kojo found and returned a wallet
kojo took a wallet to the police
kojo found a wallet and took it to the police
hints: What is the most important action?
It involves a wallet and honesty.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kojo found and returned a lost wallet.
questions.misconception: Including the detail about being thanked as the main idea.

questions.stem: Sentence: 'The pupils were exhausted after the long race.' Which is the best restatement in own words?
options: The pupils were very tired after the race.
The pupils ran a long race.
hints: Restate means say the same thing in different words.
Which option uses different words with the same meaning?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils were very tired after the race' restates the original sentence in different words.
questions.misconception: Copying the original sentence.

questions.stem: Restate this sentence in your own words: 'The market was crowded with many buyers and sellers.'
answer: many people were buying and selling
the market was full of people
lots of people were at the market
the market had many buyers and sellers
hints: Use different words for 'crowded'.
What is the sentence saying about the market?
questions.explanation: A good restatement says the market was full of people buying and selling.
questions.misconception: Copying the original sentence word for word.

questions.stem: Sentence: 'The dilapidated house had broken windows and a leaking roof.' Which restatement is best?
options: The old house was in bad condition.
hints: Restate the whole idea.
What does the condition of the house tell you?
questions.explanation: 'The old house was in bad condition' captures the overall meaning of the original sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the whole idea.

questions.stem: Summarise this sentence in fewer words: 'This is the boy who killed the snake.'
hints: Remove unnecessary words.
Keep the main action and the person.
questions.explanation: The summary is 'The boy killed the snake.' It removes the unnecessary words while keeping the main meaning.
questions.misconception: Changing the meaning while summarising.

questions.stem: Summarise this sentence in fewer words: 'The pupils who had finished their work were allowed to go home early.'
answer: pupils who finished work went home early
those who finished went home early
the pupils finished and went home early
hints: Remove the extra words.
Keep the main action and the result.
questions.explanation: A good summary is 'Pupils who finished work went home early.'
questions.misconception: Changing the meaning while shortening.

questions.stem: Summarise: 'The man who was walking slowly down the road suddenly stopped and looked at the sky.'
options: The man stopped and looked at the sky.
The man walked down the road.
hints: What is the most important action?
The summary should keep the main event.
questions.explanation: The main event is that the man stopped and looked at the sky. The other details can be left out.
questions.misconception: Keeping too many details.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama wanted to buy a new dress. She saved her pocket money for three months. Finally, she bought the dress and wore it to a party.' What is the best summary?
options: Ama saved money and bought a dress for a party.
Ama saved money for three months.
hints: The summary should cover the beginning, middle and end.
What was the result of Ama's saving?
questions.explanation: The best summary covers all three parts: Ama saved money, bought a dress and wore it to a party.
questions.misconception: Choosing a summary that covers only one part.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo found a wallet. He took it to the police station. The owner was found and thanked him.' Write a one-sentence summary.
answer: kojo found a wallet and took it to the police where the owner thanked him
kojo found a wallet and returned it
kojo took a wallet to the police and the owner thanked him
hints: Cover the main events.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A good summary covers Kojo finding the wallet, taking it to the police and the owner thanking him.
questions.misconception: Including unnecessary details.

questions.stem: Read: 'The school garden has tomatoes, onions and pepper. The pupils water the garden every morning and weed it on Fridays. They sell the vegetables and buy books for the library.' What is the main idea?
options: The pupils grow vegetables to buy books for the library.
hints: What is the whole paragraph about?
The vegetables are used to help the library.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the pupils grow vegetables in the garden and sell them to buy books for the library.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi wanted to improve her reading. She joined the reading club. She read a new book every week. By the end of the year, her reading had improved greatly.' Write a summary in two sentences.
hints: Cover her goal, her action and the result.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A strong summary explains that Esi joined the reading club, read many books and improved her reading.

questions.stem: After reading a short passage, summarise it orally in one or two sentences.
hints: Focus on the main idea.
Keep it short and clear.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a clear, concise oral summary of the passage.

questions.stem: Read a short paragraph and tell the class the main idea in one sentence.
hints: Use your own words.
Keep it short.
questions.explanation: The pupil states the main idea in one clear sentence.

questions.stem: Read this sentence and restate it in your own words in two sentences: 'The pupils who had completed their assignments were allowed to leave early.'
hints: Use different words for 'completed' and 'allowed'.
Keep the same meaning.
questions.explanation: A strong restatement says the pupils who finished their work could go home early.

questions.stem: After reading a short passage, summarise it orally and explain why you chose that summary.
hints: Summarise the main points.
Explain that you focused on the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a clear summary and explains the reasoning behind it.

criteria.description: Explains why the summary was chosen

questions.stem: Read: 'The school decided to plant trees around the compound. The pupils brought young trees from the nursery. They watered the trees every morning. Soon the compound was green and beautiful.' Write a three-sentence summary.
hints: Cover the beginning, middle and end.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A strong summary covers the decision to plant trees, the pupils' actions and the result.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom, swept the floor, arranged the desks and washed the windows.' What is the main idea?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom thoroughly.
hints: What is the sentence mostly about?
All the actions are part of cleaning.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the pupils cleaned the classroom thoroughly.
questions.misconception: Choosing one detail as the main idea.
