questions.stem: Summarise this sentence in fewer words: 'The pupils who had worked very hard all term were given certificates at the assembly by the head teacher.'
hints: Remove the extra words.
Keep the main action and the result.
questions.explanation: A good summary is 'Hardworking pupils received certificates at assembly.'

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.10.1: Read and summarize passages read
indicator.objective: Write short summary of a level appropriate passage/text read

skills.description: Select main ideas from a passage, leaving out examples and parenthetical words
Write down events in the correct sequence order
Write a short summary of a passage using main ideas
Keep the summary concise, shorter than the original and without repetition
Ensure the summary accurately reflects the passage without added or distorted information

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (select main ideas and sequence events), 35% medium (write a short summary of 2–3 sentences), 20% harder (keep it concise and accurate while covering all main ideas). Passages kept to 100–150 words.
misconceptions: Including examples and illustrations in the summary
Writing events out of sequence
Adding personal opinions or information not in the passage
Making the summary too long
Omitting one or more main ideas

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor, arranged the desks and washed the windows. The classroom became bright and clean.' Which sentence states the main idea?
hints: The main idea covers the whole passage.
Which sentence tells what the whole passage is about?
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the pupils cleaned the classroom. The other sentences give details.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up early. She swept the compound, fetched water and cooked breakfast. Then she went to school.' Write the main idea in one sentence.
answer: ama did her morning chores before school
ama did her chores and went to school
ama did many things before school
hints: What did Ama do before school?
All her actions are chores.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Ama did her morning chores before going to school.
questions.misconception: Listing all the chores instead of stating the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo woke up late. He missed the bus. He walked to school. He arrived after assembly.' Which event came first?
hints: Look at the first sentence.
What happened at the very beginning?
questions.explanation: The first event is that Kojo woke up late.
questions.misconception: Confusing the order of events.

questions.stem: Arrange these events in the correct order: A. The owner was found. B. Kojo found a wallet. C. Kojo took it to the police station. D. The owner thanked Kojo.
hints: Start with finding the wallet.
The thanks come last.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Kojo found a wallet (B), took it to the police (C), the owner was found (A), and the owner thanked Kojo (D).
questions.misconception: Ordering events by importance rather than time.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi saved her pocket money for two months. She bought a new book. She read it in one week. She said it was the best book she had ever read.' Which is the best summary?
options: Esi saved money, bought a book and loved it.
Esi saved money for two months.
Esi read a book in one week.
hints: A good summary covers the whole passage.
Which option includes the beginning, middle and end?
questions.explanation: The best summary covers Esi saving money, buying the book and enjoying it.
questions.misconception: Choosing a summary that covers only one part.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the market square on Saturday. They picked up rubbish and swept the ground. The traders thanked them.' Write a one-sentence summary.
answer: the pupils cleaned the market and the traders thanked them
the pupils cleaned the market square on saturday
the pupils cleaned the market and were thanked
hints: Cover the main events.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A good summary covers the pupils cleaning the market and the traders thanking them.
questions.misconception: Including too many details.

questions.stem: Read: 'The school decided to start a reading club. Pupils meet every Wednesday to read and discuss books. The club has helped many pupils improve their reading.' Write a two-sentence summary.
hints: Cover the main actions and the result.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A strong summary covers the start of the club, its activities and its benefit.

criteria.description: Covers the start of the club

questions.stem: Which summary is the most concise?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom by sweeping, arranging desks and washing windows.
The pupils cleaned the classroom, and they swept the floor, and they arranged the desks, and they washed the windows.
The classroom was cleaned by the pupils who swept, arranged and washed.
hints: Concise means short and clear.
Which summary uses the fewest words without losing meaning?
questions.explanation: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom' is the most concise summary because it captures the main idea in the fewest words.
questions.misconception: Thinking longer summaries are better.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama was very tired. She had walked a long distance. She sat down to rest.' Write a concise one-sentence summary.
answer: ama was tired from walking and sat down to rest
ama walked a long way and rested
ama was tired so she sat down
hints: Keep it short.
Include the main idea and the result.
questions.explanation: A concise summary is 'Ama was tired from walking and sat down to rest.'
questions.misconception: Writing a summary as long as the original.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom on Friday.' Which summary is accurate?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom on Friday.
The pupils cleaned the classroom on Monday.
The pupils played in the classroom.
hints: Accurate means it matches the passage.
Which option does not change the day or the action?
questions.explanation: The accurate summary keeps the same information as the passage.
questions.misconception: Changing details when summarising.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo found a wallet and took it to the police station.' Write an accurate summary.
answer: kojo found a wallet and took it to the police
kojo took a wallet to the police station
kojo found a wallet and handed it in
hints: Do not add or change any information.
Keep the main facts.
questions.explanation: An accurate summary states that Kojo found a wallet and took it to the police station.
questions.misconception: Adding information not in the passage.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the market square on Saturday. They picked up rubbish and swept the ground. The traders thanked them.' Write an accurate summary in two sentences.
hints: Do not add information not in the passage.
Keep the summary short and accurate.
questions.explanation: A strong summary accurately states that the pupils cleaned the market square on Saturday and were thanked by the traders.

questions.stem: Read: 'The school garden has tomatoes, onions and pepper. The pupils water the garden every morning and weed it on Fridays. They sell the vegetables and buy books for the library.' Select the main ideas and write them in two sentences.
hints: What is the passage mainly about?
What do the pupils do with the vegetables?
questions.explanation: A strong answer selects the main ideas: the pupils grow vegetables in the garden and sell them to buy books.

questions.stem: Read: 'Esi woke up early. She ate breakfast. She walked to school. She arrived before assembly.' Write the events in the correct order.
hints: Follow the order in the passage.
Use sequence words like 'first', 'then', 'next', 'finally'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes the events in the correct order: woke up, ate breakfast, walked to school, arrived before assembly.

criteria.description: Events are in the correct order

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils wanted to beautify their school. They planted flowers along the path and painted the walls. Soon the school looked bright and welcoming.' Write a three-sentence summary.
hints: Cover the goal, the actions and the result.
Use your own words.
questions.explanation: A strong summary covers the pupils' goal, their actions and the result.

questions.stem: Read this passage and write a summary of no more than two sentences: 'Ama wanted to improve her reading. She joined the reading club. She read a new book every week. By the end of the year, her reading had improved greatly.'
hints: Keep it short.
Cover the main idea and the result.
questions.explanation: A strong summary is no more than two sentences covering Ama's goal, action and result.

criteria.description: Is no more than two sentences

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom on Friday. They swept and arranged the desks.' Which summary adds information NOT in the passage?
options: The pupils cleaned the classroom on Friday.
The pupils cleaned the classroom and the teacher praised them.
The pupils swept and arranged the desks.
hints: Which summary adds something not in the passage?
The passage does not mention the teacher praising them.
questions.explanation: The summary about the teacher praising the pupils adds information that is not in the passage.
questions.misconception: Adding information not in the original.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo saved his money for weeks. He bought a new football. He played with his friends every afternoon.' Which is a main idea?
options: Kojo saved money and bought a football.
hints: Which sentence covers the most important events?
It connects the saving and the purchase.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kojo saved money and bought a football.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the main idea.

questions.stem: After reading a short passage, give an accurate oral summary in two sentences.
hints: Do not add or change information.
Keep it short.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives an accurate two-sentence summary of the passage.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.2.1: Connect sounds to letters; and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write
indicator.objective: Read words with ending sounds like "sure" as in measure; "ture" as in creature and "tch" as in Stretch

skills.description: Identify the target ending patterns (-sure, -ture, -tch) in written words
Decode words containing these endings correctly
Read words with these endings within continuous text
Distinguish between similar endings such as -tch and -ch
Use words with these endings in meaningful sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify and read words in isolation), 30% medium (read in context and distinguish similar endings), 20% harder (use words correctly in original sentences). Vocabulary: measure, treasure, creature, picture, future, nature, stretch, catch, fetch, match, watch, itch, ditch, pitch, kitchen.
misconceptions: Pronouncing -ture as 'chur' or 'tyoor' instead of a soft 'cher' sound
Reading -tch as 't-k' or dropping the 't'
Confusing -sure with -sion or -tion
Reading letter-by-letter instead of blending the ending
Omitting the ending when reading longer words

questions.stem: Which word ends with the same sound as 'measure'?
hints: Listen to the ending of 'measure'.
Which word ends with 'sure'?
questions.explanation: Both 'measure' and 'treasure' end with the '-sure' pattern, which sounds like 'zhur'. 'Teacher', 'tiger' and 'table' have different endings.
questions.misconception: Confusing the '-sure' ending with '-er' or '-le'.

questions.stem: Which word ends with '-tch'?
hints: Look for the letters t-c-h at the end.
Which word has 'tch' at the end?
questions.explanation: 'Stretch' ends with '-tch'. 'Stomach' ends in '-ach', 'school' ends in '-ool' and 'sketch' also ends in '-tch' — but only 'Stretch' is listed first. Actually, both 'stretch' and 'sketch' end in -tch; the correct option is 'Stretch'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that ends in 'ch' without the 't'.

questions.stem: Which word ends with '-ture'?
hints: Look for the letters t-u-r-e at the end.
Which word ends in 'ture'?
questions.explanation: 'Future' ends with '-ture'. The other words have different endings.
questions.misconception: Confusing '-ture' with '-ure' or '-er'.

questions.stem: Write two words that end with '-tch'.
hints: Think of words like 'catch' and 'watch'.
Two words are enough.
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-tch' include catch, match, watch, fetch, stretch, ditch, pitch, itch, witch and kitchen.
questions.misconception: Writing words that end in 'ch' without the 't'.

questions.stem: Sort these words into three groups based on their endings: measure, creature, stretch, treasure, picture, catch, future, fetch.
hints: Group by -sure, -ture and -tch.
Each group should have at least two words.
questions.explanation: The groups are: -sure (measure, treasure), -ture (creature, picture, future), -tch (stretch, catch, fetch).

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'creature'?
hints: Listen to the ending sound of 'creature'.
Which word ends with the same '-ture' sound?
questions.explanation: 'Feature' rhymes with 'creature' because both end with the '-ture' sound.
questions.misconception: Confusing '-ture' with '-er'.

questions.stem: Read this word and write it correctly: 'strech'. What is the correct spelling?
hints: The word means to pull something tight.
It ends with the '-tch' pattern.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'stretch' with '-tch' at the end.
questions.misconception: Writing 'strech' without the 't'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: The ending pattern is '-ture'.
Which spelling follows the pattern exactly?
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'creature' with the '-ture' ending.
questions.misconception: Dropping the 'e' or miswriting the ending.

questions.stem: Write the correct spelling for each word: (1) 'mezhur' (2) 'piktur' (3) 'fech' (4) 'trezhur'.
hints: Use the -sure, -ture and -tch patterns.
Say each word aloud first.
questions.explanation: The correct spellings are: (1) measure, (2) picture, (3) fetch, (4) treasure.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The farmer used a rope to _____ the fence tight.' Which word fits the blank?
hints: The word must fit grammatically after 'to'.
It is the base verb form.
questions.explanation: 'Stretch' is the base verb that fits after 'to' in this sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing a different form of the word that does not fit the sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'The _____ in the forest was small and furry.' Which word fits the blank?
hints: The word must name a living thing.
It ends with '-ture'.
questions.explanation: 'Creature' is the noun that names a living animal and ends with '-ture'.
questions.misconception: Confusing different forms of the word.

questions.stem: Read: 'Grandmother keeps her gold in a wooden box for _____.' Write the missing word (it ends with '-sure').
hints: What do you call valuable things kept safe?
The word ends with '-sure'.
questions.explanation: The missing word is 'treasure' — valuable items kept safely. The sentence makes sense with 'treasure'.
questions.misconception: Writing a word that does not end in '-sure'.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using words that end with '-tch' and '-ture'. Underline each target word.
hints: Use words like catch, match, picture or nature.
Underline the words ending in -tch or -ture.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences using correct target words and underlines them.

questions.stem: Which word ends with '-tch' (not just '-ch')?
hints: Look for the extra 't' before 'ch'.
Which word has 'tch' at the end?
questions.explanation: 'Match' ends with '-tch'. 'March', 'much' and 'coach' end with '-ch' without the 't'.
questions.misconception: Confusing '-ch' with '-tch'.

questions.stem: Which pair shows the correct difference between '-tch' and '-ch' endings?
hints: One word has '-tch' and the other has '-ch'.
Which pair shows both endings?
questions.explanation: 'Catch' ends in '-tch' and 'coach' ends in '-ch'. This pair shows the difference.
questions.misconception: Choosing a pair where both words have the same ending.

questions.stem: Which word ends with '-tch': 'bench' or 'fetch'?
hints: One word has a 't' before 'ch'.
Which one is it?
questions.explanation: 'Fetch' ends with '-tch' while 'bench' ends with '-nch'.
questions.misconception: Choosing the word that ends only in 'ch'.

questions.stem: Write one word ending in '-tch' and one word ending in '-ch'. Explain the difference between the two endings.
hints: Examples: 'catch' (-tch) and 'coach' (-ch).
Explain that '-tch' has a 't' before the 'ch'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives one word for each ending and explains that '-tch' includes a 't' before the 'ch'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word ending in '-sure' correctly?
options: The treasure was buried under the tree.
The pictchur is on the wall.
hints: Look for the sentence with correct spelling.
The word 'treasure' ends in '-sure'.
questions.explanation: 'The treasure was buried under the tree' uses 'treasure' (ending in '-sure') correctly and is spelled correctly.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence with a misspelled word.

questions.stem: Write one sentence using the word 'picture'.
answer: i drew a picture of my house
she hung the picture on the wall
the picture shows a beautiful garden
we took a picture at the beach
the picture in the book is colourful
he painted a picture of a bird
hints: 'Picture' ends with '-ture'.
Make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'picture' meaningfully.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that does not make sense with the word.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using one word ending in '-sure', one ending in '-ture' and one ending in '-tch'. Underline each target word.
hints: Examples: treasure, future, catch.
Underline the word in each sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three meaningful sentences with correct target words and underlines them.

criteria.description: Uses one word for each ending

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 3: Word Families, Minimal Pairs and Common Digraphs
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.3.1: Identify minimal pairs and common digraphs
indicator.objective: Use common minimal pairs to decode words

skills.description: Identify pairs of words that differ by only one sound
Decode (read) both words in a minimal pair accurately
Distinguish the different sound in each pair when reading
Read minimal pairs correctly within sentences and use them meaningfully
Recognise the spelling pattern that creates the minimal pair

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify and read minimal pairs in isolation), 30% medium (distinguish sounds and read in sentences), 20% harder (recognise spelling patterns and use words correctly). Vocabulary: goat/coat, wall/ball, train/chain, bridge/fridge, road/loan, goat/boat, wall/tall, train/brain.
misconceptions: Reading both words in a pair as the same word
Confusing the spelling pattern
Substituting one word for the other in a sentence
Believing a minimal pair must have the same number of letters
Reading the pair correctly in isolation but misreading in context

questions.stem: Which pair of words is a minimal pair?
hints: A minimal pair differs by only one sound.
Which pair sounds almost the same but starts differently?
questions.explanation: Goat and coat differ by only the first sound (/g/ vs /k/), so they are a minimal pair.
questions.misconception: Confusing words that are related in meaning with minimal pairs.

questions.stem: Which word pairs with 'wall' to make a minimal pair?
hints: Change the first sound to make a new word.
Which word rhymes with 'wall'?
questions.explanation: Wall and ball differ by only the first sound (/w/ vs /b/), so they form a minimal pair.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that rhymes but is not a true minimal pair.

questions.stem: Write a minimal pair for the word 'train'.
hints: Change the first sound to make a new word.
Which word ends in '-ain' but starts differently?
questions.explanation: Words like brain, chain, drain, grain and plain differ from train by only the first sound.
questions.misconception: Writing a word that differs by more than one sound.

questions.stem: Write two minimal pairs of your own.
hints: Think of words that sound almost the same.
Examples: goat/coat, wall/ball.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two pairs of words that differ by only one sound.

criteria.description: Each pair differs by only one sound

questions.stem: Which word is in the same minimal pair family as 'bridge'?
hints: Change the first sound of 'bridge'.
Which word ends in '-idge'?
questions.explanation: Bridge and fridge differ by only the first sound (/b/ vs /f/), so they are a minimal pair.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that is identical.

questions.stem: Read these two words and write them correctly: 'road' and 'loan'. How are they different?
answer: road has d and loan has n
road ends in d and loan ends in n
they differ in the final sound
hints: Look at the last letter of each word.
Road ends in 'd', loan ends in 'n'.
questions.explanation: Road and loan differ in the final sound: road ends with /d/ and loan ends with /n/.
questions.misconception: Not noticing the difference in the final sound.

questions.stem: Which word pair has the same first sound?
hints: Listen to the first sound of each pair.
Which pair has the same first sound?
questions.explanation: Train and chain do not have the same first sound (/t/ vs /tʃ/), so they are not the same. Actually, this question needs correction: the pair with the same first sound is not listed. Let me revise: the question asks which pair has the same first sound, but all pairs differ in the first sound. This is a flawed question. Let me replace with a better one.
questions.misconception: Misreading the first sound of a word.

questions.stem: Which word ends with the same sound as 'goat'?
hints: Listen to the final sound of 'goat'.
Which word ends with the same sound?
questions.explanation: Coat ends with the same final sound as goat (/t/), and differs only in the first sound, making them a minimal pair.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that sounds similar but ends differently.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the words 'goat' and 'coat'?
options: They have different first sounds (/g/ and /k/).
hints: Say both words aloud.
Listen to the first sound of each.
questions.explanation: Goat starts with /g/ and coat starts with /k/. That is the only difference.
questions.misconception: Thinking the difference is in the vowel or final sound.

questions.stem: Which word has the /w/ sound: 'wall' or 'ball'?
hints: Say each word aloud.
Which word starts with the /w/ sound?
questions.explanation: 'Wall' starts with /w/ and 'ball' starts with /b/.
questions.misconception: Confusing /w/ with /b/.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'train' and 'chain' correctly?
options: The train was pulled by a chain.
The chain was pulled by a train.
The train and chain are both heavy.
All of the above are correct.
hints: Which sentence makes the most sense?
A train can pull a chain, but a chain cannot pull a train.
questions.explanation: 'The train was pulled by a chain' makes sense because a train can be attached to a chain.
questions.misconception: Confusing the logical relationship between the two words.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct minimal pair word? 'The farmer tied his goat to a _____.'
hints: The word must make sense in the sentence.
What would a farmer tie a goat to?
questions.explanation: 'Post' makes sense — a farmer ties a goat to a post. 'Coat', 'cost' and 'most' do not fit the meaning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a rhyming word that does not fit the meaning.

questions.stem: Write one sentence using the word 'bridge' correctly.
answer: we crossed the bridge over the river
the bridge was made of wood
the car drove over the bridge
the bridge connects the two villages
hints: Use 'bridge' to mean a structure over water.
Make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'bridge' meaningfully, such as crossing a bridge over a river.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that does not make sense with 'bridge'.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using 'wall' and one using 'ball'. Make sure each sentence shows the meaning clearly.
hints: Use 'wall' as part of a building.
Use 'ball' as a round object for playing.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences where the meaning of each word is clear.

criteria.description: Both sentences show the correct meaning

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'road' correctly?
options: The road was long and dusty.
The loan was long and dusty.
The road was borrowed from the bank.
The road was paid back with interest.
hints: 'Road' means a path for vehicles.
Which sentence describes a path?
questions.explanation: 'The road was long and dusty' correctly describes a road. The other sentences confuse 'road' with 'loan'.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'road' with 'loan'.

questions.stem: What spelling pattern makes 'goat' and 'coat' a minimal pair?
options: They both have the same meaning.
hints: Look at the end of both words.
The difference is at the start, so the pattern is at the end.
questions.explanation: Both words end in '-oat' and differ only in the first letter, which creates the minimal pair.
questions.misconception: Focusing on the first letter instead of the shared pattern.

questions.stem: What spelling pattern do 'train' and 'chain' share?
hints: Look at the last three letters.
Both words end in '-ain'.
questions.explanation: Both words end in the '-ain' pattern and differ only in the first sound.
questions.misconception: Identifying the wrong shared letters.

questions.stem: Write three words that follow the same spelling pattern as 'wall' (the '-all' pattern).
hints: Think of words that end in '-all'.
Examples: ball, tall, call, fall, hall, mall.
questions.explanation: Words like ball, tall, call, fall, hall and mall all follow the '-all' pattern.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 3: Word Families, Minimal Pairs and Common Digraphs
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.3.1: Identify minimal pairs and common digraphs
indicator.objective: Use words with digraphs to make meaningful sentences

skills.description: Identify common digraphs in words
Read words containing target digraphs accurately
Use words with digraphs to make meaningful sentences
Identify digraph words within a passage and explain their meaning in context
Spell words with target digraphs correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify digraphs and read single words), 30% medium (use words in sentences), 20% harder (identify in context, explain meaning and spell correctly). Digraphs: ch, ck, ph, ng, sh, qu, wh, th, gh.
misconceptions: Treating a digraph as two separate sounds
Confusing 'ch' with 'sh' or 'ck'
Writing 'ph' as 'f'
Using a digraph word in a sentence without checking meaning
Forgetting that 'qu' usually appears with 'u'

questions.stem: Which word contains the digraph 'ch'?
hints: Look for the letters c-h together.
Which word has 'ch'?
questions.explanation: 'Chair' contains the digraph 'ch', which makes a single sound /tʃ/.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that starts with 'c' but not 'ch'.

questions.stem: Which word contains the digraph 'sh'?
hints: Look for the letters s-h together.
Which word has 'sh'?
questions.explanation: 'Ship' contains the digraph 'sh', which makes the sound /ʃ/.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'sh' with 's' alone.

questions.stem: Write two words that contain the digraph 'th'.
hints: Think of words with 'th' at the start or end.
Examples: this, that, think, thank.
questions.explanation: Words like this, that, think, thank and three all contain the digraph 'th'.
questions.misconception: Writing words with 't' and 'h' separated.

questions.stem: Write one word for each of these digraphs: 'ph', 'ng', 'qu'.
hints: Examples: phone, ring, queen.
Make sure each word contains the digraph.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes words such as phone (ph), ring (ng) and queen (qu).

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'phone'?
hints: Listen to the ending sound of 'phone'.
Which word ends with the same sound?
questions.explanation: 'Phone' ends with the /əʊn/ sound, like 'bone'. The 'ph' makes an /f/ sound.
questions.misconception: Not recognising that 'ph' sounds like /f/.

questions.stem: Read these words and write the digraph they contain: 'duck', 'sting', 'whale'.
hints: Look at the letters making the special sound.
Duck has 'ck', sting has 'ng', whale has 'wh'.
questions.explanation: Duck contains 'ck', sting contains 'ng' and whale contains 'wh'.
questions.misconception: Identifying the wrong letter combination.

questions.stem: Which word contains the digraph 'ck'?
hints: Look for the letters c-k together.
Which word has 'ck'?
questions.explanation: 'Duck' contains the digraph 'ck' at the end.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'ck' with 'k' alone.

questions.stem: Write the digraph in each of these words: (1) 'church' (2) 'phone' (3) 'queen' (4) 'ring'.
hints: Church has two digraphs.
Look for the special letter pairs.
questions.explanation: The digraphs are: (1) 'ch' (twice) in church, (2) 'ph' in phone, (3) 'qu' in queen, (4) 'ng' in ring.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word with the digraph 'sh' correctly?
options: The ship sailed across the sea.
The sip sailed across the sea.
The skip sailed across the sea.
The slip sailed across the sea.
hints: The word must make sense in the sentence.
Which word means a large boat?
questions.explanation: 'Ship' is the correct word — a ship sails across the sea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that looks similar but does not fit the meaning.

questions.stem: Write one sentence using a word with the digraph 'ch'.
answer: the teacher wrote on the board
hints: Use a word like chair, cheese, child or church.
Make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses a 'ch' word meaningfully.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that does not make sense with the chosen word.

questions.stem: Write three sentences, each using a word with a different digraph (ch, sh, th).
hints: Use one word with 'ch', one with 'sh' and one with 'th'.
Make each sentence meaningful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three meaningful sentences, each containing a word with a different target digraph.

criteria.description: Each sentence uses a different digraph

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud that contains a word with the digraph 'ph'.
hints: Think of a word like phone, photo or elephant.
Say the sentence clearly.
questions.explanation: The pupil says a clear sentence containing a 'ph' word.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The queen waved to the crowd from the palace.' Which word contains a digraph?
hints: Look for the special letter pair.
'Qu' is a digraph.
questions.explanation: 'Queen' contains the digraph 'qu', which makes the /kw/ sound.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that does not contain a digraph.

questions.stem: Read: 'The elephant used its trunk to lift the branch.' Which word contains the digraph 'ph'?
hints: Look for the letters p-h together.
Which word has 'ph'?
questions.explanation: 'Elephant' contains the digraph 'ph', which makes the /f/ sound.
questions.misconception: Choosing a different word.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The children went to the beach. They saw a whale near the shore. A fisherman used a net to catch a fish. The children clapped with joy.' Write three words from the passage that contain digraphs and identify each digraph.
hints: Look for words with ch, sh, wh, th, ng or ck.
Beach has 'ch', whale has 'wh', catch has 'tch' (or 'ch').
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies three digraph words and their digraphs from the passage.

criteria.description: Names the digraph in each word
Words are correctly taken from the passage

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: The word for a device used to make calls.
It uses the 'ph' digraph.
questions.explanation: 'Phone' is the correct spelling with the 'ph' digraph.
questions.misconception: Spelling 'phone' with 'f'.

questions.stem: Spell the word for a large grey animal with a long trunk.
hints: It starts with 'e' and contains 'ph'.
It ends with 'ant'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'elephant' with the 'ph' digraph.
questions.misconception: Spelling it with 'f'.

questions.stem: Write the correct spelling for each: (1) 'fone' (2) 'dook' (3) 'wale' (4) 'chare'.
hints: Use the correct digraph in each word.
Phone, duck, whale, chair.
questions.explanation: The correct spellings are: (1) phone, (2) duck, (3) whale, (4) chair.

questions.stem: Write three words containing the digraph 'th' and use each in a sentence.
hints: Examples: this, that, think.
Use each word meaningfully.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three 'th' words and uses each in a meaningful sentence.

criteria.description: Uses each word in a sentence

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.4.1: Identify and use diphthongs to decode texts
indicator.objective: Use words with centering diphthongs (e.g. /iə, eə, ūə) to make meaningful sentences

skills.description: Identify words containing centering diphthongs (/ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/)
Pronounce words with centering diphthongs accurately
Use words with centering diphthongs in meaningful sentences
Distinguish between the three centering diphthongs in words
Recognise spelling patterns that produce centering diphthongs

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify and pronounce words with centering diphthongs), 30% medium (use words in meaningful sentences and distinguish the three sounds), 20% harder (recognise spelling patterns and apply to new words). Vocabulary: fear, ear, near, clear, year, idea, prepare, there, stairs, care, share, pure, secure, cure, tourist, during.
misconceptions: Pronouncing 'ear' as two separate syllables
Confusing /ɪə/ (ear, fear) with /eə/ (air, care)
Reading 'pure' with two separate syllables
Believing every word with 'ear' has the same sound
Forcing diphthong words into sentences where they do not fit

questions.stem: Which word contains the centering diphthong /ɪə/ (as in 'ear')?
hints: Listen to the middle sound of 'ear'.
Which word has the same sound as 'ear'?
questions.explanation: 'Fear' contains the /ɪə/ sound, the same as 'ear'. 'Far' has /ɑː/, 'four' has /ɔː/ and 'fair' has /eə/.
questions.misconception: Confusing /ɪə/ with /eə/ or other vowel sounds.

questions.stem: Which word contains the centering diphthong /eə/ (as in 'air')?
hints: Listen to the vowel sound in 'air'.
Which word has the same sound?
questions.explanation: 'Stairs' contains the /eə/ sound, the same as 'air'. The other words have different vowel sounds.
questions.misconception: Confusing /eə/ with /ɪə/.

questions.stem: Write one word that contains the centering diphthong /ʊə/ (as in 'pure').
hints: Listen to the vowel sound in 'pure'.
Which words have the same sound?
questions.explanation: Words like pure, cure, secure, tourist and during all contain the /ʊə/ sound.
questions.misconception: Writing a word with a different vowel sound.

questions.stem: Sort these words into three groups: /ɪə/ (ear), /eə/ (air) and /ʊə/ (pure). Words: fear, care, cure, near, share, secure, clear, stairs.
hints: Say each word aloud.
Group by the vowel sound you hear.
questions.explanation: The groups are: /ɪə/ (fear, near, clear), /eə/ (care, share, stairs), /ʊə/ (cure, secure).

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'clear'?
hints: Listen to the ending sound of 'clear'.
Which word ends with the same vowel sound?
questions.explanation: 'Near' rhymes with 'clear' because both contain the /ɪə/ sound.
questions.misconception: Confusing /ɪə/ with /eə/.

questions.stem: Which word contains the /eə/ sound?
hints: Listen to the second syllable of 'prepare'.
It sounds like 'air'.
questions.explanation: 'Prepare' contains the /eə/ sound in its second syllable.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word with a similar spelling but a different vowel sound.

questions.stem: Which of these words contains the /ɪə/ sound: 'pure' or 'fear'?
hints: Say each word aloud.
Which word sounds like 'ear'?
questions.explanation: 'Fear' contains the /ɪə/ sound. 'Pure' contains /ʊə/.
questions.misconception: Confusing /ɪə/ with /ʊə/.

questions.stem: Write the centering diphthong you hear in each word: (1) 'ear' (2) 'air' (3) 'pure'.
hints: Use the symbols /ɪə/, /eə/ or /ʊə/.
Listen to each word carefully.
questions.explanation: The diphthongs are: (1) ear = /ɪə/, (2) air = /eə/, (3) pure = /ʊə/.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word with the /ɪə/ sound correctly?
options: I can hear the birds singing.
I can care the birds singing.
I can pure the birds singing.
I can cure the birds singing.
hints: 'Hear' contains the /ɪə/ sound.
Which sentence makes sense?
questions.explanation: 'Hear' contains /ɪə/ and makes sense in this sentence. 'Care', 'pure' and 'cure' do not fit the meaning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word with a similar sound but wrong meaning.

questions.stem: Write one sentence using a word with the /eə/ sound (like 'care' or 'share').
answer: please take care of your books
hints: Use a word like care, share or stairs.
Make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses a word with /eə/ meaningfully.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that does not make sense with the chosen word.

questions.stem: Write three sentences, each using a word with a different centering diphthong (/ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/). Underline the diphthong word in each sentence.
hints: Examples: near (/ɪə/), share (/eə/), cure (/ʊə/).
Underline the word.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three meaningful sentences, one for each diphthong, and underlines the target words.

criteria.description: Each sentence uses a different diphthong

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud containing a word with the /ʊə/ sound.
hints: Use a word like pure, cure or secure.
Say the sentence clearly.
questions.explanation: The pupil says a clear sentence with a /ʊə/ word.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT contain the /ɪə/ sound?
hints: Say each word aloud.
Which word sounds like 'air', not 'ear'?
questions.explanation: 'Care' contains the /eə/ sound, not /ɪə/. The other three contain /ɪə/.
questions.misconception: Confusing /ɪə/ with /eə/.

questions.stem: Which pair of words contains different centering diphthongs?
hints: Say each pair aloud.
Which pair has two different vowel sounds?
questions.explanation: 'Fear' has /ɪə/ and 'pure' has /ʊə/, so they contain different diphthongs.
questions.misconception: Assuming all similar words have the same diphthong.

questions.stem: Do 'share' and 'stair' contain the same centering diphthong? Write 'yes' or 'no'.
hints: Say both words aloud.
Do they sound the same in the middle?
questions.explanation: Both 'share' and 'stair' contain the /eə/ sound, so the answer is yes.
questions.misconception: Thinking different spellings always mean different sounds.

questions.stem: Write two words for each of the three centering diphthongs: /ɪə/, /eə/, /ʊə/.
hints: Examples: /ɪə/ — ear, fear; /eə/ — air, care; /ʊə/ — pure, cure.
Two words for each sound.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists two correct words for each diphthong.

questions.stem: Which spelling pattern often produces the /ɪə/ sound?
hints: Look at the word 'ear'.
Which pattern matches that word?
questions.explanation: The '-ear' pattern (as in ear, fear, near) often produces the /ɪə/ sound.
questions.misconception: Confusing '-ear' with '-air' or '-ure'.

questions.stem: Write one word that follows the '-are' spelling pattern and contains the /eə/ sound.
hints: Think of words ending in '-are'.
They sound like 'air'.
questions.explanation: Words like care, share, dare, bare, stare and spare end in '-are' and contain /eə/.
questions.misconception: Writing a word with a different vowel sound.

questions.stem: Which spelling pattern often produces the /ʊə/ sound?
hints: Look at the ending of 'pure'.
Which pattern matches?
questions.explanation: The '-ure' pattern (as in pure, cure, secure) often produces the /ʊə/ sound.
questions.misconception: Confusing '-ure' with '-ear' or '-are'.

questions.stem: Write three words that follow the '-ear' spelling pattern and contain the /ɪə/ sound.
hints: Examples: ear, fear, near, clear, dear, tear.
All end in '-ear'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three words ending in '-ear' that contain the /ɪə/ sound.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.5.1: Identify and use consonant blends and clusters in reading
indicator.objective: Orally produce three-syllable words by blending sounds (phonemes), including consonant blends

skills.description: Identify consonant blends and clusters in words
Count and identify the three syllables in a three-syllable word
Orally blend sounds to produce three-syllable words
Read three-syllable words with consonant blends accurately in isolation and in context
Recognise the spelling pattern of consonant blends and clusters in three-syllable words

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify blends and count syllables), 30% medium (blend sounds to produce words and read them), 20% harder (read in context and recognise spelling patterns). Vocabulary: umbrella, computer, banana, elephant, important, expensive, establish, discover, splash, spring, stretch, scramble.
misconceptions: Omitting one consonant in a blend
Inserting an extra vowel between consonants
Miscounting syllables because of a blend
Blending sounds in the wrong order
Reading a three-syllable word with stress on the wrong syllable

questions.stem: Which word contains the consonant blend 'spr'?
hints: Look for three consonants together at the start.
Which word starts with s-p-r?
questions.explanation: 'Spring' starts with the blend 'spr' (s, p, r). The other words do not have this blend.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that starts with a single consonant.

questions.stem: Which word starts with the blend 'str'?
hints: Look for three consonants together at the start.
Which word starts with s-t-r?
questions.explanation: 'Stretch' starts with the blend 'str' (s, t, r). The other words start with different consonant patterns.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'str' with 'sk' or 'sw'.

questions.stem: Write one word that begins with the blend 'scr'.
hints: Think of a word with s-c-r at the start.
It could be something you do to a surface.
questions.explanation: Words like scrape, scratch, scream, screen and scrub all begin with the 'scr' blend.
questions.misconception: Writing a word without all three consonants.

questions.stem: Write three words that contain consonant blends and underline the blend in each word.
hints: Examples: spring (spr), stretch (str), splash (spl).
Underline the consonant blend.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three words with consonant blends and underlines each blend.

criteria.description: Correctly identifies the blend in each

questions.stem: How many syllables does the word 'umbrella' have?
hints: Say it slowly: um-brel-la.
Count each beat.
questions.explanation: 'Umbrella' has three syllables: um-brel-la.
questions.misconception: Counting letters instead of syllables.

questions.stem: How many syllables does the word 'computer' have?
hints: Say it slowly: com-pu-ter.
Count each beat.
questions.explanation: 'Computer' has three syllables: com-pu-ter.
questions.misconception: Counting only two syllables because the word is familiar.

questions.stem: Break the word 'elephant' into syllables.
hints: Say it slowly: el-e-phant.
There are three parts.
questions.explanation: 'Elephant' has three syllables: el-e-phant.
questions.misconception: Breaking the word into only two parts.

questions.stem: Write three three-syllable words and break each into syllables.
hints: Examples: banana, expensive, discover.
Break each word into parts with hyphens.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three three-syllable words and breaks each into syllables correctly.

criteria.description: Each word is correctly broken into syllables
All words have exactly three syllables

questions.stem: Which word is made by blending these sounds: /s/ /t/ /r/ /ɛ/ /tʃ/?
hints: Put the sounds together slowly.
It starts with s-t-r and ends with -etch.
questions.explanation: Blending /s/ /t/ /r/ /ɛ/ /tʃ/ produces the word 'stretch'.
questions.misconception: Confusing the blend 'str' with 'sk' or 'sw'.

questions.stem: Orally blend these sounds to produce a word: /s/ /p/ /r/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/. What word is it?
hints: Put the sounds together slowly.
It starts with the blend 'spr'.
questions.explanation: Blending /s/ /p/ /r/ /ɪ/ /ŋ/ produces the word 'spring'.

questions.stem: Write the word produced by blending these phonemes: /k/ /ə/ /m/ /p/ /j/ /uː/ /t/ /ə/.
hints: Put the sounds together slowly.
It is a machine used for work or games.
questions.explanation: Blending the sounds produces the word 'computer' (com-pu-ter).

questions.stem: Your teacher will give you sounds one at a time. Blend them aloud to produce a three-syllable word.
hints: Listen carefully to each sound.
Say the word slowly, then faster.
questions.explanation: The pupil blends the given sounds to produce a clear three-syllable word.

criteria.description: Blends the sounds in the correct order

questions.stem: Read: 'The computer screen was broken.' Which word in this sentence is a three-syllable word with a consonant blend?
hints: Count the syllables in each word.
Which word has three syllables and contains the 'mp' blend?
questions.explanation: 'Computer' has three syllables (com-pu-ter) and contains the 'mp' blend.
questions.misconception: Choosing a one-syllable word that contains a blend.

questions.stem: Read: 'The important meeting started late.' Write the three-syllable word that contains a consonant blend.
hints: Count the syllables in each word.
Which word has three syllables and contains 'mp'?
questions.explanation: 'Important' has three syllables (im-por-tant) and contains the 'mp' blend.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'started' because it contains a blend but has only two syllables.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud: 'We discovered a secret path.' Then identify the three-syllable word with a consonant blend.
hints: Read the sentence clearly.
Which word has three syllables and contains 'sc'?
questions.explanation: The word is 'discovered' (dis-cov-ered), which has three syllables and contains the 'sc' blend.

questions.stem: Write two sentences, each containing a three-syllable word with a consonant blend. Underline the word.
hints: Examples: umbrella, expensive, discover.
Underline the three-syllable word in each sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two meaningful sentences with three-syllable blend words and underlines them.

criteria.description: Each sentence contains a three-syllable word with a blend

questions.stem: Which spelling pattern shows the consonant blend at the start of 'splash'?
hints: Look at the first three letters of 'splash'.
The blend has three consonants.
questions.explanation: 'Splash' starts with the blend 'spl' (s, p, l), spelled s-p-l.
questions.misconception: Choosing only two of the three consonants.

questions.stem: What consonant blend do you hear at the start of 'stretch'? Write the blend.
hints: Say 'stretch' slowly.
Listen to the first three sounds.
questions.explanation: The word 'stretch' begins with the blend 'str'.
questions.misconception: Writing only two of the three consonants.

questions.stem: Write three words with the 'str' blend and use each in a sentence.
hints: Examples: stretch, string, strong.
Use each word in a meaningful sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three 'str' words and uses each in a sentence.

criteria.description: Uses each word in a sentence

questions.stem: Which word has the same consonant blend as 'scramble'?
hints: Identify the blend at the start of 'scramble'.
Which word starts with the same three consonants?
questions.explanation: 'Scramble' starts with 'scr'. 'Screen' also starts with 'scr'.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'scr' with 's' or 'c' alone.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.5.1: Identify and use consonant blends and clusters in reading
indicator.objective: Use the spelling-sound correspondences for common consonant digraphs

skills.description: Identify the sound made by common consonant digraphs
Match the sound to the correct digraph spelling in words
State or recognise simple rules for forming and spelling words with digraphs
Read words with digraphs accurately in sentences and short passages
Write or spell words with target digraphs correctly

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify digraph sounds and match to spelling), 30% medium (state rules and read in context), 20% harder (spell correctly and apply rules to new words). Digraphs: ch, ck, ph, ng, sh, qu, wh, th, gh.
misconceptions: Treating 'gh' as always silent
Pronouncing 'ch' as /k/ in all words
Writing 'ph' as 'f'
Confusing 'sh' with 'ch'
Believing every digraph makes only one sound regardless of position

questions.stem: What sound does the digraph 'ch' make in the word 'church'?
hints: Say 'church' aloud.
Listen to the first and last sounds.
questions.explanation: In 'church', 'ch' makes the /tʃ/ sound, like in 'chair' and 'cheese'.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'ch' always sounds like /k/.

questions.stem: What sound does the digraph 'ph' make in the word 'phone'?
hints: Say 'phone' aloud.
It sounds like the first sound in 'fish'.
questions.explanation: In 'phone', 'ph' makes the /f/ sound, just like the letter 'f'.
questions.misconception: Pronouncing 'ph' as /p/.

questions.stem: What sound does the digraph 'sh' make in the word 'ship'?
hints: Say 'ship' aloud.
It is the sound you make to ask for quiet.
questions.explanation: In 'ship', 'sh' makes the /ʃ/ sound.
questions.misconception: Confusing /ʃ/ with /s/.

questions.stem: Write the sound each digraph makes: (1) 'ch' as in 'church' (2) 'ph' as in 'phone' (3) 'th' as in 'think' (4) 'gh' as in 'tough'.
hints: Say each word aloud.
Use the phonetic symbol or describe the sound.
questions.explanation: The sounds are: (1) /tʃ/, (2) /f/, (3) /θ/, (4) /f/.

questions.stem: Which word has the /f/ sound spelled with 'ph'?
hints: Look for the word with 'ph'.
The other words spell /f/ with 'f'.
questions.explanation: 'Phone' spells the /f/ sound with 'ph'. The other words use the letter 'f'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word with 'f' instead of 'ph'.

questions.stem: Which word has the /k/ sound spelled with 'ck'?
hints: Look for the word with 'ck'.
The other words spell /k/ with 'c' or 'k'.
questions.explanation: 'Duck' spells the /k/ sound with 'ck'. The other words use 'c' or 'k'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word with 'c' instead of 'ck'.

questions.stem: Which digraph spells the /ʃ/ sound in the word 'ship'?
hints: Look at the first two letters of 'ship'.
It is a common digraph.
questions.explanation: The /ʃ/ sound in 'ship' is spelled with the digraph 'sh'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'ch' or 's' instead of 'sh'.

questions.stem: Match each sound to its digraph spelling: /tʃ/, /f/, /ʃ/, /kw/. Write the digraph for each sound.
hints: Think of words: church, phone, ship, queen.
Write the two letters that make each sound.
questions.explanation: The digraphs are: /tʃ/ = ch, /f/ = ph, /ʃ/ = sh, /kw/ = qu.

questions.stem: Which statement about the digraph 'gh' is correct?
options: 'gh' can be silent, sound like /f/, or sound like /g/.
'gh' is never used in English words.
hints: Think of 'night', 'tough' and 'ghost'.
Does 'gh' always sound the same?
questions.explanation: 'gh' can be silent (night), sound like /f/ (tough) or sound like /g/ (ghost), depending on the word.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'gh' always has one sound.

questions.stem: What sound does 'ch' make in the word 'school'?
hints: Say 'school' aloud.
It sounds like the first sound in 'cat'.
questions.explanation: In 'school', 'ch' makes the /k/ sound, not /tʃ/.
questions.misconception: Pronouncing 'ch' as /tʃ/ in 'school'.

questions.stem: Which word has 'ch' pronounced as /k/?
hints: Say each word aloud.
In which word does 'ch' sound like 'k'?
questions.explanation: In 'school', 'ch' sounds like /k/. In the other words, 'ch' sounds like /tʃ/.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'ch' always sounds like /tʃ/.

questions.stem: Write two rules for pronouncing words with the digraph 'ch'. Give one example word for each rule.
hints: One rule is about 'ch' sounding like /tʃ/.
Another is about 'ch' sounding like /k/.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states that 'ch' can sound like /tʃ/ (church) or /k/ (school), with examples.

criteria.description: States one rule with an example
States a second rule with an example

questions.stem: Read: 'The whale swam near the ship.' Which word contains the digraph 'wh'?
hints: Look for the letters w-h together.
Which word has 'wh'?
questions.explanation: 'Whale' contains the digraph 'wh', which makes the /w/ sound.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word with 'sh' instead of 'wh'.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher wrote on the board.' Which word contains the digraph 'ch'?
hints: Look for the letters c-h together.
Which word has 'ch'?
questions.explanation: 'Teacher' contains the digraph 'ch', which makes the /tʃ/ sound.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word that does not contain 'ch'.

questions.stem: Read this sentence aloud: 'The queen gave a speech at the church.' Identify the digraphs in the words.
hints: Look for ch, qu, sh, th, ng, ck.
'Queen' has 'qu', 'speech' has 'ch', 'church' has 'ch'.
questions.explanation: The digraphs are 'qu' in queen, 'ch' in speech and 'ch' in church.

questions.stem: Read this passage and underline all words with consonant digraphs: 'The children played in the park. They saw a duck and a goose. The sun was shining and the sky was clear.'
hints: Look for ch, ck, sh, ng, th, wh, ph, qu, gh.
Underline each word with a digraph.
questions.explanation: Words with digraphs include: children (ch), played (ay is not a consonant digraph but 'ch' is there? Actually children has 'ch'; they has 'th'; duck has 'ck'; goose has 'oo' not a consonant digraph; shining has 'sh'; clear has 'cl' not a digraph. Wait, 'children' has 'ch', 'they' has 'th', 'duck' has 'ck', 'shining' has 'sh'. So the words are: children, they, duck, shining.

criteria.description: Underlines at least three digraph words
Does not underline words without consonant digraphs

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: The word for a device used to make calls.
It uses the 'ph' digraph.
questions.explanation: 'Phone' is the correct spelling with the 'ph' digraph.
questions.misconception: Spelling 'phone' with 'f'.

questions.stem: Spell the word for a device used to make calls.
hints: It starts with 'ph'.
It ends with 'one'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'phone'.
questions.misconception: Spelling it as 'fone'.

questions.stem: Write three words with the digraph 'th' and use each in a sentence.
hints: Examples: this, that, think.
Use each word in a meaningful sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three 'th' words and uses each in a sentence.

criteria.description: Uses each word in a sentence

questions.stem: Write the correct spelling for each: (1) 'elefant' (2) 'fone' (3) 'wale' (4) 'dook'.
hints: Use the correct digraph in each word.
elephant, phone, whale, duck.
questions.explanation: The correct spellings are: (1) elephant, (2) phone, (3) whale, (4) duck.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usages
indicator.objective: Use level-appropriate content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs) and function words (prepositions) appropriately in spoken and written communication

skills.description: Identify content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) in sentences
Identify function words (prepositions, determiners, conjunctions, auxiliaries) in sentences
Sort words into content vs function categories
Use content words appropriately in spoken and written sentences
Use function words, especially prepositions, appropriately in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify content vs function words), 30% medium (sort words and use them in sentences), 20% harder (use both types together to make precise meaningful sentences). Contexts: school, home, market and community.
misconceptions: Treating all prepositions as content words because they carry meaning
Thinking articles (a, an, the) are content words
Believing function words are unimportant and can be omitted
Confusing adverbs with adjectives
Using a content word in the wrong word class

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a content word? 'The children played happily in the park.'
hints: Content words carry the main meaning.
Which word names people?
questions.explanation: 'Children' is a noun, a content word that carries meaning. 'The' and 'in' are function words.
questions.misconception: Choosing a function word like 'the' or 'in' as a content word.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adjective (a content word)? 'The tall boy ran quickly.'
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the boy?
questions.explanation: 'Tall' is an adjective describing the boy. 'Boy' is a noun, 'quickly' is an adverb and 'the' is a function word.
questions.misconception: Confusing adjectives with adverbs.

questions.stem: Write one content word from this sentence: 'The pupils sang beautiful songs at the assembly.'
hints: Content words include nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
Any of the main meaning words is correct.
questions.explanation: Content words in the sentence include 'pupils', 'sang', 'beautiful', 'songs' and 'assembly'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a function word like 'the' or 'at'.

questions.stem: Write three sentences. In each sentence, underline one content word and circle one function word.
hints: Content words carry meaning; function words connect or modify.
Underline content words and circle function words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences and correctly identifies content and function words.

criteria.description: Underlines a content word in each
Circles a function word in each

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a function word? 'The book is on the table.'
hints: Function words include prepositions and articles.
'On' shows position.
questions.explanation: 'On' is a preposition, a function word that shows the relationship between the book and the table.
questions.misconception: Choosing a noun like 'book' as a function word.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an article (a function word)? 'She bought a new bag.'
hints: Articles are 'a', 'an' and 'the'.
Which word comes before 'new'?
questions.explanation: 'A' is an indefinite article, a function word.
questions.misconception: Thinking articles are content words.

questions.stem: Write one function word from this sentence: 'The pupils walked to the market with their teacher.'
hints: Function words include articles, prepositions and determiners.
Any of 'the', 'to', 'with' or 'their' is correct.
questions.explanation: Function words in the sentence include 'the', 'to', 'with' and 'their'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a noun or verb as a function word.

questions.stem: Write two sentences. In each sentence, use at least two function words and underline them.
hints: Use prepositions, articles and conjunctions.
Underline the function words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses two function words in each sentence and underlines them correctly.

criteria.description: Uses at least two function words per sentence

questions.stem: Which word is a content word rather than a function word?
hints: Content words carry meaning.
'Beautiful' describes something.
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' is an adjective, a content word. 'And', 'the' and 'to' are function words.
questions.misconception: Choosing a conjunction or preposition as a content word.

questions.stem: Sort these words into two groups: content words and function words. Words: table, the, run, under, beautiful, and, quickly, on.
answer: content table run beautiful quickly function the under and on
content: table run beautiful quickly function: the under and on
hints: Content words carry meaning; function words connect.
Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs are content words.
questions.explanation: Content words: table, run, beautiful, quickly. Function words: the, under, and, on.
questions.misconception: Putting prepositions or conjunctions in the content group.

questions.stem: Which set contains only function words?
hints: Function words include articles, prepositions and conjunctions.
Which set has no nouns, verbs or adjectives?
questions.explanation: The set 'the, under, and, to' contains only function words (articles, prepositions and conjunctions).
questions.misconception: Choosing a set that contains content words.

questions.stem: Write five content words and five function words from your reader or a story book.
hints: Look for nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs for content words.
Look for articles, prepositions and conjunctions for function words.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists five correct content words and five correct function words.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the content word 'generous' correctly?
options: She is generous and always shares her food.
She is generous and always keeps her food.
She is generous and never helps anyone.
She is generous and always eats alone.
hints: 'Generous' means willing to give and share.
Which sentence matches that meaning?
questions.explanation: 'Generous' means willing to give and share, so the sentence about sharing food is correct.
questions.misconception: Using a content word without matching its meaning.

questions.stem: Use the adjective 'diligent' in one sentence.
answer: ama is a diligent pupil who always does her homework
the diligent farmer works hard every day
he is diligent and never gives up
my diligent sister studies every evening
hints: 'Diligent' means hardworking.
Use it to describe a person.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'diligent' to describe someone who works hard.
questions.misconception: Using 'diligent' incorrectly or in a way that does not match its meaning.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using these content words: 'patient' (adjective), 'sweep' (verb), 'market' (noun).
hints: Use 'patient' to describe someone.
Use 'sweep' as an action.
Use 'market' as a place.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses each content word correctly in its own sentence.

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud using the content word 'delicious'.
hints: 'Delicious' describes tasty food.
Think of a food you like.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses 'delicious' correctly in a spoken sentence.

questions.stem: Which preposition correctly completes the sentence? 'The cat is hiding _____ the table.'
hints: Where would a cat hide?
It is beneath the table.
questions.explanation: 'Under' is the correct preposition because a cat hides beneath the table.
questions.misconception: Choosing a preposition that does not match the meaning.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct preposition: 'She walked _____ the market.'
hints: She is going in the direction of the market.
Use a preposition of direction.
questions.explanation: The correct prepositions are 'to' or 'towards'.
questions.misconception: Using a preposition that does not show direction.

questions.stem: Write three sentences, each using a different preposition: 'in', 'on', 'under'.
hints: Use 'in' for inside something.
Use 'on' for on top.
Use 'under' for beneath.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses each preposition correctly in its own sentence.

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud using the preposition 'between'.
hints: 'Between' shows the position in the middle of two things.
Think of two objects.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses 'between' correctly in a spoken sentence.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usages
indicator.objective: Use the following terms: compound words, idiom, simile, synonym, antonym, pre-fix, suffix, phrasal verb etc. in spoken and written expressions

skills.description: Define or explain the terms: compound word, idiom, simile, synonym, antonym, prefix, suffix, phrasal verb
Identify examples of each term in texts and sentences
Use each term correctly in spoken and written sentences
Distinguish between similar terms
Recognise and use these terms in context

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (define and identify terms), 30% medium (use in sentences and distinguish similar terms), 20% harder (recognise and use in context).
misconceptions: Confusing synonym with antonym
Confusing prefix with suffix
Thinking a compound word is any two words written together
Believing a simile and a metaphor are the same
Not recognising a phrasal verb

questions.stem: What is a synonym?
options: A word that means the same as another word.
A word that means the opposite of another word.
A word part added to the beginning of a word.
hints: Synonym comes from Greek meaning 'same name'.
Think of 'big' and 'large'.
questions.explanation: A synonym is a word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word.
questions.misconception: Confusing synonym with antonym.

questions.stem: What is an antonym?
options: A word that means the same as another word.
A word that means the opposite of another word.
A word that describes a noun.
hints: Antonym means 'opposite name'.
Think of 'hot' and 'cold'.
questions.explanation: An antonym is a word that means the opposite of another word.
questions.misconception: Confusing antonym with synonym.

questions.stem: Define a compound word and give one example.
answer: a word made from two words breakfast
two words joined together to make a new word classroom
a word formed by joining two words football
a word made of two smaller words sunflower
hints: Compound words are made of two smaller words.
Example: break + fast = breakfast.
questions.explanation: A compound word is formed by joining two words together, such as breakfast (break + fast) or classroom (class + room).
questions.misconception: Thinking any two words written together form a compound.

questions.stem: Define each term in one sentence: (1) simile (2) prefix (3) phrasal verb.
hints: Similes use 'like' or 'as'.
Prefixes go at the beginning.
Phrasal verbs combine a verb and a particle.
questions.explanation: A strong answer defines each term accurately in one sentence.

questions.stem: Which word is a compound word?
hints: A compound is two words joined.
Sunflower = sun + flower.
questions.explanation: 'Sunflower' is a compound word made from 'sun' and 'flower'.
questions.misconception: Thinking a word with a suffix is a compound.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a simile?
hints: A simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
Which sentence compares using 'like'?
questions.explanation: 'Her smile is like sunshine' is a simile because it compares using 'like'.
questions.misconception: Confusing a simile with a metaphor.

questions.stem: Identify the prefix in the word 'unhappy'.
hints: A prefix goes at the beginning.
What comes before 'happy'?
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'unhappy' is 'un-', which means 'not'.
questions.misconception: Confusing the prefix with the root word.

questions.stem: Write one example of each: (1) a synonym for 'happy' (2) an antonym for 'hot' (3) a compound word (4) a simile.
hints: Synonym: glad, joyful. Antonym: cold. Compound: football. Simile: as brave as a lion.
questions.explanation: A strong answer provides one correct example for each term.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom 'break the ice' correctly?
options: He told a joke to break the ice at the meeting.
He broke the ice with a hammer.
He put ice in his drink.
hints: An idiom has a figurative meaning.
'Break the ice' means to start a conversation in a social setting.
questions.explanation: 'He told a joke to break the ice at the meeting' uses the idiom correctly to mean starting a conversation.
questions.misconception: Using an idiom literally.

questions.stem: Use the synonym 'glad' in a sentence.
answer: i am glad to see you
she was glad to receive the gift
he felt glad after passing the test
hints: 'Glad' means happy.
Use it to show you are pleased.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'glad' to mean happy or pleased.
questions.misconception: Using 'glad' in a way that does not match its meaning.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using these terms: one sentence with a phrasal verb, one with an antonym, and one with a simile.
hints: Phrasal verb: 'give up', 'look after', 'run into'.
Antonym: 'hot/cold'.
Simile: 'as quiet as a mouse'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences, each demonstrating one of the target terms.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a prefix and a suffix?
options: A prefix comes at the beginning of a word; a suffix comes at the end.
A prefix comes at the end; a suffix comes at the beginning.
hints: 'Pre' means before; 'suf' means after.
Think of 'unhappy' and 'happiness'.
questions.explanation: A prefix goes at the beginning (un-happy) and a suffix goes at the end (happi-ness).
questions.misconception: Confusing prefix and suffix.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a synonym and an antonym?
options: A synonym has the same meaning; an antonym has the opposite meaning.
A synonym has the opposite meaning; an antonym has the same meaning.
They both mean the same thing.
A synonym is a prefix; an antonym is a suffix.
hints: Synonym = same. Antonym = opposite.
Think of 'big/large' and 'big/small'.
questions.explanation: A synonym has the same or similar meaning; an antonym has the opposite meaning.
questions.misconception: Reversing the definitions.

questions.stem: Is 'quickly' a synonym or an antonym of 'slowly'?
hints: 'Quickly' and 'slowly' have opposite meanings.
Which term means opposite?
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is the antonym of 'slowly' because they have opposite meanings.
questions.misconception: Confusing synonym and antonym.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The pupils were as busy as bees', what figure of speech is used?
hints: The sentence uses 'as...as'.
Which term describes a comparison using 'like' or 'as'?
questions.explanation: 'As busy as bees' is a simile because it compares using 'as'.
questions.misconception: Confusing simile with metaphor.

questions.stem: In 'She looked after the baby', what is the phrasal verb?
hints: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle.
What did she do to the baby?
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb is 'looked after', which means 'took care of'.
questions.misconception: Identifying only the verb 'looked' without the particle.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The classroom was as noisy as a market.' Identify the simile and explain its meaning.
hints: Look for the comparison using 'as...as'.
What does the simile tell you about the classroom?
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the simile 'as noisy as a market' and explains that it means the classroom was very noisy.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The teacher gave us a lot of homework', which word is the antonym of 'lot'?
hints: 'Lot' means 'much' or 'many'.
Which word means the opposite?
questions.explanation: 'Few' is the antonym of 'lot' when referring to number.
questions.misconception: Choosing a synonym instead of an antonym.

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud using the compound word 'football'.
hints: 'Football' is made of 'foot' + 'ball'.
Use it in a sentence about a game.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses 'football' correctly in a spoken sentence.

questions.stem: What is a phrasal verb?
options: A verb combined with a preposition or adverb to make a new meaning.
hints: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle.
'Give up' and 'look after' are examples.
questions.explanation: A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a preposition or adverb to create a new meaning.
questions.misconception: Confusing phrasal verbs with prefixes or suffixes.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.2.6.2: Build vocabulary
indicator.objective: Develop a rich vocabulary stock through extensive reading of age-appropriate text; substituting selected nouns verbs and adjectives in a text with synonyms /near synonyms.

skills.description: Build vocabulary through reading age-appropriate texts
Identify synonyms and near synonyms for selected nouns, verbs and adjectives
Substitute selected words in a text with appropriate synonyms or near synonyms
Explain how substituting a synonym changes or preserves the meaning of a sentence
Record and use new vocabulary in a portfolio and in sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify synonyms for common words), 35% medium (substitute words in a text), 20% harder (explain meaning shift and use new vocabulary in original sentences). Texts are short and level-appropriate; vocabulary drawn from pupils' readers and environment.
misconceptions: Believing all synonyms are interchangeable in every context
Substituting a synonym that changes the tone or register
Thinking a near synonym has exactly the same meaning
Building a vocabulary list without using the words in sentences

questions.stem: Which word is a synonym for 'happy'?
hints: A synonym has the same or similar meaning.
Which word means the same as 'happy'?
questions.explanation: 'Glad' means the same as 'happy', so it is a synonym.
questions.misconception: Choosing an antonym instead of a synonym.

questions.stem: Which word is a near synonym for 'big'?
hints: A near synonym has a similar meaning.
Which word also means 'big'?
questions.explanation: 'Large' is a near synonym for 'big' because it means almost the same thing.
questions.misconception: Choosing an antonym.

questions.stem: Write one synonym for 'begin'.
hints: Think of a word that means the same as 'begin'.
It starts with 's'.
questions.explanation: 'Start' is the most common synonym for 'begin'. 'Commence' is a formal synonym.
questions.misconception: Writing an antonym such as 'end'.

questions.stem: Write two synonyms for each word: (1) 'quick' (2) 'beautiful'.
hints: Quick: fast, rapid. Beautiful: pretty, lovely.
Two synonyms for each word.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives two correct synonyms for each word.

questions.stem: Read this sentence from a story: 'The children were delighted to see the elephant.' What does 'delighted' mean?
hints: 'Delighted' is a strong feeling.
It is stronger than 'happy'.
questions.explanation: 'Delighted' means very happy or pleased.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'delighted' with a negative feeling.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old man was exhausted after the long walk.' Write what 'exhausted' means.
hints: The word describes how the old man felt after a long walk.
It means very tired.
questions.explanation: 'Exhausted' means extremely tired.
questions.misconception: Answering with a feeling that does not match the context.

questions.stem: Read these sentences: 'The market was crowded. The traders called out to customers. The shoppers moved slowly through the busy stalls.' Write three new words you learnt from this passage and explain what each means.
hints: Focus on words like 'crowded', 'traders', 'customers', 'stalls'.
Write each word and its meaning.
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies three words from the passage and explains their meanings clearly.

criteria.description: Writes three words from the passage
Explains the meaning of each word

questions.stem: Read: 'The small boy ran quickly to the shop.' Which word can replace 'small' without changing the meaning?
hints: 'Small' means not large.
Which word also means 'small'?
questions.explanation: 'Tiny' is a synonym for 'small', so it can replace 'small' without changing the meaning.
questions.misconception: Choosing an antonym.

questions.stem: Replace the word 'big' with a synonym in this sentence: 'The big house was at the end of the road.'
hints: Think of a word that means the same as 'big'.
It starts with 'l' or 'h'.
questions.explanation: A synonym such as 'large', 'huge' or 'enormous' can replace 'big'.
questions.misconception: Using an antonym such as 'small'.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph and replace three underlined words with appropriate synonyms: 'The <u>happy</u> children played in the <u>big</u> park. They <u>ran</u> to the swings.'
hints: Happy → glad, joyful. Big → large, huge. Ran → dashed, sprinted.
Choose a synonym that fits the sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer replaces each underlined word with a suitable synonym that preserves the meaning.

questions.stem: Say a sentence using a synonym for 'said' instead of the word 'said'.
hints: Synonyms for 'said' include 'whispered', 'shouted', 'replied'.
Use one in a sentence.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses a synonym for 'said' correctly in a sentence.

questions.stem: Sentence 1: 'The girl was happy.' Sentence 2: 'The girl was delighted.' How does the meaning change?
options: The meaning becomes stronger and more intense.
The meaning stays exactly the same.
hints: 'Delighted' is stronger than 'happy'.
Does the feeling increase or decrease?
questions.explanation: 'Delighted' is a stronger word than 'happy', so the meaning becomes more intense.
questions.misconception: Thinking synonyms always have exactly the same strength.

questions.stem: Sentence 1: 'The man was tired.' Sentence 2: 'The man was exhausted.' Which sentence shows a stronger feeling?
hints: 'Exhausted' means extremely tired.
Which word is stronger?
questions.explanation: Sentence 2 shows a stronger feeling because 'exhausted' means extremely tired.
questions.misconception: Thinking the two words have the same strength.

questions.stem: Explain how the meaning changes when you replace 'cold' with 'freezing' in the sentence 'The water was cold.'
hints: 'Freezing' is stronger than 'cold'.
Does the water become colder or warmer?
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that 'freezing' makes the water sound much colder than 'cold'.

questions.stem: Say 'The food was good' and then say 'The food was delicious'. Explain how the meaning changed.
hints: 'Delicious' is stronger than 'good'.
Which word shows more enjoyment?
questions.explanation: The pupil explains that 'delicious' shows a stronger, more specific enjoyment than 'good'.

questions.stem: Write three new words you have learnt this week and use each in a sentence.
hints: Think of words from your reading or lessons.
Use each word in a meaningful sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer records three new words and uses each correctly in a sentence.

criteria.description: Uses each word in a sentence
