questions.misconception: Choosing a describing word instead of the verb.

questions.stem: Write the main verb in this sentence: 'The pupils wrote a letter.'
hints: What did the pupils do?
The word shows the action.
questions.explanation: 'Wrote' is the main verb showing the pupils' action.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'letter' instead.

questions.stem: Which word is a primary auxiliary verb? 'She has finished her homework.'
hints: Primary auxiliaries include be, have and do.
Which word helps the main verb 'finished'?
questions.explanation: 'Has' is a primary auxiliary that helps the main verb 'finished'.
questions.misconception: Choosing the main verb 'finished' instead.

questions.stem: Which word is a primary auxiliary verb?
hints: Primary auxiliaries are forms of be, have and do.
Which of these is a form of 'be'?
questions.explanation: 'Are' is a form of 'be', so it is a primary auxiliary. 'Can', 'will' and 'must' are modals.
questions.misconception: Choosing a modal instead of a primary auxiliary.

questions.stem: Write one primary auxiliary verb in this sentence: 'They do not like fish.'
hints: It is a form of 'do'.
It helps the main verb 'like'.
questions.explanation: 'Do' is the primary auxiliary that helps the main verb 'like'.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'not' or 'like' instead.

questions.stem: Which word is a modal auxiliary verb? 'She can swim very well.'
hints: Modals include can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would.
Which word shows ability?
questions.explanation: 'Can' is a modal auxiliary showing ability.
questions.misconception: Choosing the main verb 'swim'.

questions.stem: Which word is a modal auxiliary verb? 'You must finish your work.'
hints: Modals show obligation, ability, possibility etc.
Which word shows strong obligation?
questions.explanation: 'Must' is a modal auxiliary showing obligation.
questions.misconception: Choosing the main verb 'finish'.

questions.stem: Write the modal auxiliary verb in this sentence: 'We should respect our elders.'
hints: It shows advice or obligation.
It is one of the modals.
questions.explanation: 'Should' is the modal auxiliary showing obligation or advice.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'respect' as the modal.

questions.stem: In this sentence, which word is the main verb and which is the auxiliary? 'The pupils are reading books.'
hints: The main verb shows the action.
The auxiliary helps the main verb.
questions.explanation: 'Reading' is the main verb and 'are' is the auxiliary helping it.
questions.misconception: Reversing the main verb and auxiliary.

questions.stem: In this sentence, which word is the main verb and which is the auxiliary? 'The children have eaten their food.'
hints: The main verb is the action word.
The auxiliary comes before the main verb.
questions.explanation: 'Eaten' is the main verb and 'have' is the auxiliary.
questions.misconception: Thinking 'have' is the main verb when it is helping another verb.

questions.stem: Identify the auxiliary verb in this sentence: 'She will come tomorrow.'
hints: It is a modal auxiliary.
It helps the main verb 'come'.
questions.explanation: 'Will' is the auxiliary helping the main verb 'come'.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'come' as the auxiliary.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one with only a main verb and one with a main verb plus an auxiliary. Underline the main verb and circle the auxiliary.
hints: Example: 'She sings.' (main only) / 'She is singing.' (main + auxiliary).
Underline the main verb; circle the auxiliary.
questions.explanation: A strong answer shows one sentence with only a main verb and one with a main verb and an auxiliary, marked clearly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the auxiliary correctly?
hints: A modal is followed by the base form of the verb.
Do not add 'to' or '-s' or '-ing' after a modal.
questions.explanation: After a modal such as 'can', use the base form of the verb: can swim.
questions.misconception: Adding 'to', '-s' or '-ing' after a modal.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: 'They' takes 'are' as the auxiliary.
After 'are', the main verb takes '-ing'.
questions.explanation: 'They are going' is correct because 'they' takes 'are' and the main verb takes '-ing'.
questions.misconception: Wrong subject-verb agreement or wrong verb form after the auxiliary.

questions.stem: Complete with the correct auxiliary: 'She _____ finished her work.' (use 'have' or 'has')
hints: 'She' is singular.
Use 'has' with singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'She has finished' is correct because 'she' takes 'has'.
questions.misconception: Using 'have' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using these auxiliaries correctly: 'is', 'have', 'must'. Each sentence must also have a main verb.
hints: 'Is' goes with a singular subject.
'Have' goes with I/you/we/they.
'Must' is a modal followed by the base verb.
questions.explanation: A strong answer uses each auxiliary correctly with a main verb in a meaningful sentence.

criteria.description: Each sentence contains a main verb

questions.stem: In 'They have a new house', is 'have' a main verb or an auxiliary?
hints: There is no other verb in the sentence for 'have' to help.
When 'have' stands alone, it is the main verb.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'have' stands alone and shows possession, so it is the main verb.
questions.misconception: Assuming every 'have' is an auxiliary.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a modal auxiliary correctly?
hints: Modals are followed by the base form.
No 'to', '-s' or '-ing' after a modal.
questions.explanation: 'She might come' is correct because 'might' is followed by the base form 'come'.
questions.misconception: Changing the verb form after a modal.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: 'The pupils should be studying for their exams.' Identify the modal auxiliary, the primary auxiliary and the main verb.
hints: There are three verbs: should, be, studying.
Should = modal; be = primary auxiliary; studying = main verb.
questions.explanation: 'Should' is the modal auxiliary, 'be' is the primary auxiliary and 'studying' is the main verb.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use appropriate subject-verb agreement (indefinite pronouns, Singular/plural and Collective nouns

skills.description: Match a singular subject with a singular verb
Match a plural subject with a plural verb
Use a singular or plural verb with collective nouns appropriately
Match indefinite pronouns to the correct verb
Identify and correct agreement errors in a short passage

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (singular/plural agreement), 35% medium (collective and indefinite pronoun agreement), 20% harder (identify and correct errors in context). Contexts: school, family, community, sports, market.
misconceptions: Using a plural verb with a singular subject
Using a singular verb with a plural subject
Treating every collective noun as plural
Using plural verbs with singular indefinite pronouns
Using singular verbs with plural indefinite pronouns
Being confused by intervening phrases

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The girl are running to school.
hints: The subject 'girl' is singular.
A singular subject takes a singular verb ending in -s.
questions.explanation: 'The girl runs' is correct because 'girl' is singular and takes the singular verb 'runs'.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: The boy is in the classroom.
The boy are in the classroom.
The boy be in the classroom.
The boy were in the classroom.
hints: 'Boy' is a singular subject.
Use 'is' with a singular subject.
questions.explanation: 'The boy is' is correct because 'boy' is singular.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
hints: 'Girls' is plural.
Use a plural verb with a plural subject.
questions.explanation: 'The girls are playing' is correct because 'girls' is plural and takes 'are'.
questions.misconception: Using a singular verb with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: 'Pupils' is plural.
Use 'have' with plural subjects.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils have finished' is correct because 'pupils' is plural.
questions.misconception: Using 'has' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Complete with 'is' or 'are': 'The children _____ playing in the park.'
hints: 'Children' is plural.
Use the plural verb 'are'.
questions.explanation: 'The children are playing' is correct because 'children' is plural.
questions.misconception: Using 'is' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Complete with 'runs' or 'run': 'The dog _____ fast.'
hints: 'Dog' is singular.
A singular subject takes the verb ending in -s.
questions.explanation: 'The dog runs fast' is correct because 'dog' is singular.
questions.misconception: Using the base form with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: When a collective noun acts as one unit, use a singular verb.
The team plays as one group.
questions.explanation: 'The team is playing' is correct because the team acts as a single unit.
questions.misconception: Treating every collective noun as plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct when the group is acting as individuals?
options: The class is arguing among themselves.
The class are arguing among themselves.
The class be arguing among themselves.
The class was arguing among themselves.
hints: When the members of a group act individually, use a plural verb.
The word 'themselves' signals that the group is treated as individuals.
questions.explanation: 'The class are arguing among themselves' is correct because the members are acting individually.
questions.misconception: Using a singular verb when the group acts as individuals.

questions.stem: Complete with 'is' or 'are': 'The family _____ going on a trip.'
hints: The family acts as one unit.
Use a singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'The family is going' is correct because the family acts as one unit.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with a collective noun acting as one unit.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: The committee have made its decision.
The committee has made its decision.
The committee have made their decision.
hints: The committee acts as one unit here.
Use a singular verb and a singular possessive pronoun.
questions.explanation: 'The committee has made its decision' is correct because the committee acts as a single unit.
questions.misconception: Mixing a plural verb with a singular pronoun, or vice versa.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: 'Everyone' is singular.
Use a singular verb with 'everyone'.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone is here' is correct because 'everyone' takes a singular verb.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with 'everyone'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Both of the boys is here.
Both of the boys are here.
Both of the boys be here.
Both of the boys was here.
hints: 'Both' refers to two people and takes a plural verb.
Use 'are' with 'both'.
questions.explanation: 'Both of the boys are here' is correct because 'both' is plural.
questions.misconception: Using a singular verb with 'both'.

questions.stem: Complete with 'is' or 'are': 'Somebody _____ knocking at the door.'
hints: 'Somebody' is singular.
Use a singular verb.
questions.explanation: 'Somebody is knocking' is correct because 'somebody' is singular.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with 'somebody'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Each of the pupils have a book.
Each of the pupils has a book.
Each of the pupils are having a book.
Each of the pupils be having a book.
hints: 'Each' is singular.
Even though 'pupils' is plural, 'each' controls the verb.
questions.explanation: 'Each of the pupils has a book' is correct because 'each' is singular.
questions.misconception: Being confused by the plural noun after 'each'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Neither of the boys are ready.
Neither of the boys is ready.
Neither of the boys be ready.
Neither of the boys were ready.
hints: 'Neither' is singular in formal English.
Use a singular verb with 'neither'.
questions.explanation: 'Neither of the boys is ready' is correct because 'neither' is singular.
questions.misconception: Being confused by the plural noun after 'neither'.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The pupils of Basic 6 is very hardworking. They studies every day. Their teacher are proud of them.' Which sentence contains an agreement error?
options: The pupils of Basic 6 is very hardworking.
Their teacher are proud of them.
hints: Check each subject and verb pair.
Pupils = plural; they = plural; teacher = singular.
questions.explanation: All three sentences contain errors: 'pupils...is' should be 'are'; 'they studies' should be 'study'; 'teacher are' should be 'is'.
questions.misconception: Missing agreement errors in context.

questions.stem: Read this passage and correct the subject-verb agreement errors: 'The girls in my class is very friendly. They helps each other with homework. One of them have a kind heart.' Write the corrected passage.
hints: Girls = plural; they = plural; one = singular.
Change 'is' to 'are', 'helps' to 'help', 'have' to 'has'.
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'The girls in my class are very friendly. They help each other with homework. One of them has a kind heart.'

questions.stem: Read: 'The bag of books are heavy. The pupils carries it together.' Which option corrects the agreement errors?
options: The bag of books is heavy. The pupils carry it together.
The bag of books are heavy. The pupils carry it together.
The bag of books is heavy. The pupils carries it together.
The bag of books are heavy. The pupils carries it together.
hints: The subject of the first sentence is 'bag', not 'books'.
The subject of the second sentence is 'pupils'.
questions.explanation: The correct version is: 'The bag of books is heavy. The pupils carry it together.'
questions.misconception: Being confused by the plural noun in the phrase 'of books'.

questions.stem: Write two sentences about your class using correct subject-verb agreement. Use one singular subject and one plural subject.
hints: Singular subject → singular verb (ends in -s).
Plural subject → plural verb (no -s).
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with correct agreement for singular and plural subjects.

criteria.description: Writes a sentence with a singular subject and verb
Writes a sentence with a plural subject and verb

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use different forms of verbs: − Irregular − Infinitive to talk about personal activities E.g.: I asked my friend to read the story.

skills.description: Form the simple past of irregular verbs
Form the past participle of irregular verbs
Identify the infinitive form (to + base verb) in a sentence
Use infinitives to talk about personal activities
Use irregular verbs correctly in spoken and written sentences about personal activities

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify the infinitive; form simple irregular pasts), 35% medium (use infinitives for personal activities), 20% harder (past participles and mixed use in context). Contexts: daily activities, school, home, sports, community.
misconceptions: Adding -ed to irregular verbs
Confusing past simple and past participle
Omitting 'to' before an infinitive
Using the infinitive after modals
Using 'to' as a preposition and confusing it with the infinitive marker

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'go'?
hints: 'Go' is an irregular verb.
The past form is not 'goed'.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'go' is 'went'. 'Gone' is the past participle.
questions.misconception: Adding -ed to an irregular verb.

questions.stem: What is the simple past form of 'eat'?
hints: 'Eat' is irregular.
The past form changes the vowel.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'eat' is 'ate'. 'Eaten' is the past participle.
questions.misconception: Adding -ed to an irregular verb.

questions.stem: Write the simple past form of 'see'.
hints: 'See' is irregular.
See → saw.
questions.explanation: The simple past of 'see' is 'saw'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'seed' or 'seen'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct past form of 'take'?
hints: 'Take' is irregular.
The past form is 'took'.
questions.explanation: 'She took the book' uses the correct simple past form of 'take'.
questions.misconception: Adding -ed to an irregular verb.

questions.stem: Write the simple past forms of these irregular verbs: 'write', 'buy', 'drink', 'run'.
hints: Write → wrote; buy → bought; drink → drank; run → ran.
Use the correct irregular forms.
questions.explanation: The simple past forms are: wrote, bought, drank, ran.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of 'go'?
hints: The past participle is used after have/has/had.
Go → went → gone.
questions.explanation: The past participle of 'go' is 'gone'. We use it after have/has/had.
questions.misconception: Confusing the simple past with the past participle.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct past participle?
hints: After 'has', use the past participle.
The past participle of 'go' is 'gone'.
questions.explanation: 'She has gone home' uses the correct past participle after 'has'.
questions.misconception: Using the simple past instead of the past participle after 'has'.

questions.stem: Write the past participle of 'eat'.
hints: It is used after have/has/had.
Eat → ate → eaten.
questions.explanation: The past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'ate' instead of 'eaten'.

questions.stem: Write the past participle forms of these irregular verbs: 'see', 'write', 'take', 'break'.
hints: See → seen; write → written; take → taken; break → broken.
Use the correct participle forms.
questions.explanation: The past participle forms are: seen, written, taken, broken.

questions.stem: What is the infinitive form of the verb in this sentence? 'I want to read a book.'
hints: An infinitive is 'to' + base verb.
Which phrase has 'to' plus a verb?
questions.explanation: 'To read' is the infinitive form.
questions.misconception: Choosing the main verb 'want'.

questions.stem: Which of these is an infinitive?
hints: An infinitive starts with 'to'.
Which option has 'to' plus a base verb?
questions.explanation: 'To sing' is the infinitive form.
questions.misconception: Choosing the '-ing' form or past form.

questions.stem: Identify the infinitive in this sentence: 'She asked me to help her.'
hints: It starts with 'to'.
It is followed by the base verb 'help'.
questions.explanation: 'To help' is the infinitive in the sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'help' alone instead of 'to help'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an infinitive correctly?
options: I want to go to the market.
I want go to the market.
I want going to the market.
I want went to the market.
hints: After 'want', use the infinitive.
'To go' is the infinitive.
questions.explanation: 'I want to go' is correct because 'want' is followed by the infinitive 'to go'.
questions.misconception: Omitting 'to' before the infinitive.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an infinitive to talk about a personal activity?
hints: An infinitive is 'to' + base verb.
Which option uses 'to play'?
questions.explanation: 'I like to play football' uses the infinitive 'to play' to talk about a personal activity.
questions.misconception: Confusing the infinitive with the '-ing' form.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with an infinitive: 'I asked my friend _____ me with my homework.' (help)
hints: Use 'to' + base verb.
The verb is 'help'.
questions.explanation: 'I asked my friend to help me' is correct.
questions.misconception: Writing 'help' without 'to'.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about personal activities using an infinitive in each sentence. Underline the infinitive.
hints: Use verbs like want, like, ask, try, hope.
Follow each with 'to' + base verb.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with infinitives used correctly to talk about personal activities.

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud using an infinitive to describe something you plan to do this week.
hints: Use 'I plan to...' or 'I want to...'.
Follow with the base verb.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses an infinitive correctly in a spoken sentence about a plan.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the irregular verb correctly?
options: She goed to the market yesterday.
She went to the market yesterday.
She gone to the market yesterday.
She going to the market yesterday.
hints: 'Go' is irregular.
The simple past is 'went'.
questions.explanation: 'She went to the market yesterday' uses the correct irregular past form.
questions.misconception: Adding -ed to an irregular verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: After 'have', use the past participle.
The past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.
questions.explanation: 'I have eaten my lunch' uses the correct past participle after 'have'.
questions.misconception: Using the simple past 'ate' after 'have'.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about your personal activities. Use the irregular verbs 'went', 'saw' and 'ate' in the simple past.
hints: Use each verb in a separate sentence.
Make the sentences meaningful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with the irregular verbs used correctly in the simple past.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the simple present form of verbs in sentences: − For scheduled future actions. − for future possibilities or plans

skills.description: Identify simple present verbs used for scheduled future actions
Use the simple present for scheduled future actions in sentences
Use the simple present in conditional/future possibility structures
Identify time markers that signal future meaning
Distinguish the simple present used for habit vs for future

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify scheduled future and time markers), 35% medium (use simple present for scheduled future), 20% harder (conditional future possibility and distinguishing uses). Contexts: school timetable, transport (tro-tro, bus), sports fixtures, events.
misconceptions: Using 'will' for every future meaning even when a schedule is meant
Confusing habitual present with scheduled future
Using the future tense in the 'if' clause
Using the simple present for an unscheduled plan
Missing time markers that signal future meaning

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present for a scheduled future action?
options: The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.
The bus left at 6 a.m. yesterday.
The bus will leave at 6 a.m. tomorrow.
hints: Scheduled future uses the simple present with a future time marker.
The action is planned for tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow' uses the simple present 'leaves' for a scheduled future event.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' when a schedule is meant.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present for a scheduled future action?
options: The match starts at 3 p.m. on Saturday.
The match started at 3 p.m. on Saturday.
The match will start at 3 p.m. on Saturday.
hints: The match is scheduled for Saturday.
Use the simple present for timetabled events.
questions.explanation: 'The match starts at 3 p.m. on Saturday' uses the simple present 'starts' for a scheduled event.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' for a scheduled event.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence signals a future scheduled action? 'The school reopens next Monday.'
hints: Look for a time expression.
Which words tell you when the school reopens?
questions.explanation: 'Next Monday' is the time marker that signals the future scheduled action.
questions.misconception: Missing the time marker.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple present for a scheduled future action?
options: The tro-tro leaves at 7 a.m. tomorrow.
The tro-tro will leave at 7 a.m. tomorrow.
The tro-tro left at 7 a.m. tomorrow.
The tro-tro is leaving at 7 a.m. tomorrow.
hints: Scheduled actions use the simple present.
The time is given for tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'The tro-tro leaves at 7 a.m. tomorrow' uses the simple present for a scheduled future action.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' for a timetable event.

questions.stem: Complete with the simple present form of 'start': 'The assembly _____ at 8 a.m. tomorrow.'
hints: Use the simple present for a scheduled event.
'Assembly' is singular, so add -s.
questions.explanation: 'The assembly starts at 8 a.m. tomorrow' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'will start' instead of the scheduled present.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about scheduled future events using the simple present. Use 'leaves', 'starts' and 'closes'.
hints: Use a time marker like 'tomorrow' or 'next week'.
Use the simple present for each scheduled event.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with scheduled future meaning using the simple present.

criteria.description: Uses 'leaves', 'starts' and 'closes' in the simple present
Each sentence has a future time marker

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple present for a future possibility?
options: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If it will rain, we will stay at home.
If it rained, we will stay at home.
If it is raining, we will stay at home.
hints: Use the simple present in the 'if' clause.
Do not use 'will' in the 'if' clause.
questions.explanation: 'If it rains, we will stay at home' uses the simple present 'rains' in the 'if' clause for a future possibility.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' in the 'if' clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple present for a future possibility?
options: If he comes early, we shall go together.
If he will come early, we shall go together.
If he came early, we shall go together.
If he is coming early, we shall go together.
hints: The 'if' clause uses the simple present.
'Comes' is the simple present.
questions.explanation: 'If he comes early, we shall go together' uses the simple present 'comes' in the 'if' clause.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' in the 'if' clause.

questions.stem: Complete with the simple present form of 'pass': 'If you _____ the exam, you will get a prize.'
hints: Use the simple present in the 'if' clause.
The subject is 'you', so use the base form.
questions.explanation: 'If you pass the exam' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'will pass' in the 'if' clause.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using the simple present in 'if' clauses to talk about future possibilities.
hints: Start with 'If...' and use the simple present.
The main clause can use 'will' or 'shall'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with the simple present in 'if' clauses for future possibilities.

criteria.description: Uses the simple present in 'if' clauses

questions.stem: Which time marker signals a future meaning?
hints: Future time markers point to time ahead.
Which word means the day after today?
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' signals a future meaning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a past time marker.

questions.stem: Which time marker signals a future meaning in this sentence? 'The train leaves at 6 a.m. next Monday.'
hints: Look for the time expression that points to the future.
'Next Monday' is a future time marker.
questions.explanation: 'Next Monday' is the future time marker in the sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing the verb or subject instead of the time marker.

questions.stem: Write one future time marker you could use with the simple present to show a scheduled event.
hints: Think of words that point to the future.
Examples: tomorrow, next week, next month.
questions.explanation: Future time markers include tomorrow, next week, next Monday and next month.
questions.misconception: Writing a past time marker.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the simple present used for a habit?
options: The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.
The match starts at 3 p.m. on Saturday.
hints: A habit is something done regularly.
'Every evening' signals a habit.
questions.explanation: 'She reads every evening' uses the simple present for a habitual action.
questions.misconception: Confusing habitual present with scheduled future.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the simple present used for a scheduled future action?
options: He walks to school every day.
The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow.
hints: Look for a future time marker.
'Tomorrow' signals a scheduled future event.
questions.explanation: 'The bus leaves at 6 a.m. tomorrow' uses the simple present for a scheduled future action.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence that describes a habit.

questions.stem: Does 'She reads every evening' use the simple present for a habit or for a future action? Write 'habit' or 'future'.
hints: 'Every evening' signals a regular action.
It is not about a scheduled future event.
questions.explanation: 'She reads every evening' uses the simple present for a habit.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is a future action because of the present tense.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using the simple present for a habit and one using it for a scheduled future action.
hints: Habit: use words like 'every day'.
Scheduled future: use a future time marker like 'tomorrow'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence for a habit and one for a scheduled future action, both using the simple present.

criteria.description: Writes a sentence for a habit
Writes a sentence for a scheduled future action
Both use the simple present correctly

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the simple present for a scheduled future action?
options: The pupils are going to the museum tomorrow.
The pupils go to the museum tomorrow at 9 a.m.
The pupils went to the museum yesterday.
The pupils will go to the museum tomorrow.
hints: Scheduled actions use the simple present.
The time is given for tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils go to the museum tomorrow at 9 a.m.' uses the simple present for a scheduled future action.
questions.misconception: Using 'will go' for a timetable event.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the simple present for a future possibility?
options: Unless you study hard, you will fail.
Unless you will study hard, you will fail.
Unless you studied hard, you will fail.
Unless you are studying hard, you will fail.
hints: 'Unless' works like 'if not'.
Use the simple present in the 'unless' clause.
questions.explanation: 'Unless you study hard' uses the simple present 'study' for a future possibility.
questions.misconception: Using 'will' in the 'unless' clause.

questions.stem: Read: 'The school closes on Friday for the holidays.' Is the simple present used for a habit or a scheduled future action? Explain your answer.
hints: The action is planned for a specific time.
Is it something that happens regularly or a one-time scheduled event?
questions.explanation: The sentence uses the simple present for a scheduled future action because the school closing on Friday is a planned event.

criteria.description: Identifies it as a scheduled future action

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the past continuous form of verbs to talk about actions/events which were going on when a second one took place e.g. We were playing football when the fire broke out.

skills.description: Form the past continuous correctly (was/were + -ing verb)
Identify the past continuous verb in a sentence
Identify the two actions in a sentence and show which was ongoing and which interrupted it
Use 'when' with the interrupting action and 'while' with the ongoing action correctly
Write original sentences using past continuous for the ongoing action plus simple past for the second action

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (form and identify past continuous), 35% medium (identify the two actions; use when/while), 20% harder (write original sentences combining both actions). Contexts: school, home, market, community, sports.
misconceptions: Using the simple past for both actions without showing which was ongoing
Forgetting the auxiliary
Using 'while' with the short interrupting action
Mixing up 'was' and 'were' with singular/plural subjects
Using the past continuous for the interrupting action instead of the simple past
Adding -ing without dropping final 'e'

questions.stem: Which is the correct past continuous form of 'play' for 'we'?
hints: 'We' is plural.
Use 'were' with plural subjects.
questions.explanation: The past continuous for 'we' is 'we were playing'.
questions.misconception: Using 'was' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Which is the correct past continuous form of 'read' for 'she'?
hints: 'She' is singular.
Use 'was' with singular subjects.
questions.explanation: The past continuous for 'she' is 'she was reading'.
questions.misconception: Using 'were' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Complete with the past continuous form of 'cook': 'They _____ dinner when I arrived.'
hints: 'They' is plural.
Use 'were' + the -ing form.
questions.explanation: 'They were cooking' is the past continuous form.
questions.misconception: Using 'was cooking' or forgetting the auxiliary.

questions.stem: Write the past continuous forms of these verbs for the subjects given: (1) run (he) (2) swim (they) (3) make (she) (4) sit (we).
hints: Use was/were + -ing form.
Remember spelling rules: double consonants, drop 'e'.
questions.explanation: The correct forms are: he was running, they were swimming, she was making, we were sitting.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence is in the past continuous? 'We were playing football when the fire broke out.'
hints: Past continuous = was/were + -ing.
Which phrase has 'were' plus an '-ing' verb?
questions.explanation: 'Were playing' is the past continuous verb.
questions.misconception: Choosing the simple past 'broke out' as the past continuous.

questions.stem: Identify the past continuous verb in this sentence: 'The pupils were sweeping the classroom when the bell rang.'
hints: Look for 'was' or 'were' plus an '-ing' verb.
It describes the ongoing action.
questions.explanation: 'Were sweeping' is the past continuous verb describing the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'rang' as the past continuous.

questions.stem: In 'She was reading when the lights went out', which action was going on?
hints: The ongoing action uses the past continuous.
Which action was happening first and continued?
questions.explanation: 'She was reading' is the ongoing action in the past continuous.
questions.misconception: Confusing the ongoing action with the interrupting one.

questions.stem: In 'We were playing football when the fire broke out', which action interrupted the other?
hints: The interrupting action is the short one.
What happened while they were playing?
questions.explanation: 'The fire broke out' is the interrupting action, happening while they were playing.
questions.misconception: Confusing the interrupting action with the ongoing one.

questions.stem: Complete with 'when' or 'while': '_____ I was walking home, it started to rain.'
hints: Use 'while' with the ongoing action.
The walking was ongoing.
questions.explanation: 'While I was walking home' is correct because 'while' introduces the ongoing action.
questions.misconception: Using 'when' with an ongoing action in this structure.

questions.stem: Complete with 'when' or 'while': 'She was cooking _____ the phone rang.'
hints: The ringing is the short interrupting action.
Use 'when' with the interrupting action.
questions.explanation: 'She was cooking when the phone rang' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'while' with the interrupting action.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'when' and 'while' correctly?
options: While I was reading, the doorbell rang.
While I was reading, the doorbell rang while.
When I was reading, the doorbell rang while.
While I read, the doorbell was ringing when.
hints: Use 'while' for the ongoing action and 'when' for the interrupting action.
Which sentence uses the two correctly?
questions.explanation: 'While I was reading, the doorbell rang' uses 'while' for the ongoing action and the simple past for the interruption.
questions.misconception: Misplacing 'when' and 'while'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the past continuous for the ongoing action and simple past for the interruption?
options: I was walking home when I saw a snake.
I walked home when I was seeing a snake.
I was walking home when I was seeing a snake.
I walked home when I saw a snake.
hints: Ongoing action = past continuous; interrupting action = simple past.
Which sentence shows this pattern?
questions.explanation: 'I was walking home when I saw a snake' uses the past continuous for the ongoing action and the simple past for the interruption.
questions.misconception: Using the simple past for both actions.

questions.stem: Write a sentence using the past continuous and simple past to describe an interruption. Use 'read' and 'knock'.
answer: i was reading when someone knocked on the door
i was reading when the door was knocked
i was reading when the knock came
i was reading when someone knocked
hints: Use 'was reading' for the ongoing action.
Use 'knocked' for the interrupting action.
questions.explanation: 'I was reading when someone knocked on the door' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using the simple past for the ongoing action.

questions.stem: Write three sentences, each using the past continuous for the ongoing action and the simple past for the interrupting action. Use different subjects.
hints: Example: 'They were playing when it started to rain.'
Use different subjects and different verbs.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with the correct pattern of past continuous + simple past.

criteria.description: Uses past continuous for the ongoing action
Uses simple past for the interrupting action

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: 'Boys' is plural.
Use 'were' with plural subjects.
questions.explanation: 'The boys were playing football' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'was' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using 'while' with the past continuous, and one using 'when' with the simple past interrupting action.
hints: While + past continuous.
When + simple past.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'while' + past continuous and one with 'when' + simple past.

criteria.description: Writes a sentence with 'while' + past continuous
Writes a sentence with 'when' + simple past

questions.stem: Read: 'While the teacher was explaining the lesson, a pupil sneezed loudly.' Identify the ongoing action and the interrupting action.
hints: The ongoing action uses past continuous.
The interrupting action uses simple past.
questions.explanation: Ongoing action: 'the teacher was explaining the lesson'. Interrupting action: 'a pupil sneezed loudly'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past continuous correctly?
options: She were singing when I entered.
She was singing when I entered.
She was sang when I entered.
hints: 'She' is singular.
Use 'was' + -ing verb.
questions.explanation: 'She was singing when I entered' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'were' or the past participle.

questions.stem: Say a sentence aloud about something you were doing when a second event happened.
hints: Use 'I was ... when ...'.
Describe a real or imagined situation.
questions.explanation: The pupil says a clear sentence using the past continuous and simple past.

criteria.description: Uses simple past for the second action

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.5.1: Apply the knowledge of verbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use the imperative form of verb to give warning and express prohibitions E.g. Break the glass, and you will pay for it.

skills.description: Form imperative verbs (base form) for commands and warnings
Use the 'imperative + and + consequence' structure to give a warning
Express prohibitions using 'Do not / Don't + base verb'
Distinguish an imperative warning or prohibition from a statement
Use imperative forms for warnings and prohibitions in original sentences about safety

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (form imperative verbs and simple prohibitions), 35% medium (use warning structure), 20% harder (distinguish from statements and write original warnings). Contexts: road safety, home safety, school rules, health and hygiene.
misconceptions: Using the infinitive with 'to' for imperatives
Using the wrong subject with imperatives
Confusing a prohibition with a positive command
Forgetting 'and' or 'or' in the warning structure
Confusing the consequence marker 'or' vs 'and'
Making imperatives sound like statements by adding a subject

questions.stem: Which sentence is an imperative (command)?
hints: An imperative tells someone to do something.
It starts with a verb and has no subject.
questions.explanation: 'Close the door' is an imperative because it tells someone to do something.
questions.misconception: Choosing a statement as an imperative.

questions.stem: Which word is an imperative verb?
hints: An imperative uses the base form of the verb.
Which is the base form?
questions.explanation: 'Stop' is the base form, used for imperatives.
questions.misconception: Choosing a past or present participle form.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence as an imperative command: 'You should run to the classroom.'
hints: Remove 'You should'.
Start with the base verb.
questions.explanation: The imperative form is 'Run to the classroom'.
questions.misconception: Keeping 'You should' in the command.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the warning structure correctly?
options: Break the glass, and you will pay for it.
Break the glass, or you will pay for it.
You break the glass and pay for it.
Breaking the glass pays for it.
hints: The warning structure is 'imperative + and + consequence'.
'And' shows that the consequence will follow if the action is done.
questions.explanation: 'Break the glass, and you will pay for it' is the correct warning structure.
questions.misconception: Using 'or' instead of 'and' in the warning structure.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a warning using the imperative structure?
options: Touch the wire, and you will get a shock.
You will get a shock if you touch the wire.
Touching the wire gets a shock.
hints: Look for 'imperative + and + consequence'.
'Touch the wire, and...' uses the warning structure.
questions.explanation: 'Touch the wire, and you will get a shock' uses the imperative warning structure.
questions.misconception: Choosing a conditional statement instead of the warning structure.

questions.stem: Complete the warning: 'Run across the road without looking, and _____.'
answer: you could be hit by a car
hints: The consequence should be a danger.
What can happen if you run across the road without looking?
questions.explanation: A suitable consequence is 'you may be knocked down' or 'a car may hit you'.
questions.misconception: Giving a consequence that is not a warning.

questions.stem: Write two warnings using the 'imperative + and + consequence' structure. Use these topics: (1) playing with fire, (2) disobeying school rules.
hints: Example: 'Play with fire, and you will get burnt.'
Make the consequences clear.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two correct warning sentences.

criteria.description: Uses the imperative + and + consequence structure

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses a prohibition?
hints: A prohibition tells someone NOT to do something.
Look for 'Do not' or 'Don't'.
questions.explanation: 'Do not touch the wire' is a prohibition.
questions.misconception: Choosing a statement as a prohibition.

questions.stem: Which is the correct prohibition form?
options: Do not run in the corridor.
Do not running in the corridor.
Do not ran in the corridor.
Do not to run in the corridor.
hints: Use 'Do not' + base verb.
Do not add '-ing' or 'to'.
questions.explanation: 'Do not run' uses the base verb correctly.
questions.misconception: Adding '-ing' or 'to' after 'Do not'.

questions.stem: Rewrite this as a prohibition: 'You must not play with matches.'
hints: Use 'Do not' + base verb.
Remove 'You must'.
questions.explanation: The prohibition is 'Do not play with matches'.
questions.misconception: Keeping 'You must' in the prohibition.

questions.stem: Write three prohibitions for your classroom using 'Do not' or 'Don't'. Each prohibition must start with an imperative verb.
hints: Examples: 'Do not shout in class.' 'Don't fight.'
Use 'Do not' + base verb.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three clear prohibitions for the classroom.

criteria.description: Prohibitions are relevant to the classroom

questions.stem: Which sentence is an imperative (warning), not a statement?
options: You will pay for the broken glass.
Break the glass, and you will pay for it.
hints: An imperative tells or warns someone to do something.
It starts with a verb and includes a consequence.
questions.explanation: 'Break the glass, and you will pay for it' is an imperative warning. The others are statements.
questions.misconception: Confusing a statement with an imperative warning.

questions.stem: Is 'The pupils should not make noise' an imperative or a statement? Write 'imperative' or 'statement'.
hints: It has a subject ('the pupils') and 'should not'.
An imperative does not have a subject and uses the base verb.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils should not make noise' is a statement, not an imperative.
questions.misconception: Confusing a statement with an imperative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correct warning about road safety?
options: You cross the road without looking and a car hits you.
Cross the road without looking, and you may be hit by a car.
Crossing the road without looking is dangerous.
The road is dangerous without looking.
hints: Use the imperative + and + consequence structure.
The warning should start with a verb.
questions.explanation: 'Cross the road without looking, and you may be hit by a car' is a correct warning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a statement or a factual sentence instead of a warning.

questions.stem: Write one prohibition about health and hygiene.
answer: do not eat food with dirty hands
do not skip washing your hands
hints: Think about keeping healthy.
Use 'Do not' + base verb.
questions.explanation: A suitable prohibition is 'Do not eat food with dirty hands'.
questions.misconception: Writing a statement instead of a prohibition.

questions.stem: Write three imperative sentences about safety: one warning and two prohibitions.
hints: Warning: 'Touch the fire, and you will get burnt.'
Prohibitions: 'Do not play with knives.'
Use the correct structures.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one warning and two prohibitions using the correct imperative forms.

questions.stem: Give one warning and one prohibition aloud about keeping safe at school.
hints: Warning: imperative + and + consequence.
Prohibition: 'Do not' + base verb.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a clear warning and prohibition.

questions.stem: Which warning is correctly formed?
options: Cheat in the exam, and you will be punished.
Cheat in the exam, or you will be punished.
You cheat in the exam and you will be punished.
Cheating in the exam punishes you.
hints: Use 'and' to show the consequence will follow.
'Or' would change the meaning.
questions.explanation: 'Cheat in the exam, and you will be punished' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'or' instead of 'and'.

questions.stem: Which prohibition is correctly formed?
options: Do not to cross the road alone.
Do not cross the road alone.
Do not crossing the road alone.
Do not crossed the road alone.
hints: Use 'Do not' + base verb.
Do not add 'to', '-ing' or '-ed'.
questions.explanation: 'Do not cross the road alone' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using the wrong verb form after 'Do not'.

questions.stem: Write one imperative warning and one statement. Explain how they are different.
hints: Warning: starts with a verb, gives a consequence.
Statement: has a subject and gives information.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one warning and one statement, and explains the difference.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.6.1: Apply the knowledge of different types of adverbs in communication
indicator.objective: Use adverbs to express degree and reason

skills.description: Identify adverbs of degree in sentences
Identify adverbs or adverbials that express reason
Use adverbs of degree correctly to modify adjectives or adverbs
Use adverbs or adverbials of reason correctly in sentences
Distinguish between adverbs of degree and adverbs of reason in context

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify degree and reason adverbs in given sentences), 30% medium (use them in original sentences), 20% harder (distinguish the two types in context and select the appropriate one). Contexts: school, home, market, weather, feelings, daily activities.
misconceptions: Confusing 'too' with 'to' or 'two'
Using 'very' where 'too' is needed
Placing 'enough' before an adjective instead of after
Treating 'because' only as a conjunction and not recognising it as expressing reason
Confusing 'so' as a degree adverb with 'so' as a reason connector
Using 'therefore' and 'because' interchangeably
Placing 'very' before a verb instead of an adjective or adverb
Using 'too much' with a count noun where 'too many' is needed
Confusing 'hardly' with 'hard'

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adverb of degree? 'The soup was very hot.'
hints: Adverbs of degree tell us how much or to what extent.
Which word modifies the adjective 'hot'?
questions.explanation: 'Very' is an adverb of degree that tells us how hot the soup was.
questions.misconception: Choosing the adjective 'hot' instead of the adverb that modifies it.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adverb of degree? 'She was too tired to walk.'
hints: Adverbs of degree modify adjectives or other adverbs.
'Too' means more than is wanted or needed.
questions.explanation: 'Too' is an adverb of degree showing an excessive amount of tiredness.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'too' with 'to' or 'two'.

questions.stem: Identify the adverb of degree in this sentence: 'The pupils worked extremely hard.'
hints: It tells how hard they worked.
It means 'very'.
questions.explanation: 'Extremely' is the adverb of degree modifying 'hard'.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'hard' instead of the adverb that modifies it.

questions.stem: Write two sentences, each containing a different adverb of degree. Underline the adverb of degree in each sentence.
hints: Use words like very, too, so, quite, rather, almost, enough, hardly.
Underline the adverb in each sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with different adverbs of degree and underlines them.

criteria.description: Each contains an adverb of degree

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence expresses reason? 'She was late because the bus broke down.'
hints: Reason tells us why something happened.
Which word introduces the reason?
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason why she was late.
questions.misconception: Choosing the subject or verb instead of the word that shows reason.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence expresses reason? 'It rained heavily; therefore, the match was cancelled.'
hints: Reason shows the result or consequence.
'Therefore' introduces the result of the rain.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' expresses the reason or result of the heavy rain.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'therefore' with 'because' (they show opposite directions of reason).

questions.stem: Identify the word that expresses reason in this sentence: 'Since it was raining, we stayed indoors.'
hints: It introduces the reason for staying indoors.
It means 'because'.
questions.explanation: 'Since' expresses the reason for staying indoors.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'raining' instead of the reason connector.

questions.stem: Write two sentences, each using a different word that expresses reason. Underline the reason word in each sentence.
hints: Use words like because, since, therefore, so, as a result.
Underline the reason word.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with different reason words and underlines them.

criteria.description: Each contains a different reason word

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the adverb of degree correctly?
options: The shirt is too small for me.
The shirt is very small for me to wear.
The shirt is enough small for me.
The shirt is small too for me.
hints: 'Too' means more than is needed or wanted.
Which sentence shows the shirt does not fit?
questions.explanation: 'The shirt is too small for me' correctly uses 'too' to show it does not fit.
questions.misconception: Placing 'enough' before an adjective or misplacing 'too'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the adverb of degree correctly?
options: She is enough tall to reach the shelf.
She is tall enough to reach the shelf.
She is too tall enough to reach the shelf.
She is very enough tall to reach the shelf.
hints: 'Enough' comes after the adjective.
Which sentence places 'enough' correctly?
questions.explanation: 'She is tall enough' places 'enough' after the adjective, which is correct.
questions.misconception: Placing 'enough' before the adjective.

questions.stem: Complete with the correct adverb of degree: 'The box is _____ heavy for me to carry.' (Use 'too' or 'very')
hints: The box cannot be carried because it is excessively heavy.
Use the adverb that means 'more than is wanted'.
questions.explanation: 'Too heavy' is correct because it shows the box cannot be carried.
questions.misconception: Using 'very' instead of 'too'.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using 'too' and 'enough' correctly as adverbs of degree.
hints: Use 'too' before an adjective to show excess.
Use 'enough' after an adjective to show sufficiency.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'too' and one with 'enough', both used correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the reason word correctly?
options: I was late because I missed the bus.
I was late because I miss the bus.
I was late because I will miss the bus.
I was late because I am missing the bus.
hints: The reason happened in the past.
Use the past tense after 'because'.
questions.explanation: 'Because I missed the bus' uses the correct past tense to show the reason.
questions.misconception: Using the wrong tense after a reason word.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'therefore' correctly?
options: It rained heavily; therefore, the match was cancelled.
It rained heavily; therefore, the match was not cancelled.
Therefore it rained heavily, the match was cancelled.
It rained heavily therefore because the match was cancelled.
hints: 'Therefore' introduces the result of a cause.
Which sentence shows the logical result?
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' correctly introduces the result of the heavy rain.
questions.misconception: Misusing 'therefore' or combining it with 'because'.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with a reason word: '_____ the pupils worked hard, they passed the exam.'
hints: The reason is that they worked hard.
Use 'because', 'since' or 'as'.
questions.explanation: 'Because', 'since' or 'as' all correctly introduce the reason.
questions.misconception: Using 'therefore' or 'so' in this position.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using 'because', 'since' and 'therefore' correctly.
hints: 'Because' and 'since' introduce a reason.
'Therefore' introduces a result.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences, each using one of the reason words correctly.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adverb of degree and which expresses reason? 'She was very tired, so she went to bed early.'
hints: 'Very' tells how tired she was.
'So' introduces the reason for going to bed early.
questions.explanation: 'Very' is the adverb of degree and 'so' expresses the reason.
questions.misconception: Confusing the two types of adverbs.

questions.stem: Read: 'The box was too heavy; therefore, we could not carry it.' Which word is the adverb of degree and which is the reason word?
hints: 'Too' shows the extent of heaviness.
'Therefore' introduces the result.
questions.explanation: 'Too' is the adverb of degree and 'therefore' is the reason word.
questions.misconception: Swapping the two types.

questions.stem: Identify the adverb of degree and the reason word in this sentence: 'She was extremely happy because she won the prize.'
hints: 'Extremely' tells how happy she was.
'Because' gives the reason.
questions.explanation: The adverb of degree is 'extremely' and the reason word is 'because'.
questions.misconception: Missing one of the two words.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using only an adverb of degree and one using only a reason word. Underline the target word in each sentence.
hints: Use words like very, too, extremely for degree.
Use because, since, therefore for reason.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with an adverb of degree and one with a reason word, underlining each.

criteria.description: Writes a sentence with an adverb of degree
Writes a sentence with a reason word

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an adverb of degree, not a reason word?
options: She was happy because she won.
She was happy, so she danced.
She was happy since it was her birthday.
hints: Degree words tell how much or to what extent.
Which sentence has no word that means 'why'?
questions.explanation: 'She was very happy' uses 'very' as an adverb of degree with no reason word.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence with a reason word.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.7.1: Understand and use idiomatic expressions appropriately in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: identify, explain and use idiomatic expressions correctly.

skills.description: Identify idiomatic expressions in sentences and short texts
Explain the meaning of an idiom in context
Interpret an idiom as used in a sentence or short passage
Use idiomatic expressions correctly in original sentences
Distinguish idiomatic meaning from literal meaning
Recognise idioms from the learner's own culture and match them to English equivalents

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify an idiom and match to a simple meaning), 30% medium (explain and interpret idioms in context), 20% harder (use idioms correctly in original sentences and distinguish literal vs idiomatic meaning). Idioms restricted to those named in the document ('take after', 'pull down') plus common, level-appropriate English idioms.
misconceptions: Interpreting an idiom word-by-word
Believing every phrase with a verb and preposition is an idiom
Using an idiom in the wrong context
Assuming idioms translate word-for-word into English
Using idioms that are too informal in formal writing
Thinking idioms have no fixed form

questions.stem: Which of these is an idiomatic expression?
options: The book is on the table.
hints: An idiom has a meaning that is not literal.
'Take after' means to resemble someone.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' is an idiom meaning to resemble a family member.
questions.misconception: Choosing a literal statement as an idiom.

questions.stem: Which of these is an idiomatic expression?
hints: An idiom's meaning is figurative.
To 'pull down' someone means to destroy their reputation.
questions.explanation: 'Pull down someone's reputation' is idiomatic. 'Pull down a house' is literal.
questions.misconception: Confusing the literal use with the idiomatic use.

questions.stem: Identify the idiom in this sentence: 'She takes after her mother in everything she does.'
hints: Look for a phrase whose meaning is not literal.
It means 'resembles'.
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'takes after', meaning to resemble.
questions.misconception: Choosing a literal phrase instead.

questions.stem: Write two sentences, each containing a different idiom. Underline the idiom in each sentence.
hints: Use idioms like 'take after', 'pull down', 'a piece of cake', 'under the weather'.
Underline the idiom.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences with different idioms and underlines them.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'take after' mean in this sentence? 'Kojo takes after his father.'
hints: The meaning is not literal.
It is about appearance or character.
questions.explanation: 'Take after' means to resemble someone, usually a family member.
questions.misconception: Interpreting the idiom literally.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'pull down' mean in this sentence? 'They tried to pull down the head teacher.'
options: They tried to make him fall.
They tried to destroy his reputation.
They tried to lift him up.
hints: The meaning is figurative.
It is about reputation, not physical action.
questions.explanation: 'Pull down' someone means to destroy their reputation.
questions.misconception: Interpreting the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Explain the meaning of 'a piece of cake' in this sentence: 'The exam was a piece of cake.'
hints: The meaning is not literal.
It describes something that is easy to do.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' means something is very easy.
questions.misconception: Taking the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were under the weather, so they did not go to school.' Explain the meaning of the idiom and how it fits the sentence.
hints: 'Under the weather' does not mean literally under weather.
It is about feeling unwell.
questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means feeling unwell, which explains why the pupils did not go to school.

criteria.description: Explains that the idiom means unwell
Connects the meaning to the sentence

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher told the pupils to hit the books before the exam.' What did the teacher tell them to do?
options: Hit their books with their hands
hints: The meaning is idiomatic, not literal.
'Hit the books' means to study.
questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to study hard.
questions.misconception: Interpreting the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.' What did Ama do?
hints: The meaning is figurative.
What does 'letting the cat out of the bag' mean for a surprise?
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret.
questions.misconception: Interpreting the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Read: 'The two friends are like two peas in a pod.' What does this idiom mean?
hints: Compare the two friends to two peas.
It describes how alike they are.
questions.explanation: 'Like two peas in a pod' means very similar.
questions.misconception: Interpreting the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom 'take after' correctly?
options: She takes after her mother in her kindness.
She takes after school every day.
hints: 'Take after' means to resemble someone.
Which sentence uses it about a person resembling another?
questions.explanation: 'She takes after her mother in her kindness' uses the idiom correctly.
questions.misconception: Using the idiom incorrectly.

questions.stem: Use the idiom 'under the weather' in a sentence.
answer: i am feeling under the weather today
she was under the weather and stayed home
he was under the weather so he did not go to work
they felt under the weather after the journey
hints: It means feeling unwell.
Use it in a sentence about someone who is sick.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'under the weather' to mean feeling unwell.
questions.misconception: Using the idiom literally.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using these idioms correctly: 'pull down', 'a piece of cake', 'hit the books'.
hints: 'Pull down' = destroy reputation; 'a piece of cake' = very easy; 'hit the books' = study hard.
Use each in its own sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with the idioms used correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'pull down' literally?
options: They tried to pull down the old building.
They tried to pull down his reputation.
They tried to pull down the head teacher.
They tried to pull down the government.
hints: Literal means the actual, physical meaning.
Which sentence is about physically pulling something down?
questions.explanation: 'Pull down the old building' is literal, meaning physically demolish it.
questions.misconception: Confusing the literal and idiomatic uses.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'take after' idiomatically?
options: She takes after her father in her sense of humour.
hints: Idiomatic means figurative.
Which sentence is about resembling someone?
questions.explanation: 'She takes after her father in her sense of humour' uses the idiom correctly.
questions.misconception: Confusing the literal and idiomatic uses.

questions.stem: In this sentence, is 'break the ice' used literally or idiomatically? 'He told a joke to break the ice.'
hints: The meaning is not literal.
It means to start a conversation.
questions.explanation: 'Break the ice' is used idiomatically to mean starting a conversation.
questions.misconception: Calling it literal.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using 'pull down' literally and one using it idiomatically.
hints: Literal: physically demolishing something.
Idiomatic: destroying someone's reputation.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with the literal meaning and one with the idiomatic meaning.

questions.stem: In Ghanaian culture, saying 'the child has inherited the father's legs' is similar to which English idiom?
hints: Both expressions are about resemblance.
Which idiom means to resemble someone?
questions.explanation: 'Take after' is the English idiom meaning to resemble a family member.
questions.misconception: Choosing an idiom unrelated to resemblance.

questions.stem: Write one English idiom that means the same as the saying 'do not count your chickens before they hatch'.
answer: don't count your chickens before they hatch
do not count your chickens before they hatch
hints: The saying is already an English proverb.
It warns against expecting success too early.
questions.explanation: The English proverb is 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch'.
questions.misconception: Writing an unrelated idiom.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.8.1: Apply the knowledge of conjunctions in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Identify and use simple conjunctions - so that, when, while, if etc. to: − show purpose − express time − condition, etc.

skills.description: Identify conjunctions in sentences
Use 'so that' to show purpose
Use 'when', 'while', 'before', 'after', 'until', 'since', 'as' to express time relationships
Use 'if' and 'unless' to express condition
Distinguish the meaning relationship each conjunction signals (purpose vs time vs condition)
Use conjunctions correctly in original sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify conjunctions and their basic meaning), 35% medium (use time and condition conjunctions correctly), 20% harder (use 'so that' for purpose and distinguish between purpose/time/condition). Contexts: school, home, market, weather, daily routines, community events.
misconceptions: Using 'so that' interchangeably with 'so' (which can also show result)
Confusing 'when' (time) with 'if' (condition)
Using 'while' for a short action instead of an ongoing one
Using 'unless' with a negative clause
Confusing 'before' and 'after' in time sequences
Using a conjunction without checking that the two ideas are logically linked
Omitting the comma when the subordinate clause comes first

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a conjunction? 'She stayed at home because it was raining.'
hints: A conjunction links two ideas.
Which word joins the two parts of the sentence?
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a conjunction linking the idea of staying home to the reason (rain).
questions.misconception: Choosing the subject or verb instead of the linking word.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a conjunction? 'We will go to the beach if the sun shines.'
hints: A conjunction joins two clauses.
'If' introduces a condition.
questions.explanation: 'If' is a conjunction that introduces a condition.
questions.misconception: Choosing the auxiliary 'will' instead of the conjunction.

questions.stem: Identify the conjunction in this sentence: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom before the bell rang.'
hints: It links two actions in time.
Which word tells you the order of events?
questions.explanation: 'Before' is the conjunction linking the two events in time.
questions.misconception: Choosing 'cleaned' instead.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct conjunction to show purpose: 'She studied hard _____ she could pass the exam.'
hints: Purpose means 'in order to'.
Which conjunction introduces a purpose?
questions.explanation: 'So that' introduces the purpose of studying hard.
questions.misconception: Using a time or condition conjunction instead of a purpose conjunction.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'so that' to show purpose?
options: I left early so that I would not miss the bus.
I left early so that I missed the bus.
I left early so that when I missed the bus.
I left early so that if I missed the bus.
hints: Purpose means the reason for doing something.
Which sentence shows the reason for leaving early?
questions.explanation: 'I left early so that I would not miss the bus' uses 'so that' to show purpose.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'so that' with other conjunctions.

questions.stem: Complete with 'so that': 'She watered the plants _____ they would grow well.'
hints: The purpose is for the plants to grow well.
Use 'so that'.
questions.explanation: 'She watered the plants so that they would grow well' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'because' or 'when' instead.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using 'so that' to show purpose. Use different subjects.
hints: Example: 'I wore a coat so that I would not feel cold.'
Make sure the purpose is clear.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two sentences using 'so that' to express purpose.

criteria.description: Purpose is clear in each sentence

questions.stem: Which conjunction completes the sentence to show time? 'The pupils went home _____ the bell rang.'
hints: The action happened after the bell rang.
'After' shows the time relationship.
questions.explanation: 'After' shows the time relationship between going home and the bell ringing.
questions.misconception: Using a purpose or condition conjunction instead of a time conjunction.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a time conjunction correctly?
options: She was reading while the phone rang.
She was reading while the phone was ringing.
She was reading while she reads the phone.
She was reading while the phone will ring.
hints: 'While' links two ongoing actions.
Both actions should be in the past continuous.
questions.explanation: 'She was reading while the phone was ringing' uses 'while' correctly with two ongoing actions.
questions.misconception: Using 'while' with a short interrupting action.

questions.stem: Complete with a time conjunction: 'We waited at the station _____ the bus arrived.' (Use 'until')
hints: They waited up to the time the bus arrived.
Use 'until'.
questions.explanation: 'We waited at the station until the bus arrived' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'if' or 'so that'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'when' correctly?
options: When I was walking home, it started to rain.
When I was walking home, it was starting to rain.
When I walked home, it started to rain.
When I was walking home, it will start to rain.
hints: 'When' introduces the action that interrupts or happens at a specific time.
The walking is ongoing; the rain is the interruption.
questions.explanation: 'When I was walking home, it started to rain' uses 'when' correctly with the past continuous and simple past.
questions.misconception: Confusing 'when' and 'while' usage.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using two different time conjunctions: 'while' and 'after'.
hints: While = during the time that; after = following in time.
Make each sentence meaningful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'while' and one with 'after', both used correctly.

questions.stem: Which conjunction completes the sentence to show a condition? 'You will pass the exam _____ you study hard.'
hints: A condition is something that must happen first.
'If' introduces a condition.
questions.explanation: 'If' introduces the condition for passing the exam.
questions.misconception: Using a time or purpose conjunction instead of a condition conjunction.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless'?
options: Unless you study hard, you will fail.
Unless you don't study hard, you will fail.
Unless you will study hard, you will fail.
Unless you studied hard, you will fail.
hints: 'Unless' means 'if not'.
Do not use a negative clause with 'unless'.
questions.explanation: 'Unless you study hard, you will fail' is correct because 'unless' already means 'if not'.
questions.misconception: Using 'unless' with a negative clause.

questions.stem: Complete with 'if' or 'unless': 'You will be late _____ you leave now.'
hints: The meaning is 'if you do not leave now'.
Use 'unless'.
questions.explanation: 'You will be late unless you leave now' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'if' without a negative.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using 'if' and 'unless' correctly. One sentence should show a positive condition, the other a negative condition.
hints: If = positive condition; unless = negative condition (if not).
Make sure both are meaningful.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'if' and one with 'unless', both correctly used.

questions.stem: What is the meaning relationship of the conjunction 'so that' in this sentence? 'He ran fast so that he would catch the bus.'
hints: 'So that' introduces the reason for an action.
It shows why he ran fast.
questions.explanation: 'So that' signals purpose — the reason for running fast.
questions.misconception: Confusing purpose with time or condition.

questions.stem: What is the meaning relationship of the conjunction 'if' in this sentence? 'If it rains, we will stay at home.'
hints: 'If' introduces something that must happen first.
It states a condition.
questions.explanation: 'If' signals a condition — something that may or may not happen.
questions.misconception: Confusing condition with time or purpose.

questions.stem: Does 'while' in 'While I was reading, the bell rang' show time, purpose or condition? Write the answer.
hints: 'While' tells us when something happened.
It relates to the timing of events.
questions.explanation: 'While' is a time conjunction showing when the bell rang.
questions.misconception: Confusing time with condition or purpose.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using these conjunctions correctly: 'so that', 'when', 'unless'.
hints: 'So that' = purpose; 'when' = time; 'unless' = condition.
Use each in a separate sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences using 'so that', 'when' and 'unless' correctly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.strand: Strand 3: Grammar Usage at Word and Phrase Levels
indicator.content_standard: B6.3.9.1: Apply the knowledge of modals in speech and in writing
indicator.objective: Use modals to express a variety of meanings

skills.description: Use 'can' and 'could' to express ability
Use 'may', 'can', 'could', 'would' to ask for permission and show politeness
Use 'must', 'have to', 'ought to', 'need to', 'should' to express obligation and necessity
Use 'may', 'might', 'could' to express possibility
Use 'shall' and 'will' for prediction, intention and determination
Use 'used to' for past activities or events that no longer happen
Match a modal to the meaning it expresses in context

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (use can/will/must for basic meanings), 35% medium (permission, possibility and past habit), 20% harder (distinguish similar modals by meaning in context — may vs might, must vs should, could vs would). Contexts: school rules, home chores, market, transport, weather, health and daily life.
misconceptions: Using 'can' for past ability instead of 'could'
Using 'must' and 'should' as if they mean the same
Confusing 'may' with 'might'
Using 'will' where 'would' is needed for polite requests
Adding 'to' after a modal
Using 'used to' in the present
Using 'ought' without 'to'
Using double modals

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly shows present ability?
options: She could swim very well when she was five.
hints: Present ability uses 'can'.
'Could' is for past ability.
questions.explanation: 'She can swim very well' shows present ability.
questions.misconception: Using 'could' for present ability.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly shows past ability?
options: When I was young, I can climb trees.
When I was young, I could climb trees.
When I was young, I must climb trees.
When I was young, I may climb trees.
hints: Past ability uses 'could'.
The sentence is about when the speaker was young.
questions.explanation: 'When I was young, I could climb trees' shows past ability.
questions.misconception: Using 'can' for past ability.

questions.stem: Complete with 'can' or 'could': 'She _____ play the piano when she was ten years old.'
hints: The sentence is about past ability.
Use 'could' for past ability.
questions.explanation: 'She could play the piano when she was ten' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using 'can' for a past ability.

questions.stem: Write two sentences: one using 'can' to show present ability and one using 'could' to show past ability.
hints: Present: 'I can...'
Past: 'When I was younger, I could...'
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'can' (present) and one with 'could' (past).

criteria.description: Writes a sentence with 'can' for present ability
Writes a sentence with 'could' for past ability

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to ask for permission?
hints: Polite requests use 'May I' or 'Could I'.
Which option asks rather than demands?
