It helps the reader focus on the argument.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that a formal style makes the argument more credible and respectful.

criteria.description: Explains one reason for maintaining formal style

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.13.2: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence
indicator.objective: Provide a concluding statement that follows from argument presented and pose a rhetorical question on the topic.

skills.description: Identify the concluding statement in a model argument
Write a conclusion that follows logically from the argument presented
Identify a rhetorical question
Form a rhetorical question on the topic
Write a full conclusion combining a concluding statement and a rhetorical question

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify conclusion and rhetorical question), 30% medium (write a conclusion that follows from the argument), 20% harder (combine a concluding statement with an appropriate rhetorical question). Topics drawn from school, community and national issues at Basic 6 level.
misconceptions: Writing a conclusion that introduces new arguments or evidence
Writing a conclusion that simply repeats the introduction word-for-word
Confusing a rhetorical question with a genuine question that needs an answer
Writing a rhetorical question unrelated to the argument
Ending the argument abruptly without a concluding statement
Using a rhetorical question as the entire conclusion without a concluding statement

questions.stem: Read this argument: 'Pupils should not use mobile phones in school. Phones distract pupils during lessons. They can also be used to cheat in exams. Therefore, phones should be banned in schools.' Which sentence is the concluding statement?
options: Pupils should not use mobile phones in school.
They can also be used to cheat in exams.
Therefore, phones should be banned in schools.
hints: The conclusion comes at the end.
It usually begins with a word like 'therefore' or 'in conclusion'.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, phones should be banned in schools' is the concluding statement that follows from the reasons.
questions.misconception: Choosing a reason as the conclusion.

questions.stem: Read this argument: 'Every child should learn to swim. Swimming can save lives. It is also good exercise. In conclusion, swimming lessons should be part of the school curriculum.' Which sentence is the concluding statement?
options: Every child should learn to swim.
In conclusion, swimming lessons should be part of the school curriculum.
hints: The conclusion comes at the end and summarises the argument.
Look for 'In conclusion'.
questions.explanation: 'In conclusion, swimming lessons should be part of the school curriculum' is the concluding statement.
questions.misconception: Choosing a reason as the conclusion.

questions.stem: Read: 'We should plant more trees. Trees provide shade and clean the air. They also prevent soil erosion. Therefore, planting trees should be encouraged in every community.' Write the concluding statement.
answer: therefore planting trees should be encouraged in every community
planting trees should be encouraged in every community
hints: The conclusion comes at the end.
It often begins with 'therefore'.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore, planting trees should be encouraged in every community' is the concluding statement.
questions.misconception: Choosing a reason as the conclusion.

questions.stem: Argument: 'Pupils should eat breakfast. Breakfast gives energy for the day. It also helps pupils concentrate in class. Therefore, _____' Which conclusion follows logically?
options: breakfast is the most important meal for pupils
pupils should eat breakfast every morning
hints: The conclusion should follow from the reasons.
The reasons all support eating breakfast.
questions.explanation: 'Pupils should eat breakfast every morning' follows logically from the reasons.
questions.misconception: Choosing a conclusion that contradicts the argument.

questions.stem: Argument: 'We should keep our environment clean. Clean environments reduce the spread of diseases. They also make our surroundings pleasant. Therefore, _____' Which conclusion follows logically?
options: everyone should help keep the environment clean
only adults should clean the environment
hints: The conclusion should follow from the reasons.
The reasons support keeping the environment clean.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone should help keep the environment clean' follows logically from the reasons.
questions.misconception: Choosing a conclusion that contradicts the argument.

questions.stem: Write a concluding statement for this argument: 'Reading is important. It improves vocabulary. It helps us learn new things. It is also enjoyable.'
answer: reading should be encouraged for all pupils
we should all develop the habit of reading
reading is valuable and should be encouraged
hints: The conclusion should summarise the reasons.
It should state what people should do.
questions.explanation: A good conclusion states that reading should be encouraged or that everyone should read regularly.
questions.misconception: Writing a conclusion that does not follow from the reasons.

questions.stem: Write a full argument (3–4 sentences) about why pupils should keep their school clean, ending with a concluding statement that follows logically.
hints: Start with the claim.
Give reasons.
End with a conclusion that summarises the argument.
questions.explanation: A strong answer has a clear claim, reasons and a conclusion that follows logically.

criteria.description: Ends with a conclusion that follows logically

questions.stem: Which of these is a rhetorical question?
options: Can we truly say we care for our environment if we keep littering?
hints: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer.
Which question makes a point rather than asking for information?
questions.explanation: 'Can we truly say we care for our environment if we keep littering?' is a rhetorical question that makes a point.
questions.misconception: Confusing a rhetorical question with a genuine question.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a rhetorical question?
options: Do you know where the library is?
Is it not time we took responsibility for our own health?
What time does the bus leave?
How many pupils are in your class?
hints: A rhetorical question does not expect an answer.
Which question challenges the reader to think?
questions.explanation: 'Is it not time we took responsibility for our own health?' is rhetorical because it makes a point.
questions.misconception: Choosing a genuine question as rhetorical.

questions.stem: Explain in one sentence what makes a rhetorical question different from a normal question.
answer: a rhetorical question is asked for effect not for an answer
it does not need an answer
it makes a point rather than asking for information
hints: Think about the purpose of the question.
Does it need an answer?
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question is asked for effect or to make a point, not to get an answer.
questions.misconception: Thinking a rhetorical question requires a real answer.

questions.stem: Which rhetorical question best concludes an argument about keeping the school clean?
options: What is the name of our school?
Can we call ourselves responsible pupils if we let our school become dirty?
How many classrooms does our school have?
hints: The rhetorical question should relate to the argument.
It should make the reader think about responsibility.
questions.explanation: 'Can we call ourselves responsible pupils if we let our school become dirty?' is a rhetorical question that relates to the argument.
questions.misconception: Choosing a question unrelated to the topic.

questions.stem: Write a rhetorical question to conclude an argument about why pupils should not litter.
answer: can we truly be proud of our school if we litter it
is it fair to make others clean up after us
why should we spoil the beauty of our school
do we want to learn in a dirty environment
hints: The question should make the reader think about littering.
Use a question that makes a point.
questions.explanation: A good rhetorical question challenges the reader to think about the effects of littering.
questions.misconception: Writing a genuine question instead of a rhetorical one.

questions.stem: Write two rhetorical questions that could be used at the end of an argument about the importance of reading.
hints: Make each question challenge the reader to think.
They should relate to reading.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two rhetorical questions that make points about reading.

questions.stem: Which conclusion combines a concluding statement and a rhetorical question?
options: Therefore, pupils should eat breakfast every day. After all, can we expect to learn well on an empty stomach?
Pupils should eat breakfast every day.
Can we expect to learn well on an empty stomach?
hints: Look for both a concluding statement and a rhetorical question.
Option A has both parts.
questions.explanation: Option A has a concluding statement ('Therefore, pupils should eat breakfast every day') and a rhetorical question ('Can we expect to learn well on an empty stomach?').
questions.misconception: Choosing a conclusion with only one part.

questions.stem: Write a full conclusion (2–3 sentences) for an argument about why pupils should keep their school clean. Include a concluding statement and a rhetorical question.
hints: Start with a concluding statement that summarises the argument.
End with a rhetorical question that makes a point.
questions.explanation: A strong answer includes both a concluding statement and a rhetorical question.

questions.stem: Write a full conclusion for an argument about why every child should learn to swim. Include a concluding statement and a rhetorical question.
hints: Summarise the argument in one sentence.
Ask a rhetorical question that challenges the reader.
questions.explanation: A strong answer includes both parts, relating to the argument about swimming.

questions.stem: Say a conclusion aloud for an argument about why pupils should not litter. Include a concluding statement and a rhetorical question.
hints: State the conclusion first.
End with a rhetorical question.
questions.explanation: The pupil gives a conclusion with both parts.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the concluding statement in this argument? 'We should plant more trees. Trees provide shade and clean the air. They also prevent soil erosion. In conclusion, planting trees is essential for a healthy community.'
options: Trees provide shade and clean the air.
In conclusion, planting trees is essential for a healthy community.
hints: The conclusion often begins with 'In conclusion'.
It summarises the argument.
questions.explanation: 'In conclusion, planting trees is essential for a healthy community' is the concluding statement.
questions.misconception: Choosing a reason as the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which of these is a rhetorical question?
options: Is it fair that some children cannot go to school?
hints: A rhetorical question makes a point about fairness or justice.
Which question challenges the reader to think about fairness?
questions.explanation: 'Is it fair that some children cannot go to school?' is a rhetorical question that makes a point about fairness.
questions.misconception: Choosing a genuine question as rhetorical.

questions.stem: Write a concluding statement that follows logically from these reasons: (1) Exercise keeps the body healthy. (2) It helps the mind stay sharp. (3) It can be fun.
hints: The conclusion should summarise the reasons.
It should state that exercise is important.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion states that exercise is important and should be part of daily life.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.14.2: Write the event of the day
indicator.objective: Write short paragraphs to describe incidents. E.g. accidents, fire outbreak.

skills.description: Recall and identify the stages of the writing process and their features
Select a topic about an incident and brainstorm ideas
Organise points into a paragraph plan
Write a short paragraph describing an incident with a clear topic sentence and supporting details
Draft, self-edit and peer-edit an incident paragraph
Present the finished incident paragraph in groups

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (recall writing-process stages; select and brainstorm a topic), 35% medium (organise points and write a short incident paragraph), 25% harder (self/peer-edit and present a polished paragraph). Incidents drawn from pupils' environment: road accidents, fire outbreaks, floods, market incidents, school incidents. Paragraphs kept to 5–8 sentences.
misconceptions: Confusing an incident description with a narrative
Writing a vague paragraph with no topic sentence
Omitting key facts (where, when, who, what happened, what was done)
Adding personal opinion or emotion where a factual report is expected
Confusing the writing-process stages
Presenting a first draft without revising or editing
Using sensational or exaggerated language for a factual incident report

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the writing process?
hints: Prewriting comes first and publishing comes last.
Which order follows the stages correctly?
questions.explanation: The correct order is prewriting, drafting, revising, editing, publishing.
questions.misconception: Putting the stages in the wrong order.

questions.stem: Which stage of the writing process involves correcting spelling and punctuation?
hints: Correcting conventions happens after revising.
Which stage focuses on conventions?
questions.explanation: Editing is the stage where you correct spelling, punctuation and capitalisation.
questions.misconception: Confusing editing with revising or drafting.

questions.stem: Name two stages of the writing process you would use to write a paragraph about an incident.
hints: There are five stages.
Any two correct stages are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Any two stages of the writing process are correct.
questions.misconception: Naming unrelated activities.

questions.stem: Explain in three sentences what you do at each stage of the writing process when writing about an incident.
hints: Mention prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and publishing.
Explain what happens at each stage.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains the stages and what happens at each.

criteria.description: Explains what happens at each stage

questions.stem: Which of these is the best topic for a short incident paragraph?
options: A fire outbreak at the local market
The history of the whole world
hints: An incident is a specific event that happened.
Which topic is focused on one event?
questions.explanation: 'A fire outbreak at the local market' is a focused incident topic.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too broad or not an incident.

questions.stem: Write one incident topic you could write a short paragraph about.
answer: a road accident near the school
a fire outbreak in the market
an accident during a football match
hints: Choose a specific event that happened in your community.
It should be an incident, not a general topic.
questions.explanation: A good incident topic is specific, such as a road accident, a fire outbreak or a flood.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general topic instead of an incident.

questions.stem: Choose an incident you have heard about and write three ideas you could include in a paragraph about it.
hints: Think about what happened, where, when and who was involved.
Write at least three ideas.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists three relevant ideas about the incident.

questions.stem: You are writing a paragraph about a fire outbreak. Which plan is best?
options: What happened, where it happened, who was involved, what was done
The history of fire, types of fire, fire safety in other countries
My opinion about fire, my feelings about fire, my favourite colour
A story about a dragon that breathes fire
hints: An incident paragraph reports the key facts.
Which plan covers the key facts?
questions.explanation: The best plan covers what happened, where, who was involved and what was done.
questions.misconception: Including irrelevant or fictional details.

questions.stem: Organise these facts into a paragraph plan about a road accident: (1) two cars collided (2) at the junction near the market (3) on Monday morning (4) one driver was injured (5) he was taken to the hospital.
hints: Group the facts logically: what, where, when, who, what was done.
Order the facts as they happened.
questions.explanation: A strong plan orders the facts logically to describe the incident.

questions.stem: Write one question you should answer when planning a paragraph about an incident.
hints: Think about the key facts of an incident.
Who, what, where, when, why or how?
questions.explanation: Key questions include what happened, where, when, who was involved and what was done.
questions.misconception: Asking a question unrelated to the incident.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about a fire outbreak?
options: A fire broke out at the Techiman market on Tuesday morning.
Some people sell tomatoes at the market.
hints: A topic sentence introduces the incident.
It should state what happened, where and when.
questions.explanation: Option A clearly introduces the incident with the key facts.
questions.misconception: Choosing a general statement instead of an incident topic sentence.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (5–6 sentences) about a road accident. Include a topic sentence and key facts: what happened, where, when, who was involved and what was done.
hints: Start with a topic sentence.
Include the key facts clearly.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph has a clear topic sentence and includes all the key facts.

criteria.description: Includes key facts (what, where, when, who, what was done)

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (6–8 sentences) about a fire outbreak at a market. Include the topic sentence, key facts and what was done to help.
hints: Start with the topic sentence.
Include what happened, where, when, who was involved and what was done.
Keep the tone factual.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph includes a topic sentence and all key facts in a factual tone.

criteria.description: Includes key facts and what was done

questions.stem: Which is the best revision for this draft sentence: 'The accident was bad and people were sad.'?
options: The accident was bad and people were sad.
Two cars collided at the junction, and one driver was injured.
People were very sad about the accident.
hints: A revision should add specific facts.
Which option gives specific details about the incident?
questions.explanation: Option B replaces vague words with specific facts about what happened.
questions.misconception: Thinking vague language is acceptable for an incident report.

questions.stem: Revise this draft sentence to make it more factual: 'The fire was really scary and everyone was running.'
answer: the fire spread quickly and people ran to safety
the fire destroyed several stalls and people fled
the fire broke out and people ran away
the fire caused damage and people ran to safety
hints: Replace emotional words with factual ones.
Say what actually happened.
questions.explanation: A good revision replaces 'scary' and 'everyone was running' with factual details.
questions.misconception: Keeping emotional language in a factual report.

questions.stem: Read this draft and revise it for a factual incident report: 'There was a really bad accident yesterday. It was so scary. People were crying and shouting. The cars were smashed.'
hints: Remove emotional language.
Add specific facts about what, where, when and who.
Keep the tone factual.
questions.explanation: A strong revision removes emotional language and presents the facts clearly.

questions.stem: Present your incident paragraph to the class. Read it clearly and emphasise the key facts.
hints: Speak clearly and at a good pace.
Emphasise the key facts.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the paragraph clearly and emphasises the key facts.

questions.stem: In groups, present your incident paragraphs on a poster or chart. Each group member should explain one key fact.
hints: Prepare a clear poster or chart.
Each member explains one part.
questions.explanation: The group presents the incident paragraph clearly, with each member explaining one key fact.

criteria.description: Each member explains one key fact

questions.stem: Which of these is an incident?
options: A fire outbreak at a market
hints: An incident is a specific event that happened.
Which option describes a specific event?
questions.explanation: A fire outbreak at a market is a specific incident.
questions.misconception: Confusing a general topic with a specific incident.

questions.stem: When writing an incident paragraph, what should you include first?
options: A topic sentence stating what happened
A long description of the weather
The names of all the people in the town
hints: The topic sentence introduces the incident.
It should state what happened.
questions.explanation: An incident paragraph should begin with a topic sentence stating what happened.
questions.misconception: Starting with opinion or irrelevant details.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.14.2: Write the event of the day
indicator.objective: Write articles on varied topics

skills.description: Identify the features of a short article: title/headline, introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion
Select a varied topic and brainstorm ideas
Organise ideas into an article plan (headline, lead paragraph, body, conclusion)
Write a short article on a chosen topic with clear structure and relevant facts
Use appropriate informative language (facts, examples, clear explanations)
Revise, edit and prepare the article for publication
Write with a clear audience in mind

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (identify article features; select a topic and plan), 35% medium (write a short structured article with informative language), 25% harder (edit, publish and adapt to a clear audience). Topics drawn from varied domains at Basic 6 level; articles kept to 3 short paragraphs.
misconceptions: Writing an article as a personal narrative
Omitting a headline or giving a headline that does not match the content
Writing an introduction that gives away the whole article in one sentence
Using opinion where facts and explanations are expected
Using sensational language in an informative article
Forgetting to consider the audience
Presenting the first draft as the published article
Writing an article with no clear conclusion

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of an article?
hints: An article begins with a title that catches the reader's attention.
What do we call the title of an article?
questions.explanation: A headline is the title of an article and is a key feature.
questions.misconception: Confusing article features with story features.

questions.stem: Which part of an article gives the main idea and catches the reader's attention?
hints: The first thing a reader sees is the headline.
It tells you what the article is about.
questions.explanation: The headline gives the main idea and catches the reader's attention.
questions.misconception: Confusing the headline with the introduction or body.

questions.stem: Name two features of an article.
hints: An article has a title and paragraphs.
It has an introduction and a conclusion.
questions.explanation: An article has a headline, introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion.
questions.misconception: Naming only one feature or naming features of a story.

questions.stem: Write three features of an article and explain what each one does.
hints: Think about the headline, introduction and body.
Explain the purpose of each feature.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names three features and explains their functions.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best topic for a short article?
options: How to keep our school clean
The history of the whole world
hints: A good article topic is focused and informative.
Which topic can be covered in a short article?
questions.explanation: 'How to keep our school clean' is focused and suitable for a short article.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too broad or not informative.

questions.stem: Write one suitable topic for a short informative article.
answer: how to keep the environment clean
hints: Choose a topic that informs readers.
It should be focused enough for a short article.
questions.explanation: A good article topic is focused and informative, such as malaria prevention or the benefits of exercise.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too broad or personal.

questions.stem: Choose a topic for an article and write three ideas you could include in the body.
hints: Choose a focused topic.
Write three facts or ideas about it.
questions.explanation: A strong answer chooses a focused topic and lists three relevant ideas.

questions.stem: How should an article be organised?
hints: An article has a specific structure.
It starts with a headline and ends with a conclusion.
questions.explanation: An article is organised with a headline, introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion.
questions.misconception: Confusing article structure with narrative structure.

questions.stem: Organise these ideas into an article plan: (1) what malaria is (2) how it is spread (3) how to prevent it. Write a simple plan with a headline, introduction, body and conclusion.
hints: The headline should catch attention.
The introduction presents the topic.
The body develops the ideas.
questions.explanation: A strong plan has a clear headline, an introduction, body paragraphs covering the ideas and a conclusion.

criteria.description: Organises ideas into introduction, body and conclusion

questions.stem: What should the introduction of an article do?
answer: state what the article is about
catch the reader's attention and present the topic
give a brief overview of the topic
hints: The introduction comes after the headline.
It tells the reader what the article is about.
questions.explanation: The introduction introduces the topic and gives a brief overview.
questions.misconception: Thinking the introduction gives all the details.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best introduction for an article about keeping the school clean?
options: Keeping our school clean is important for our health and learning.
I went to the market yesterday.
hints: The introduction should present the topic clearly.
Which sentence is about keeping the school clean?
questions.explanation: Option A clearly introduces the topic of keeping the school clean.
questions.misconception: Choosing an unrelated sentence as the introduction.

questions.stem: Write a short article (3 paragraphs) about the importance of reading. Include a headline, introduction, body and conclusion.
hints: Start with a headline.
Write an introduction that presents the topic.
Develop the body with facts.
End with a conclusion.
questions.explanation: A strong article has a clear headline, introduction, body and conclusion.

questions.stem: Write a short article (3 paragraphs) on the topic 'How to Prevent Malaria'. Include a headline, introduction, body and conclusion. Use facts and clear explanations.
hints: Include a headline that catches attention.
The body should give facts about prevention.
The conclusion should summarise.
questions.explanation: A strong article includes a headline, introduction, body and conclusion, with facts about malaria prevention.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses informative language suitable for an article?
options: Malaria is spread by the bite of an infected mosquito.
Malaria is really scary and awful.
Malaria is the worst thing ever.
hints: Informative language presents facts clearly.
Which sentence gives a fact without emotion?
questions.explanation: Option A presents a clear fact in an informative way.
questions.misconception: Using emotional or sensational language in an informative article.

questions.stem: Rewrite this sentence in informative language: 'Exercise is, like, super good for you and you should totally do it.'
answer: exercise is good for your health and should be done regularly
regular exercise is beneficial for health
exercise is important for good health
hints: Remove slang and informal words.
State the fact clearly.
questions.explanation: The rewrite uses clear, informative language without slang.
questions.misconception: Keeping informal language in an informative article.

questions.stem: Write two sentences of informative language about the importance of trees for an article.
hints: Use facts and clear explanations.
Avoid opinions and emotion.
questions.explanation: A strong answer presents clear facts about trees in an informative tone.

questions.stem: What should you check before publishing an article?
options: Headline, spelling, punctuation and clear paragraphs
hints: Check all aspects of the article.
It should be polished before publishing.
questions.explanation: Before publishing, check the headline, spelling, punctuation and paragraphing.
questions.misconception: Thinking only one aspect needs checking.

questions.stem: Edit this draft article introduction: 'pollution is bad it makes people sick we should stop it.' Write the corrected version.
hints: Add capital letters and full stops.
Correct the punctuation.
questions.explanation: The corrected version is: 'Pollution is bad. It makes people sick. We should stop it.'

questions.stem: You are writing an article for your school magazine. Who is your audience?
options: Pupils and teachers in your school
hints: The audience is who will read the article.
Where is the school magazine read?
questions.explanation: The audience for a school magazine article is pupils and teachers in the school.
questions.misconception: Confusing the audience with a different group.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining how you would change an article about the importance of reading for different audiences: younger pupils and adults.
hints: Younger pupils need simpler language.
Adults can handle more complex vocabulary.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that simpler language suits younger pupils while more formal language suits adults.

criteria.description: Explains how to adapt for younger pupils
Explains how to adapt for adults

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.15.1: Write informal letters on given topics
indicator.objective: Write to friends to express their views on given topics using appropriate letter formats

skills.description: Identify the features of an informal friendly letter
Compare informal letters with formal letters and state similarities and differences
Identify the purpose and audience of the letter and make a mind map to plan
Express personal views on a given topic in the letter body
Use the correct informal letter format
Edit and revise the letter, including peer editing
Use appropriate informal but polite language

spec.difficultyPlan: 40% easy (identify features; plan purpose and audience), 35% medium (express views and use correct format), 25% harder (edit/revise and use appropriate informal language). Topics: school, family, holidays, community and national issues at Basic 6 level.
misconceptions: Using formal letter conventions in a friendly letter
Omitting the address or date
Writing the body as one long paragraph
Using slang or disrespectful language
Forgetting to sign the letter
Writing a friendly letter as a narrative instead of expressing views
Not editing the letter after the first draft
Confusing sender's address with recipient's address

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of an informal (friendly) letter?
hints: An informal letter is written to a friend or family member.
Which greeting is friendly and personal?
questions.explanation: 'Dear Ama' is a friendly, informal greeting. 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Yours faithfully' belong to formal letters.
questions.misconception: Using formal letter features in a friendly letter.

questions.stem: Which of these should an informal letter include?
hints: A friendly letter starts with your address and the date.
Formal letters may have reference numbers or subject lines.
questions.explanation: An informal letter includes the sender's address and the date, but not a reference number or subject line.
questions.misconception: Including formal features such as a reference number.

questions.stem: Name three features of an informal letter.
answer: address, date, salutation, body, closing, signature
sender's address, date, dear friend, closing
hints: Think about what comes at the beginning and end.
The greeting, body and closing are important.
questions.explanation: Features include the sender's address, date, salutation, body paragraphs, closing and signature.
questions.misconception: Naming only one or two features.

questions.stem: Write three features of an informal letter and explain what each one does.
hints: Think about the address, greeting and closing.
Explain the purpose of each feature.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names three features and explains their functions.

questions.stem: Which greeting is used in a formal letter but NOT in an informal letter?
hints: Formal letters use titles and surnames.
Informal letters use first names.
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir/Madam' is formal. Informal letters use first names such as 'Dear Ama'.
questions.misconception: Using formal greetings in informal letters.

questions.stem: Which closing is used in an informal letter?
hints: Informal closings are friendly.
Which closing sounds like something you would say to a friend?
questions.explanation: 'Best wishes' is an informal closing. The others are formal.
questions.misconception: Using formal closings in informal letters.

questions.stem: Write one difference between a formal letter and an informal letter.
answer: informal letters use first names while formal letters use titles
informal letters are to friends while formal letters are official
informal letters use 'best wishes' while formal letters use 'yours faithfully'
formal letters are more polite and official
hints: Think about the greeting and closing.
Who is the letter written to?
questions.explanation: A key difference is the greeting: informal letters use first names, formal letters use titles or 'Sir/Madam'.
questions.misconception: Confusing formal and informal features.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining how an informal letter is different from a formal letter.
hints: Mention the greeting, closing and tone.
Use complete sentences.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that informal letters are friendly and personal, while formal letters are official and polite.

questions.stem: You are writing a letter to your friend about your holidays. Who is your audience?
hints: Audience means who will read the letter.
Who are you writing to?
questions.explanation: The audience is your friend.
questions.misconception: Confusing the audience with someone else.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of writing a letter to a friend about your holidays?
options: To share your experiences and news
To complain to the head teacher
hints: A friendly letter shares personal news.
What do you tell a friend about your holidays?
questions.explanation: The purpose is to share experiences and news with a friend.
questions.misconception: Confusing the purpose with a formal request.

questions.stem: Write one purpose for a letter to a friend about a school event.
answer: to tell your friend about the event
to share news about the event
to invite your friend to the event
to describe the event to your friend
hints: A friendly letter can share news or invite someone.
What would you want your friend to know?
questions.explanation: The purpose could be to tell your friend about the event or invite them.
questions.misconception: Giving a purpose unrelated to the topic.

questions.stem: Make a short mind map for a letter to a friend about 'How I spent my holidays'. Include at least three ideas.
hints: Think of places you visited, people you met and things you did.
Write three ideas in your mind map.
questions.explanation: A strong mind map has at least three ideas related to holiday experiences.

questions.stem: Which sentence expresses a personal view suitable for a letter to a friend about school rules?
options: I think our school rules are fair and help us learn.
hints: A personal view states what you think or feel.
Which sentence gives an opinion?
questions.explanation: Option A expresses a personal view about school rules.
questions.misconception: Choosing a factual statement instead of a view.

questions.stem: Write one sentence expressing your view on the topic 'Pupils should help with housework'.
answer: i think pupils should help with housework
i believe helping with housework is good for children
pupils should help with housework because it teaches responsibility
i think children should not do too much housework
hints: Use 'I think' or 'I believe'.
State your opinion clearly.
questions.explanation: A good sentence clearly expresses a personal view on the topic.
questions.misconception: Giving a factual statement instead of a view.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) expressing your views on 'Why pupils should read every day' for a letter to a friend.
hints: Start with your opinion.
Give reasons for your view.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph clearly expresses a personal view with reasons.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of an informal letter?
options: Address, date, greeting, body, closing, signature
Date, address, body, greeting, signature, closing
Greeting, address, body, date, signature, closing
Body, greeting, address, date, closing, signature
hints: Address and date come first.
The greeting comes before the body.
questions.explanation: The correct order is address, date, greeting, body, closing and signature.
questions.misconception: Putting the parts in the wrong order.

questions.stem: Write the correct closing and signature line for an informal letter to your friend Ama.
hints: Use a friendly closing.
Sign your own name.
questions.explanation: A good closing is 'Best wishes' followed by your name.
questions.misconception: Using a formal closing such as 'Yours faithfully'.

questions.stem: Write the opening of an informal letter to your friend Esi about your holidays. Include the address, date and greeting.
hints: Start with your address and date.
Use a friendly greeting.
questions.explanation: A strong opening includes the address, date and a friendly greeting.

questions.stem: What should you check when editing an informal letter?
hints: Editing checks all aspects of the letter.
Look at spelling, punctuation and tone.
questions.explanation: When editing, check spelling, punctuation, paragraphing and that the tone is friendly.
questions.misconception: Thinking only one aspect needs checking.

questions.stem: Edit this draft sentence from a friendly letter: 'i went to the market with my mother we bought tomatoes onions and pepper.' Write the corrected version.
hints: Add capital letters and full stops.
Add commas in the list.
questions.explanation: The corrected version is: 'I went to the market with my mother. We bought tomatoes, onions and pepper.'

questions.stem: Which sentence uses appropriate informal but polite language for a friendly letter?
options: I hope you are doing well and I miss you.
I am writing to inform you of my recent activities.
hints: Informal language is friendly but not rude.
Which sentence sounds like something you would say to a friend?
questions.explanation: Option A is friendly, polite and appropriate for an informal letter.
questions.misconception: Using slang or overly formal language in a friendly letter.

questions.stem: Write two sentences in friendly, polite language that you could include in a letter to a friend about a school event.
hints: Use a friendly tone.
Be polite and clear.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes friendly, polite sentences about a school event.

criteria.description: Sentences relate to a school event

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.2.1: Copy and rewrite sentences correctly
indicator.objective: Write with a legible, fluent and personal handwriting style

skills.description: Write sentences and short passages in legible, readable handwriting
Write in a joint (joined-up) script consistently and fluently
Maintain consistent spacing between words and letters, and write on a straight line
Develop and maintain a consistent personal handwriting style
Copy sentences from a text or board accurately, preserving spelling and punctuation

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (write legibly with clear letter formation), 35% medium (use joint script with consistent spacing and alignment), 20% harder (maintain a personal style while copying accurately). Texts kept to 2–4 sentences.
misconceptions: Writing so fast that letters become unclear
Mixing print and joint script in the same piece
Inconsistent letter sizes within a word
Leaving no space between words or too much space
Copying inaccuracies while focusing only on neatness
Believing personal style means ignoring legibility

questions.stem: Write this sentence in your best legible handwriting: 'The pupils walked to school early.'
hints: Take your time.
Make each letter clear and easy to read.
questions.explanation: The pupil should write the sentence with clear, readable letters and even spacing.

questions.stem: Write these words legibly: 'market', 'teacher', 'school', 'pupil'.
hints: Keep each letter distinct.
Do not rush.
questions.explanation: Each word should be written with clear, distinct letters.

questions.stem: Write this sentence in joined-up (joint) script: 'The boy is reading a book.'
hints: Join each letter within a word.
Keep the joins smooth and consistent.
questions.explanation: The letters within each word should be joined consistently.

questions.stem: Write these words in joint script: 'and', 'kettle', 'can', 'catch'.
hints: Join the letters smoothly.
Keep the letters the same size.
questions.explanation: Each word should be written in joined-up letters.

questions.stem: Which is the best handwriting spacing?
hints: Words need space between them.
Which option is easiest to read?
questions.explanation: Clear space between words makes handwriting easy to read.
questions.misconception: Thinking spacing does not matter.

questions.stem: Copy this sentence on a straight line: 'The sun shines brightly in the sky.'
hints: Use the ruled line to keep your writing straight.
Leave even spaces between words.
questions.explanation: The writing should sit on the line with even spacing.

questions.stem: What does a 'personal handwriting style' mean?
options: Writing in any style that is not legible.
A consistent style that is your own but still readable.
hints: Personal style is your own consistent way of writing.
It must still be readable.
questions.explanation: A personal style is a consistent, readable way of writing that belongs to you.
questions.misconception: Thinking personal style means ignoring legibility.

questions.stem: Write two sentences in your own handwriting style. Make sure the style is consistent throughout.
hints: Use the same letter shapes and size throughout.
Keep it neat and readable.
questions.explanation: The pupil should show a consistent personal style across both sentences.

questions.stem: Copy this sentence accurately: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom, swept the floor and arranged the desks.'
hints: Check every word, comma and full stop.
Do not change anything.
questions.explanation: The copied sentence should match the original exactly, including punctuation.

questions.stem: Copy this short passage accurately in your best handwriting: 'The market was crowded. Traders called out their prices. Buyers moved from stall to stall.'
hints: Copy each sentence carefully.
Check spelling and punctuation after copying.
questions.explanation: The copied passage should match the original exactly and be neatly written.

questions.stem: Write this sentence legibly, using your best handwriting: 'Reading every day helps us learn new words.'
hints: Form every letter clearly.
Keep the size of the letters even.
questions.explanation: The pupil should write with clear letters and even size.

questions.stem: Write these words in joint script: 'at', 'am', 'et', 'de'.
hints: Join the two letters in each pair smoothly.
Keep the joins consistent.
questions.explanation: Each pair should be written with smooth, consistent joins.

questions.stem: Copy this list neatly, keeping the items aligned: 'tomatoes, onions, pepper, rice'.
hints: Keep the commas in the correct places.
Write the items evenly spaced.
questions.explanation: The list should be neatly written with clear spacing and correct commas.

questions.stem: Write this paragraph in your own consistent handwriting style: 'The rain fell heavily. The pupils stayed in the classroom. They read books and played games.'
hints: Use the same style throughout.
Keep the handwriting neat and readable.
questions.explanation: The paragraph should show a consistent personal style that is readable.

questions.stem: Copy this passage accurately and neatly: 'Kojo found a wallet on the road. He took it to the police station. The owner thanked him.'
hints: Copy every word carefully.
Check for full stops and capital letters.
questions.explanation: The copy should match the original and be neatly presented.

criteria.description: Capital letters and full stops are correct

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.2.1: Copy and rewrite sentences correctly
indicator.objective: Write complex sentences clearly and correctly

skills.description: Identify simple and compound sentences to distinguish them from complex sentences
Identify the structure of a complex sentence: main clause plus subordinate clause
Use subordinating conjunctions correctly to form complex sentences
Construct complex sentences clearly and correctly in original writing
Use commas correctly in complex sentences

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify main and subordinate clauses), 35% medium (join pairs of simple sentences into complex sentences), 20% harder (construct original complex sentences with correct punctuation and clear meaning). Contexts: school, home, community, daily life.
misconceptions: Using 'and' or 'but' to join clauses and calling the result a complex sentence
Omitting the subordinating conjunction so the sentence becomes two simple sentences or a fragment
Using a comma when the main clause comes first
Using the wrong subordinator for the meaning relationship
Writing a subordinate clause as a complete sentence
Using double subordinators in one clause

questions.stem: Which sentence is a simple sentence?
options: The boy ran to school, and he met his friend.
When the boy ran to school, he met his friend.
The boy ran to school because he was late.
hints: A simple sentence has one main clause.
It has one subject and one verb.
questions.explanation: 'The boy ran to school' has one main clause, so it is a simple sentence.
questions.misconception: Confusing a compound or complex sentence with a simple sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: She sang, and her brother danced.
When she sang, her brother danced.
She sang because she was happy.
hints: A compound sentence has two main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.
Look for 'and', 'but' or 'or' joining two full clauses.
questions.explanation: 'She sang, and her brother danced' has two main clauses joined by 'and', so it is a compound sentence.
questions.misconception: Confusing a compound sentence with a complex one.

questions.stem: In this complex sentence, which part is the subordinate clause? 'When you come, we will go.'
options: When you come, we will go
hints: The subordinate clause begins with a subordinating conjunction.
'When' introduces the subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: 'When you come' is the subordinate clause; 'we will go' is the main clause.
questions.misconception: Choosing the main clause as the subordinate clause.

questions.stem: Identify the main clause in this sentence: 'Although it was raining, the pupils went to school.'
hints: The main clause can stand alone.
It does not begin with a subordinating conjunction.
questions.explanation: The main clause is 'the pupils went to school'.
questions.misconception: Choosing the subordinate clause as the main clause.

questions.stem: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
hints: Subordinating conjunctions introduce subordinate clauses.
'Because' introduces a reason clause.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction.
questions.misconception: Confusing coordinating conjunctions with subordinating ones.

questions.stem: Which subordinating conjunction best completes the sentence? '_____ it rained, the match was cancelled.'
hints: The sentence shows a reason for cancelling the match.
'Because' introduces a reason.
questions.explanation: 'Because it rained, the match was cancelled' is correct.
questions.misconception: Using a coordinating conjunction instead of a subordinating one.

questions.stem: Join these two simple sentences using 'when': 'I saw him. He was crossing the road.'
answer: i saw him when he was crossing the road
when i saw him he was crossing the road
hints: Use 'when' to link the two ideas in time.
Make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.explanation: A correct complex sentence is: 'I saw him when he was crossing the road.'
questions.misconception: Using 'and' instead of 'when'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correctly formed complex sentence?
options: She was tired, but she finished her work.
She was tired because she had worked all day.
She was tired, hungry and thirsty.
hints: A complex sentence has one main clause and one subordinate clause.
'Because she had worked all day' is a subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: 'She was tired because she had worked all day' is a complex sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing a compound or simple sentence instead.

questions.stem: Write two original complex sentences using the subordinating conjunctions 'although' and 'unless'.
hints: 'Although' introduces a contrast; 'unless' introduces a condition.
Use one subordinator per sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence with 'although' and one with 'unless', both correctly formed.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a complex sentence?
options: When you come we will go.
When you come, we will go.
When, you come we will go.
We will go, when you come.
hints: Use a comma after the subordinate clause when it comes first.
The main clause follows.
questions.explanation: 'When you come, we will go' correctly places the comma after the subordinate clause.
questions.misconception: Omitting the comma or placing it incorrectly.

questions.stem: Add the correct punctuation to this complex sentence: 'Although it rained the pupils went to school.'
answer: although it rained the pupils went to school
although it rained, the pupils went to school
hints: The subordinate clause comes first.
Add a comma after it.
questions.explanation: 'Although it rained, the pupils went to school' needs a comma after the subordinate clause.
questions.misconception: Omitting the comma after the subordinate clause.

questions.stem: Write three complex sentences using these subordinating conjunctions: 'because', 'although', 'if'.
hints: Each sentence must have one main and one subordinate clause.
Use the correct punctuation.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three correct complex sentences with the given conjunctions.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: She sings because she is happy.
She sings, and her sister dances.
hints: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause.
'Because she is happy' is a subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: 'She sings because she is happy' is a complex sentence.
questions.misconception: Confusing compound and complex sentences.

questions.stem: In 'The pupils went home after the bell rang', what is the main clause?
hints: The main clause can stand alone.
It does not start with a subordinating conjunction.
questions.explanation: 'The pupils went home' is the main clause.
questions.misconception: Choosing the subordinate clause as the main clause.

questions.stem: Write one complex sentence and underline the subordinate clause.
hints: Use a subordinating conjunction like 'when', 'because', 'if' or 'although'.
Underline the clause that starts with it.
questions.explanation: The pupil should write a complex sentence and correctly underline the subordinate clause.

questions.stem: Which subordinating conjunction shows a condition?
hints: A condition is something that must happen first.
'If' introduces a condition.
questions.explanation: 'If' shows a condition.
questions.misconception: Confusing condition with reason or time.

questions.stem: Join each pair of simple sentences into one complex sentence using the subordinator given: (1) She was tired. She kept working. (although) (2) You must study. You will pass. (if)
hints: Place the subordinator correctly in each sentence.
Use a comma where needed.
questions.explanation: A strong answer: (1) Although she was tired, she kept working. (2) If you study, you will pass.

criteria.description: Joins the first pair correctly with 'although'
Joins the second pair correctly with 'if'

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Although it was raining, the pupils played outside.
Although it was raining the pupils played outside.
Although, it was raining the pupils played outside.
Although it was raining; the pupils played outside.
hints: Use a comma after the subordinate clause.
The subordinate clause comes first.
questions.explanation: 'Although it was raining, the pupils played outside' is correctly punctuated.
questions.misconception: Omitting the comma or using the wrong punctuation.

questions.stem: Write two complex sentences: one with the subordinate clause first, and one with the main clause first. Use commas correctly.
hints: Subordinate first → comma after the subordinate clause.
Main clause first → no comma needed before the subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one sentence of each type with correct punctuation.

criteria.description: Writes a complex sentence with the subordinate clause first
Writes a complex sentence with the main clause first

questions.stem: Write one simple sentence, one compound sentence and one complex sentence. Label each type.
hints: Simple = one clause; compound = two main clauses; complex = main + subordinate clause.
Label each sentence clearly.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one correct example of each sentence type and labels them.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.6.1: Develop, organise and express ideas cohesively in writing and representing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts
indicator.objective: Choose appropriate ways and modes of writing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts, and organise facts, ideas and/or points of view in a way appropriate to the mode of delivery, using appropriate text features

skills.description: Identify the mode of writing in a sample text
Identify the purpose and audience of a sample text
Organise facts, ideas or points of view to suit the chosen mode
Use text features appropriate to the mode
Choose an appropriate mode of writing for a given purpose and audience
Rearrange jumbled paragraphs into a coherent piece

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify mode, purpose and audience), 35% medium (organise content to suit a mode; select mode for a purpose), 20% harder (apply mode-appropriate text features in a short piece). Sample texts kept short and level-appropriate; contexts: school, community, national issues.
misconceptions: Confusing narrative with descriptive
Believing persuasive and argumentative writing are identical
Choosing a mode that does not fit the purpose
Ignoring the audience when choosing mode and vocabulary
Writing in one mode but using features of another

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'First, wash the tomatoes. Next, cut them into small pieces. Then add salt and pepper. Finally, cook for ten minutes.' What mode of writing is this?
hints: The passage gives steps to do something.
Process writing explains how something is done.
questions.explanation: The passage gives a sequence of steps, so it is process (expository) writing.
questions.misconception: Confusing process writing with narrative.

questions.stem: Read: 'The old house stood at the end of the road. Its walls were cracked and grey, and the roof sagged like a tired old man.' What mode of writing is this?
hints: The passage paints a picture of the house.
It describes what the house looks like.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the appearance of the house, so it is descriptive writing.
questions.misconception: Confusing descriptive writing with narrative.

questions.stem: Read: 'Smoking should be banned in all public places. It harms not only the smoker but also those around. Studies show that second-hand smoke causes serious diseases.' What mode of writing is this?
hints: The writer takes a position and gives reasons.
It argues for a point of view.
questions.explanation: The passage states an opinion and supports it with reasons, so it is argumentative writing.
questions.misconception: Confusing argumentative with descriptive writing.

questions.stem: Read: 'Yesterday I went to the market with my mother. We bought tomatoes and fish. On the way home, it started to rain.' What mode of writing is this?
hints: The passage tells a story of events.
It has a beginning, middle and end.
questions.explanation: The passage narrates a sequence of events, so it is narrative writing.
questions.misconception: Calling it descriptive because it mentions the market.

questions.stem: A letter to a friend telling about your holidays has what purpose?
hints: The letter is to a friend.
What do you usually share with a friend?
questions.explanation: A letter to a friend about holidays is written to share personal news.
questions.misconception: Confusing the purpose with argumentation.

questions.stem: An article titled 'Why We Should Stop Littering' is written for which purpose and audience?
options: To persuade the community to stop littering
To tell a story about littering
To explain how to build a bin
hints: The title says 'Why We Should...'
That is a persuasive purpose.
questions.explanation: The article aims to persuade readers — likely the community — to stop littering.
questions.misconception: Confusing persuasion with narration.

questions.stem: You are writing a process paragraph on how to plant a tree. Which order is best?
options: Steps in logical order: dig a hole, place the seedling, cover with soil, water it.
Describe the tree first, then the farmer.
Give your opinion about trees, then three reasons.
Tell a story about a tree.
hints: Process writing follows a logical sequence of steps.
The steps must be in the order they are done.
questions.explanation: Process writing organises the steps in the order they are carried out.
questions.misconception: Organising the paragraph like a narrative or argument.

questions.stem: You are writing a descriptive paragraph about a market. What should you organise your details around?
answer: what you see hear and smell
hints: Descriptive writing uses sensory details.
What would help a reader picture the market?
questions.explanation: Descriptive writing organises details around what you see, hear, smell, feel and taste.
questions.misconception: Organising by time or argument instead of sensory detail.

questions.stem: An argumentative paragraph should be organised how?
hints: Argumentation needs a claim and reasons.
Which structure fits argumentation?
questions.explanation: An argumentative paragraph has a claim, reasons and a conclusion.
questions.misconception: Organising argumentation like a narrative.

questions.stem: Write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) in narrative mode about a pupil who found a lost book. Organise the events in order.
hints: Begin with the beginning of the event.
Then tell what happened next.
End with how it turned out.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes a short narrative with events in chronological order.

criteria.description: Paragraph has a clear beginning, middle and end

questions.stem: Which text feature is most suitable for a process paragraph?
hints: Process writing follows steps.
What words show the order of steps?
questions.explanation: Order words such as 'first', 'next', 'then' and 'finally' are suitable for a process paragraph.
questions.misconception: Choosing sensory words instead of order words.

questions.stem: Which text feature is most suitable for a descriptive paragraph?
hints: Descriptive writing paints a picture.
What words help readers see, hear and smell?
questions.explanation: Sensory details and adjectives help readers picture what is being described.
questions.misconception: Using order words instead of sensory details.

questions.stem: What text feature is most suitable for an argumentative paragraph?
hints: Arguments need support.
What do you use to convince readers?
questions.explanation: Argumentative writing uses evidence, reasons and examples to support a claim.
questions.misconception: Using personal feelings without evidence.

questions.stem: Write a short descriptive paragraph (3–4 sentences) about the school compound. Use at least three sensory details.
hints: Use details of sight, sound and smell.
Help the reader picture the compound.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the compound with sensory details.

criteria.description: Uses at least three sensory details

questions.stem: You want to convince your classmates to join the reading club. Which mode of writing should you use?
hints: You want to convince people.
That is the purpose of persuasion.
questions.explanation: Persuasive/argumentative writing is used to convince readers to take a stand or take action.
questions.misconception: Choosing narrative or descriptive writing for a persuasive purpose.

questions.stem: You want to explain how to prepare kenkey to a younger pupil. Which mode of writing should you use?
hints: You are explaining steps.
That is process writing.
questions.explanation: Process (expository) writing is used to explain how something is done.
questions.misconception: Choosing narrative for an explanation.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks you to write about 'A Day I Will Never Forget'. Which mode should you use and why? Write one sentence giving the mode and one giving the reason.
hints: The topic is about an event in your life.
Which mode tells the story of an event?
questions.explanation: A strong answer chooses narrative because the topic tells about a personal event.

questions.stem: These sentences form a process paragraph: A. Next, add the eggs and stir. B. First, heat the oil in a pan. C. Finally, serve the food on a plate. D. Then add the chopped onions. What is the correct order?
hints: Look for order words: first, then, next, finally.
'First' must come first and 'finally' last.
questions.explanation: The order is B (first), D (then), A (next), C (finally).
questions.misconception: Ignoring the order words in the sentences.

questions.stem: Arrange these sentences to form a good paragraph: A. Finally, the pupils cleaned the windows. B. The pupils arrived at school early. C. Then they swept the floor. D. First, they arranged the desks. Write the letters in order.
hints: Start with the event that happens first.
Use the order words to guide you.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: B (arrived), D (first arranged), C (then swept), A (finally cleaned windows).
questions.misconception: Ordering the sentences arbitrarily.

questions.stem: Which feature is most suitable for a narrative paragraph?
hints: Narratives tell a story in order.
What words show the order of events?
questions.explanation: Chronological connectors help organise events in a narrative.
questions.misconception: Using argumentative features for a narrative.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.6.1: Develop, organise and express ideas cohesively in writing and representing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts
indicator.objective: use key words, phrases or clauses to introduce the main idea in the paragraph.

skills.description: Identify the main idea of a model paragraph
Identify the topic sentence in a paragraph
Identify key words, phrases or clauses that introduce the main idea
Write a topic sentence that clearly introduces the main idea of a paragraph
Identify sentences that support the main idea and distinguish them from the topic sentence

spec.difficultyPlan: 50% easy (identify main idea and topic sentence), 30% medium (identify key words/phrases; write a topic sentence), 20% harder (distinguish supporting sentences from the topic sentence and write a paragraph with a clear topic sentence). Paragraphs kept short (4–6 sentences).
misconceptions: Thinking the first sentence is always the topic sentence
Confusing a supporting detail with the main idea
Writing a topic sentence that is too broad or too narrow
Believing every sentence in a paragraph states the main idea
Writing a paragraph with no clear topic sentence

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks. They also washed the windows. The classroom looked bright and clean.' What is the main idea?
hints: The main idea covers all the sentences.
What is the whole paragraph about?
questions.explanation: All the sentences describe how the pupils cleaned the classroom, so that is the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail as the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama woke up early. She swept the compound. She fetched water. She cooked breakfast. Then she went to school.' What is the main idea?
hints: What do all the actions have in common?
They are all chores done in the morning.
questions.explanation: All the actions are morning chores, so the main idea is that Ama did her morning chores.
questions.misconception: Choosing one action as the main idea.

questions.stem: Read: 'Kojo found a wallet. He took it to the police station. The owner was found and thanked him.' Write the main idea in one sentence.
answer: kojo found and returned a wallet
kojo took a wallet to the police
hints: What is the most important action?
It involves a wallet and honesty.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that Kojo found and returned a lost wallet.
questions.misconception: Including the detail about being thanked as the main idea.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph and write the main idea in one sentence: 'The market was busy. Traders called out their prices. Buyers moved from stall to stall. The noise was loud.'
hints: What is the whole paragraph about?
All sentences describe the market.
questions.explanation: The main idea is that the market was busy.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the topic sentence in this paragraph? 'The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks. They also washed the windows. The classroom looked bright and clean.'
options: The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom.
They swept the floor and arranged the desks.
The classroom looked bright and clean.
hints: The topic sentence introduces the main idea.
It usually comes first.
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces the main idea that the pupils cleaned the classroom.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail as the topic sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'The school garden is full of vegetables. The pupils planted tomatoes and onions. They water the garden every morning. They also weed it on Fridays.' Which sentence is the topic sentence?
options: The school garden is full of vegetables.
The pupils planted tomatoes and onions.
They water the garden every morning.
They also weed it on Fridays.
hints: The topic sentence states the main idea.
It is the first sentence here.
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces the main idea that the garden is full of vegetables.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting sentence as the topic sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a very kind girl. She shares her food with others. She helps her mother at home. She comforts her friends when they are sad.' Which sentence is the topic sentence? Write it.
answer: ama is a very kind girl
hints: The topic sentence tells us what the paragraph is about.
It is the first sentence.
questions.explanation: The first sentence 'Ama is a very kind girl' is the topic sentence.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail.

questions.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about the importance of reading.
hints: The topic sentence should state the main idea.
Keep it clear and specific.
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence might be: 'Reading is important for many reasons.'

criteria.description: Sentence introduces the main idea about reading

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks. They also washed the windows.' Which key words introduce the main idea?
hints: The key words are in the topic sentence.
They tell us what the paragraph is about.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'cleaned the classroom' introduces the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing supporting details as key words.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a very kind girl. She shares her food with others. She helps her mother at home.' Write the key phrase that introduces the main idea.
hints: Look at the first sentence.
Which words tell us about Ama's character?
questions.explanation: The key phrase 'very kind girl' introduces the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail instead of the key phrase.

questions.stem: Which phrase best introduces the main idea for a paragraph about keeping the school clean?
options: Keeping the school clean is important.
hints: The phrase should state the main idea.
Which option is a general statement about cleanliness?
questions.explanation: 'Keeping the school clean is important' introduces the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a supporting detail as the main idea.

questions.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about the importance of exercise. Underline the key words that introduce the main idea.
hints: The key words should state the main idea.
Underline the words that tell us what the paragraph is about.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes a clear topic sentence and underlines the key words.

criteria.description: Underlines the key words that introduce the main idea

questions.stem: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the school library?
options: The school library is a useful place.
hints: The topic sentence should state the main idea.
Which sentence is the most general and clear?
questions.explanation: 'The school library is a useful place' is the best topic sentence because it introduces the main idea.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail as the topic sentence.

questions.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about the importance of trees.
hints: State the main idea clearly.
Keep it general but focused.
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence states that trees are important.
questions.misconception: Writing a sentence that is too specific or too broad.

questions.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about a busy market. Then write two supporting sentences.
hints: The topic sentence should state the main idea about the market.
Supporting sentences should give details.
questions.explanation: A strong answer has a clear topic sentence and two supporting sentences.

questions.stem: Which sentence supports the main idea in this paragraph? 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks. They also washed the windows.'
options: They swept the floor and arranged the desks.
hints: Supporting sentences give details about the main idea.
Which sentence tells how they cleaned?
questions.explanation: 'They swept the floor and arranged the desks' supports the main idea by giving details.
questions.misconception: Choosing the topic sentence as a supporting sentence.

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama is a very kind girl. She shares her food with others. She helps her mother at home.' Which sentence is a supporting sentence?
answer: she shares her food with others
she helps her mother at home
hints: Supporting sentences give examples or details.
They come after the topic sentence.
questions.explanation: Both 'She shares her food with others' and 'She helps her mother at home' are supporting sentences.
questions.misconception: Choosing the topic sentence as a supporting sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT support the main idea 'The market was busy'?
options: Buyers moved from stall to stall.
hints: Supporting sentences should give details about busyness.
Which sentence gives unrelated information?
questions.explanation: 'The market is in Accra' does not support the idea that the market was busy.
questions.misconception: Thinking any sentence about the market supports the main idea.

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (3–4 sentences) with a clear topic sentence and at least two supporting sentences. Underline the topic sentence.
hints: Start with a topic sentence.
Follow with details that support it.
Underline the topic sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph has a clear topic sentence and supporting details.

criteria.description: Writes a paragraph with a clear topic sentence
Includes at least two supporting sentences

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.6.1: Develop, organise and express ideas cohesively in writing and representing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts
indicator.objective: Elaborate on, explain and/or justify the main ideas of a paragraph by providing relevant details and examples

skills.description: Add relevant details to elaborate on a main idea
Explain a main idea with reasons or examples
Justify a main idea with evidence or examples
Ensure supporting details and examples are relevant to the main idea
Write a paragraph that elaborates on a given topic sentence

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (add one relevant detail), 35% medium (explain and justify with examples), 20% harder (write a full elaborated paragraph with relevant, varied support). Topic sentences kept simple; contexts: school, family, community, environment.
misconceptions: Adding details that are off-topic
Repeating the main idea in different words instead of elaborating
Giving opinions without examples or reasons
Adding too many unrelated details
Believing one example is enough for every point

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The school compound is kept clean by the pupils.' Which detail best elaborates this idea?
options: The pupils sweep the compound every morning.
hints: A relevant detail should explain how the pupils keep the compound clean.
Which option mentions an action related to cleaning?
questions.explanation: Sweeping the compound every morning is a relevant detail that shows how the pupils keep it clean.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail about the school that is not about cleanliness.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Ama is a very kind girl.' Which detail best elaborates this idea?
options: She shares her food with hungry classmates.
hints: Kindness is shown through actions toward others.
Which detail shows kindness?
questions.explanation: Sharing food with hungry classmates is a detail that shows kindness.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that does not show kindness.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The market was busy.' Write one detail that elaborates this idea.
answer: buyers moved from stall to stall
hints: What makes a market busy?
Think of sounds and movement.
questions.explanation: Details such as traders calling out prices or many people moving about elaborate the idea of a busy market.
questions.misconception: Repeating the topic sentence without adding a detail.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Exercise is good for the body.' Write three sentences that elaborate this idea with details.
hints: Explain what exercise does for the body.
Give examples such as running, jumping or playing football.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives details such as exercise strengthens the heart, builds muscles and keeps the body fit.

criteria.description: Details are relevant to exercise and health

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Reading is important for pupils.' Which sentence best explains this idea?
options: Reading helps pupils learn new words and do well in school.
hints: An explanation tells why the main idea is true.
Which sentence gives a reason reading matters?
questions.explanation: The sentence about learning new words and doing well explains why reading is important.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that does not explain the importance.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Water is important for good health.' Write one sentence explaining why.
answer: water keeps our body working well
we need water to stay healthy
our bodies need water to survive
hints: Think about what water does in the body.
Use a reason to explain the topic sentence.
questions.explanation: A good explanation states that the body needs water to work well and stay healthy.
questions.misconception: Repeating the topic sentence without explaining why.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Homework helps pupils learn better.' Which explanation best supports this idea?
options: Homework gives pupils extra practice with what they learned in class.
Some pupils do not like homework.
Homework is written in exercise books.
hints: An explanation tells how homework helps learning.
Which sentence describes the benefit of homework?
questions.explanation: Extra practice with classwork is a clear explanation of how homework helps learning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a fact about homework that does not explain its benefit.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Trees are important to us.' Write two sentences explaining why trees are important.
hints: Think about what trees provide and do for us.
Use reasons that explain the topic sentence.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that trees provide shade, clean the air or give fruits and wood.

criteria.description: Sentences are relevant to the topic

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The pupils of Basic 6 are hardworking.' Which example best justifies this idea?
options: They study every evening and help each other with homework.
hints: A justification gives evidence for the idea.
Which example shows hard work?
questions.explanation: Studying every evening and helping with homework is evidence of hard work.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that does not justify the idea.
