questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The market is well organised.' Write one example that justifies this idea.
answer: traders arrange their goods in rows
similar goods are sold in the same area
there are clear walking paths between stalls
the market has a waste disposal area
hints: What makes a market well organised?
Think of how stalls and goods are arranged.
questions.explanation: An example such as goods arranged in rows or clear walking paths justifies the idea that the market is organised.
questions.misconception: Repeating the topic sentence without an example.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Our school is a good place to learn.' Which evidence best justifies this idea?
options: The school has a library, qualified teachers and clean classrooms.
The school has a green gate.
The school is near a river.
hints: Evidence should support the idea that learning is good.
Which option mentions facilities and teachers?
questions.explanation: A library, qualified teachers and clean classrooms are evidence that the school supports learning.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail that does not relate to learning.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The pupils worked hard to prepare for the festival.' Write two examples that justify this idea.
hints: Think of actions that show hard work and preparation.
Give specific examples.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives examples such as practising the song every day or decorating the classroom after school.

criteria.description: Examples justify the idea of hard work and preparation

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'Ama keeps her desk neat.' Which detail is most relevant?
options: She arranges her books and pencils carefully.
hints: A relevant detail should support the idea about neatness.
Which option is about organising things on a desk?
questions.explanation: Arranging books and pencils carefully is relevant to keeping a desk neat.
questions.misconception: Choosing a detail about appearance instead of neatness.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The school garden is productive.' Which detail is NOT relevant?
options: The pupils harvest vegetables every month.
The garden has rows of tomato plants.
The pupils water the garden every morning.
The school gate is painted green.
hints: Relevant details support the idea of productivity.
Which option is about something other than the garden?
questions.explanation: The colour of the school gate is not related to the productivity of the garden.
questions.misconception: Thinking any detail about the school supports the idea.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The pupils respect their teacher.' Write one relevant detail that supports this idea.
hints: Respect is shown through actions.
What actions show respect to a teacher?
questions.explanation: A relevant detail is an action that shows respect, such as greeting politely or listening carefully.
questions.misconception: Giving a detail unrelated to respect.

questions.stem: Topic sentence: 'The market was noisy and busy.' Write three sentences that elaborate this idea with relevant details. One sentence should NOT be relevant — underline the irrelevant sentence.
hints: Two or three sentences should be relevant details.
One sentence should be off-topic.
questions.explanation: A strong answer includes relevant sensory details (noise, movement, crowds) and one clearly unrelated sentence.

criteria.description: Writes at least two relevant details

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (4–5 sentences) that elaborates on this topic sentence: 'Our school has a beautiful compound.'
hints: Start with the topic sentence.
Add details about what makes it beautiful.
Use descriptive words.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph elaborates the topic sentence with relevant descriptive details.

criteria.description: Adds at least three relevant details
Paragraph is coherent and well organised

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (4–5 sentences) that elaborates on this topic sentence: 'Reading is a valuable habit for pupils.' Include at least one reason and one example.
hints: Start with the topic sentence.
Explain why reading is valuable.
Give an example.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph elaborates with a reason and an example that support the topic sentence.

criteria.description: Paragraph is coherent and well organised

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.6.1: Develop, organise and express ideas cohesively in writing and representing for a variety of purposes, audience, and contexts
indicator.objective: Use cohesive devices pronoun references, repeated key terms or grammatical structures to link ideas in a paragraph. E.g. use connectors to link contrasting ideas. Show results and purpose.

skills.description: Identify cohesive devices in a paragraph
Use connectors correctly to link contrasting ideas, show results and purpose
Use pronoun references to link sentences and avoid repetition
Repeat key terms or grammatical structures to link ideas coherently
Write a coherent paragraph using a range of cohesive devices

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify cohesive devices), 35% medium (use connectors and pronoun references correctly), 20% harder (write a coherent paragraph using repeated key terms and appropriate connectors). Paragraphs kept short; contexts: school, community, environment, daily life.
misconceptions: Overusing 'and' as the only connector
Using the wrong connector for the relationship
Using a pronoun without a clear antecedent
Repeating the same noun in every sentence instead of using pronouns
Misplacing connectors
Believing repeated key terms are always bad

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor and arranged the desks.' Which word is a cohesive device?
hints: Cohesive devices link ideas in a text.
'They' refers back to 'the pupils'.
questions.explanation: 'They' is a pronoun reference that links the second sentence to the first.
questions.misconception: Choosing a noun instead of the cohesive device.

questions.stem: Read: 'The market was crowded. However, the traders were happy.' Which word is a cohesive device?
hints: Cohesive devices link ideas together.
'However' links two contrasting ideas.
questions.explanation: 'However' is a connector that shows contrast between the two sentences.
questions.misconception: Choosing an adjective instead of the connector.

questions.stem: Identify the pronoun reference in this paragraph: 'Ama found a wallet. She took it to the head teacher.'
hints: Pronouns refer back to nouns.
Which words replace 'Ama' and 'wallet'?
questions.explanation: 'She' refers to Ama and 'it' refers to the wallet.
questions.misconception: Choosing the nouns instead of the pronouns.

questions.stem: Write two sentences that use a pronoun reference to link them. Underline the pronoun reference.
hints: Use a pronoun to refer back to a noun in the first sentence.
Underline the pronoun.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two linked sentences and underlines the pronoun reference.

criteria.description: Uses a pronoun reference to link them

questions.stem: Which connector best shows contrast between these ideas? 'The food was delicious. _____, it was very expensive.'
hints: The two ideas are opposite: good food but high price.
Use a contrast connector.
questions.explanation: 'However' shows the contrast between the delicious food and the high price.
questions.misconception: Using a connector that does not show contrast.

questions.stem: Which connector best shows a result? 'It rained heavily. _____, the match was cancelled.'
hints: The second sentence is the result of the first.
Use a result connector.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' shows that the cancellation was the result of the heavy rain.
questions.misconception: Using a contrast connector for a result.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with a result connector: 'The pupils studied hard. _____, they passed the exam.'
hints: The second sentence is the result of the first.
Use a connector that shows result.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore', 'as a result', 'so' or 'consequently' all correctly show the result.
questions.misconception: Using 'however' for a result.

questions.stem: Write two sentences using 'however' to link contrasting ideas and two sentences using 'therefore' to show a result.
hints: 'However' links opposite ideas; 'therefore' shows a result.
Use each connector in its own pair of sentences.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes one pair of sentences with 'however' and one pair with 'therefore'.

criteria.description: Writes two sentences with 'however' showing contrast
Writes two sentences with 'therefore' showing result

questions.stem: Read: 'Ama has a new bag. She bought it from the market.' What does 'it' refer to?
hints: A pronoun refers back to a noun.
'It' replaces a thing, not a person.
questions.explanation: 'It' refers to the new bag.
questions.misconception: Choosing the person instead of the object.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pronoun reference correctly?
options: Kojo found a wallet. He took it to the police station.
Kojo found a wallet. They took it to the police station.
Kojo found a wallet. She took it to the police station.
Kojo found a wallet. It took him to the police station.
hints: The pronoun must match the noun it refers to.
Kojo is male and singular.
questions.explanation: 'He' correctly refers to Kojo and 'it' refers to the wallet.
questions.misconception: Using a pronoun that does not match the noun.

questions.stem: Replace the repeated noun with a pronoun: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. The pupils swept the floor.'
answer: the pupils cleaned the classroom they swept the floor
they cleaned the classroom they swept the floor
the pupils cleaned the classroom and they swept the floor
hints: Use 'they' for the pupils.
Avoid repeating 'the pupils'.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence uses 'they' to replace 'the pupils': 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor.'
questions.misconception: Keeping the repeated noun.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils of Basic 6 cleaned the classroom. The classroom looked bright and clean.' What cohesive device is used?
hints: Look for a repeated word.
'Classroom' appears in both sentences.
questions.explanation: The repeated word 'classroom' links the two sentences.
questions.misconception: Confusing repeated key terms with pronoun reference.

questions.stem: Write a second sentence that uses a repeated key term to link to: 'The school garden is full of vegetables.'
answer: the garden has tomatoes and onions
the garden is watered every morning
the school garden is looked after by the pupils
hints: Repeat 'garden' or 'school garden'.
Make sure the sentence links to the first.
questions.explanation: A sentence that repeats 'garden' links clearly to the first sentence.
questions.misconception: Not using the key term in the second sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a repeated key term to link with 'The library has many books'?
options: The books are arranged by subject.
hints: Look for the repeated word.
Which sentence repeats 'books'?
questions.explanation: The sentence 'The books are arranged by subject' repeats the key term 'books'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a sentence without the key term.

questions.stem: Write three sentences about the school library, using repeated key terms to link them. Underline the repeated key terms.
hints: Choose a key term like 'library', 'books' or 'pupils'.
Repeat it naturally across the sentences.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three linked sentences with clearly underlined repeated key terms.

criteria.description: Uses repeated key terms to link the sentences

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (3–4 sentences) about the importance of keeping the school clean. Use at least two cohesive devices (pronoun reference and a connector).
hints: Start with a topic sentence.
Use a pronoun and a connector to link ideas.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph uses at least two cohesive devices to link ideas smoothly.

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (4–5 sentences) about a visit to the market. Use at least three cohesive devices: a pronoun reference, a repeated key term and a connector.
hints: Choose a key term to repeat.
Use a pronoun to avoid repetition.
Add a connector to show a relationship.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph uses at least three different cohesive devices.

questions.stem: Which connector shows purpose? 'The pupils studied hard _____ they could pass their exams.'
hints: Purpose means the reason for doing something.
'So that' introduces a purpose.
questions.explanation: 'So that' shows the purpose of studying hard.
questions.misconception: Confusing purpose with result or contrast.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'The pupils cleaned the compound. They swept the floor. The compound looked clean. However, the windows were still dirty.' Identify three cohesive devices used in the paragraph.
hints: Look for pronouns, repeated key terms and connectors.
There is one of each in the paragraph.
questions.explanation: The cohesive devices are: 'They' (pronoun reference), 'compound' (repeated key term) and 'However' (contrast connector).

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (4–5 sentences) about how to keep your community clean. Use at least three cohesive devices and underline them.
hints: Use a pronoun, a repeated key term and a connector.
Underline each cohesive device.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph uses at least three cohesive devices and underlines them.

criteria.description: Uses at least three cohesive devices

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.9.1: Apply the skills and strategies for idea generation, selection, development, organisation and revision in writing
indicator.objective: Select a topic of choice on a national issue or from different learning areas, brainstorm ideas and organize them before writing

skills.description: Select a suitable topic on a national issue or from another learning area
Generate ideas on a chosen topic through brainstorming without judging ideas
Organise brainstormed ideas into a writing plan using an outline, chart or graphic organiser
Identify the stages of the writing process and place pre-writing in sequence
Identify the purpose and audience for a chosen topic before writing

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (select a topic and brainstorm ideas), 35% medium (organise ideas into a plan), 20% harder (choose purpose/audience and produce a coherent plan). Topics drawn from national issues and other learning areas at Basic 6 level.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad to write about in a short piece
Judging or discarding ideas during brainstorming instead of listing them
Skipping the organising stage and going straight to writing
Making a plan that does not match the topic
Believing pre-writing is optional

questions.stem: Which of these is the best topic for a short piece of writing on a national issue?
options: The history of the whole world
How to reduce plastic waste in Ghana
hints: A good topic is focused, not too broad.
Which topic can be covered in a short piece?
questions.explanation: 'How to reduce plastic waste in Ghana' is focused and manageable. The others are too broad.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too wide to cover.

questions.stem: Write one suitable topic on a national issue that you could write about.
answer: why we should keep our environment clean
hints: Choose a topic that affects many people in Ghana.
It should be focused enough for a short piece.
questions.explanation: Any focused national issue such as malaria prevention, bush fires or education is suitable.
questions.misconception: Choosing a topic that is too broad.

questions.stem: What should you do during brainstorming?
options: Write down every idea that comes to mind without judging it.
Write only one idea and stop.
hints: Brainstorming means generating many ideas.
Do not judge ideas yet.
questions.explanation: During brainstorming, you write down all ideas without judging them. You can select the best ones later.
questions.misconception: Thinking you should judge ideas during brainstorming.

questions.stem: Brainstorm three ideas for a piece of writing about keeping the school clean.
hints: Think of causes, effects and solutions.
Write down at least three ideas.
questions.explanation: A strong answer lists at least three ideas such as: rubbish attracts flies, we should use bins, pupils can form a cleaning club.

criteria.description: Ideas are relevant to keeping the school clean

questions.stem: After brainstorming, what should you do with your ideas before writing?
options: Organise them into a plan or outline.
Copy them into the final draft.
hints: Organising helps you structure your writing.
A plan groups and orders your ideas.
questions.explanation: You should organise your ideas into a plan, outline or graphic organiser before writing.
questions.misconception: Thinking you can start writing immediately after brainstorming.

questions.stem: Name one type of graphic organiser you could use to organise your ideas.
hints: Graphic organisers help you group ideas visually.
Examples include mind maps, charts and outlines.
questions.explanation: Graphic organisers such as mind maps, charts, outlines and line diagrams help organise ideas.
questions.misconception: Not knowing what a graphic organiser is.

questions.stem: What is the first stage of the writing process?
hints: The first stage comes before writing.
It involves planning and generating ideas.
questions.explanation: Prewriting is the first stage of the writing process.
questions.misconception: Thinking drafting comes first.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the prewriting stage?
hints: Prewriting is before writing.
It involves planning and idea generation.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming and organising ideas are prewriting activities.
questions.misconception: Confusing prewriting with editing or publishing.

questions.stem: You are writing about the dangers of bush fires for your classmates. What is your audience?
hints: Audience means the people who will read or hear your writing.
Who is in your class?
questions.explanation: The audience for a piece written for your classmates is your classmates.
questions.misconception: Confusing audience with someone else.

questions.stem: Write one purpose for a piece of writing about keeping the environment clean.
answer: to persuade people to keep the environment clean
to inform people about the importance of cleanliness
to encourage people to stop littering
to teach people how to keep the environment clean
hints: Why would you write about cleanliness?
The purpose could be to inform or persuade.
questions.explanation: A suitable purpose is to inform or persuade people about keeping the environment clean.
questions.misconception: Giving a purpose unrelated to the topic.

questions.stem: Which topic is from a different learning area rather than a national issue?
options: The importance of education for all
hints: A different learning area could be Science, Maths or Social Studies.
Which topic belongs to Science?
questions.explanation: 'How plants make food' is a Science topic, not a national issue.
questions.misconception: Not recognising topics from different learning areas.

questions.stem: Why is brainstorming useful before writing?
options: It helps you gather many ideas to choose from.
It is only for older pupils.
hints: Brainstorming generates ideas.
More ideas give you more to choose from.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming helps you gather many ideas so you can choose the best ones for your writing.
questions.misconception: Thinking brainstorming is unnecessary.

questions.stem: You have brainstormed these ideas about malaria: mosquitoes spread it, use treated nets, clear stagnant water, it causes fever. Organise them into a simple plan with three groups: Causes, Prevention, Effects.
hints: Group the ideas into the three categories.
Write each group clearly.
questions.explanation: A strong plan groups the ideas: Causes: mosquitoes; Prevention: treated nets, clear stagnant water; Effects: fever.

criteria.description: Groups ideas into causes, prevention and effects
Places each idea in the correct group

questions.stem: List the five stages of the writing process in order.
hints: Start with prewriting.
The last stage is publishing.
questions.explanation: The five stages are: prewriting, drafting, revising, editing and publishing.

criteria.description: Stages are in the correct order

questions.stem: You are writing about the importance of reading. Identify your purpose and audience, and explain why.
hints: Purpose: why you are writing. Audience: who will read it.
Explain your choices.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the purpose (e.g. to encourage reading) and audience (e.g. classmates) and explains why.

questions.stem: Choose one topic on a national issue and write two reasons why you chose it.
hints: Choose a topic you know well or care about.
Give two clear reasons.
questions.explanation: A strong answer names a focused topic and gives two reasons, such as importance to the community or personal experience.

criteria.description: Gives two reasons for choosing it

questions.stem: What is the best way to organise ideas for a persuasive piece about stopping littering?
hints: Persuasive writing needs a claim and reasons.
Which structure fits persuasion?
questions.explanation: A persuasive piece is best organised as: claim, reasons and conclusion.
questions.misconception: Organising a persuasive piece like a narrative.

questions.stem: In a group, brainstorm five ideas about the topic 'Keeping our community clean'. Share them with the class.
hints: Do not judge ideas during brainstorming.
Write down every idea that comes to mind.
questions.explanation: The group generates five ideas without judging them.

criteria.description: Ideas are relevant to the topic

questions.stem: Tell the class your purpose and audience for a piece of writing about the dangers of drug abuse.
hints: Think about why you are writing and who will read it.
Explain your choices.
questions.explanation: The pupil states a clear purpose and audience and explains why.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.9.2: Develop and express ideas coherently and cohesively in writing
indicator.objective: Develop ideas into a three-paragraph draft without considering the writing conventions, linking ideas within and across paragraphs with a wider range of cohesive devices, e.g. as a result, on the other hand, however.

skills.description: Develop a writing plan into a three-paragraph draft
Link ideas within paragraphs using cohesive devices
Link ideas across paragraphs using a wider range of cohesive devices
Draft for content and organisation without stopping to perfect conventions
Give each paragraph a clear function (introductory, developing, concluding)
Select appropriate cohesive devices that match the relationship between ideas

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (develop a plan into a draft of three paragraphs), 35% medium (use cohesive devices within and across paragraphs), 20% harder (select appropriate cohesive devices that match the relationship between ideas). Drafts produced from plans; contexts from national issues and school/community life.
misconceptions: Writing a draft and stopping at every error instead of getting ideas down
Producing three paragraphs that all say the same thing
Using the same connector repeatedly regardless of the relationship
Using 'however' for addition instead of contrast
Writing a draft with no clear introduction or conclusion
Confusing a draft with a final copy

questions.stem: How many paragraphs should a three-paragraph draft have?
hints: The task asks for a three-paragraph draft.
Count the paragraphs.
questions.explanation: A three-paragraph draft has three paragraphs.
questions.misconception: Confusing the number of paragraphs with the number of sentences.

questions.stem: You have a plan with these ideas: (1) what pollution is (2) causes and effects (3) what we can do. How should you organise them into three paragraphs?
options: Introduction: what pollution is; Body: causes and effects; Conclusion: what we can do
Introduction: causes and effects; Body: what pollution is; Conclusion: what we can do
All three ideas in one paragraph
hints: The introduction sets the scene.
The body develops the main ideas.
The conclusion suggests action.
questions.explanation: The introduction explains pollution, the body gives causes and effects, and the conclusion suggests solutions.
questions.misconception: Putting all ideas in one paragraph or misordering them.

questions.stem: Write a three-paragraph draft on the topic 'Keeping Our School Clean'. Use a plan with: (1) why cleanliness matters (2) what pupils can do (3) a concluding call to action.
hints: Each paragraph should have one main idea.
Do not worry about perfect spelling; focus on getting ideas down.
questions.explanation: A strong answer has three paragraphs with clear introductory, developing and concluding functions.

criteria.description: Each paragraph develops one main idea

questions.stem: Which cohesive device best links these two sentences within a paragraph? 'The classroom was dirty. _____, the pupils cleaned it.'
hints: The second sentence is the result of the first.
Use a result connector.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' shows that cleaning was the result of the classroom being dirty.
questions.misconception: Using a contrast connector for a result.

questions.stem: Write one sentence using the connector 'as a result' to link two ideas.
answer: it rained heavily as a result the match was cancelled
he studied hard as a result he passed the exam
the pupils littered as a result the compound was dirty
she woke up late as a result she missed the bus
hints: Use 'as a result' to show a consequence.
The second idea should follow from the first.
questions.explanation: A correct sentence uses 'as a result' to show the consequence of the first idea.
questions.misconception: Using 'as a result' without a clear consequence.

questions.stem: Write a paragraph (4–5 sentences) about the importance of exercise. Use at least two cohesive devices within the paragraph.
hints: Use connectors like 'first', 'also', 'therefore'.
Link the sentences smoothly.
questions.explanation: A strong paragraph uses at least two cohesive devices to link ideas.

criteria.description: Uses at least two cohesive devices

questions.stem: Which cohesive device best links two paragraphs with contrasting ideas?
hints: Contrasting ideas need a contrast connector.
'On the other hand' shows contrast.
questions.explanation: 'On the other hand' links paragraphs that present contrasting ideas.
questions.misconception: Using an addition or result connector for contrast.

questions.stem: Which cohesive device best links two paragraphs where the second adds more information?
hints: Addition means adding more of the same kind of idea.
'Furthermore' adds information.
questions.explanation: 'Furthermore' links paragraphs where the second adds more information.
questions.misconception: Using a contrast connector for addition.

questions.stem: Name one cohesive device you can use to link paragraphs when giving an example.
hints: Think of words that introduce examples.
'For example' and 'for instance' are good.
questions.explanation: Cohesive devices for giving examples include 'for example', 'for instance' and 'to illustrate'.
questions.misconception: Using a contrast connector for an example.

questions.stem: Write a two-paragraph piece on 'The Importance of Trees'. Use at least two cohesive devices to link the paragraphs.
hints: Use connectors like 'moreover', 'in addition', 'as a result'.
Link the two paragraphs smoothly.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes two linked paragraphs using cohesive devices across them.

criteria.description: Uses at least two cohesive devices across paragraphs

questions.stem: What should you focus on when writing a first draft?
options: Getting your ideas down on paper
hints: A first draft is about ideas.
You can correct conventions later.
questions.explanation: A first draft should focus on getting ideas down, not on perfecting conventions.
questions.misconception: Thinking a first draft must be perfect.

questions.stem: Why should you not stop to correct every spelling mistake while drafting?
answer: it stops the flow of ideas
you may lose your train of thought
hints: Drafting is about getting ideas down.
Corrections come in the editing stage.
questions.explanation: Stopping to correct mistakes interrupts your flow of ideas. Corrections belong in the editing stage.
questions.misconception: Thinking drafting and editing happen at the same time.

questions.stem: What is the function of the first paragraph in a three-paragraph draft?
hints: The first paragraph comes first.
It sets up the writing.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph introduces the topic.
questions.misconception: Confusing the introductory paragraph with the body or conclusion.

questions.stem: What is the function of the middle paragraph in a three-paragraph draft?
options: To develop the main ideas with details
hints: The middle paragraph comes after the introduction.
It develops the ideas.
questions.explanation: The middle paragraph develops the main ideas with details and examples.
questions.misconception: Confusing the developing paragraph with the introduction or conclusion.

questions.stem: What is the function of the last paragraph in a three-paragraph draft?
answer: to bring the writing to a close
hints: The last paragraph comes at the end.
It wraps up the writing.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph concludes the piece by summarising or giving a final thought.
questions.misconception: Thinking the last paragraph introduces new ideas.

questions.stem: Write a three-paragraph draft on 'The Importance of Reading'. Each paragraph should have a clear function: introduction, development and conclusion.
hints: The first paragraph introduces the topic.
The second develops the ideas.
The third concludes.
questions.explanation: A strong answer has three clearly functioning paragraphs.

criteria.description: Each paragraph has a clear function

questions.stem: Which cohesive device correctly shows the relationship between these ideas? 'The pupils studied hard. _____, they passed their exams.'
hints: The second idea is the consequence of the first.
Use a result connector.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' shows the consequence of studying hard.
questions.misconception: Using a contrast or example connector for a result.

questions.stem: Which cohesive device correctly shows the relationship? 'The food was delicious. _____, it was very expensive.'
hints: The two ideas are contrasting: good food but high price.
Use a contrast connector.
questions.explanation: 'However' shows the contrast between delicious food and high price.
questions.misconception: Using a result connector for contrast.

questions.stem: Write three pairs of sentences using these cohesive devices correctly: (1) 'however' (2) 'therefore' (3) 'for example'.
hints: 'However' shows contrast; 'therefore' shows result; 'for example' gives an example.
Use each in a pair of sentences.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three pairs of sentences with the connectors used correctly.

questions.stem: Write a three-paragraph draft on 'The Dangers of Drug Abuse'. Focus on getting your ideas down without worrying about spelling or punctuation. Use a plan: (1) what drug abuse is (2) its effects on young people (3) how to avoid it.
hints: Follow the plan for your three paragraphs.
Do not stop to correct conventions.
questions.explanation: A strong answer has three paragraphs following the plan, with ideas developed in each.

questions.stem: Say two sentences aloud using the connector 'however' to show contrast.
hints: 'However' shows contrast between two ideas.
The two ideas should be opposite.
questions.explanation: The pupil uses 'however' correctly to link two contrasting ideas.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.9.3: Apply strategies for improving drafts for publishing
indicator.objective: Review, and revise the draft to produce a coherent piece by proposing grammar and vocabulary for improvement.

skills.description: Use revision guide questions to review a draft
Identify and propose grammar improvements in a draft
Identify and propose vocabulary improvements in a draft
Revise a draft to make it more coherent
Read a partner's draft and offer suggestions for improvement

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (apply revision guide questions), 35% medium (propose grammar and vocabulary improvements), 20% harder (revise for coherence and give helpful peer feedback). Sample drafts kept short (2–3 paragraphs).
misconceptions: Thinking revision means only correcting spelling
Changing content without checking whether the new content fits the topic
Offering 'It is good' as peer feedback instead of specific suggestions
Making so many changes that the original ideas are lost
Confusing revision (content/organisation) with editing (conventions)

questions.stem: Which question is a good revision guide question?
options: Does my beginning catch the reader's attention?
How many words are in my draft?
How long did I take to write?
hints: Revision questions help improve the content and organisation.
Which question helps you review your writing?
questions.explanation: 'Does my beginning catch the reader's attention?' is a revision question that helps improve the writing.
questions.misconception: Choosing a question unrelated to improving the writing.

questions.stem: Which revision question helps check if the ideas are organised?
options: Are my ideas in order and easy to understand?
Did I use a blue pen?
hints: Organisation is about the order of ideas.
Which question asks about order and understanding?
questions.explanation: 'Are my ideas in order and easy to understand?' helps check the organisation of ideas.
questions.misconception: Confusing organisation with handwriting or pen colour.

questions.stem: Write one revision question you could ask about the conclusion of a draft.
answer: does my conclusion summarise the main points
does the conclusion follow from the ideas
does the ending wrap up the writing
hints: Think about what a conclusion should do.
Does it bring the writing to a close?
questions.explanation: A good revision question about the conclusion asks whether it summarises the main points or brings the writing to a close.
questions.misconception: Asking a question unrelated to the conclusion.

questions.stem: Write three revision guide questions you would use to review a draft.
hints: Ask about the beginning, the ideas and the ending.
Make each question help improve the writing.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three useful revision questions.

questions.stem: Read this draft sentence: 'The pupils goes to school every day.' How should you revise it?
hints: Check subject-verb agreement.
'Pupils' is plural, so the verb should be 'go'.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'pupils' needs the plural verb 'go', so change 'goes' to 'go'.
questions.misconception: Not recognising the subject-verb agreement error.

questions.stem: Draft sentence: 'She don't like fish.' What is the best revision?
hints: 'She' is singular.
Use 'doesn't' with singular subjects.
questions.explanation: 'She doesn't like fish' is the correct form.
questions.misconception: Using 'don't' with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Revise this sentence: 'The boys is playing football.'
hints: 'Boys' is plural.
Use 'are' with a plural subject.
questions.explanation: The correct revision is 'The boys are playing football.'
questions.misconception: Keeping 'is' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Read this draft and propose three grammar improvements: 'The pupils was very happy. They has finished their work. The teacher give them a prize.'
hints: Check subject-verb agreement in each sentence.
Change 'was' to 'were', 'has' to 'have', 'give' to 'gave'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies and corrects the three grammar errors.

questions.stem: Draft sentence: 'The food was good.' Which revision improves the vocabulary?
hints: Choose a stronger, more precise word.
'Delicious' is more descriptive than 'good'.
questions.explanation: 'Delicious' is a stronger and more precise word than 'good'.
questions.misconception: Thinking all synonyms improve the vocabulary equally.

questions.stem: Draft: 'The boy ran fast to the shop.' Which revision improves the vocabulary?
options: The boy sprinted to the shop.
The boy ran quickly to the shop.
The boy went to the shop.
The boy walked to the shop.
hints: Choose a more precise verb.
'Sprinted' is more precise than 'ran fast'.
questions.explanation: 'Sprinted' is a more precise and vivid verb than 'ran fast'.
questions.misconception: Choosing a weaker word instead of a stronger one.

questions.stem: Improve the vocabulary in this sentence: 'The girl was very happy.'
hints: Replace 'very happy' with a stronger adjective.
Use a more precise word.
questions.explanation: 'Delighted', 'overjoyed' or 'thrilled' are stronger and more precise than 'very happy'.
questions.misconception: Keeping 'very happy' without improvement.

questions.stem: Read this draft and propose three vocabulary improvements: 'The big dog ran quickly to the old house. It was very hungry. The food was good.'
hints: Replace 'big', 'quickly' and 'good' with more precise words.
Examples: 'huge', 'sprinted', 'delicious'.
questions.explanation: A strong answer suggests more precise vocabulary for the underlined words.

criteria.description: Suggests an improvement for 'quickly' or 'very hungry'

questions.stem: Draft: 'The pupils cleaned the classroom. The classroom was dirty. They swept the floor.' Which revision improves coherence?
options: The classroom was dirty, so the pupils cleaned it. They swept the floor.
The pupils cleaned the classroom. The classroom was dirty. They swept the floor.
The classroom was dirty. The pupils cleaned the classroom. They swept the floor.
They swept the floor. The classroom was dirty. The pupils cleaned the classroom.
hints: Coherence means the ideas flow logically.
The cause should come before or connect to the effect.
questions.explanation: Option A links the cause (dirty classroom) to the effect (cleaning) coherently.
questions.misconception: Not recognising the need for logical ordering.

questions.stem: Revise this draft to improve coherence: 'She woke up late. She missed the bus. She arrived at school late.'
answer: she woke up late so she missed the bus and arrived at school late
because she woke up late she missed the bus and arrived at school late
she woke up late therefore she missed the bus and arrived at school late
hints: Link the causes and effects clearly.
Use connectors like 'so', 'because' or 'therefore'.
questions.explanation: A coherent revision links the events with appropriate connectors.
questions.misconception: Leaving the sentences disconnected.

questions.stem: Read this draft and revise it for coherence: 'The market was busy. The traders called out prices. The buyers moved from stall to stall. The noise was loud.' Write the revised version.
hints: Use connectors to link the ideas.
Organise the details logically.
questions.explanation: A strong revision links the details smoothly and logically.

questions.stem: Which is the best peer feedback?
options: Your story has a clear beginning, but the ending could be stronger. Try adding how the character felt.
hints: Good feedback is specific and helpful.
Which option gives a specific suggestion?
questions.explanation: Option B gives specific, helpful feedback about the ending.
questions.misconception: Thinking vague feedback is helpful.

questions.stem: What should you do when giving peer feedback?
options: Point out specific strengths and suggest specific improvements.
Only say the work is bad.
Only say the work is good.
hints: Good feedback is balanced and specific.
Mention what works and what can improve.
questions.explanation: Good peer feedback points out specific strengths and suggests specific improvements.
questions.misconception: Thinking peer feedback should be all negative or all positive.

questions.stem: Read your partner's draft: 'The dog ran. The dog was happy. The dog played.' Write one specific suggestion to improve it.
answer: use a pronoun to avoid repeating dog
use 'it' instead of repeating the dog
hints: What is repeated too often?
How can the sentences be improved?
questions.explanation: A good suggestion is to use a pronoun to avoid repeating 'the dog' or to combine the sentences.
questions.misconception: Giving a vague suggestion without specifics.

questions.stem: Read this draft and write two specific suggestions for improvement: 'The pupils went to the market. The pupils bought food. The pupils went home.'
hints: Look for repeated words and short sentences.
Suggest combining sentences or using pronouns.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives two specific suggestions, such as using a pronoun and combining sentences.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.9.3: Apply strategies for improving drafts for publishing
indicator.objective: Edit/proofread draft, checking capitalisation, usage, punctuation and spelling

skills.description: Check and correct capitalisation
Check and correct punctuation
Check and correct spelling errors
Check and correct usage errors (subject-verb agreement, verb tense)
Edit a partner's draft and prepare a neat final copy

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (find and correct one type of error, e.g. capitals), 35% medium (correct multiple types of errors), 20% harder (edit a passage with mixed errors and prepare a clean final copy). Sample drafts kept short.
misconceptions: Reading for meaning and missing mechanical errors
Correcting spelling only and ignoring punctuation
Believing editing means rewriting the whole piece
Missing errors in proper nouns
Forgetting to use apostrophes in contractions and possessives
Not proofreading the final copy after making corrections

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalisation error?
hints: Every sentence must start with a capital letter.
Which sentence begins with a small letter?
questions.explanation: 'my name is Ama' should start with a capital letter: 'My name is Ama.'
questions.misconception: Missing the sentence-start capitalisation error.

questions.stem: Which word should be capitalised in this sentence? 'We visited kumasi last week.'
hints: Proper nouns need capital letters.
Kumasi is the name of a city.
questions.explanation: 'Kumasi' is a proper noun and should be capitalised.
questions.misconception: Not recognising proper nouns that need capitalisation.

questions.stem: Correct the capitalisation in this sentence: 'my friend ama lives in accra.'
answer: my friend ama lives in accra
my friend Ama lives in Accra.
hints: Start the sentence with a capital.
Capitalise the proper nouns 'Ama' and 'Accra'.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence is: 'My friend Ama lives in Accra.'
questions.misconception: Missing one of the capital letters.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
hints: A statement ends with a full stop.
Which sentence has the correct end punctuation?
questions.explanation: 'She is my sister.' is a statement and ends with a full stop.
questions.misconception: Not knowing which punctuation mark ends a statement.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the comma correctly?
options: She bought rice beans and oil.
She bought rice, beans and oil.
She bought, rice beans and oil.
She bought rice beans, and oil.
hints: Commas separate items in a list.
Place the comma between the listed items.
questions.explanation: 'She bought rice, beans and oil' correctly places commas between the items in the list.
questions.misconception: Placing the comma incorrectly in a list.

questions.stem: Add the correct punctuation to this sentence: 'where is my book'
hints: The sentence asks a question.
Use a question mark.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence is: 'Where is my book?'
questions.misconception: Using a full stop for a question.

questions.stem: Punctuate this passage correctly: 'the pupils went to the market they bought tomatoes onions and pepper they returned home in the evening'
hints: Start each sentence with a capital.
Add commas in the list and full stops at the end of sentences.
questions.explanation: The punctuated passage is: 'The pupils went to the market. They bought tomatoes, onions and pepper. They returned home in the evening.'

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: The correct word means 'correct'.
It begins with 'r' and ends with 't'.
questions.explanation: 'Right' is the correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Choosing a similar-sounding word.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling error?
hints: Check each word's spelling.
Also check for grammar errors.
questions.explanation: 'The boys is happy' has both a spelling error ('boys' is fine) and a usage error ('is' should be 'are').
questions.misconception: Missing the usage error while checking spelling.

questions.stem: Correct the spelling in this sentence: 'The elefant is a big animal.'
answer: the elephant is a big animal
the elephant is a big animal.
hints: The word is spelled with 'ph'.
Elephant starts with 'ele-'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'elephant'.
questions.misconception: Spelling 'elephant' with 'f'.

questions.stem: Correct the spelling errors in this passage: 'The pupils recieved a gift. They were very happy. They went to the libary to read.'
hints: Check 'recieved' and 'libary'.
The correct forms are 'received' and 'library'.
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'The pupils received a gift. They were very happy. They went to the library to read.'

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The girl are running to school.
hints: The subject 'girl' is singular.
A singular subject takes a verb ending in -s.
questions.explanation: 'The girl runs' is correct because 'girl' is singular.
questions.misconception: Using a plural verb with a singular subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct verb tense?
options: She will go to school yesterday.
hints: 'Yesterday' shows the action happened in the past.
Use the past tense.
questions.explanation: 'She went to school yesterday' uses the correct past tense.
questions.misconception: Using the present tense with a past time marker.

questions.stem: Correct the usage error in this sentence: 'The boys is playing in the field.'
answer: the boys are playing in the field
the boys are playing in the field.
hints: 'Boys' is plural.
Use 'are' with a plural subject.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'The boys are playing in the field.'
questions.misconception: Keeping 'is' with a plural subject.

questions.stem: Correct the usage errors in this passage: 'The pupils was very happy. They has finished their work. The teacher give them a prize.'
hints: Check subject-verb agreement in each sentence.
Change 'was' to 'were', 'has' to 'have' and 'give' to 'gave'.
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'The pupils were very happy. They have finished their work. The teacher gave them a prize.'

questions.stem: What should you check when editing a partner's draft?
hints: Editing checks many aspects of writing.
Look at capitals, punctuation, spelling and grammar.
questions.explanation: When editing, check capitalisation, punctuation, spelling and usage.
questions.misconception: Thinking editing only means checking spelling.

questions.stem: Edit this draft and write the corrected version: 'the pupils went to the market they bought tomatoes onions and pepper they returned home'
hints: Check capitals, punctuation and spelling.
Add commas and full stops.
questions.explanation: The corrected version is: 'The pupils went to the market. They bought tomatoes, onions and pepper. They returned home.'

questions.stem: Rewrite this passage with correct capitalisation: 'my name is kojo. i live in ghana. my friend ama lives in kumasi.'
hints: Capitalise the first word of each sentence.
Capitalise proper nouns and the pronoun 'I'.
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'My name is Kojo. I live in Ghana. My friend Ama lives in Kumasi.'

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe?
hints: An apostrophe shows possession.
One girl owns the bag, so use the singular possessive.
questions.explanation: 'The girl's bag is new' correctly shows that one girl owns the bag.
questions.misconception: Confusing singular and plural possession.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 'its' and 'it's' correctly?
hints: 'Its' shows possession; 'it's' means 'it is'.
Which sentence uses the possessive correctly?
questions.explanation: 'The dog wagged its tail' uses the possessive 'its' correctly.
questions.misconception: Confusing the possessive 'its' with the contraction 'it's'.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.4.9.3: Apply strategies for improving drafts for publishing
indicator.objective: Publish writing piece for other peers to read and in the school magazine.

skills.description: Prepare a writing piece in a publishable format with a neat copy, title, author and clear layout
Share writing with peers, family and the school community
Revise and edit a piece specifically for publication
Reflect on the writing process and identify what was learnt
Identify appropriate places to publish writing
Present a published piece to an audience

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (produce a neat, publishable copy), 35% medium (share with a wider audience and follow publication conventions), 20% harder (reflect on the process and identify improvements). Contexts: class magazine, school notice board, school magazine, The Junior Graphic.
misconceptions: Submitting a first draft for publication
Ignoring the audience when preparing the published version
Believing publication means only the teacher reads it
Forgetting to include a title and author's name
Thinking the writing process ends at editing (publishing is the final stage)

questions.stem: Which of these should a publishable piece include?
options: A title and the author's name
hints: A published piece needs a title and author.
Readers should know who wrote it.
questions.explanation: A publishable piece should include a title and the author's name.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to include a title or author's name.

questions.stem: What does a neat, publishable copy look like?
options: Clear handwriting, no crossing out, even spacing and correct spelling
Writing on a scrap of paper
hints: Publishable means ready for others to read.
It should be neat and correct.
questions.explanation: A neat, publishable copy has clear handwriting, no crossings out, even spacing and correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Thinking any draft can be published.

questions.stem: Write one thing you should check before preparing your final copy for publication.
answer: that there are no crossing outs
hints: Check the conventions of writing.
Make sure the piece is correct before publishing.
questions.explanation: Before publishing, check spelling, punctuation, capitalisation and grammar.
questions.misconception: Thinking no checks are needed before publishing.

questions.stem: Write a title and an author line for a piece you have written about keeping the school clean.
hints: The title should be short and interesting.
Write your name as the author.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes a clear title and an author line.

criteria.description: Both are appropriate to the topic

questions.stem: Besides your teacher, who else can read your published piece?
options: Your classmates, family and the school community
hints: Publication means sharing with others.
Think about who reads the school notice board or magazine.
questions.explanation: Published writing can be read by classmates, family and the school community.
questions.misconception: Thinking published writing is only for the teacher.

questions.stem: Name one audience you could share your published writing with.
hints: Think beyond the teacher.
Who would benefit from reading your writing?
questions.explanation: Audiences include classmates, family, pupils in other classes and readers of the school magazine.
questions.misconception: Naming only the teacher.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining why it is important to share your writing with others.
hints: Think about feedback and purpose.
Sharing helps others learn and gives you feedback.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that sharing allows others to read your ideas and gives you feedback.

questions.stem: What should you do before publishing your final copy?
options: Proofread it one more time for errors
hints: Check for any remaining errors.
A final proofread ensures the piece is correct.
questions.explanation: Before publishing, proofread the final copy to catch any remaining errors.
questions.misconception: Thinking no final check is needed.

questions.stem: Your published piece has a spelling mistake. What should you do?
options: Ask someone else to write it
hints: Published work should be correct.
Fix the error before sharing.
questions.explanation: Correct any mistakes before publishing the piece.
questions.misconception: Thinking mistakes do not matter in published work.

questions.stem: Write one thing you should check after making your final copy.
answer: that the author's name is included
hints: Do a final check before sharing.
Look for any remaining errors.
questions.explanation: Check spelling, punctuation and capitalisation on the final copy.
questions.misconception: Thinking no checks are needed after the final copy.

questions.stem: Write two sentences explaining the steps you would take to prepare a piece for publication.
hints: Think about revising, editing and making a neat copy.
Mention at least two steps.
questions.explanation: A strong answer mentions revising, editing and making a neat final copy before publishing.

questions.stem: What does reflecting on your writing process mean?
options: Thinking about what you did well and what you can improve
hints: Reflection is thinking about the process.
What went well? What could be better?
questions.explanation: Reflecting means thinking about what you did well and what you could improve.
questions.misconception: Thinking reflection is just reading the work.

questions.stem: Write one thing you learnt during the writing process.
hints: Think about what you practised.
What did you do better after revising?
questions.explanation: Any genuine reflection on a skill learnt during the process is acceptable.
questions.misconception: Giving an unrelated statement.

questions.stem: Write three sentences reflecting on your writing process: what you did well, what was difficult and what you would do better next time.
hints: Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses.
Give specific examples.
questions.explanation: A strong answer reflects on strengths, challenges and improvements.

criteria.description: Mentions an improvement for next time

questions.stem: Where can you publish a writing piece for other pupils to read?
options: On the class or school notice board
At the bottom of your bag
hints: Think of places where pupils can see written work.
A notice board is a good place.
questions.explanation: The class or school notice board is a place where pupils can read published work.
questions.misconception: Thinking publication means hiding the work.

questions.stem: Which of these is a publication outlet for pupils in Ghana?
hints: Think of a newspaper for young people.
The Junior Graphic is for pupils.
questions.explanation: The Junior Graphic is a publication where pupils can share their writing.
questions.misconception: Choosing a non-publication item.

questions.stem: Name one place where you could publish your writing at school.
hints: Think of places where other pupils can read.
Notice boards and magazines are good options.
questions.explanation: Places include the class or school notice board, class magazine, school magazine or library.
questions.misconception: Naming a place where writing is not shared.

questions.stem: Read your published piece aloud to the class with clear voice and expression.
hints: Speak clearly and at a good pace.
Show expression as you read.
questions.explanation: The pupil reads the published piece aloud clearly and with expression.

questions.stem: Prepare a short presentation about your published piece. Write three sentences: (1) the title of your piece (2) what it is about (3) why you chose the topic.
hints: Be clear and brief.
Explain your choice of topic.
questions.explanation: A strong answer states the title, topic and reason for choosing it.

criteria.description: Explains what the piece is about
Explains why the topic was chosen

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.5.1.1: Use capital letters to start the first word in direct speech.
indicator.objective: Follow appropriate mechanical convention.

skills.description: Capitalise the first word of every sentence
Capitalise proper nouns (names of people, places, organisations, days, months, festivals, languages, nationalities)
Capitalise the first word in direct speech
Capitalise titles appropriately (Mr, Mrs, Dr, Prof; book/newspaper titles)
Capitalise the pronoun 'I' wherever it appears
Apply capitalisation alongside other mechanical conventions in a short written piece
Identify and correct capitalisation errors in a short passage

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (capitalise sentence starts and proper nouns), 35% medium (direct speech, titles, pronoun 'I'), 20% harder (mixed mechanical conventions and error correction in a short passage). Contexts: school writing, letters, stories, news reports, personal writing.
misconceptions: Writing the pronoun 'i' in lower case
Failing to capitalise proper nouns
Capitalising common nouns in the middle of a sentence
Forgetting to capitalise the first word after a direct speech comma
Capitalising every word in a sentence for emphasis
Confusing titles (Mr, Dr) with common nouns for capitalisation
Forgetting to capitalise the first word after a full stop
Believing all nouns should be capitalised

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct capitalisation?
hints: Every sentence starts with a capital letter.
Only the first word needs a capital.
questions.explanation: Option B correctly capitalises the first word of the sentence.
questions.misconception: Capitalising every word or none at all.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly capitalised?
hints: Capitalise the first word.
Proper nouns also need capitals.
questions.explanation: 'My name is Ama.' correctly capitalises the first word and the proper noun 'Ama'.
questions.misconception: Capitalising the wrong words.

questions.stem: Correct the capitalisation in this sentence: 'the sun rises in the east.'
answer: the sun rises in the east
The sun rises in the east.
hints: Capitalise the first word.
The rest of the sentence stays the same.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence is 'The sun rises in the east.'
questions.misconception: Capitalising more words than necessary.

questions.stem: Which word should be capitalised? 'We live in ghana.'
hints: Proper nouns name specific places.
Ghana is a country name.
questions.explanation: 'Ghana' is a proper noun and should be capitalised.
questions.misconception: Not recognising proper nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct capitalisation of proper nouns?
hints: Capitalise names of places and months.
Kumasi and December are proper nouns.
questions.explanation: Both 'Kumasi' (a place) and 'December' (a month) should be capitalised.
questions.misconception: Capitalising only one of the proper nouns.

questions.stem: Write the correct capitalisation for this sentence: 'ama and kojo are from techiman.'
answer: Ama and Kojo are from Techiman.
ama and kojo are from techiman
hints: Capitalise names of people and places.
The first word also needs a capital.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'Ama and Kojo are from Techiman.'
questions.misconception: Missing one of the proper nouns.

questions.stem: Write three sentences using proper nouns for a person, a place and a festival, all correctly capitalised.
hints: Use names like Ama, Kumasi, Homowo.
Capitalise each proper noun.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes three sentences with correctly capitalised proper nouns.

criteria.description: Each contains a different proper noun

questions.stem: Which sentence capitalises direct speech correctly?
hints: The first word inside quotation marks needs a capital.
Only the first word and 'I' need capitals.
questions.explanation: The first word of the direct speech ('I') should be capitalised.
questions.misconception: Not capitalising the first word in direct speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
hints: The first word inside the quotation marks needs a capital.
Only the first word needs a capital.
questions.explanation: 'Open your books' correctly capitalises the first word of the direct speech.
questions.misconception: Capitalising every word in direct speech.

questions.stem: Add correct capitalisation to this direct speech: 'she said, "we are going to the market."'
answer: she said, "we are going to the market."
she said, "We are going to the market."
hints: Capitalise the first word inside the quotation marks.
The word 'we' should be 'We'.
questions.explanation: The correct version is: 'She said, "We are going to the market."'
questions.misconception: Not capitalising the first word in direct speech.

questions.stem: Which is correctly capitalised?
hints: Titles like Mr, Mrs, Dr take capitals.
The name also takes a capital.
questions.explanation: 'Mr. Mensah' capitalises both the title and the name.
questions.misconception: Not capitalising titles or names.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct capitalisation of a title?
hints: Capitalise the title 'Dr'.
Capitalise the name 'Kwame'.
questions.explanation: 'Dr. Kwame' correctly capitalises the title and the name.
questions.misconception: Capitalising only the name or only the title.

questions.stem: Write the correct capitalisation for 'mrs. adjoa boateng'.
hints: Capitalise the title and both names.
Mrs. Adjoa Boateng.
questions.explanation: The correct capitalisation is 'Mrs. Adjoa Boateng'.
questions.misconception: Not capitalising both names.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly capitalised?
hints: The pronoun 'I' is always capitalised.
Only 'I' and the first word need capitals.
questions.explanation: 'I like reading.' correctly capitalises the pronoun 'I'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'i' in lower case.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct capitalisation?
options: My friend and i went to the market.
My friend and I went to the market.
My friend and i Went to the market.
My Friend and I went to the Market.
hints: The pronoun 'I' must be capitalised.
Only the first word and 'I' need capitals.
questions.explanation: 'My friend and I went to the market.' correctly capitalises 'I'.
questions.misconception: Capitalising other words unnecessarily.

questions.stem: Correct the capitalisation in this sentence: 'kojo and i are friends.'
hints: Capitalise the name 'Kojo'.
Capitalise the pronoun 'I'.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence is 'Kojo and I are friends.'
questions.misconception: Missing the capital 'I'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses capitalisation and punctuation correctly?
options: the pupils went to kumasi on monday.
The pupils went to Kumasi on Monday.
The Pupils went to Kumasi on Monday.
The pupils went to kumasi on Monday.
hints: Capitalise the first word and proper nouns.
Do not capitalise every word.
questions.explanation: Option B correctly capitalises the first word and the proper nouns 'Kumasi' and 'Monday'.
questions.misconception: Capitalising too many or too few words.

questions.stem: Rewrite this passage with correct capitalisation: 'my name is kojo. i live in ghana. my friend ama lives in kumasi.'
hints: Capitalise the first word of each sentence.
Capitalise proper nouns and 'I'.
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'My name is Kojo. I live in Ghana. My friend Ama lives in Kumasi.'

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is incorrectly capitalised? 'The Pupils went to school on monday.'
hints: Common nouns should not be capitalised mid-sentence.
'Pupils' is a common noun.
questions.explanation: 'Pupils' should not be capitalised because it is a common noun.
questions.misconception: Capitalising common nouns unnecessarily.

questions.stem: Correct the capitalisation error in this sentence: 'We visited the Market yesterday.'
hints: The word 'Market' is a common noun here.
It should be lower case.
questions.explanation: The corrected sentence is 'We visited the market yesterday.'
questions.misconception: Capitalising common nouns.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.5.10.1: Spell words accurately
indicator.objective: Check pieces of literary work for spelling

skills.description: Identify wrongly spelt words in a short extract or piece of literary work
Correct wrongly spelt words accurately using spelling rules, patterns and a dictionary
Apply a checking procedure: read, underline doubtful words, check each one and rewrite correctly
Write a continuation of a story or extract with correct spelling
Edit spelling in group writing and create additional activities to correct spellings

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (spot and correct one or two obvious misspellings), 35% medium (correct several misspellings applying rules and patterns), 20% harder (proofread a longer extract and write a correctly spelt continuation). Texts kept short; contexts from local stories and pupils' own writing.
misconceptions: Reading for meaning and overlooking spelling errors
Correcting one error but missing others
Relying on sound only instead of checking spelling patterns
Correcting spelling but introducing new errors in the rewrite
Confusing homophones (their/there, to/too/two, its/it's)
Not checking proper nouns for capitalisation as part of spelling accuracy
Editing only own work and not group work

questions.stem: Which word is spelled incorrectly in this sentence? 'The pupils recieved a prize for their hard work.'
hints: The word means 'got something'.
It follows the rule 'i before e except after c'.
questions.explanation: 'Recieved' should be 'received' — 'i before e except after c'.
questions.misconception: Missing the spelling error because the word sounds correct.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled incorrectly in this sentence? 'She was very happy to see the beautiful flower.'
hints: The word has one 'l' at the end, not two.
Beautiful ends with '-ful'.
questions.explanation: 'Beautifull' should be 'beautiful' — it ends with one 'l'.
questions.misconception: Adding an extra 'l' to words ending in '-ful'.

questions.stem: Identify the misspelt word in this sentence: 'The children went to the libary to read books.'
hints: The word means a place where books are kept.
It has an 'r' after the 'b'.
questions.explanation: 'Libary' should be 'library' — it has two 'r's.
questions.misconception: Writing 'library' as 'libary'.

questions.stem: Read this passage and write down all the misspelt words: 'The pupils were very exited about the trip. They packed their bags and waited patiently. They finaly boarded the bus.'
hints: Look for words that look or sound wrong.
Check words ending in '-ed' and '-ly'.
questions.explanation: The misspelt words are: 'exited' (excited) and 'finaly' (finally).

criteria.description: Does not list correctly spelt words

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling?
hints: 'I before e except after c'.
The word follows the 'ei' rule.
questions.explanation: 'Receive' is correct because 'ei' follows 'c'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'recieve'.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling?
hints: The word ends with '-ful', not '-full'.
It has one 'l' at the end.
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' is the correct spelling with one 'l'.
questions.misconception: Adding an extra 'l'.

questions.stem: Correct the spelling of 'neccessary'.
hints: It has one 'c' and two 's's.
It comes from 'necessity'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'necessary'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'neccessary' with two 'c's.

questions.stem: Correct the spelling errors in these words: (1) 'acommodate' (2) 'definately' (3) 'seperate' (4) 'untill'.
hints: Accommodate has two 'c's and two 'm's.
Definitely has no 'a' in the middle.
Separate has 'par' in the middle.
Until has one 'l'.
questions.explanation: The correct spellings are: accommodate, definitely, separate, until.

questions.stem: What is the first step in checking a piece of writing for spelling?
options: Ask a friend to rewrite it
hints: You need to find the errors first.
Read before you mark or rewrite.
questions.explanation: The first step is to read the whole piece carefully to find spelling errors.
questions.misconception: Skipping the reading step.

questions.stem: What should you do after identifying a doubtful word during spelling check?
hints: You need to find the correct spelling.
Use a dictionary or spelling rule.
questions.explanation: After identifying a doubtful word, you should check its correct spelling in a dictionary or using a spelling rule.
questions.misconception: Guessing without checking.

questions.stem: Describe the four steps you would use to check a piece of writing for spelling.
hints: Read, underline, check, rewrite.
Explain each step.
questions.explanation: A strong answer describes reading, underlining doubtful words, checking each word, and rewriting correctly.

questions.stem: Story: 'Cinderella wore the shoes and she was taken away to marry the prince.' Which continuation has all words spelt correctly?
options: She lived happily with the prince and they had a beautiful wedding.
She lived hapily with the prince and they had a beutiful wedding.
She lived happily with the prince and they had a beatiful wedding.
She lived happily with the prince and they had a beautifull wedding.
hints: Check each word's spelling.
Happily and beautiful are correct in option A.
questions.explanation: Option A has all words spelt correctly.
questions.misconception: Missing spelling errors in the continuation.

questions.stem: Write a short continuation (one sentence) of this story with correct spelling: 'The farmer planted his maize and waited for the rain.'
answer: soon the rain came and the maize began to grow
after a few weeks the maize started to grow
the rain fell and the maize grew well
when the rain came the maize grew tall
hints: Write a logical next sentence.
Check every word's spelling.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes a logical continuation with correctly spelt words.
questions.misconception: Writing a continuation with spelling errors.

questions.stem: Write a three-sentence continuation of this story with correct spelling: 'Ama found a lost puppy near the market. She took it home and fed it.'
hints: Continue the story logically.
Check every word's spelling.
questions.explanation: A strong answer writes a three-sentence continuation with all words spelt correctly.

questions.stem: In group writing, what should you do to check spelling?
options: One person reads aloud while others check the spelling
hints: Collaboration helps catch errors.
Reading aloud helps others spot mistakes.
questions.explanation: In group work, one person reads aloud while others check the spelling, which helps catch more errors.
questions.misconception: Thinking spelling is not important in group work.

questions.stem: Your group has written this passage with spelling errors: 'The pupils were exited about the compitition. They practised everyday.' Correct the spelling and rewrite the passage.
hints: Change 'exited' to 'excited'.
Change 'compitition' to 'competition'.
Change 'everyday' to 'every day' (if used as two words).
questions.explanation: The corrected passage is: 'The pupils were excited about the competition. They practised every day.'

questions.stem: Work in a group. Read a short passage aloud while others check the spelling. Discuss any errors you find.
hints: Read slowly and clearly.
Other group members should listen and check.
questions.explanation: The group reads aloud and checks spelling collaboratively.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled incorrectly? 'She wrote a letter to her freind.'
hints: The word means a person you like.
It follows the 'i before e except after c' rule.
questions.explanation: 'Freind' should be 'friend' — 'i before e'.
questions.misconception: Missing the 'ie' spelling rule.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling?
hints: It has one 'm' and two 'r's.
Tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' is the correct spelling.
questions.misconception: Adding extra 'm's or 'r's.

questions.stem: Explain to the class the steps you use to check spelling in your own writing.
hints: Read, underline, check, rewrite.
Be specific about each step.
questions.explanation: The pupil explains the four-step checking procedure clearly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B6.5.2.1: Show understanding of how punctuations are used appropriately in writing
indicator.objective: Use : − the comma around a phrase for the modifying of the proceeding noun; − quotation marks to indicate direct speech; − apostrophe to show plural possession;

skills.description: Use commas to set off a modifying phrase that describes the noun before it
Use quotation marks correctly to enclose direct speech
Place punctuation correctly with quotation marks
Use the apostrophe to show plural possession
Distinguish singular possession from plural possession
Insert missing punctuation marks into an unpunctuated text

spec.difficultyPlan: 45% easy (identify and use commas around modifying phrases; use quotation marks for simple direct speech), 35% medium (place quotation marks and punctuation correctly; use apostrophe for plural possession), 20% harder (distinguish singular vs plural possession; punctuate an unpunctuated passage with mixed target punctuation). Contexts: school writing, stories, letters, news reports, conversations.
misconceptions: Omitting both commas around a modifying phrase
Using only one comma around the modifying phrase
Writing direct speech without quotation marks
Putting the comma outside the closing quotation mark
Using a full stop outside the closing quotation mark
Placing the apostrophe after the 's' for singular possession
Placing the apostrophe before the 's' for plural possession
Confusing the plural possessive apostrophe with the contraction apostrophe
Forgetting that some plural nouns end in 's' already and only need an apostrophe after the 's'
Using quotation marks for indirect or reported speech

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly around a modifying phrase?
options: Kofi my friend will help me.
Kofi, my friend, will help me.
Kofi, my friend will help me.
Kofi my friend, will help me.
hints: A modifying phrase needs commas on both sides.
Which sentence has a comma before and after 'my friend'?
questions.explanation: 'Kofi, my friend, will help me' correctly places commas around the modifying phrase 'my friend'.
questions.misconception: Using only one comma or none at all.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Our teacher, Mr. Mensah, is very kind.
Our teacher Mr. Mensah is very kind.
Our teacher, Mr. Mensah is very kind.
Our teacher Mr. Mensah, is very kind.
hints: The phrase 'Mr. Mensah' modifies 'our teacher'.
It needs commas on both sides.
questions.explanation: 'Our teacher, Mr. Mensah, is very kind' correctly sets off the modifying phrase with commas.
questions.misconception: Omitting one or both commas.

questions.stem: Add commas to this sentence: 'Ama the tallest girl in the class won the race.'
answer: ama, the tallest girl in the class, won the race
Ama, the tallest girl in the class, won the race.
hints: The phrase 'the tallest girl in the class' modifies 'Ama'.
Use commas on both sides.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'Ama, the tallest girl in the class, won the race.'
questions.misconception: Adding only one comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
hints: Direct speech needs quotation marks around the spoken words.
Both opening and closing quotation marks are needed.
questions.explanation: Option B correctly places quotation marks around the spoken words.
questions.misconception: Omitting one or both quotation marks.

questions.stem: Add quotation marks to this sentence: 'The teacher said, Open your books.'
hints: Place quotation marks around the exact words spoken.
The spoken words are 'Open your books.'
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'The teacher said, "Open your books."'
questions.misconception: Placing quotation marks around the wrong words.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
hints: A comma goes before the closing quotation mark when a reporting clause follows.
The comma is inside the quotation marks.
questions.explanation: '"I like football," said Ama' correctly places the comma inside the quotation marks.
questions.misconception: Placing the comma outside the quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly places a full stop with quotation marks?
hints: The full stop goes inside the closing quotation mark when the speech ends the sentence.
Look at where the full stop is placed.
questions.explanation: The full stop is inside the quotation marks: 'She said, "I am tired."'
questions.misconception: Placing the full stop outside the quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly shows plural possession?
options: The girl's bags are on the table.
The girls' bags are on the table.
The girls bags are on the table.
The girls's bags are on the table.
hints: Plural possession: apostrophe after the 's'.
More than one girl owns the bags.
questions.explanation: 'The girls' bags' correctly places the apostrophe after the 's' to show plural possession.
questions.misconception: Putting the apostrophe before the 's' for plural possession.

questions.stem: Rewrite this phrase to show plural possession: 'the books belonging to the boys'
hints: Plural possession uses an apostrophe after the 's'.
Boys → boys' books.
questions.explanation: The correct phrase is 'the boys' books'.
questions.misconception: Writing 'the boy's books'.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'the girl's bag' and 'the girls' bag'?
options: 'The girl's bag' means one girl owns the bag; 'the girls' bag' means more than one girl owns the bag.
'The girl's bag' means more than one girl owns the bag.
'The girls' bag' means no one owns the bag.
hints: Singular possessive = apostrophe before 's'.
Plural possessive = apostrophe after 's'.
questions.explanation: The position of the apostrophe shows whether one girl (girl's) or more than one girl (girls') owns the bag.
questions.misconception: Thinking both phrases mean the same.

questions.stem: Write the correct possessive form: 'the toys belonging to the child'.
hints: One child owns the toys, so use singular possessive.
Add apostrophe + s.
